en: Now begins the first chapter.
Homage to Śrī.
Homage to Śrī Rāmacandra.
Salutations to the illustrious great preceptor Vikhanas;
salutations to the illustrious Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, and Kaśyapa. This concludes the section on miscellaneous matters.

Now begins the first chapter. Salutations to Vikhanas, the knower of the meaning of all the Vedas, by whom every rite— whether prescribed by the Śruti or the Smṛti and so forth— was succinctly formulated.
I bow to the ocean of the Vaikhanasas, which is filled with the rivers of Śruti and Smṛti, agitated by the waves of the scriptures,
and purified by the water of devotion to Viṣṇu.
The sages' reply. The sages said:
O best of sages, son of Brahmā, salutations to you, the foremost among embodied beings!
You alone are the knower of all; you alone are the best among speakers.
Therefore, O Lord, we, your wretched disciples, desire to know through your grace the sequence of the examination of the ground and other rites pertaining to Viṣṇu. BhS 1.2.
Since you are a knower of all things in detail, you ought to speak of them at length:
by which path, with which mantras, and while worshipping which deity does a person [attain success]? BhS 1.3.
"Tell me truly, O voice, what worlds does one attain?
Bhṛgu said:
"Having prostrated before the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the discus and the sword-bannered one..."
I shall explain in detail; listen with full concentration:
the examination of the auspicious moments (muhūrta) is recommended for every undertaking when the sun is situated in the north.
The period known as *apraśasta* (unfavorable),
extending from the month of Puṣya for six months along with the southern path, is traditionally regarded as the day of the gods.
It is recorded in tradition that whatever is performed during this month leads to increase;
the night at the beginning of the month of Āṣāḍha is joined with all ritual acts.
The first, second, third, fifth,
as well as the sixth, seventh, tenth, and eleventh [days].
The thirteenth lunar day and the full moon are considered auspicious;
as are the constellations Rohiṇī, Aśvinī, Citrā, Puṣya, Revatī, and the three Uttaras.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Āditya (Punarvasu), Maghā, Svātī, Hasta, and Śravaṇa are auspicious;
the movable signs should be avoided, while the dual and fixed signs are excellent for [undertakings] involving fear.
The days of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are remembered as the most excellent; the aspects of these planets are desired through their divisions, decans, and horās. BhS_1.11 //
Among these, the portion of rising is auspicious; however, without the rising of the Moon, it indeed causes affliction by disease when there is a cruel or quadruple asterism.
The Sun, Saturn, and Mercury are auspicious when situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses;
likewise, when they occupy the ascendant, they cause disease, sorrow, and fear.
All planets situated in the eighth house cause misfortune for the doer;
all those situated in the eleventh house are known to bring security and health.
Bhārgava (Venus) situated in the second, seventh, or tenth house is said to cause fear; Jupiter situated in the second, seventh, fifth, or ninth house is very auspicious.
Indeed, it brings great happiness to the kingdom and to the sacrificer;
on Sunday, the asterisms Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā), Hasta, Revatī, and the three Uttarās are auspicious.
On Saturday, Sunday, and Tuesday, it is said that [the asterisms] Rohiṇī and Svātī are auspicious;
likewise, on Wednesday, one should avoid Hasta and Āśvinī.
One should avoid Thursday; likewise, both the Saumya (Mṛgaśīrṣa) and Uttarā constellations, as well as Śravaṇa and Puṣya, should be avoided on Friday.
The lunar mansion Uttarāṣāḍhā on Monday is auspicious; likewise, the second lunar day joined with Mercury, and the sixth lunar day conjoined with Jupiter.
Soma, when conjoined with the eleventh lunar day, causes a risk to life;
Pūṣan, however, when conjoined with the seventh, burns the subjects like fire.
One who is one-eyed, as well as those born under the asterisms of Tūṇa, Dhanakṣatra, Guru, and Viṣī, should be avoided;
likewise, [one should avoid setting out] during an earthquake, when the quarters are ablaze, on a foul day, or when there is a violent wind.
A day accompanied by the sound of thunder is declared to be censurable;
likewise, one should avoid [studying] during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during eclipses.
Even if a house has been built during the six auspicious periods (ṣaḍaśīti), it will perish;
therefore, one who desires his own welfare should act only after such examination.
The wise one should perform the rites beginning with the consecration of the ears and ending with the installation;
then, having first examined the ground, he should begin the plowing.
The examination of the ground:
land that is white is said to belong to a Brāhmaṇa, while that which is red belongs to a Kṣatriya; yellow land belongs to a Vaiśya, and black land is declared to belong to a Śūdra.
The Brāhmaṇī woman is said to bestow liberation; the Kṣatriyā grants victory;
the Vaiśyā is the ground that bestows wealth; and the Śūdrā bestows abundance of sons.
One should avoid ground frequented by those who act against the natural order and the like, as well as ground abounding in anthills;
having dug a pit one cubit deep, one should fill it again with that same soil. (BhS 1.26)
If the [number of] days is greater, it is fertile ground; if fewer, it is to be rejected; if equal, it is even.
When protected, it sprouts after three nights; otherwise, it is not fit ground for acceptance.
Having placed it upon a support made from that [lotus], one should look at the water contained within a lotus-bowl,
which flows primarily clockwise and possesses steady bubbles.
Likewise, water that turns to the left, is undesirable, and full of many bubbles;
it should be taken when the lotus is facing upward, but not when the lotus is facing downward.
Having examined it thus, one should take possession of it and have the proclamation of an auspicious day made;
having examined it in this way through many methods, one should perform the most excellent consecration of the ground.
The ploughing [should be done by] two bulls that are either white or tawny, not lacking in limbs, nor emaciated; or else, they may be of other colors, provided they are healthy and full of strength.
Having bound a pair of milk-trees (kṣīravṛkṣa) together with a śamī tree,
or else an asana or khadira tree, he fashioned a plowshare for the seat.
Then, having yoked [the oxen] with a pair of ropes made of cowhair,
one should construct a water-shed (prapā) in its western region according to the prescribed rule.
Having first prepared a seat of grain and worshipped Deveśa in the east according to the sequence accompanied by the three Vedas, one should thereafter worship the Cakra.
Having worshipped Garuḍa facing in all directions, one should present the offerings;
having performed the Vāstuyajña sacrifice, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Placing a stream of water in front, the teacher, by way of circumambulation,
[proceeds] with unwashed garments, an upper cloth, and finger-rings.
Having adorned a bull there with white garlands and ointments according to the prescribed ritual, he led it forth while saying, "O Bull! (BhS 1.37).
Having yoked a bull to the right while saying, "O son of Surabhi," he should thereafter yoke the strong oxen to the left.
One should again yoke the plough with the mantra, "yugaṃ yugaśṛṅgam," and having firmly grasped the bull with the mantra, "ṛṣabhaṃ gṛhṇāmi. (BhS 1.39)
One should perform self-protection with the mantra, “May Viṣṇu protect me,” and dismiss those who have taken refuge with the mantra, “Those who live in this place. (BhS 1.40)
With the mantra beginning with "halakṛṣṭe," one should break up that auspicious earth;
one should plow the ground toward the northeast using Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Then, having summoned a plowman, he should have him plow everywhere;
and likewise, having honored the noble one along with the two bulls.
Having performed the first plowing, one should perform the second plowing;
then, taking all the seed, one should perform the sprinkling with ritual consecrations.
“May these seeds sprout!”—having sown the seven kinds of cultivated seeds beyond that, while reciting the mantra: “O Goddess, in you! (BhS 1.44).
Having recited, "Duhatām uhadiva," one should then offer the sacrificial fee;
having properly performed the protection rites there, one should honor the preceptor.
Having bowed to the ripened grain with the mantra beginning with "sasyā" and having likewise performed the propitiation (śānti), one should worship it with the mantras beginning with "viṣvaksena."
One should properly offer [the gift] to the cows with this mantra: "śuddhā asi. (BhS 1.47)
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.
Hereafter, I shall explain the installation of the gnomon (śaṅku), the most excellent method of installing the gnomon.
Likewise, when the sun enters Aries and Taurus, on that day as well.
Having made the ground level, one should smear it with cow dung; then, one should draw two threads around its exterior according to these measurements.
For the determination of the east,
one should mark the shadow of the gnomon on both the forenoon and the afternoon;
then, one should fix three threads passing through the middle of the gnomon.

If it is excessive, one should rotate [the cord]; if it is deficient, one should increase it by that same amount. By measuring with that cord according to the eastern direction, one should determine the center.
Having laid out a north-south line there and made it square,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Regarding the worship of the deities of the site:
having divided the site into eighty-one squares, one should worship the deities of the site;
having worshipped those beginning with Īśāna, one should worship the thirty-two who share in the portions.
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jaya, Mahendra, Āditya, Satyaka, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa— these are the deities of the eastern quarter.
Agni, Pūṣan, Cavi-tatha, Graha, Akṣata, and Yama; likewise Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the Ṛṣis are the deities of the right foot.
In the west are Nirṛti and Dauvārika,
as well as Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, and the Asura.
Śoṣaṇa and Rāga—these eight are declared to be the gods;
furthermore, Ugratara, Javana, the preeminent Nāga, and Bhallāṭa.
Somar’gala, Aditi, and likewise Sūrideva;
Brahmā enjoys the ninefold station, especially in the center of the site (vāstu).
Aryaman, Daṇḍabhṛt, Pāśabhṛt, and likewise Dhanada—
these stand in the four directions of Brahmā, partaking of six steps each.
Apa and Apavatsa, Savitṛ and Sāvitra, Indra and Indrajā, Rudra and Rudrajā. (BhS 2.13)
These gods, who consume the offerings of bipeds and dwell in the six directions,
are Carakī, Devatārī, Pūtanā, and the wicked Rākṣasī.
In the outer corners starting from Īśāna, [the deities] are situated on squares devoid of [central] plots;
having thus assigned the deities, one should then fashion the Vāstudeva.
The characteristics of the Vāstupuruṣa: One should perform the worship of the Vāstu deity with its head in the Īśāna direction and its feet in the Nairṛti direction;
its two hands are to be known as being at the confluence of rivers, and its arm is said to be in the Agni direction. (BhS 2.16)
The throat is said to be Apikaṇṭha, and the heart is Apavatsaka;
the navel is reckoned as Brahmā, and the belly is named Savitṛ.
In the case of Indra and Indrāṇī, according to the prescribed rule, the secret place is at the root of the thighs;
the right side is declared [for them], and one should arrange the left side in the same manner.
Having reached the site-ground, the deity of the site (Vāstudeva) lies there with his face turned downward;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should perform the sprinkling with ritual purifications (prokṣaṇa).
One should worship with flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps, accompanied by salutations joined with one's own names preceded by the syllable *praṇava*. (BhS 2.20)
At the conclusion of the worship, the practitioner should touch the part where the thorn is located and observe that specific limb;
one should likewise declare the thorn to be in the body of the site (vāstu) exactly as it is.
If there is a thorn in the head, one should indicate it by measuring two hand-spans from the touch-point;
if it is in the throat or the neck, one should indicate it as being at the distance of one hand-span.
From contact with three hands, one should predict an iron chain or a spike;
from contact with a single hand measuring only one cubit, one should predict a bedstead leg.
Due to excessive contact by the performer, [the defect] is three cubits from the stage edge;
it is rendered defective by scorpions, snakes, and the like, at a measurement of two spans (vitasti).
It is said that a "foot-thorn" measures six vitastis;
one should perform [the ritual] there by touching the little finger and the thumb together to form a hand-span.
When there are four cubits remaining after subtracting the expenditure, one should then touch the ground with the knees; having cleared away any debris from that spot, one should level the surface.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship the deities of the site (vāstudeva). Then,
for the offering to the deities of the site,
one should cook one *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of rice.
One should offer a bali-oblation consisting of curd, molasses, and ghee to all [the deities], beginning with Brahmā; "Homage to you" or "svāhā to you"—this shall be the bali. (BhS 2.28)
Having performed the offering of the bali-oblation, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Thus ends the second chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Lord according to the *Śrīvaikhānasa* tradition.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.
The various types of celestial palaces (vimāna) and their forms of arrangement shall now be described in due order:
the Śrīvatsa is declared first, and the Nandyāvarta is second.
One should know the third to be the Svastika; the fourth is remembered as the Bhadraka;
the fifth they call the Daṇḍaka, and the sixth is said to be the Vedika.
One should know the seventh to be the *kumbhaka* [posture], and likewise the eighth the *padmaka*;
the ninth shall be the *rathapada*, while the tenth is the *prakīrṇaka*.
I shall describe their form correctly and in due order:
everything except for the Daṇḍaka [forest] is endowed with a circular enclosure.
And for that [mandala], the Śrīvatsa and other [symbols] are prescribed by means of the boundary marks at the corners;
it has one row of paths facing east and rows of paths facing north.
It should be known as the Śrīvatsa, considered equal to all vidyās;
it has a central corner and four gates, arranged clockwise starting from the east and the lords of the directions.
That which has the path of individual trees at its corners is known as the Nandyāvarta;
the Svastika has the path of individual trees at its ends, while the Bhadra has a central alleyway.
A *kumbhaka* is described as having a single ancient pillar, being square with a four-cornered altar (*vedikā*), and circular; a *padmaka* should have two altars.
Having the shape of a chariot, a footpath, or a city with eight gates and the treasury of Brahmā,
and sloping toward the northeast, it is declared to be the "scattered" (prakīrṇaka) type.
The mind may become engaged through two doors or four doors;
the worship of a deity by one whose doors are not disciplined is not prescribed.
The grasping of the womb is said to occur through the measuring of the thief by means of the staff;
having understood the body, its limbs, and its minor members, one should fashion the womb accordingly.
The village is the body, and the limbs are the possessions of gods and brahmins;
the palaces, mansions, and so forth have become the minor limbs. (BhS 3.12)
The dispute regarding the first two [measures] is settled by the staff, while the other is determined by the hand;
one should multiply the width and length of the staff each by three.
Having divided each by sixty, one should indicate the remaining [number] as the birth sign (*yoni*). In the case of a conjunction of two hands, one should multiply it by three and divide by eight.
One should recognize the remaining birth-source from the sequence beginning with the banner and smoke;
or, in all cases, one should determine the birth-source by means of the result of those two groups.
The womb is the most excellent among the great directions; it is considered to be seven spans and three finger-breadths in height.
It is known by the wise to be skillfully fashioned as a square, with its length extending according to these measures.
The others should have eight, six, and four parts respectively; in this manner, one should arrange the application of proportions for each individual limb. (BhS 3.17)
The length should be twice the width, with the width being either one-quarter less or one-quarter more;
it is prescribed that the width may be reduced by half, while the increase is not permitted.
They know that the length of the body, including the feet and the topknot, should be greater than the width of the site; or, specifically, it should be twice as long.
One should make it equal on all sides, except for the body and the staff;
or one may increase the length by sixteen times the thickness of the staff.
One should make the staff eightfold, or its length according to the rules;
the width of the limbs and the various types of staffs are also to be applied accordingly.
In other cases, one should inflict punishment, especially regarding transgressions;
they know that the fall occurs within the lines of the width, or even within two lines.
One should also have two neck-threads made as subsidiary parts;
however, a distinction in the ritual procedure must be observed, especially regarding the portion for Brahmā.
In this sequence, one who knows the treatises should properly fashion the body.
Having installed Janārdana according to the rite of the five forms in the region of Vāyu, which is a portion of Brahmā, above a thousand Brahmins, he performed the installation of Viṣṇu.
One should worship Puruṣottama with highly fortunate Vaikhānasa brahmins who are devoted to Vedic worship and are knowers of the Vedānta.
The installation of Śaṅkara and others, as well as Īśāna and Īśvara, or even Someśāna; Keśava’s station is in the west, and the abode of Śaṅkara is in the northeast.

The ritual procedure (kalpa) is of three kinds: the secondary procedure (anukalpa), the alternative procedure (vikalpa), and the primary procedure (kalpa). Whatever rite begins with the examination of the ground is known as the secondary procedure (anukalpa). (BhS 3.28)
One should fashion the conceptual construction for the gods and other beings, as well as for the sages; wherever there is a temple made of clay, one should perform the ritual of installation there.
Having thus determined the location, one should designate the site for the foundation;
or else, for the sake of the height of the celestial palace (vimāna) to be constructed here, [one should designate it] on all sides.

The wise man should have pillars brought from water, tree-trunks, or stone as appropriate; having dug outside the boundary of the length and width for the sake of stability, he should establish them firmly.
Having filled it on all sides with sand to the height of one, two, or three cubits, respectively, one should order its stabilization.

For those who are capable, the installation of the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) may take place even without a separate hall for the child-form (bālāgāra); however, for those who are incapable, if there is to be an installation of the permanent worship, one should not construct a hall for the child-form.
Thus ends the third chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The laying of the first bricks. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the first brick of the site (vāstu):
having prepared four first bricks during the first part of the night. (BhS 4.1)
One should fashion [the images] endowed with the proper characteristics, either from stone or from clay;
those made of stone should be free from defects, and those made of clay should be well-baked.
The bricks are said to be six, five, or four finger-breadths in width;
for the rites beginning with the highest class, their length is double their width.
The thickness of the bricks has been declared according to their measurement;
having constructed a water-shed (prapā) facing the temple, the wise man [should proceed].
In the middle of that, having constructed an altar measuring one cubit in width,
its breadth being the same, and its height half of that.
Having duly established the sacrificial fire of the assembly, one should perform the Aghora rite according to the rules;
then, having performed the earth-sacrifice, one should proceed with seven water-pots in sequence.
Having bathed him and clothed him in a new garment upon the bed,
and having tied the protective amulet (kautuka), one should then have him lie down on the bed.
Having offered the *Ātmapuruṣasūkta* and thereafter the *Viṣṇusūkta*,
one should worship in sequence with the mantras beginning with those of the four Vedas and the *Śrībhūsūkta*.
Or else, one should remember the first syllable of the name of the bricks or the stones;
then, one should pass the remainder of the night in sequence with dances, songs, and musical instruments.
At dawn, one should first worship the preceptor together with the artisans;
the preceptor is qualified for the mantras, while the artisans are qualified for the ritual work.
Its placement in the right-side bolt of the door is praised;
at an auspicious moment, the wise man should lay down four bricks in sequence.
One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the four directions with the mantras beginning with the four Vedas;
then, in the center of those, one should fill the pit with water.
In that very place, one should dissolve the nine jewels in successive order.
Now, I shall explain specifically the sequence of the procedure for the deposition in the womb (garbha-nyāsa). BhS 4.13.
One endowed with the insertion of a central chamber (garbha) achieves all prosperity;
therefore, at the outset, the insertion of the garbha should be performed, for it bestows abundance. (BhS 4.14)
There should be three at the base of the palace; the first should be on the first brick, the middle one above the threshold, and the last one at the very top.

One should cause [the water] to be held at ground level for those of the Śūdra caste; for kings (Kṣatriyas) and Vaiśyas, with the water vessel held at the waist; and for Brāhmaṇas, held above the mouth, according to the order of the castes.
The rite pertaining to the earth, which brings about all accomplishments and is auspicious,
one should arrange between the directions of Indra and Agni, at the eastern gate.
One should perform it to the south of the door, or likewise to the west;
or else, when the door-panel and bolt are joined, one should perform the recitation of the limbs (*anyastavyāṅgabhāvanam*) elsewhere.
A spittoon made of gold, copper, or crystal is recommended;
it should have legs and a base of equal width, and be adorned with auspicious signs.
If there are cracks or fissures in the vajra, [one should apply] a thick layer equal to one-twentieth of its thickness, or even half of that, or a quarter of that. BhS 4.20.
The height of the wall of the inner chamber should be one-fourth of the width;
the best [height] is equal to the [width], while the middling is recorded as three-quarters [of it].
Now, they declare that the height of the half-bench is threefold:
one part should be the single-layer construction, and two parts should constitute the layering.

In the internal arrangement, the length should be one finger-breadth less than that [measurement], the width half of that, and it should be reduced by half the thickness of the joint. Thus it should be in the interior.
Having washed the body and the vessel with the five products of the cow so that they are purified,
[one should place them] in front of the Ālaya in a well-decorated pavilion.
Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day;
thereafter, the best of mantra-knowers should deposit red seeds and minerals.
Reciting the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta, and having uttered the verse "Viṣṇur yonim," one should cause the embryo to be placed within the womb. (BhS 4.26)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, within the *Bhagavacchāstra* of the venerable Vaikhānasa tradition.
Now begins the fifth chapter: the characteristics of the temple (*prāsāda*).
Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of palaces,
by which one constructs a palace that is highly renowned.
The division of the finger-breadth is declared to be threefold according to its measurement:
first is the measure-finger (mānāṅgula), and after that is the measure-of-quantity finger (mātrāṅgula). BhS 5.2.
The third [unit] is declared to be the *deha*, obtained from its own measure;
likewise, eight *rathareṇu*s make an *aṇu*, and eight *aṇu*s make an *īkṣāyūka*.
Know that the finger-measure (mānāṅgula) is traditionally defined as eight kuṇas in sequence;
the middle joint of the middle finger is traditionally known as the paryamātrāṅguli.
By means of the division of finger-breadths and the counting of palm-lengths, the vessel [is measured];
however, the finger-breadth (aṅgula) is declared according to the measurement obtained from the body. BhS 5.5.
The construction of palaces and pavilions is according to the rule of the *mānāṅgula*,
whereas the sacrificial implements are according to the rule of the *mātrāṅgula*.
One should have the image made according to the proportions obtained from the body;
likewise, twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) are said to constitute a cubit (kiṣku).
A *prājāpatya* is declared to consist of twenty-five [units];
twenty-six is a handful of grain (*dhānyamuṣṭi*), and twenty-seven is a *dhanu-graha*.

The characteristics of the hands have been declared according to the rule of the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger-breadth); the arrangement beginning with one palm and so forth starts from three cubits (*hasta*) and extends up to nine cubits. (BhS 5.9)
A wise man should construct a single-story [temple] with an odd number of cubits;
thereafter, he may construct a two-story one with thirteen cubits.
A temple of three stories should be fifteen cubits in height;
one should increase the measurement by six cubits specifically for each successive floor.
One should construct the measurement of the width up to twelve stories;
they declare that the height should be twice the width for the best [type].
When the width is divided into seven parts, twelve parts shall be the middle [measure],
and eleven parts the lowest, when the width is divided into seven parts.
In this manner, the height up to twelve stories is prescribed;
one should mark out sixteen squares using threads directed toward the east and the north.
The inner chamber is declared to have four sides of medium length;
one should arrange twelve sides on the exterior for the purpose of the walls.
With six [verses] for each of those sūtras, there are twenty-five words;
the remaining portion is stated for the purpose of the walls in the center of the nine-celled house. BhS 5.16.
It is declared to be of three kinds:
likewise, those in the form of palaces;
and it becomes threefold as Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara.
That which is square at the top of the stūpa is declared to be the Nāgara style;
that which is octagonal from the neck upwards is the Drāviḍa temple.
That which extends from the neck downwards is declared to be the *dveṣa* (aversion) line;
wherever the image (*bera*) was previously situated, it should be determined according to the position of that image.
The pedestal (pīṭha) indeed has a width equal to one-third of the base;
the inner chamber (garbha) is three times the size of the pedestal, and the wall (bhitti) is said to be half the size of the inner chamber.
One should construct a wall there, occupying one-third of the interior of the chamber;
in front of it, one should make a pavilion with a width equal to that of the palace.
One should construct a front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) measuring one-tenth of the temple's total length,
and at the front of the temple, one should fashion a door endowed with the proper characteristics.
The height of the door is said to be up to the upper limit of the enclosure;
the width of the best door is declared to be half that height.
That which is reduced by one-tenth of half the height is called the middle [size];
that which is reduced by one-twentieth would be the width of the inferior [size]. (BhS 5.24)
One should fashion both the body and the secondary body according to their height;
one part shall be the base, and the height shall consist of the earth.
Two parts should be for the feet; this portion is called the *prastāra*.
One part is declared to be the neck, and the two parts shall constitute the crest (*śikhara*).
The region above the hips is known as the "belly" (bhāgasthya), and thus the height is described;
this has been declared according to desire, and now the secondary body (anukāya) is being discussed.
One should make the width of the temple twenty-four parts;
its breadth shall be one part, and likewise its thickness one part.
In a two-storey building it should be ten finger-breadths, and in a three-storey building twelve finger-breadths;
for each subsequent storey, it should be increased by four finger-breadths.
One-eighth of this foot,
which is wide and firm, should be dug out at the top of the pillar according to the measurement of the body.
The two feet at the front should extend beyond the support;
having divided the base into three parts, one part indeed becomes the jagatī.
One should cause the *kumuda* to be made with a second part;
having completed the entire [structure], one should make the *paṭṭikā* with a single part.
One should make the neck one and a half [units]; the remainder is called the horse.
This is known as the "foot-binding" [style], honored in all undertakings. (BhS 5.33)
Or one should perform the ritual of receding (pratikramaṇa) according to the dimensions of the foundation;
likewise for the base (jagatī), and then the lotus (kumuda) is said to be attached.
Having divided it into parts as before, one should perform the remaining fourth part;
likewise, the *megha* and *astarika* should be made using the *paṭṭika* alone.
One should make two facing [images]; this is called the *pratikrama* (counter-step), known as the *adhiṣṭhāna* (foundation). Now the measurement of the feet will be explained.
It may be square, octagonal, or circular—thus it is of three kinds;
likewise, some maintain it is provided with a pitcher, while others hold it to be without a pitcher.
Some indeed remember the foot as being joined with two *vaikuṃbha* jewels,
equal in width, or even twice as wide at its base.
Having abandoned the square shape, one should make it circular, or indeed octagonal,
as is appropriate, or else sixteen-sided.
The form of the feet has been declared; now the characteristics of the pitcher (kumbha) are being stated:
it should be one and a half times the height of the feet, or twice the height minus one-quarter of a foot.
Its height should be double its width at the base;
it is called Śrīkara, Candrakānta, Saumukhya, and Priyadarśana.
The names should be applied specifically according to their respective order:
*Śrīkara* for those with feet in the *vṛtta* meter, and likewise *Kalāśrāṇa* for those with feet in the *kalā* meter.
Furthermore, the moonstone (candrakānta) is octagonal and is known as a "fragment of the moon" (somakhaṇḍa);
it is said to be "pleasing to behold" when used in pillars that bear great weight.
Having made the water-pot (kumbha) nine parts, one part is said to be the heart;
the neck portion is declared to consist of four parts.
It is said that one part should be for the mouth, and the remainder should be made with two staffs;
likewise, it may be circular with a single lotus-petal design or otherwise.
The width of the two pillars is said to be twice the width of the *kumbha*;
the width of the mouth is one and a half times that, like the base of the pillar for the support of the *hāra*.
Thus the extent has been described; now the characteristic of the maṇḍala is stated: the height of the maṇḍalas should be three-quarters [of the width], and the width should be four times that.
One-third [of the width] shall be for the lotus, and likewise one part for the reed;
the space for the planks shall be two parts, and the space for the reeds shall be like the form of the foot.
One should construct the shoulder according to the measurement of the tip of the foot, following the prescribed rule;
its width at the top of the pillar should be equal to that of the *vīrakānta* type, measured in three parts.

Above that, one should fashion a foot-protrusion (*pāda*) with a width equal to one-quarter of the base; its height is said to be one-quarter, one-half, or [one-third] of the base. This is called the elevation of the *bodhika*.
The height of the Bodhi tree is said to be three *daṇḍas* for the lowest, four *daṇḍas* for the middling, and five *daṇḍas* for the highest. BhS 5.51.
At the edge of the courtyard, at the edge of the lotus pond, or again at the edge of the paved walkway,
one should construct the path for the water's exit and the entry of the stalk.
It should be one *haṃsapāda* or *tripāda* in length, or specifically one *vitasti*;
it should have a channel for the passage of urine, and likewise be made of stone.

One should appoint a woman whose form resembles that of an elephant's lip, who has a face superior in its lion-like shape, who is like a lion among beings, and who possesses an excellent head and a preeminent voice.
The double-staff or triple-staff [of the teacher] should be equal to the depth of the womb-chamber of the temple, or equal to the height of the image, or twice that, or even three times that.
The width at the base of the spout should be one-third [of the vessel's diameter], while the width at its tip should be one-third of that;
the thickness should be one-third less than one-third of the width.
Deep with the movement of water, characterized by the sound *jhajhara*,
it was neither low nor high, yet it appeared to slope due to the rapidity of its flow.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma accompanied by all musical instruments and auspicious recitations, one should thereafter worship the preceptor.
Thereafter, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction,
the preceptor, with a serene mind, should worship the artisan and recite the Vāruṇa hymn.
A carpenter should gradually fix a very smooth and firm tube into the interior of the temple of the image,
reaching as far as the limit of the palm tree.
Should a wise person perform the *dhārāntu* and *kevala* rites on a wall?
The installation of the image (*bera*) is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (BhS 5.61)
At the conclusion of the *dhārā* and *dala*, the installation (*sthāpana*) would be the most excellent; prior to the closing of the door, the installation would be middling. (BhS 5.62)
The installation of the smallest [stone] should take place to the east of the stone at the summit;
for whoever does otherwise acts indeed for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
Having thus established the nāla and the prastara, as well as the uttara and so forth,
the viṣkaṃbha should have a width of one pāda, and its height should be of three kinds.
The height of the best [type] should be equal to its width; the middle should be three-quarters [of that];
and the lowest should be half the height of the best, according to the rule.
One-third of the top of the pillar shall be the upper fillet (paṭṭikā); the neck (nigama) is said to be equal to that. This is the characteristic of the fillet.
Above that, however, the lotus-band (padmapaṭṭika) should be made with two parts;
the *kapota* should be two *daṇḍas*, and it should be provided with a cornice (*upāna*).
The remaining layout should be made fivefold;
one part should be used for the frieze, and one should be made for the neck.
Above that, two parts should be made, and a fillet (paṭṭikā) with one part;
thus the layout has been described, and now the archway (toraṇa) will be explained.
Toranas should likewise be constructed at the two sides and at the back;
the support for the torana should be at the northern boundary of the enclosure.
The width, however, should be half of that; the width [of the base] is five parts.
The remainder is known as the foot, being one-third of the Makara-part.
Alternatively, the width of the arch at the end of the base should be made exactly as previously described, according to the measurement of one-eighth of a *makara*.
The measurement of the nose has been stated according to its characteristics;
however, its proportions shall now be explained as determined by the authoritative treatises.
The great hall (mahānāsī) is said to have a width equal to half the interior of the courtyard;
the *nigama* should be half of that, or three-quarters, or even equal [to the courtyard].
One should make a single nose on the four peaks in the cardinal directions;
its width should be half [the height], and there should be eight noses on the corner-towers (kapota).
The characteristic of the *kūṭa* has been declared; the *kūṭa-śāla* is prescribed.
Having divided the temple (*prāsāda*) into six parts, one part is to be set aside for it.
The kūṭa-śālā should consist of one part, and the fifth part should be half a part;
the kūpa should be fourfold, and the śālā should have the form of a gopura.
The side walls should be made according to the measurement of the hall's width;
a cage provided with a single opening is thus described.
Then, one should increase the pinnacle (śikhara) by a measure of half the neck;
it is said that the height of the pinnacle is twice the length of the neck.
Outside the Nigama-vartana, one should construct the vardhana at half that measure;
the staff (daṇḍa), joined with the sthūpī, the ikku, and the bhas, should be made according to the prescribed rule.
The summit is said to be of that same measurement in width;
above that is called the neck, and above that is the cornice.
"One should gradually make it thin until it reaches the edge of the tooth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Lord belonging to the Śrī Vaikhānasa tradition.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
the procedure for the *mūrdhan* brick. Hereafter, I shall explain specifically the sequence of the procedure for the *mūrdhan* brick.
And having constructed the sacrificial hall at the forefront, the wise one [proceeded].
Having prepared the center of the altar according to the measurement of the stūpa’s pinnacle-pin,
and having prepared the assembly hall facing east, one should perform the āghāra offering according to the rules.
The wise one should place upon the middle of the altar four bricks that are very smooth, free of cracks, and firm,
having first recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra over them in due order.
The tip may be somewhat depressed and the base somewhat elevated;
the back part would be below and the face part above.
Then, one should cause the syllables to be written using flour made from śāli rice:
the letter *ya* should be written in the east, and the letter *ra* should be placed in the south.
One should draw the letter *la* in the west and the letter *va* in the north;
there, the wise man should place a stūpa made either of metal or of wood.
The length of the foot is one and a half [units], its width is equal to the foot;
the tip is one finger-breadth in width, and it tapers accordingly.
The base should be square, such that one-third of it is equal [to the height];
above that one should make it circular, and one should place a śīlī-foot below.
Its length should be three times its width, and its breadth should be equal to its width;
having joined it with those two [sides], it should stand as a spike (śūla) with its face turned downward.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
having performed the Vāstuyajña sacrifice, one should carry out the ritual of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the fire oblation according to the rule for the crown-brick,
the wise and righteous preceptor, accompanied by the patron, [should do so] again at dawn.
Having taken up the stone and other materials, he should place them upon the celestial chariot (vimāna) in that manner;
having grasped them with both hands, facing either eastward or northward.
One should place the stone upon Indra and the other [deities] with mantras beginning with the four Vedas;
then, having recited the Dhruva-sūkta, one should likewise fix the stūpa in the center.
Having summoned a skilled artisan and honored him especially,
one should perform the consolidation by placing stones and other materials upon it.
In the foot-binding, the neck, and the pavilion, the deities of the pavilion are to be placed in order around it;
one should place Viṣṇu in the east, where his residence is in the inner sanctum.
One should arrange the placement thus: of the embodiment of Satya in the south, of Acyuta in the west, and of Aniruddha in the north.
The form of Gajapuruṣa is in the south, Nārasiṃha in the west,
Varāha in the west, and Hayagrīva likewise in the north.
Seated upon a comfortable throne, adorned with all ornaments,
and having a serpent raised at one corner, [he is] Viṣṇu or the Lord of Beasts (Śiva).
Having thus properly installed Vakratuṇḍa and Durgā upon the walls of the front pavilion, one should worship them according to what is available.
One should thus arrange the stationing of the gatekeepers at the gates;
the characteristics of the palace have been declared, and now those of the pavilions are described.
A pavilion established with sixteen pillars is known as Śrīpratiṣṭhita;
one joined with twelve pillars is remembered as Bījāsana.
That which is endowed with thirty-two bodily marks is celebrated as Jayabhadra;
that which is endowed with thirty-six bodily marks is the most beautiful Nandyāvarta.
That which is endowed with sixty-four pillars is known as the Śrībhadraka;
that which is endowed with hundreds of pillars is designated as the Viśāla.
The expansion [of the mandala] should be described as being like a palace, according to its proportions;
it should be constructed upon a horse, and the supporting elements should likewise consist of digits.
The pillar, the crossbeam, and the height should each be one-fourth as wide [as the base];
the *jayantī* architrave should be level with them, its width measured according to the span of the *tulā*.
Then, extending half a *daṇḍa* in thickness along its length,
one should cover it from above with bricks, provided with *galakas*.
The length of the pavilion should be made in four ways: one and a quarter [the width], one and a half, double, and less by a quarter.
Regarding the length as appropriate, the rule for the pillars is stated:
they should be two cubits, or three cubits, or even four cubits.
The space between the pillars should be constructed according to the specific rules;
thus has the sequence been fully explained, and now the enclosure wall is described.
One should construct a wall surrounding the palace according to its dimensions;
the width of that wall is here called its "staff" (daṇḍa).
They call the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala) one and a half daṇḍas in measure;
the innermost load is a prastha, while the middle load is two daṇḍas.
The boundary wall should be constructed with a measurement of four *daṇḍas*,
while the great boundary wall should be seven *daṇḍas* in measure.
One and a half times, twice, three times, or even four times the width of the gate is declared to be the length of the ramparts specifically.
One should construct a wall with a height of one cubit and a width of a hand, topped with a pigeon-ornament (kapota) and provided with a watch-tower and an enclosure wall.

The height of the base (talotsedha) originating from the foundation is prescribed as one cubit; alternatively, it may be raised according to availability. This is known as the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
One should construct a series of six finger-breadths for the successive lower ramparts;
the exit path for water should be at the end of the platform or even on the bank.
One should likewise arrange the door of the first enclosure at the front;
as for the door of the second enclosure, there is no fault if it is not aligned.
It should be one-fourth the height of the palace, or less by a quarter, or even half that size;
it may be joined with separate gate-towers or raised on all sides.
It may thus have five enclosures, or even three;
in the case of three enclosures, it should be six finger-breadths deep at the bottom in three places.
One should know that the height of the wall up to the edge of the *kapota* (dove-cot) is the best;
up to the *utkara* (projection) is the middling; and likewise, up to the *kalaśa* (pitcher-finial) is the lowest.
Thus, in connection with the enclosure wall, the height is threefold in sequence;
or it may be one-fifth of the height, or indeed four parts out of five.
One may make the width of the wall threefold by means of one-sixth [of the total],
or else the wall of the temple should be equal to that, as indeed is the wall itself.
In the womb [of the temple], the offering pedestal (balipīṭha) should likewise be made such that its height is eight parts for the best, two-sevenths for the middling,
and one-fifth for the lowest.
One part out of five, three, or two [parts] of the womb-measure...;
in the ninefold [system], six, four, or [three] parts constitute the medium, the inferior, and the superior [measures] respectively.
The Paiśācika [mantra] is of three kinds from the seat (pīṭha):
it is said to be one cubit, up to two cubits, up to three cubits, and up to four cubits in sequence.
The Piśāca-pīṭha is of three kinds— inferior, middling, and superior—
and its height is equal to twenty-seven parts.
The footstool is known to have two parts, the birth [pedestal] they know to have four parts,
the water-pot they say has three parts, and the neck likewise has four.
They say that one-sixth is for the *karaṇa*, two parts are for the *valaka* alone,
four parts are for the *kapotas*, and one part is for the upper frieze (*agrapaṭṭikā*).
One and a half [parts] are for the lotus flower, and one half is for the lotus bud;
having understood this correctly, one should designate them according to their respective portions.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the section on the *Prakīrṇa-adhikāra* of the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavac-chāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The characteristics of the retinue and the abode. Now, therefore, follows the description of the abodes of the retinue:
one should construct them as being either one-quarter less than the celestial palace (vimāna) or half its size. (BhS 7.1)
Then, one should fashion Viṣvaksena between Someśa and Īśāna, [the former] endowed with color and excellent, while the latter is devoid of color. BhS 7.2.
To the south of the door is Indra, and in the southeast is the kitchen;
to the west of that is the place for water.
The bed is prescribed for the south, the sacrificial pavilion to its east,
the flower-garden in the northeast, and the store of garments in the south.
Likewise, the installation [of the deity] between Īśāna and Soma is prescribed;
and the location for grain is likewise praised as being between Indra and Agni.
One should worship Śrībhūta, facing outward, in the middle of the steps;
one should worship Garuḍa in front of him, facing toward the deity.
The guardians of the celestial palaces, the guardians of the directions, together with the Sun;
the discus, the banner, the conch, and the spirit who is indeed the leader of spirits.
One should worship them in their respective locations within the first enclosure,
especially by performing festivals and offerings that are never-ending.
Furthermore, one should perform circumambulation even of that which is immeasurable:
[the image] of the deity up to the limit of the neck, externally up to the limit of the breasts.
Or specifically, one should visualize the arising of the retinue in sequence up to the navel;
specifically, the retinue beginning with Dhātṛ and ending with Bhūta.

In the section on ritual procedures (*kriyādhikāra*), I have already clearly stated the characteristics [of the deities] according to their colors, vehicles, banners, and so forth, preceded by their names and asterisms. (BhS 7.11)
The Characteristics of the Bera (The Classification of Materials):
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme characteristics of the *bera* [the image]:
that made of stone, that made of gems, that made of minerals, and likewise that made of wood. (BhS 7.12)
"Likewise, it may be made of clay; thus the image of Āveśa is said to be fivefold.
The stone image may be of four kinds, and likewise the jewel-made image is sevenfold."
That which is born of metal is said to be of eight kinds, and that which is born of wood is declared to be sixteenfold;
that which is made of clay is said to be of two kinds—their characteristics are now stated in order.
Regarding the characteristics of stone (śailaja):
white, red, yellow, and black—these four are declared to be the varieties of stone; their characteristics are now described. (BhS 7.15)
A stone that resembles cow's milk, or resembles a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, is declared to be white; it bestows the power of subjugation. (BhS 7.16)
The stone resembles the hibiscus flower, it is like blood,
it is comparable to the bandhūka blossom, and it is similar to natural cinnabar.
A stone that is red is declared to be victorious when it possesses the [proper] characteristics;
one that is yellow resembles gold or is like the powder of turmeric. (BhS 7.18)
A stone endowed with auspicious marks bestows wealth, grain, and happiness;
it resembles black gram, mung beans, or is like the fruit of the jambu tree.
The black stone, resembling a bee or a blue lotus, is known to increase progeny; it bestows all accomplishments upon everyone. (BhS 7.20)
For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, [the colors] are white, red, yellow, and black respectively, according to the rule. (BhS 7.21)
For the twice-born and those of the three [other] castes, a red stone bestows victory;
a white stone is declared to bestow liberation, especially for Brāhmaṇas.
If one should cause a permanent image to be made out of devotion, [using] ruby, coral, lapis lazuli, and likewise sphatika; BhS_7.23 //
Emerald, topaz, and sapphire—these are born from gems;
ruby is said to bring prosperity, and coral brings about subjugation.
Lapis lazuli effects attraction; crystal bestows the increase of sons; emerald causes dissension; and topaz effects immobilization.
A blue [amulet] should be made with turuṣka; it shall yield the fruit of those born of jewels.
One should prepare an amulet from these, and for others as well, the same procedure is prescribed.
Gold, silver, copper, bronze, brass,
iron, lead, and tin— these are the minerals derived from the elements.
Gold is said to bestow prosperity, silver grants a kingdom,
copper is for the sake of attaining sons, and bell-metal causes enmity.
In its utterance, copper causes imprisonment, iron is the cause of destruction,
lead produces floods of water, and tin brings about the ruin of one's lifespan.
Thus has that which is made of metal been described; next, that which is made of wood is mentioned:
namely, *devadāru*, the *śamī* tree, the *pippala*, and likewise the *nandana*.
The *āsana* tree, the *khadira*, the *vakula*, the *śaṅkhinī*, the *vātana*, as well as the *mayūra*, the *padma*, the *ḍuṇḍūka*, and the *karṇikāra*.
Likewise, the *nibūka*, the *añjanikā*, the *plakṣa*, and the *audumbara*—
these four are to be avoided due to the transgression of the twice-born.
Earthenware is said to be of two kinds: namely, the fired and the unfired;
the fired is perishable, while the unfired is conducive to all accomplishments.
Regarding the observation of signs (auspicious omens):
with a resolute mind, one should go to that place where the stones are;
at the time of departure, auspicious birds bestow favorable results. (BhS 7.34)
Auspicious are water-jars filled with pure speech, bones, the king of elephants, and the best of birds;
auspicious are hides, meat, curds, milk, and the sound of kettledrums. (BhS 7.35)
I shall likewise describe the inauspicious signs as they appear in the future:
the sight of those with disheveled hair, naked, and smeared with blood, fat, and oil. (BhS 7.36)
The mention of an empty pitcher being stopped, or the sight of an oil vessel at the time of departure,
are considered lost omens that yield contrary results.
One should set out on the journey after remaining in a place characterized by auspicious signs;
having reached the stone at a favorable location, one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.
Having performed the ritual sprinkling with the Vaiṣṇava Sūkta, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, and likewise the Śrībhū Sūkta, one should then properly place five water-pots.

Having set out earth, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and muttered prayers, as well as water with all medicinal herbs, and having worshipped them with water for the feet and other offerings, one should worship those respective deities.
One should consecrate the stone with the thread during a moment endowed with auspicious characteristics;
having cut the stone with the mantra beginning with "atodevā," the wise one [should proceed].
One should arrange the lower part there as the mouth and the head above; alternatively, one may arrange the head portion toward the east or the north.
Having marked the face, the back, as well as the feet, the sides, and likewise the head according to the prescribed rule, one should then proceed with the carving.
A woman who is endowed with auspicious marks should be known as a young girl, a young woman, or an old woman;
one who is smooth, soft, and inclined, as well as having a voice like milk, is a young girl.
That stone which possesses a beautiful sound and is endowed with luster is known as "young";
that stone which is black, rattling, rough, aged, and devoid of sound is [known as] "old."
A stone that is immature is said to cause destruction; one that is youthful bestows great prosperity;
and one that is aged brings about the ruin of undertakings. Thus, stones should be accepted only after they have been examined.
Having performed the smoothing of the surface, one should observe the defects of the stone;
then, having smeared the stone with milk, clarified butter, lead, and red ochre.
Then, having thoroughly washed the stone that has been left overnight with water and having examined any defects in the stone, one should perform what is enjoined by the ritual rules.
A line, a dot, and a stain are proclaimed to be defects of the stone;
however, a circle should be present there where one would designate the *garbha*.
On a red maṇḍala, however, there is a snake; on a yellow maṇḍala, a chameleon; on a crimson one, there would be a lizard; and on a dark-red one, a frog. (BhS 7.50)
In a tawny [dream], a mouse is proclaimed; in a black-colored one, a scorpion;
and in one that is a mixture of white and red, a white and red scorpion.
If mixed with blood, it becomes a frog;
in the color of vermilion, a firefly; and in the color of a dove, a house-lizard. (BhS 7.52)
One should avoid stones with the color of molasses, water that lacks natural luster, and ground containing subterranean cavities as well as that which is stained by impurities.
The stainless [metal] is known as gold-bronze (hemakāṃsya) and iron; these three are traditionally recognized.
Having thus examined them, one should act accordingly according to the prescribed measure.
Whether according to the measurement of the interior of the temple or according to the measurement of the cubit,
the measurement of the door shall be explained as having three distinct varieties for each.
One and a half times the door-measure, as well as one and a quarter times the door-measure;
thus the middle and the smallest door are prescribed.
Between the lowest and the highest, the wise one should divide [the length] into eight parts;
three should be known as the smallest, and likewise three as the middle.
One should know that the height consists of three plus one part, making nine parts in total;
the height above the pillar is one and a half parts, which is the specific measure for the *uttama* [type].

Between the best and the lowest, one should apply the measurement according to the size of the door; the middle [size] should be equal to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), and the lowest should be three-quarters of that.
It should be understood that a size exceeding [the standard] by one-quarter is indeed prescribed as the best;
(one should apply the measurement of the door between the best and the lowest). Likewise, I shall describe the measurement in cubits: nine cubits is the highest. BhS 7.60.
With six *aṅgulas* for the others, up to a limit of two and a half cubits;
such is the praised measurement of height for a stationary [image].
