as well as the other Sādhyas, are considered to be threefold and nine tālas in height.
The lords of the Daityas and Yakṣas, as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, along with Mars,
the Sun, and Rāhu, are esteemed for the excellent nine-beat tāla.
One should honor the sages and the hosts with nine *tālas*;
likewise, the celestial singers (*uṅgās*) and other *cāraṇas* have a height measured by nine *tālas*.
Mortals are said to be eight *tālas* in height; for the *pretas*, it is seven *tālas*.
The *kubjakas* are said to be six *yamās* tall, while the *vāmanas* reach five *tālas*.
Those dwelling on the earth have four *tālas*; the *kinnaras* have three;
the *kūśmāṇḍas* have two; and the headless trunks (*kabandhas*) have one.
Among those, there are three types of proportions—superior, middling, and inferior.
I shall now explain the procedure for working with beeswax according to the specific prescriptions.
Either in the house of the sacrificer or in a delightful temple,
having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, one should prepare the aupāsana fire-pit.
Having performed the libation according to the rules, one should likewise worship Viṣṇu;
and having offered oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta, one should likewise offer those of Brahmā and Rudra.
Having properly offered oblations to the Viśvaśaiṣika-cakras and to Vighneśa,
one should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains to the south of that fire.
Then, having spread out a square and a circle as is auspicious,
one should duly worship the Cakras, Śaiṣikas, and Vīśas in their proper sequence.
Having taken purified beeswax with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should fashion the primary limb [of the image] with the mantra: “*iṣe tvorje tvā*. (BhS 9.49)
Having thus abandoned the syllables, meditated upon them, and touched them,
one should then offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and dismiss the other deities.
There, the attendants beginning with the Goddess should be offered oblations with their respective mantras;
having placed that prepared offering into the hand of the artisan while recollecting Hari, [one should proceed].
Just as one would place the male organ into the female organs for the purpose of grasping,
so too, having grasped the thread, one should establish the embryo.
A wise artisan should work according to the measurements of weight, height, and proportion;
having gradually coated [the mold] and allowed it to dry, he should apply external layers of clay and iron.
Having bound it with cloths according to the ritual procedure and having smeared it again, one should let it dry;
then, under a lunar mansion favorable to the patron, one should perform the fire offering as before.
Likewise, having established it as equal according to the sequence of water-equivalence,
and having attained the appropriate accomplishment, one should heat that embryo.
Having gradually excavated the earth according to the prescribed rite, one should extract the image.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Vaikhānasa-Phagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall describe the ritual of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) following the rites such as the examination of the ground;
for the God of gods, Viṣṇu, the sowing of sprouts is performed according to the prescribed rule.
In the ninth, the seventh, or even the fifth, or at the sixth; or facing the Ālaya, or in the northeast, or in the north. (BhS 10.2)
For the twice-born, it should be eleven cubits; for kings, nine cubits;
for Vaiśyas, seven cubits; and for Śūdras, five cubits.
One should construct a pavilion, a wind-shelter, or a water-station according to the prescribed rite, provided with sixteen pillars and equipped with four gates. (BhS 10.4)
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should recite the mantra "Be pacified" (śāmyantu);
or else, [one may use] white cotton lintel-powder or even lime powder.
Having made it into a fine powder and likewise mixed with sand, one should place it [on the ground] with its tips pointing eastward and northward, reciting the mantra: "Somaṃ rājānam."
And having made it symmetrical, smooth, beautiful,
and lovely, he adorned it with a circular rim and embellished it with small offering-bowls and sprouts.
Having established the center of the mandala, one should have it made beautiful,
adorned with canopies, pillar-wrappings, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments.
One should establish the four presiding deities within the inner fourfold sheath: Dharma, Knowledge, Dispassion, and Sovereignty.
Having worshipped the twelve Ādityas, who are the deities of the twelve [months], according to what is appropriate, one should perform their respective rites.
Whether it be five cubits, three cubits, or even one cubit,
having divided it into twenty-five squares, one should establish the seat of Brahmā in the center.
Eight lotuses indeed should be placed all around for the purpose of movement;
furthermore, four doors are declared to be in the east and so forth, with one in the center.
On the remaining space of the sun-plate, the wise one should establish the positions of the *pālikās*;
he should arrange a row of either rice grains or husked rice according to the prescribed rule.
One should construct a square Brahmā-altar with a length of sixteen finger-breadths, raised as high as available, and provided with three altars at its corners. BhS 10.14.
The remaining [portion] to the north of the eastern gate and to the east of the southern gate shall be the pedestal for Vakratuṇḍa;
it should be to the south of the western gate.
One should worship Paṅktīśa at the northern gate and Somapīṭhaka in the west; or else, one should worship [the deities] in the jars, beginning from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having prepared a seat for the six [deities], one should perform the rite for Brahmā as previously described;
likewise, one should worship Jayā and the other Apsarases from the direction of Indra (East) to the direction of Īśāna (Northeast).
One *āḍhaka*, half of that, or a quarter, [of rice] separately with husked grains,
on a seat eight fingers wide on the outside, or even on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Square, well-rounded, triangular, bow-shaped,
staff-like, lotus-like, eight-sided, and perfectly circular.
One should arrange the seats for Jaya and the others in sequence outside the *pālikās*;
if one is capable, one should also have mandalas made for the guardians of the directions.
Or likewise, one should quickly worship upon the ground, or upon bundles of kuśa grass;
[the mandalas] being square, triangular, perfectly circular, and even the vajra-shape.
The half-moon, the hexagon, the circle, and the anklet-shaped [mandala], as well as the form of the mandala of the world-protectors, and for others, the square. BhS 10.22.
Having tied together an *aśvattha* sprout, *dūrvā* grass, and *kuśa* grass in the middle,
one who is pure should fill the *pālikā* vessels and the others in due order with clay.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra and taken [the materials] with the Praṇava, the knower of mantras,
having recited the Medinī mantra, should place the earthen vessels in the northeast and the other directions.
Having thus set down the jars, one should then place them at the left of the door;
and having recited "rākām ahaṃ," one should again [place them] to the right of the door. (BhS 10.25)

“With the mantra ‘O Sinīvālī,’ the preceptor should place [the grains] in sequence; according to the order of the castes, he should do so for those [deities] at every step of the small earthen vessels. (BhS 10.26)
On the right side of Brahmā, the teacher should sit facing north,
having taken his seat upon the Brahmā-throne while recollecting the God of gods.
First, one should visualize Brahmā and the others within the heart;
then, one should sequentially invoke them into the vessels upon the grass mats placed on the sacrificial mound.
Four-faced and four-armed, adorned with all ornaments,
his right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness, while his left rests upon his thigh.
Holding a water-pot and a rosary in his right and left hands respectively,
seated upon a lotus throne, golden-hued, clad in dark blue garments, and born from a lotus.
Having invoked Brahmā with the *mūrti-mantras*, one should worship him facing east;
likewise, [one should worship] him facing east at the eastern gate and similarly at the southern gate.
In the vimāna with the western door, and likewise in that with the northern door,
one should meditate upon the lotus-born [Brahmā] facing east, and the others according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform the meditation for those facing east and so forth, while facing east oneself; having worshipped Prajāpati in the middle of the row, one should recite the Brahma-mantra.
With a golden body, yellow garments, and two arms holding a lotus, he is seated with a casket upon his head; the remainder [of the deities] face westward toward him.
One should visualize Ananta, the lord of all nāgas and husband of Vāruṇī,
endowed with seven hoods, white in luster, and with palms joined in reverence.
The Lord, whose face is like coral, who has the face of an elephant, and who sits facing north, holds a plantain tree, a mango tree, a breadfruit tree, a noose, and a goad.
The wise one should meditate upon him who has a single tusk, four arms, and a formidable snout;
he is dark-complexioned, wears yellow garments, and carries a sword and a shield.
One should meditate upon Paṅktīśa, who has two arms, wears a crown of caskets, faces the east, is white in color,
is dressed in dark blue garments, possesses the Saunya [mark], and holds a staff in his two hands.
Adorned with a crown and a basket, she stands firmly facing the south;
possessing the luster of a cloud, wearing red garments, and holding two lotuses in her hands.
One should worship Jayā, who has limbs adorned with every ornament,
who possesses a blue luster, wears yellow garments, and holds two lotuses in her hands, in the place of Indra.
One should worship Vijayā with a garland, her entire body adorned with ornaments;
she has the luster of a white water-lily, wears green garments, possesses two hands, and is marked by a lotus.
One should worship Vindā at the southern foot, her limbs adorned with various ornaments,
resembling the leaf of the dhātakī tree, and clothed in deep blue garments.

One should worship Nandā at the south-western quarter (Nairṛti), who holds two lotuses in her hands, has the luster of washed [silver], wears yellow garments, and possesses two hands holding lotuses. (BhS 10.43)
One should worship Puṣṭikā, who belongs to Varuṇa, as being adorned with flower ornaments;
she is golden-hued, wears red garments, has two hands, and holds lotuses. (BhS 10.44)
One should worship Kumudvatī, whose limbs are adorned, in the northwest in due order;
she has a reddish luster, is clothed in garments resembling clouds, and is decked with ornaments.
One should worship her with two hands holding a lotus, gentle and adorned with earrings;
she has the luster of gold, wears green garments, and has arms joined with a lotus.
Then one should worship Viśogā, adorned with all ornaments—[the goddesses] Raktābhā, Hāṭakābhā, Hariṇī, and Nīlavarṇikā. (BhS 10.47)

Those resembling the *dhātakī* flower, those with peaceful aspirations, those like the white and blue lotus, and those with the luster of the *aśoka* tree— these, in sequence, have two arms and hold lotuses.
Some maintain that one should meditate here on Jayā and the others, who wear inverted garments, are seated comfortably upon their respective seats, and whose limbs are adorned with every ornament.
The wise one should likewise recollect Medinī, Rākā, and Sinīvālī.
One should visualize Medinī as having a dark complexion, standing with two arms, and wearing a garment with a yellow border.
Holding a flower-basket in her hands, with beautiful hair and a face turned toward that direction,
the goddess was as dear as the full moon, her countenance resembling the full moon.
One should visualize Hemāṅgī, who wears red garments and holds a water-jar, standing like the full moon;
likewise Śeṣā, and the white-limbed Chinīvalī, who wears dark blue garments.
I consider her who holds a shallow bowl to be like the earth;
having meditated upon her correctly in each respective position, or while seated, one should then worship her.
Having likewise meditated on the Moon as the seed-syllable, holding that seed with both hands,
one should stand or sit facing north or south.

Having meditated thus, one should then worship with incense and other offerings; the wise person should properly present the oblation (havis) upon the altar or cause the sacrificial offering (bali) to be given.
The colors for Jaya and the others follow their sequence in a clockwise order;
the height of the *pālikā* is one span, its width is half that, and its opening is half [the width] again.
The middle circumference is ten finger-breadths less than the broad circumference at the bottom;
the emergence of the bulb (kumbha) is equal to that, and its mouth is six finger-breadths in length.
It should be described as having a mouth like the neck of a water-pot and a belly ten finger-breadths deep;
it is joined to the door of the hermitage, and the remainder is equal to its supporting ledge.
The *śarāva* vessel should have a height equal to a *tāla*, and its mouth should be the same size as that of the *pālikā*;
it should be placed either to the north of the temple, or especially in the northeast.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should worship it;
having worshipped the peaceful wheel, one should take that clay into the belly.
Having placed it in a bronze vessel, one should set it upon the head of the disciple;
then, having circumambulated the village or circumambulated the temple.
Having filled the *pālikā* vessels and reciting the *gāyatrī* mantra,
one should place those *pālikā* vessels in the corners beginning with the northeast.
There should be a water-pot at the left of the door and a shallow bowl at the right of the door;
having wrapped them with new cloths, one should worship the *pālikā*s and the other vessels.
One should also bring grains in a vessel, such as kidney beans, mung beans, barley, niṣpāvas, mustard seeds, chickpeas, sesame, and tilva.
Having taken up the vessel of oblation, one should worship Soma in the northwest;
at that time, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day, one should cause the sounding of musical instruments.
Then, having recited the Viṣṇusūkta, the preceptor, together with the patron, should sow the sprouts while reciting the mantra beginning with "ime bīja". (BhS 10.66)
Then, with the mantra "somaṃ rāje," one should cause the sprouts to be sown;
having recited the Varuṇa mantra, one should provide water. (BhS 10.67)
If a Śūdra is the sacrificer, he should again honor his guru with garments and other offerings, give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and then have the hair shaved by that very same person.
One should cover [the vessel] with leaves of the arka, vata, or eraṇḍa plants until the end; this is considered the worship performed at the three times of day.
Having dismissed the deities here, one should have them placed in a concealed spot;
having covered the *pālikā* vessels and so forth with new cloths, one should worship them.
One should perform the offering of the sprouts immediately on the day following the new moon;
some authorities maintain that it should likewise be performed immediately even when there is an interval caused by a solar transit (saṃkrānti).
If there is an immediate sprout, whether at night or by day,
one should perform all the rites accordingly with flowers or likewise with rice grains.
One should have it sown for that rite and have it prepared immediately; if a vessel is not available, one should have it done in a clay bowl, or as may be obtained.
For the immediate offering of sprouts, one should worship pure rice grains;
one should take earthen vessels (pālikās) according to the arrangement of nine, five, or one.

One [image] should be placed facing Brahmā, while the remaining ones are around the perimeter; having worshipped the respective lords of those directions, one should worship them with their respective mantras.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as stated in the *Khila*.
The definition is likewise declared there, as are the qualities and defects in that very place.
One should always perform the gift of a perpetual lamp according to the prescribed rule;
at the conclusion of the rite, one should cast the sprouts of grain into the midst of water.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Blessed One:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme ritual for consecration;
at a highly auspicious moment, the wise one should indeed cause the consecration to be performed. (BhS 11.1)
The characteristics of the teacher: According to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, [he should choose] Brahmins who have performed the rites beginning with the *niṣeka*,
who are preeminent knowers of the Vedas, righteous, and devoted to the pursuit of knowledge.
Gentle, with senses conquered, pure, and devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu,
their minds had their doubts destroyed through the process of reasoning and refutation.
Having summoned those who are accompanied by their wives and children, peaceful, habituated to bathing, and handsome,
one should honor one among them there as the instructor for all matters.
Having chosen a teacher, one should perform everything as instructed by him;
for the ground has been examined by that guru according to the prescribed ritual.
One should have the ritual activities, from the plowing of the ground up to the consecration, performed by that very person;
likewise, even the duties of the preceptor therein should be performed by him alone.
In his absence, however, [one should offer it] to his son, grandson, or even great-grandson;
or to his brother, disciple, grand-disciple, or even his teacher.
In the absence of the former, one should likewise employ the latter fellow-celibate;
or, with his permission, another may be appointed to the position of teacher.
Otherwise, there would be great calamity; the king and the kingdom would perish, the duties of the castes would decline, and the intermixture of castes would arise.
The Agnihotra sacrifices will not be performed, the study of the Vedas will not proceed,
and other things will be reversed, with the low becoming high and the high becoming low.
Therefore, one should have all rites performed according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures,
using white perfumes and ointments, as well as white flowers and finger-rings.
Having honored and paid homage to the preceptor and others as if they were one's own deity, one should respectfully entreat the preceptor, saying: "Please perform this rite for me. (BhS 11.12)
The disciple should offer everything as a burden at the feet of the teacher;
the teacher, with a well-pleased mind and intent upon favoring the disciple, [should accept it]. (BhS 11.13)
Having made a firm resolve that it shall be exactly so, one should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa);
this should take place from the day before the commencement of the ritual onwards.
The preceptor, without delay, should perform the Kūśmāṇḍa fire-oblation in a fire produced from lotuses;
he should have his teeth and nails clean and wear a white cloth as an upper garment.
Devoted to bathing at the three periods of the day, eating sacrificial food, and having his senses subdued,
the wise man should thus proceed in this sequence together with the officiating priests.
The fire-drills, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the auspicious items, the *darvī* spoon, and the arches, in their proper order.
Having gathered nyagrodha and plakṣa wood for the sacrificial posts, as well as wood from trees belonging to the ancestors,
all endowed with the proper characteristics for the purpose of the archways.
Now I shall describe the eightfold auspicious rite (aṣṭamaṅgala), which should be two tālas in length,
one prādeśa in width, or even six aṅgulas.
It should be thick, four finger-breadths,
or it may be two finger-breadths; in its center, the wise one should draw each respective form separately.
The Śrīvatsa, the full water-jar, the drum, the mirror,
as well as the pair of fish, the goad, the conch, and the whirlpool constitute the eight auspicious signs.
I shall now describe the characteristics of the whirlpool, consisting of twenty-five squares;
starting from the northeast (īśāna) and ending at the southwest (nairṛta), one proceeds through the squares three times in sequence.
One should indeed join the initial, middle, and final words [of the mantra] in the northwest,
ending at the southeast corner, and in the north, center, and south.
The wise one, however, [should recite] eight intermediate words even without [the others];
by these seventeen [words], the *āvarta* is designated.
The conch, discus, mace, bow, and sword are the five weapons;
furthermore, the handle of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be three *prādeśas* in length.
The root should be one span in length, and its girth at the base half of that;
at the tip it should have the shape of a bilva fruit, and its circumference should be equal to one span.
Its mouth should be two finger-breadths wide, carved to a depth of two *māṣas*;
one should fashion the *sruva* ladle in this manner, or else with a width of two *prādeśas*.
The length of the *juhū* handle is twenty-four finger-breadths, and its circumference is said to be half of that; it resembles a lotus bud.
Its tip should be six finger-breadths in circumference;
its wise [maker] should make the width at the tip two finger-breadths and its length eight finger-breadths.
The remainder, however, is said to be four finger-breadths in width and height;
they know the sequence for the middle cavity and for the *juhū* ladle according to this proportion.
Thereafter, one should prepare the *upabhṛt* [ladle], three *prādeśas* in length;
it is said that its width at the base is one *prādeśa*, and from the base to the tip it is half of that. (BhS 11.31)
The staff, tapering gradually and known as "reaching to the neck," should be one span in height,
four-cornered, and six finger-breadths in thickness at the top.
Above that, one should describe the neck as being one and a half finger-breadths in length;
the remainder should be made into a square, and one should fashion it there with that very same [measurement].
The height of the wall is said to be one and a half finger-breadths above [the floor];
having determined the lip to be one finger-breadth, one should fashion a depression in its center.
Having fashioned it in the shape of a full moon, its width should be one span;
the wise man should make it gradually concave, with a depth of four barley grains at the tip.
Now, the length of the ladle should be twenty-four finger-breadths;
its tip should be six finger-breadths, and its handle five finger-breadths.
The remainder, from thirteen finger-breadths onwards, is called the staff (daṇḍa) in sequence;
that which is thick at the base is female, while that which is thick at the tip is neuter.
From the root to the tip, it is gradually rounded and described as having a masculine form;
having fashioned a garland from *darbha* grass, one should place [a bead] upon each joint of it.
Having cast out two darbha-blades at a time, one should suspend them in succession to a length of two tālas;
likewise, there should be a staff made of khadira wood, joined with a span of two tālas.
It should indeed be ten finger-breadths in circumference and perfectly round;
one should tie it from the base to the tip, joined with branches of equal finger-breadths.
Having bound it with bands of copper or iron, the wise one should make a hollow at its base and fashion a ball of the same dimensions.
Thus should the churning-stick be; one who has mastered the scriptures should prepare it, taking wood from a *śamī* tree or an *aśvattha* tree grown in the wilderness. (BhS 11.42)
The width of the ball should be six finger-breadths and its thickness likewise;
its length should be two tālas, and the wise one should have it fashioned as a flat board.
Likewise, having fashioned a handle on top,
the wise one should have a triple-stranded cord made of muñja grass for the purpose of churning.
A cloth is said to be ten, eight, or nine cubits in length;
or it is said that a cloth is three, four, or five tālas in width.
One should procure cow-derived ghee, specifically that from a tawny cow among the various types of cattle;
however, that from goats and buffaloes should be rejected, and one should avoid anything that has been kept for more than a fortnight.
Having washed his feet and sipped water, facing either east or north,
he should assume the Brahma-posture while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Having taken up the ritual grass mats, the sacrificial fuel, and so forth,
the most excellent knower of the rules should take up the mat while turning to the right.
One should construct the sacrificial hall either in front or on the right;
the sacrificial hall is a pavilion provided with sixteen pillars, or indeed a peaked roof structure.
Or one should construct a water-station there and have a pavilion built in the middle,
having clearly demarcated the low and high ground near the water and the dry land.
Having adorned [the site] in due order according to the previously stated procedure,
one should prepare an altar in the center with a measurement of one and a half times that of the image.
One should fashion the sabhya fire-pit in the eastern part outside of that;
and in the eastern part of the sabhya, one should fashion the āhavanīya fire-pit.
Furthermore, one should perform the rite again according to the rules for the domestic fire (aupāsana);
to the south of the sabhya fire-pit, one should prepare the paiṇḍarīka pit.
To the south of the altar, one should prepare the Anvāhārya fire-pit;
the wise man should then designate the place for the deities in the southwest.
One should establish the Gārhapatya fire on the western side;
one should establish the place for the collection of ashes in the northwestern quarter according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, on the northern part of the altar, one should prepare the Āvasathyā fire;
in the northeast, one should prepare a bathing pit according to the prescribed rule.
For the Sābhyapaiṇḍarīka fire-altar, three girdles are prescribed;
for all other types of altars, there are indeed only two girdles.
Each individual [pillar] should have a width and height of four finger-breadths;
for the central pillar of the assembly hall, it should be five [finger-breadths], and for that of the lotus, six finger-breadths below.
The *aupāsana* fire-altar should be like the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), but it should be raised by two finger-breadths;
the positions of the *brahman* and *soma* priests are likewise on the south and north [of the fire].
Twelve finger-breadths in length, square and well-rounded,
it should be free from thorns, clods of earth, husks, charcoal, grass, ashes, and the like.
The wise practitioner should prepare separate sacrificial pits there using either clay or sand, having first constructed a water-shed to the east of the place of sacrifice.

One should prepare a sacrificial hall for the purpose of opening the eyes; then, at the conclusion of the prescribed rites, having taken up the image, one who is free from worldly attachment should perform the opening of the eyes.
The artisan should perform the opening of the eyes according to the path of the scriptures;
he should especially place a heap of grain in front of the deity.
Having taken a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, along with her calf,
one should place them before the deity.
Having taken ghee, honey, curd, and milk into a bronze vessel,
one should place gold therein and set it down together with a lamp.
One should procure a *hūlikā* and a *tāṭanī* using gold vessels or needles, or even with silver; however, for iron, one should use a *śīlā*.
Then, on the northern side of the image, one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice;
having performed the paryagni rite, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then the Guru, facing north and having performed the purification of the body,
takes hold of the *hūlikā* and the *tāṭanī* while preceded by the mantra.
Having said, "May Viṣṇu protect you," and while recollecting the Viṣṇu-sūkta,
one should touch the head and other parts of the deity within the cloth painting in their proper sequence.
Having uttered the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should perform the ritual there;
and with the two goddesses, one should likewise recite their respective mantras in due order.
Afterwards, having grasped the bowl with two needles, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
one should consecrate the six mandalas while recollecting the presiding deity.
Having meditated upon the eyelashes, the armor, the red, the white, the black, and the luminous [elements],
one should quickly stabilize the mandala with these in due order.
May the sun, Rāhu, and Saturn, having abandoned [their malefic influence], rise before his two eyes;
may he open his eyes for the sake of the increase of all prosperity. (BhS 11.73)
If one performs [the rite] under the Andhā constellation, there will be total destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Having recited the Puruṣasūkta, one should place it upon the right eye.
In that very same way, while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra with the left eye,
one should specifically perform the rite for Śrī and Bhūmi using their two respective hymns.
Having made an oblation while touching the body of the Lord, beginning with the crown and the garland,
and likewise having made an oblation for the two Goddesses, one should offer separately with the [mantra] "dadbhyaḥ syāha".

If the celestial palace (vimāna) is new, one who is most skilled in mantras should perform oblations of incense and other offerings; he should have it consecrated with the mantra of the assembly (parṣad) and their forms.
Let the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Sviṣṭākāra offering be recited;
having uttered the Godāna-sūkta and touched the mouth and other parts [of the cow].
Having subsequently cast away the cloth, he should display the cow and other items;
then, taking those substances such as the cow, he should give them to the preceptor.

Having specifically prepared the auspicious knots (kautuka) and so forth upon the pedestal of the image according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should deposit the gems and other materials.
One should deposit jewels, mineral ores, seeds, and gold therein;
having thus established it, the wise person should heat it until it is indeed firmly solidified.
Having performed the opening of the eyes as prescribed for a fixed image (dhruvabera),
one who has mastered its mantra should thereafter carry out the preliminary rites such as the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa).
Having taken up the five products of the cow and sprinkled [the site], the wise one,
having recited "vasoḥ pavitram," should perform the ritual therein.
Afterwards, having taken milk and sprinkled [the area] while composed in meditation, and having recited "śanno devī," one should perform the ritual with that. (BhS 11.84)

The one who perceives the purpose, having taken up the lamps and placed them before the deity, should offer them; then, having prepared the water, he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) therein.

And thus, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) here, one should again perform the preliminary consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) upon his images, as well as the preliminary consecration with milk.
In the absence of these two, one should perform the preliminary consecration of the water there;
in every village, one should deposit abundant offerings during that night.
Thus, in the venerable Vaikhānasa scripture, the Bhagavacchāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The eleventh chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters in the *Saṃhitā*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
The Ritual for the Installation of the Blessed One.
Then, at the onset of night, the righteous one, a knower of mantras, should lift the deity from the water;
having brought the materials for bathing, he should bathe the deity.
Having covered it with silk cloth and the like, and further adorned it with jewels, gold, and various other beautiful flower garlands, making it enchanting; BhS_12.2 //
Having placed the Lord of Gods upon a vehicle while reciting the *Svakti-sūkta*,
and having preceded him with a stream of water, he should lead him around the village in a clockwise direction.
Having specifically established [the deity] in the western part of the pit,
one should perform the Vāstu-homa in the sacrificial hall to the north.
Having churned the fire, he should take it up, or else the very fire for the oblation;
having consecrated it according to the rule and taken it, he should lead it forward to the *gārhapatya* hearth.
The unconditioned mundane fire shall be like a fire produced by friction;
having performed the pouring of the oblation according to the rule, one should perform the rites ending with the Vaiṣṇava offering.
Then, in order, [he offers oblations] into the anvāhārya pit, then into the āhavanīya fire,
then into the āvasathya, then into the sabhya, and finally into the padma fire.
One should perform the fire-oblation everywhere according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra;
taking a jar filled with thirty-two prasthas, one should go to a crossroads.
Reciting the mantra beginning with "iṣe tvorje tvā," and having wrapped [the vessel] with a thread, he should perform the washing of the jar while reciting "śucī vo havya. (BhS 12.9)
Having taken water from a river and having purified it, one should fill [the vessel];
then, having wrapped it with a pair of cloths, one should carefully adorn it.

Having perfumed [the image] according to the ritual procedure with cardamom, black pepper, camphor, fragrant ushira-root, and unbroken rice grains, and subsequently with other fragrant flowers; BhS_12.11.
Having placed deposits of gold and precious gems, the best of mantra-knowers should then set down a cushion made of cow-hair, kuśa grass, and darbha grass.
Alternatively, one may place a ritual broom (*kūrca*) made solely of *darbha* grass;
bone is proclaimed to be the jewel, the vein the thread, and the flesh the fine clay.
Blood is red clay, water is likewise fat;
semen is said to be the brush, and the garment is indeed the wrapped skin.
"These seven elements [are found] in jars and in bowls;
one might lack any one of these, yet there is no presence of the self therein. (BhS 12.15)
Having placed the water-pot there on the right side of the deity,
the preceptor should likewise be adorned with garments, ornaments, and earrings.
Adorned with garlands and perfumes, wearing a turban bound upon his head,
he should stand on the southern side of the water-jar, facing either east or north.
Having assumed the svastika posture, with body straight and mind composed,
he should bow to Keśava and the other deities at the locations beginning with the forehead.
Having placed all the letters beginning with 'A' at all the joints,
one should then touch the water-pot well and recite the Sūktas and other prayers in sequence.
Then, having recited the Ātmasūkta and the Pauruṣasūkta,
and having recited the Ekākṣarasūkta, one should thereafter recite the Viṣṇusūkta.
Then, having recited the Śrībhūsūkta while chanting the "Sahasraśīrṣa" [Puruṣasūkta],
and having then recited the Vaiṣṇava hymn, one should meditate properly with a fully concentrated mind.
Thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) through exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka).
I shall now describe its threefold fruit, which is distinct for each type, in due order.
In that very practice, one should first perform the exhalation (recaka), which burns away all sins;
thereafter, one should perform the inhalation (pūraka), which then nourishes one with nectar.
One should perform the third breath-retention (kumbhaka) and contemplate immortality;
therefore, with every effort, one should carry out the exhalations (recaka) and the other [breath-controls].
The wise one, recollecting the water as belonging to Kumbhagaṇṭha and visualizing the mandala of Varuṇa in the shape of a half-moon, should place its seed-syllable there.
Having encircled it with the syllable *tamaṃ* and bound it firmly without flaw,
one should invoke the deity who resides within the solar disc right there.
The primordial seed-syllable, golden-hued and surrounded by *praṇavas*, should be worshipped;
thereafter, having fully honored the deity, one should perform the worship ending with the *arghya* offering.
Having taken the image and the pitcher, one should place them in the bathing pit;
and on the eastern side of the pit, one should have a row of staffs made.
One should properly bathe the deity with exactly fourteen water-pots; having bathed the deity everywhere, one should worship him up to the offering of lamps.
Having placed [the deities] upon the seat in the southwest, one should, with a concentrated mind, invoke the gods;
having thus taken hold of the two goddesses, the wise one should quickly bathe them.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, and having bowed down to the God of gods,
one should especially take up a vessel filled with rice grains.
One should place a golden or silver amulet there,
or else, having taken a thread and laid it upon the rice.
Having placed the vessel containing betel-leaf before the Lord,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited at that time, while chanting the *Svastisūkta*.
One should bind the *kautuka* (protective thread) in sequence upon the right hand of the deity and the two left hands of the two goddesses, using the mantra "svasti-dā vīti."
The preceptor, knowing the Vedic mantras, while reciting the protective mantra,
should spread six *droṇas* or half that amount of grain upon the altar.
Taking half of that amount of rice, and likewise half of that burnt [amount] of sesame seeds,
and taking half of that burnt [amount] of barley, and also half of that [amount] of *tilva* wood.
One should spread five types of coverings upon the altar-bed: those made of eggs, those made of hair, those made of wool, those made of the left side [of an animal], and those made of skin.
But if these are not obtained, one should spread out five pieces of cloth;
a pillow for the head should be made, and one should worship [the image] while it is positioned above, not below.
Taking the deity and the two goddesses, the wise man should lay them upon the bed according to the direction of the door and the head, while reciting, "That which belongs to Viṣṇu. (BhS 12.39)
One should likewise perform the same for the two goddesses and recite their respective hymns in sequence;
one should provide an upper covering and place it there reaching down to the neck.
One should worship all the deities surrounding the bed and the altar;
one should worship the deities in order, beginning with Īśāna, up to the offering of the bali.
One should [place] Śaṅkara, Balirakṣa, Vāgdevī, Bali, Śrakra,
Agni, Pavitra, and Śailūṣa, facing westward, in sequence toward the east.
One should place Bhauma, Guha, Durgā, Yama, Mandu,
Nairṛti, Rohiṇī, and the Seven Mothers facing north on the right side.
In the west, one should worship Nairṛta and the others in their proper sequence:
Vaiṣṇavī, Puruṣa, Budha, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā.
One should worship Puṣpa, Rakṣaka, and Vāyu facing east;
then, from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the northeast (Īśa), one should worship those facing south in due order.
One should worship Śukra, the tranquil Bhṛgu, as well as the seven sages (saptarṣis),
Bhāgīrathī, Kubera, Candra, and all living beings.
At each door, one should worship the door-deities, beginning with Dhātr;
having worshipped around the temple, one should worship Nyakṣa and the others in due order.
With a serene mind, the wise man should worship before the God the two beings who are never-failing, as well as Tārkṣya and Amita.
The wise man should worship the discus, conch, and lotus of the Lord Agni;
he should cause the Vedas to be studied in the cardinal directions, for the Śruti declares: "The East is the Ṛgveda. (BhS 12.49)
Having spread grain upon the sacrificial altar according to the sequence of the cloths,
one should place the jewels and other items into vessels of gold and so forth, [visualizing] their presiding deities.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite and having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana),
the wise man, reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta, should cover [the image] with a cloth.
Thereafter, having summoned a Hotṛ priest endowed with the aforementioned qualities,
and having washed his feet and sipped water, [the teacher] should seat him, who is provided with a kūrca-grass mat and is composed in mind.
And one should adorn the assembly member with flowers and other offerings, using ornaments appropriate for the five limbs,
while standing in the eastern part [of the hall] facing west.
Having merely looked at the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ should utter the syllable *praṇava*;
then, when the words "O Hotṛ, come! have been spoken, the Hotṛ should respond. (BhS 12.54)
Having said, "O Adhvaryu, O God," and having washed his feet, he should sip water;
standing there as before, he should say, "Om, obeisance to the speaker. (BhS 12.55)
One should utter the name preceded by "hotṛ," appending a word ending in "-śarman";
having said "in the past" and "in the future," one should speak [the name] preceded by the syllable "dhīṃ. (BhS 12.56)
Then the Adhvaryu priest, facing eastward, should place the fuel sticks into the fire, moving clockwise and reciting "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ" after each utterance of the syllable Om.
When the Hotṛ priest says, "O Agni, great [is your power]," the invocation of the lineage (pravara) is desired;
this may belong to the king, or to the queen, or likewise to the minister. (BhS 12.58)
If the village itself is the sacrificer, he should recite the Vasiṣṭha pravara;
or else, being learned, he should have it performed while reciting the Kāśya pravara.
If the sacrificer should be of a different caste than a Vaiśya,
one should omit his own *pravara* and recite the *Kāśyapa-pravara*.
Then, without speaking, the Blessed One turned toward the western direction;
he should then invoke all forms, from Viṣṇu down to the elemental spirits (bhūtas).
The wise one should summon the attendants by the path already described;
having performed the invocation in its proper sequence, he should offer oblations of clarified butter and perform the sacrifice.

Having strewn grass around the domestic fire (*sabhyāgni*), preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites, he should offer oblations with the mantras "Svasti caiva" and likewise "Prajāpateḥ."
Having said, "To Agni, the wise one," and likewise "To the Ādityas," "To the Viśvedevas," and "To the hosts of Maruts. (BhS 12.64)
“One should sacrifice with the four vyāhṛtis beginning with ‘Bhūr agnaye. A thousand oblations are said to consist of these [vyāhṛtis] repeated one hundred times each. (BhS 12.65)
Pouring with the *sruva* ladle, the wise one should perform the rite without interruption, reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the Puruṣa-sūkta. (BhS 12.66)
The Śrīsūkta has the Earth as its deity; the Matodevādi hymn belongs to Viṣṇu;
and the hymn beginning with the Ekākṣara is joined with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. (BhS 12.67)
Let this be offered by reciting the seven hymns four times each;
if one is unable to do this, one should perform it once here.
Some say that one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇugāyatrī mantra, using either the eight-syllable or the twelve-syllable formula. (BhS 12.69)
Then, in the Āhavanīya fire-pit, one should duly and in the proper sequence worship with the Puruṣasūkta, reciting it sixteen times with diligence.
In the Anvāhārya fire-pit, let the Viṣṇu-sūkta be well-offered;
one should likewise offer the Brāhma-sūkta, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Jaya-homas and so forth in their proper sequence.
One should offer oblations in the Gārhapatya fire with the Śrīsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns;
specifically, in the Āvasathya fire, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava and the Rudrasūkta.
One should offer oblations with the Mahīsūkta and the hymn beginning with the single-syllable [Om];
furthermore, in the Paiṇḍarīka rite, one should offer oblations accompanied by the Pāramātmika hymn.
In the absence of white lotuses, a wise person should offer a red lotus and a bilva leaf,
having soaked them in ghee, while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, and likewise barley;
sesame, *tilva*, as well as mung beans, black gram, roasted flour, and likewise jaggery.
Honey-cakes, curd, and milk are declared to be the materials for the oblation;
with these seventeen substances, the wise man should perform the Vaiṣṇava fire-sacrifice.
With both the *juhu* and the *upajuha* ladles, let the *Viṣṇu-sūkta* be well-offered;
and in the *sabhyāgni* and the *vaiṇḍarīka* fires, one should perform the rites except for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
One should perform the final oblation in the fires, such as the Āhavanīya and others;
and one should cause the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, to be taught in the four directions in their proper sequence.
In this manner, the study [of the Vedas] has been declared; such is the Vedic revelation: "With the Ṛg-verses, [one should proceed] eastward.
He should spend the remainder of the night in due order with dancing, songs, and musical instruments.
Then at dawn, the righteous-souled one, having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing and having performed the Brahma-sacrifice, should recite the twelve hymns.
Having washed his feet, sipped water, and awakened the deities with mantras,
he should discard his previous garment and adorn himself once more with another.
One should properly arrange the pedestal especially in the Brahma-position;
above that, the wise one should divide it into nine parts and arrange [the design].
One should perform the placement of the jewels (ratnanyāsa) precisely according to the previously mentioned sequence;
having filled [the vessel] with lime (sudhā), the wise one should cover it with linen cloth (kṣauma).
At that time, the patron, having bowed to the preceptor and the others,
should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of nine gold coins along with a pair of sandals.
Then one should give five niṣkas to each of the Sthāpaka and the others,
especially to the Sabhya and the Adhvaryu, and likewise to the Hotṛ as well.
For the *adhvaryu* of the *paiṇḍarīka* sacrifice, there is a gift of five *niṣkas* for each;
for the other *adhvaryus* at the *āhavanīya* and other fires, there are four for each.
In the dwellings of heretics, one should give a separate niṣka plus a quarter to the Adhvaryu and to the others; it is recited that this should be given in full.
The giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed by the command of the teacher;
it is the teaching that the sacrificer should not perform it independently.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the sacrificer, especially so;
indeed, the scriptural injunction is that a sacrifice performed without fees is fruitless.
When the auspicious moment had arrived, he uttered the Svasti-sūkta accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and the pouring of water.
The preceptor, taking the water-pot, should go first; then, in due order, the attendants should lead the deity together with the divine consort and the other [deities].
Having walked slowly in a clockwise direction and entered the temple,
he should take his place on a prepared seat of grain on the southern side of the pedestal.

The wise preceptor, having taken up the pitcher and the deity, should enter the courtyard; the discerning one, having placed the *kautuka* (protective thread) in the Brahma-position, should perform the consecration.
Having uttered "Bhūr asi bhūḥ," the wise one should properly join the deity upon the pedestal;
then, on its right side, he should establish the Śrī-devī.
In the same way, one should establish the ground firmly on the left side;
then, one should place the image for the festival on the left side of the deity.
The wise one should place the bathing vessel and the food offering for the deity on the right;
likewise, he should recite the Viṣṇusūkta together with the Puruṣasūkta.

Having recited the Dhruva-sūkta, the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta, and the two Devī-sūktas individually, and having separately recited the Śrī-sūkta and the Bhū-sūkta, one should thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having uttered the syllables specifically as "su-vabhu-nva-bhūn," the wise one should then place the letter *ya* between the two feet.
One should correctly place the supreme seed-syllable within the heart of the image—the golden-hued, supreme seed, which is the cause of all causes. (BhS 12.99)
Resembling a thousand rising suns, saluted by Brahmā and Īśvara,
the Lord of Gods is seated upon a lotus throne, his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark.
The gentle one bearing the conch and the discus, adorned with all ornaments;
the single-syllable Brahman "Oṃ" is recited as the Praṇava. (BhS 12.101)

Having uttered the syllable *Śrī* for the sake of prosperity (*śrī*), and likewise the syllable *La* for the sake of the earth (*bhuvaḥ*), one should take that water from the jar—which is joined with the Śakti—using the *kūrca* brush. (BhS 12.102)
Having recited this mantra of Viṣṇu and taken [the image] while remaining composed, one should say,
“May the Blessed One come,” and place it upon the head of the permanent image (dhruvabera).
The Śruti declares that the Lord of the gods remains pervading Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha, who are immovable.
The wise one should invoke Śrī with the mantra beginning "śriye jāta," and he should properly invoke Hariṇī with the mantra "medinī. (BhS 12.105)
During a marriage ceremony, a festival, a ritual bathing,
or the offering of a bali-oblation, one should extract the vow at that time, like a lamp from another lamp, in succession.
Having invoked [the deity] from the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should invoke it by means of the ritual grass-bundle (kūrca) in sequence;
having observed the ninefold path, according to the desire of the performer as he wishes.
One should perform the worship continuously and eternally according to the prescribed rule;
if one is unable to do so, one should not perform the consecration at all.

A wealthy man, possessing everything and desiring to build a temple for Viṣṇu, sets aside one-third of his wealth for his own purpose and assigns another third for the sake of his family. (BhS 12.109)
With the two remaining portions, one should begin the worship of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Even in times of dire distress, a wise person should not act so as to bring harm upon himself.
Just as an uninterrupted worship proceeds according to the ritual rule,
so should the wise man establish its continuity through the enjoyment of the land.
And for the sake of the worshipper’s ritual service and for the sake of his family, he should diligently provide extremely abundant land, well-suited for many crops. (BhS 12.112)
One should present it to the worshipper free from taxes and the like;
thereafter, the determination of the boundaries should be inscribed upon a copper plate or similar medium. (BhS 12.113)
One should grant that land for the livelihood of the worshipper under the very name of the deity, saying, "Let this be performed first"; for the status of Hari is dependent upon that.
The Lord Hari is the father and the worshipper is said to be the son;
one should not write the name of the son in the presence of the father according to the traditional order.
Indeed, the worshipper should have a mind solely devoted to Lord Hari;
or else, the wise man should draw [the image] using the name of the worshipper.
Likewise, it is recommended that for his residence, a dwelling be constructed very firmly with stones in the vicinity of the temple of the deity.
Just as a worshipper, being well-composed, might live without affliction,
so should he strive diligently to do so for as long as the moon and the sun endure.
When the worshipper is afflicted by afflictions, the Blessed Lord Hari is afflicted;
but when the worshipper is well-pleased, Janārdana is likewise pleased.
Two forms of Hari are proclaimed: the image (bimba) and the worshipper (arcaka).
In the image, [the Lord] is always present before the invocation; in the worshipper, He is eternally present.
Reflecting further, the righteous sacrificer, filled with joy,
refrained from any desire for power and instead performed another act of generosity.
On the five festival days, on the transits of the sun, on other auspicious days,
and for the sake of special worship and for the purpose of sacrificial offerings, one should act with diligence.
And for the purpose of ritual bathing, for festivals, and likewise for the sake of expiation,
one should provide for actors, dancers, female servants, and singers according to one's ability.
Having first assigned a livelihood in the form of land to students, devotees, and others who possess no wealth, before Lord Hari; BhS 12.124.
The teacher gives [the gift] into the hand [of the recipient], preceded by the mantra and water;
likewise for other riches and for those who seek other objects.
The best of instructors should cause the earth and other gifts to be given under those very names;
he should also provide an excellent livelihood for the preceptor under those same names.
Thus, he who performs this with devotion obtains fruit both in this world and the next,
as well as enjoyments such as cattle and servants, and especially vehicles and the like.
One shall obtain gold, jewels, grain, and so forth in abundance;
whatever evil has been committed by that person’s body perishes at that very moment.
Whatever he desires, he attains it all without doubt;
his ancestors from previous births, as well as those in his father’s lineage, [attain their desires].
And those born on the mother’s side, such as his maternal grandfathers and others—
all of them go to the third heaven and rejoice there for a long time.
Then they shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, the splendor which is peerless and unsurpassed—
[to those] who properly protect this [teaching] and who cause it to increase further.
One attains the very fruit of the construction, such as the first brick,
and having achieved the destruction of all that is inauspicious, one obtains what was desired.
Having ascended a celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
What is the use of much speaking regarding ritual injunctions? There is no destiny higher than Keśava.
One should worship that Viṣṇu constantly, the means for accomplishing all means, who eternally bestows liberation from everything and grants the fruits of all desires. (BhS 12.134)
The proper worship performed there in villages and agrahāras always bestows all accomplishments upon the residents and increases sons and grandsons. (BhS 12.135)
O you whose wealth is austerity, the Agnihotra may be common even for those who do not maintain the sacred fires;
it also serves as a means of atonement for those who do maintain the fires when the specific expiation is unknown.
Therefore, one should perform worship without interruption with every possible effort.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the nine, six, and five forms;
namely, Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aviruddhaka. (BhS 13.1)
Having likewise installed the Vārāha and Nārasiṃha [forms] by means of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, one should thus establish the ninefold form according to the prescribed rule.
One should install the five forms beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as the primordial form (Ādimūrti), in their respective order; this is here called the "sixfold form" (Ṣaṇmūrtika).
The installation of the five [deities] beginning with Viṣṇu constitutes the fivefold form;
the ritual for the ten incarnations consists of the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf.
Rāma, Rāma, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa—these ten are the Karkis;
at the time of creation, the Blessed One, having created the preceptor Vikhanas, [established them].
In former times, when the Rākṣasas such as Madhu and others had arisen together on earth at that time, he taught him the Vedas capable of protecting the world.
Having repeatedly overpowered Brahmā by force, he then carried off those Vedas;
meanwhile, [the gods] sought to slay the Rākṣasa Somaka, who possessed prowess in battle.
Having vanished from the boat, Hari assumed the form of a fish;
and having slain Somaṅka, he subsequently gave the Vedas back to the Lotus-born One.
And in all places such as villages, whether in the middle or even in the west,
[he dwells] in a celestial palace upon the back of an elephant, or in a celestial palace shaped like a water-jar.
One should make the best [image] two tālas in height; this is declared to be the measurement for every incarnation, and the *kautuka* should have four arms.
I shall here state the specific details regarding the primary lotus-arrangement in due order:
having performed the praise of the *hautra* priest, one should carry out the invocation of the deities.
“Likewise, one should invoke [the deities] as ‘Matsya’ (the Fish) and ‘Jalaja’ (the Water-born), as well as ‘Bhadra’ (the Auspicious) and ‘Krīḍātman’ (the Playful Self);

The wise one should perform all the rites, beginning with the *juṣṭākāra*, as previously described;
he should sacrifice one hundred and eight times with the mantra "rāyām īśe. (BhS 15.58)
“The mantra uttered for the sake of Sītā’s prosperity when she was born, and that [mantra] of Bharata known as ‘Tanmāyaśograh,’ are both offered in the sacrifice. (BhS 15.59)
Having uttered "śanno nidhattām," the wise one should offer oblations for Lakṣmaṇa;
having said "bhūmānantogra," he should perform the rite for Śatrughna.
“The Maruts are the supreme Self; as in the case of the Marut [deity], so it is in the Māruta [rite].
The wise one should offer the mantra everywhere one hundred and eight times. (BhS 15.61)
Just as [the gods perform] worship, festivals, and ablutions for Hari, so too did Halin [perform them] for the best of the Yadus, Mālābala, for the sake of slaying the Daityas. (BhS 15.62)
Even though Vasudeva was already wise,
Viṣṇu manifested as Balabhadra along with Balarāma for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden.
Having slain Naraka, Kaṃsa, and all others, he protected all the worlds;
thus, whoever would wish to establish Rāma in this way and cause it to be done—
Or else, O wise one, having placed the third Rāma— two-armed and white in color— upon a moon-and-star celestial chariot or upon the back of an elephant, [one should proceed].
Having formed this form with these ten measures while remaining composed,
he holds a pestle and a sword in his right and left hands respectively.
One should hold the pestle firmly with a fist as level as the hips and pubic region;
likewise, one should hold the plow in the left hand at the level of the arm-pit.
On his right side, one should fashion Rohiṇī, who possesses the splendor of Lakṣmī.
Thus one should represent her with weapons; now I shall describe her without weapons.
Having contracted the left foot and extended the right,
one should place the right hand in the gesture of fearlessness and the left upon the left thigh.
At the Āhavanīya fire, one should praise the office of the Hotṛ priest there in this sequence:
“Rāma, the best of the Yadus, Viṣṇu, Halāyudha. (BhS 15.70)
“Indirā, Revatī, Lakṣmī, and Rāmapriyā”—having performed the invocation in this manner, one should proceed as before with the *juṣṭākāra* and other rites. (BhS 15.71)
“One should perform one hundred and eight sacrifices with the mantra ‘kṣmāmekām’;
and the worship, the festival, and the ceremonial bathing should be conducted just as for Hari. (BhS 15.72)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the sacred scripture of the Lord according to the illustrious Vaikhānasa tradition.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter: The Chapter on the Ten Incarnations (Kṛṣṇa).
Now, O wise ones, I shall fully explain the installation of Kṛṣṇa;
the temple of Kṛṣṇa is prescribed to be in a potter’s vimāna.
Whether on a peak, at a city gate, or even on a mountain-shaped [spot],
[one should worship] the child-form of Kṛṣṇa, whose height is measured by a palm tree.
Starting from one year up to five years,
one should respectfully perform [the ritual] according to the circumstances by means of the sequence of three claps of the hands.
Beginning from seven years of age, it is three times six tālas; likewise, beginning from seven years of age, it is three times seven tālas.
Starting from ten years of age, there are likewise three times eight *tālas*;
starting from thirteen years of age, there are likewise three times nine *tālas*.
Thus, according to the sequence of their ages, the proportions of the palm tree (tāla) are likewise described;
[the Lord] stands upon a single pedestal together with Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
And Kṛṣṇa, with the body of a youth, dark-complexioned and clad in yellow garments;
and Rukmiṇī, who has the luster of gold, and Satyabhāmā, who is dark-complexioned.
Vāsudeva, Guḍākeśa, adorned with all ornaments,
the God holding a play-stick, endowed with the three-fold bend (tribhaṅga) and absorbed in meditation.
One should place the right foot in the svastika position and the left foot bent;
while standing, one should practice the placement of the big toes at the base of the fingers.
One should stand with the left foot placed so that its inner part is slightly bent;
likewise, the face, the body, and the region of the hips should be positioned in the same manner.
Because there is curvature in the three paths, the state of having three bends is established:
the face is on the right side, while the middle part is on the left.
On the right side of the hip, three bends are described;
the right hip and hand are joined with a playful staff.
On the right, the hand holding the staff should be raised below the navel-line by five, four,
and three finger-breadths respectively, according to the prescribed rule.
The left arm of the two goddesses rests upon [the left shoulder]; the left hand is turned downwards;
and the left elbow should be ten finger-breadths below the sūtra of the hiccough.
One should gradually measure [the height] as being six, seven, or eight finger-breadths greater, and one should join the tip of the palm of the left hand at the level of the navel. (BhS 16.15)
One should gradually press the bamboo and the *taravega* with both hands;
the bamboo should be equal in height to the upper body, and the play-stick should be of the same measure.
One should visualize him as having three bends, with a dark-complexioned body, two arms, and red garments;
or else, one may represent him with four arms, holding a conch and a discus, as the supreme being.
Well-established with the left foot, one should bind [the posture] with the right;
adorned with all ornaments, beautiful, and with gentle eyes.
One should represent him together with two goddesses, or some authorities say he may be alone;
to the left of the god, one should depict Garuḍa standing with palms joined in reverence.
One should fashion it with two wings like the base of a palm leaf;
one should likewise make it a dancer of fresh butter and a crusher of Kālīya.
The form of Pārthasārathi and that of the two goddesses are to be fashioned in sequence;
the pedestal and the height of the image should be divided into five parts and three parts, respectively.
Seven parts from nine divisions, or two parts from three, are said to be the height of a worldly image; this is the sequence for the measurement in finger-breadths (mānāṅgula).
First, it should be nine finger-breadths in length, increasing by two finger-breadths each time;
this is declared to be the measurement in nine varieties. Thus is the rule established.
By this, however, there would be a threefold division: superior, inferior, and middling;
namely, measurement (māna), weighing (pramāṇa), measuring by capacity (unmāna), and comparison by hanging down (laṃbamānopamānaka).
It is declared that it should be made five *tālas* in length and suspended;
one should employ the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types, while avoiding the latter.
Having raised the right knee to the height of the navel-line,
or else making it level with the hips and the pubic region, one should indeed place the right foot [upon the ground].
The staff in the hand should be measured [to reach] the head, or just the hair;
the right hand should be in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*); the eyebrows and the elbows and so forth [should be proportionate]. (BhS 16.27)
With the face turned slightly to the right and a somewhat smiling countenance,
the thread known as the "hair-blanket" (keśakambala) should be placed on the left side.

It may be located in the middle of the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), at the tip of the nose, in the left nostril, in the center of the navel, or on the right side of the scrotum or the thigh. (BhS 16.29)
If one hangs the central thread from the tip of the right hand on the foot, down to the front of the crown on the left, one need not employ any other thread.
The uṣṇīṣa shall be half a finger-breadth, and the face shall be eight finger-breadths;
his neck shall be half a finger-breadth, and from there to the end of the throat it shall be two finger-breadths.
The upper body is prescribed as eighteen finger-breadths in length, extending from the end of the hiccups to the heart, the navel, and the root of the penis.
The length of the thigh is prescribed as thirteen finger-breadths;
the knee shall be two finger-breadths, and the shank and the thigh are equal to that.
The foot is indeed two finger-breadths in measure; of this there is no doubt.
From the end of the *hīk* thread, the arm is traditionally recorded as being ten finger-breadths.
The forearm should be eight finger-breadths in length, and the palm seven finger-breadths in length;
the opening should be as wide as the mouth [of the vessel], and the width of the rim one finger-breadth.
The width of the neck should likewise be four finger-breadths and four barley-corns;
the length of the arm, from the shoulder to the tip, is twenty-four finger-breadths.
The space between the armpits is fourteen finger-breadths in width;
the thigh is ten finger-breadths, and the hip is eleven finger-breadths.
The width of the hips should likewise be desired at thirteen finger-breadths,
and the width of the base of the thighs should be eight finger-breadths, in that order.
The width of the knee should be six finger-breadths, and the width of the shank seven;
the width of the tube (nālikā) should be known as five and a half finger-breadths.
The extent of his feet is said to be endowed with all auspicious marks;
he is dark like a cluster of blossoms and bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
He was covered with many jewels, his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem,
made beautiful by rows of pearl necklaces, and seated upon Garuḍa.
One should visualize Kṛṣṇa, who delights in Vṛndāvana together with his two goddesses,
resplendent with a moon-like face shining with shimmering, curling locks of hair.
With her lower lip exceedingly red and adorned by two hands that are crimson,
she has drawn up her left foot and turned her right one upward.
Likewise, his right hand is in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and joined with fresh butter;
his left hand is extended upward and adorned with all ornaments.
One should perform the *saṃvara* [practice], or indeed the *vigatāmbara*;
in this manner, the wise man should perform the "newly born dancer" (*navanitanaṭa*) according to the prescribed rule.
In this very manner, one should visualize the Supreme Self dancing upon the hoods of the serpent Kālīya, with His feet alternately extended and contracted.
One should place a piece of fresh butter on the right hand,
or one may also hold a snake’s tail in the hand to perform the *kālīyamardana* [subduing of the serpent].
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, beautifully adorned with yellow garments,
he has four arms, holding a conch and a discus in his two upper hands.
With both hands lowered, playing a flute, filled with joy,
adorned with all ornaments, and seated upon Garuḍa.
One who especially desires progeny should thus visualize Kṛṣṇa accompanied by his two consorts and surrounded by sages.
Dark as a cluster of *kalāpa* flowers, with a face resembling the full moon,
wearing a crest of peacock feathers, and adorned with every ornament.
Possessing the beauty of a young woman's form, with a chest marked by the Śrīvatsa, holding a flute to his smiling, reddish lips— he who fascinates the three worlds.
One should represent Akṣamālā and Vidyā in his two upper hands;
one should represent Hari as possessing four arms, with a flute held in his two [lower] hands.
His feet were gazed upon by Śrī, who stood at his left side, whose lotus-like hands shone with the radiant luster of refined gold.
Seated upon a beautiful golden lion-throne attended by queens,
he was adorned with a white parasol resembling the orb of the moon.
The Supreme Lord was worshipped by hosts of sages such as Nārada who sought knowledge,
and was saluted by the multitudes of deities beginning with Indra.
In this way, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whose form deludes the world,
surrounded by the cowherd girls and the cows, the embodiment of supreme bliss.
Having crossed the right foot over the left and established it firmly,
[he is] four-armed, holding a conch and a discus in his two upper hands.
Holding a flute composed of the Vedas with his other two hands,
he joyfully filled the holes of the flute with his fingers.
The wise one should thus represent Kṛṣṇa, who is moved by divine and celestial music, standing in the *tribhaṅga* posture, and playing the flute.
Adorned with all ornaments and provided with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra),
he wears red garments, is dark-complexioned, and has lotus-like eyes.
He was graced on his two sides by Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā;
Rukmiṇī, possessing a golden complexion, and Satyā, appearing dark-hued.
Having beheld Vasudeva and Devakī in front and to the right, as well as Yaśodā, Nandagopa, and the Lord of Gods standing firmly established; BhS_16.63 //
Likewise, one should place Pradyumna and Sāmba with their characteristic marks on the left;
one should also depict Dāma, Sumanas, and another Gopikā.
One should fashion the tip of Kṛṣṇa’s ear so that it rests upon Sumantu on the left, or likewise, according to the proper method, making it level with the armpit and the arm in due sequence.
One should fashion them, well-adorned, according to the measurement of nine tālas;
one should represent Devakī and Vasudeva as being of dark complexion.
One should represent Yaśodā as fair-complexioned, Nanda as variegated,
Pradyumna as dark-complexioned, and Sāmba as having the luster of black collyrium.
The wise one should fashion Dāman, who resembles blood in color, as well as Gaura, Sumanas, and the white-colored Sumantu, according to the prescribed ritual.
In this way, one should perform [the worship] of Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a divine-human form;
and the sequence of their four forms is as described in the section on the abodes.
Holding a flower-staff with his right hand,
he placed the other [hand] upon the head of the royal scepter resting on the ground.
One should thus represent Kṛṣṇa in the form of a royal cowherd, accompanied by Rukmiṇī and adorned with ornaments befitting a king.
The god, wearing yellow garments, his hands radiant with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
holding a flute in the other hand, sits comfortably with a pure smile.
One should thus meditate upon Hari as Kṛṣṇa himself, whose form is that of the Lord of Wisdom (Jñānagopāla), being worshipped by sages and devoid of his two divine consorts.
The Lord of the World, with a golden radiance and noble limbs, possesses eight arms;
he holds a sugarcane bow, a goad, a flute, a conch, a discus, and beautiful arrows.
He bears a divine and auspicious form embraced by Ramā,
is adorned with all ornaments, and bestows the nectar of immortality upon the yogins.
In this way, one should perform the rite of enchantment for Kṛṣṇa in the form of a cowherd boy,
for the protection of the cows, the young cowherds, and the cowherd girls.
The Blessed Lord Hari held up the mountain named Govardhana with his left upraised hand, supporting that most excellent mountain.
One should likewise fashion the four-armed deity with one hand resting on the hip, or holding a lotus, and bearing a conch and a discus.
In this manner, one should represent Kṛṣṇa as the upholder of Govardhana;
for in ancient times, during a great battle, Hari protected Pārtha.
One should visualize Pārtha standing upon his chariot, equipped with arrows and quivers,
gazing at the Lord of Gods who stands upon his own chariot by his side.
Dark-complexioned, mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, with his hair tied up,
bearing a noose in his right hand and likewise a conch in his left hand.
Beholding the great chariot-warrior Arjuna smiling with his face turned toward him,
one should thus conceive of Kṛṣṇa as the embodiment of Pārtha’s charioteer.
Having bent the left knee and extended the other long, likewise having stretched it out and placed the left hand on the ground in front; BhS 16.83.
With one hand, beautiful in its posture upon the seat and slightly bent at the elbow,
he held ever-fresh butter.
One should thus represent Kṛṣṇa in the form of a young cowherd boy, gazing repeatedly at that which is especially worthy of being seen.
Formerly, at the time of universal dissolution, when all worlds had been withdrawn,
the Blessed Lord Hari lay asleep upon a banyan leaf.
Having playfully drawn up his right foot with his left hand, he who was in the form of a child, yet supreme beyond the supreme, lay upon a banyan leaf.
Placing his big toe in his mouth, with a smiling face as if about to suck it,
he held his right thigh with his right hand.
One should fashion a large banyan leaf with one foot extended, adorned with divine ornaments, and with the tip of its lower edge broadened.
One should likewise visualize Kṛṣṇa reclining on a banyan leaf,
his hands beautifully holding the conch, discus, mace, lotus, noose, and goad.
Holding a flute with both hands and blowing it, he who deludes all beings possesses the splendor of ten million suns and is beautifully adorned with yellow garments.
One should thus visualize the great Kṛṣṇa, who is beautiful with various ornaments, situated within a solar disc, and the deluder of all.
One should cause the form of Kṛṣṇa to be fashioned as innumerable and according to one's own will;
however, in rites such as the subduing of Kālīya, one should fashion the daughters of the Nāgas and so forth.
One should thus conceive of the various kinds of enjoyments and so forth through reasoning,
intellect, and devotion, in such a way that they become pleasing to the mind.
Having thus assumed such a form, one should perform the auspicious rite (kautuka); or else, the image (bimba) may be without the rite and endowed with four arms.

Having thus fashioned [the image] with four arms— the first showing the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the supreme one holding the conch and discus— one should commence the rite of installation.
Having arranged five fires within the previously mentioned sacrificial hall,
one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire of the *paiṇḍarīka*.
“He [worshipped] Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the meritorious lord of the thirty gods, and [he worshipped] Rukmiṇī, the beautiful goddess Ramā, as Rukmiṇī. (BhS 16.98)
“[I invoke] Satyarūpā, Satī, Sannatī, and Kṣamā. Having spoken thus, he should likewise invoke Garuḍa as before.

Having offered the oblations of clarified butter according to the very same sequence as the invocation, one should sacrifice one hundred and eight times while reciting: "Satyaḥ satyasthaḥ. (BhS 16.100)
And one should perform the rites for Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā as if for Śrī and Bhūmi;
one should have the installation and other ceremonies carried out according to the previously mentioned procedure.
At the time of the end of the age, Viṣṇu will become known as Karkī;
with sword and shield in hand, he shall slay the Mlecchas and others.
Having installed the form of Kalki on a peak, or at a city gate, or even upon a mountain-shaped structure, one should worship it within a celestial chariot (vimāna).
One should fashion the horse-faced head with a middle measurement of ten tālas, having the luster of a mass of crushed collyrium, while the rest of the body should be human in form.
And he has four arms, holding in his hands, in sequence, the weapons:
the discus, the conch, the sword, and likewise the shield.
Alternatively, one may visualize the deity as mounted on a horse, with two arms,
resembling pure crystal, and holding a sword and a shield.
In this very place, one should perform the rite of consecration (*kautuka*), fashioning a four-armed form of Viṣṇu,
after having arranged the five fires within the previously mentioned sacrificial hall.
One should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire, Paiṇḍarīka:
"Karkiṇa, Kāmarūpa, and Viṣṇu, the cause of dissolution. (BhS 16.108)
Having thus invoked according to the rite and prepared the offerings, one should sacrifice oblations of clarified butter;
having recited the verse beginning with "dhūrvo vahantām," one should sacrifice one hundred and eight times.
One should perform festivals, ritual ablutions, and other rites for [the deity] just as one does for Viṣṇu;
thus has the characteristic of the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu been described.
The Blessed Time is beginningless, and its end is not seen;
creation, maintenance, destruction, and dissolution revolve like a wheel.
Furthermore, the numerous incarnations of the Supreme Self are proclaimed for the sake of protecting the Dharma and for the thorough discipline of the wicked.
One should know that manifestation which occurs where Viṣṇu appears immediately out of compassion for his devotees as *āvirbhāva*, while the other is called *prādurbhāva*. (BhS 16.113)
The five incarnations beginning with the Fish are well known, as are the others;
they also proclaim manifestations such as the liberation of the lordly elephant.
Likewise, in the intermediate space on the right and left sides of Viṣṇu,
one should fashion Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, or perhaps within the portico itself.
