Then, having installed the *kautuka* image and the *bera* image— some say these two alone— either in the inner pavilion (*antarmaṇḍapa*) or likewise in the enclosure pavilion (*āvaraṇamaṇḍapa*).
Having fashioned the Nārasiṃha, Varāha, Vāmana, and Trivikrama [forms],
along with the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should perform the consecration (kautuka) endowed with all the proper characteristics.
Having thus installed [the image] of Viṣṇu, one should worship him in the front pavilion,
especially those of the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, and Vāmana incarnations.
One should fashion the *kautuka* as the form of Viṣṇu with four arms; however, one should not fashion it in the form of Dhruva, though in other cases it may be done as desired.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Lord according to the illustrious Vaikhānasa tradition.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter: The Ritual of the Primordial Form (Ādimūrtikalpa).
Now I shall explain in detail the specific determination of Keśava and the others:
one should fashion Keśava with a gentle form and four arms. (BhS 17.1)
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, with a golden luster,
adorned with all ornaments, and decorated with pearl necklaces.
One should fashion the Lord thus established together with the two goddesses;
one should fashion Nārāyaṇa as dark as a rain cloud and four-armed.
The god who bears the conch, the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the sword;
adorned with jewel ornaments, naked, and infallible.
And one should especially fashion the auspicious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
the most excellent, according to the measurements of ten tālas in terms of size, height, and proportion.
Seated upon the lion-throne,
with his right leg extended and his left placed upon the seat, he possessed the [auspicious] marks as before.
Having placed Lakṣmī upon his left thigh, the goddess, filled with joy, extends her hands toward his face;
she is five tālas in height.
With his left hand embracing her—who stood with palms joined in reverence and adorned with all ornaments—and with his right hand granting the gesture of fearlessness; BhS_17.8 //
With his other two hands, he holds the conch and the discus;
he is seated upon the shoulders of Tārkṣya, and everything else is as described before.
Tārkṣya [should be depicted] with a height of nine and a half tālas; his face has a slightly frowning brow.
Some wise masters maintain that Lakṣmī is situated upon his right thigh.
One should likewise represent Hari as seated upon the coils of a serpent,
endowed with seven or five expanded hoods.
One should properly fashion the remainder [of the image] with a very tall body;
and Mādhava, resembling a blue lotus, [should be depicted] with a discus, a mace, and a sword.
One should depict Hari Govinda, who has four arms, wears variegated garlands and garments, and is white in complexion. BhS_17.13 //
The wise man should have Viṣṇu fashioned holding a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus;
he should be dark blue like a water-lily, bearing the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace.
One should visualize the god Madhusūdana as adorned with all ornaments, clad in yellow garments, and possessing the luster of a red lotus; he is the infallible one.
One should meditate upon Trivikrama, who is free from ailment, blue in color, four-armed, and bearing a conch, discus, lotus, and mace.
The god who bears four arms, adorned with all ornaments,
is Vāmana, cloud-colored, possessing four arms and great strength.
One should likewise have [the deity] fashioned holding a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus, appearing in a deceptive form;
or else, one should have a jar and curd-rice placed in his two hands.
They call him Dadhivāmana, the white-complexioned Hari with two arms;
or else, he may assume the form of a young brahmin student, holding a staff and a water-pot.
One should have Hari fashioned with a golden complexion, a youthful form, and two arms;
however, one should make Śrīdhara white and black in appearance and four-armed.
One should visualize Hṛṣīkeśa as the Lord, possessing a dark complexion and four arms, bearing the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, the discus, and the lotus.
One should visualize the imperishable Hari, Padmanābha, who bears the mace, conch, discus, and lotus, and whose complexion is white and dark-blue.
One should visualize the Lord Dāmodara, the consort of Ramā, who holds the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, the lotus, and the conch in his hands, and who is white and fair in complexion.
One should represent the four-armed deity Saṃkarṣaṇa as white in color and holding a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a discus.
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, the eternal support of all, whose hands hold the conch, discus, lotus, and mace, and who resembles the rising sun.
One should meditate upon Hari, the all-pervading Lord who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, the sustainer of all,
possessing the luster of the moon or the glow of a fresh jasmine flower.
One should depict the god Pradyumna, who has a golden luster, as four-armed, holding a discus,
a conch, a mace, and a lotus— the god of great strength.
Unobstructed, with a golden luster, endowed with all ornaments,
bearing the conch, the discus, the bow, and the sword— the Lord of the lords of gods.
One should visualize the Lord of Gods, Puruṣottama, as having a white and black luster,
the four-armed deity holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Then one should fashion the bull-born [Brahmā], white as a conch shell, four-armed, holding a discus,
a conch, a mace, and a lotus, and adorned with ornaments.
One should meditate upon Nārasiṃha, who has the luster of a cloud, is adorned with all ornaments, holds a conch,
a lotus, a mace, and a discus, and bestows fearlessness upon his devotees.
One should depict the all-pervading and infallible Lord as having a white and dark-blue complexion,
resplendent with four arms marked by the mace, lotus, discus, and conch.
One should meditate upon Janārdana, the eternal deity, who possesses noble limbs, is blue in color, and holds a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus.
Alternatively, one should visualize Upendra, who has his left hand placed upon his hip,
who is dark as a rain cloud, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god who is the Lord of the world, Hari, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
possessing a pale-white and dark-blue luster, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should fashion a charming image of Kṛṣṇa, dark as a rain cloud, with eyes like white lotuses, holding a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus. (BhS 17.36)
The wise one should fashion [the image] holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
for all [deities], one should construct palaces as prescribed for Viṣṇu.
Having praised the office of the *hautra* priest there in the principal fire within the sacrificial pit of the assembly hall:
"Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, and Viṣṇu, the supreme beyond the supreme. (BhS 17.38)
“Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Viṣṇu, and the Destroyer of Naraka,” as well as “Mādhava, the Lotus-eyed One, Viṣṇu, the Soul of All. // BhS 17.39 //
“Govinda, the supreme bliss, and Viṣṇu himself, the eternal;
likewise Viṣṇu, the all-pervading, the Lord, and the sovereign of all worlds. (BhS 17.40)
“Madhusūdana, Udyoga, Mahān, Viṣṇu,” and also, “Trivikrama, Lord of the three worlds, Support of the worlds, the Eternal. (BhS 17.41)
“Vāmana, Varada, Kāśyapi, the beloved of Aditi; Śrīdhara, Puruṣa, and Viṣṇu, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark. (BhS 17.42)
“Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the World, Viṣṇu who consists of the universe;
likewise Padmanābha, the Lord of the Gods, and Viṣṇu, the Master of the World. (BhS 17.43)
“Dāmodara, the eternal support, Viṣṇu whose form is the Praṇava;
likewise Saṃkarṣaṇa, the best of the Yadus, Viṣṇu, the wielder of the plow. (BhS 17.44)
“Vāsudeva, whose form is merit; Bhadreśa, whose nature is merit;
likewise Pradyumna, the Lord of the World, and Viṣṇu, whose essence is merit. (BhS 17.45)
“Unceasing and great, dispassionate and possessing all splendor;
likewise, the Supreme Person, blissful Viṣṇu, who is fivefold. (BhS 17.46)
“Adhokṣaja, the beginningless Viṣṇu, and also the all-pervading one;
Nārasiṃha, the lord of asceticism, Mahāviṣṇu, the one of great power. (BhS 17.47)
“The infallible one, the immeasurable, the Lord of Śrī,
likewise Janārdana, the one without beginning or end, Viṣṇu, and the embodiment of splendor.”
“Upendra, Indrāvaraja, Viṣṇu, and Vaikuṇṭha;
Hari, the remover of sins—thus [one should meditate upon] Viṣṇu, whose form is auspicious. (BhS 17.49)
Having invoked Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Puṇya, and Tridaśādhipa in their proper sequence, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and perform the sacrifice.
One should offer oblations with the twelve mantras of Keśava and the other [twelve Ādityas], beginning with "viṣṇornuka," "adabhiṣṣaṭ," and likewise "rato devā adabhiḥ. (BhS 17.51)
The mantra of Kṛṣṇa as Nārasiṃha has been proclaimed first;
the ten mantras for the other ten [forms] have likewise been proclaimed.
"Viṣṇu is for all," and so forth; having aimed at whichever deity is proclaimed in each sacrifice, the one who is not indolent [should offer] with the respective mantra. (BhS 17.53)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should perform the remainder as before;
in this manner, one should everywhere worship the Lord together with the two goddesses.
One should have a marriage pavilion constructed, endowed with all auspicious characteristics;
one should perform all the rites, beginning with the ploughing, just as for Viṣṇu.
The *Lakṣmīkalpa*:
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme installation of Lakṣmī;
Lakṣmī is said to be eightfold, the first of which is the "Inseparable" (*anapāyinī*).
She, adorned with all ornaments, should be depicted on the chest of Viṣṇu,
in the divine circle above the right breast within a triangle.
Seated in the center of a lotus, her two hands gracefully holding two lotuses,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and a lotus-face with a gentle smile.
One should fashion her in such a form; she is considered the Fortune of Yoga (Yogalakṣmī).
Having installed the Fortune of Yoga, one who desires prosperity should worship her correctly.
One should perform the supreme rite of bone-retrieval (asthāpana) together with the Lord of Gods;
at another time, one may perform it again using gold, silver, and so forth.
Having fashioned it in the form of the Śrīvatsa, one should bear the imperishable Viṣṇu;
and one should make the characteristic of the Śrīvatsa in accordance with each respective image.
These—Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā—are declared in order to be the goddesses of the enjoyments and fortunes;
however, in the cases of the *dhruva* and other *beras*, Śrī and Bhūmi are on the left side of the Lord.
Nīlā, who travels upon the path to Vaikuṇṭha and is eternally resorted to, was previously established by the Lord of Gods together with Śrī and Bhūmi. (BhS 17.63)
If the Lord is devoid of his two goddesses, one should perform the installation of Śrī and Bhūmi separately at a later time,
according to the injunctions of Aṅgiras.
She is called Vīralakṣmī when she is associated with a separate temple;
one should construct a separate temple on the southern side of the main shrine.
One should fashion the Goddess with the ten-tāla measurement and endowed with the proper characteristics, holding two lotuses in her hands and bearing the gestures of veneration and fearlessness.
Adorned with a crown and a bodice, beautified by all ornaments,
seated upon a lotus throne, golden-hued, and the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
One should construct the goddess Lakṣmī, known as Vijayā, on the Godāvarī;
she should be made nine tālas in measurement and may reside in another temple.
Holding a white water-lily with her right hand,
while her other hand is outstretched, she is beautiful with her hair tied in a braided chignon.
One should have her represented as standing, adorned with all ornaments;
she is said to be born from a portion of the Earth-goddess (Godā), and one should perform the rites with her mantra.
The goddess Pākalakṣmī is described as being associated with the kitchen;
one should fashion her image in the kitchen according to a measurement of eight tālas.
One should visualize her adorned with ornaments, either seated or standing, with hands gracefully folded in the form of two lotuses, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
At the second pavilion door, one should worship Dvāralakṣmī in the middle of the lintel (pataṅgapaṭṭikā), adorned with all ornaments.
Her two hands are gracefully joined in the form of a lotus, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is seated upon a lotus throne and adorned with a crown and other ornaments.
Furthermore, one should place two elephants at the two corners [of the mandala], with golden jars in their trunks;
likewise, one should depict them sprinkling Mahālakṣmī with water from those jars.
The worship of Śrī and Bhūmi, as well as Vīra and Vijayalakṣmī,
is prescribed according to the dimensions of the permanent image (dhruvabera) when performing the worship of another image.
One may perform such curious rites as festivals and the like according to one's desire;
however, one should not perform them for other [deities], but should instead cause only the constant worship (dhruvārcā) to be performed.
In the *paiṇḍarīka*, the primary fire, one should praise the *hautra* ritual there;
then, by means of the form-mantras (*mūrti-mantra*) of Śrī and Bhūmi, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the subsequent rites in due order.
One should address her as Godā, Kṛṣṇapriyā, Lakṣmī, and Rukmiṇī;
following the sequence of invocation, one should perform the oblation with those respective mantras.
One should perform everything for the nine, six, or five forms, as well as for the temple and the sanctuary, according to the sequence prescribed for consecration, just as before.
In that same manner, one should perform the installation of the two forms, as well as the installation of the three forms,
and the installation of the other attendant deities according to the prescribed rule.
Whatever object is offered in the temple of the Lord of Gods, all of that should be established according to the prescribed rite and then presented.
But that which is unconditioned is not to be grasped; nor would it be dear to the gods, such as ornaments, garments, bowls, or other articles of equipment.
One should accept only those ornaments suitable for oneself and those that serve as adornments for one's dwelling, provided they have been properly prepared; in this way, it will be fruitful.

One should offer oblations with the mantra of the deity who is the presiding lord of each respective substance, as well as all other rites, performing them according to the procedure prescribed for consecration.
The ritual for the presiding deity of the substances has been correctly explained by me in its entirety.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now I shall describe the worship of the Blessed One, specifically the supreme worship of Viṣṇu,
which is likewise ordained by Vedic texts such as "pravaḥ pāntam andha" and others. (BhS 18.1)
That which was spoken in brief by the Great Sage, the Teacher, in the Sūtra,
has been explained at length in this Śāstra to the extent of one and a half koṭis [of verses].
But I shall describe the sequence of its worship in a well-condensed form, measuring four hundred thousand [verses]; listen, O best of sages! (BhS 18.3)

Endowed with the rites beginning from conception according to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, possessed of the qualities prescribed for an officiating priest, with well-nourished limbs, and composed in mind; BhS_18.4 //
Whether a householder or a celibate student, one should perform worship with devotion alone,
accomplishing it with various materials and likewise with infinite modes of service.
Even for Brahmā and the other gods, it is impossible to perform worship according to the prescribed rules;
what then need be said of poor men who lack self-control?
Therefore, one should perform [the rite] according to one's capacity with many worshippers,
many attendants, and likewise with others who seek various requisites.
The worship of Viṣṇu, which is to be accomplished by those endowed with faith and devotion,
must therefore be performed by nine kinds of officiating priests and attendants.
In the case of the highest [temple], the highest [number] is prescribed for the worshippers, which is twenty;
for the attendants, it is eighty. Then, in the highest [temple], the middle [number] is prescribed.
For the attendants, sixteen worshippers are prescribed for the highest [grade];
however, for the lowest, twelve worshippers are prescribed.
In the middle [mandala], there are fifty attendants;
furthermore, in the supreme [mandala], there are forty attendants, and eight worshippers are proclaimed.
In the middle [assembly], the middling [retinue] is proclaimed; six attendants are declared for each [of the others].
Furthermore, in the middle [assembly], there are twenty-five inferior attendants.
There are four worshippers there, and sixteen attendants;
for the three middle wheels, there should be nine attendants in the lowest and highest [categories].
Two worshippers who perform the service are called *adhamamadhyama*; four are *adhamamadhyama*; one who worships alone with two attendants is declared *adhamādhama*. (BhS 18.14)
The preceptor should be the supervisor, acting as the medium for the presence of the deity;
all activities, such as worship and the rest, should be performed under his direction.
For he is the decider of what must be done, the protector of dharma, and the instructor;
as a worshiper of the God of gods, he should perform the rites of mantras, seats, and so forth.
The servant and attendant shall assist the worshipper in performing the infinite ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures according to the rules. (BhS 18.17)
These attendants should be employed as those who perform many tasks;
they should likewise be sweepers and plasterers.
One who lights the lamps, one who cleans the vessel, one who brings water, and one who gathers flowers. (BhS 18.19)
He prepares incense, lamps, and the like; he is intent on grinding perfumes;
he fetches various articles of equipment, and likewise carries the sacrificial offerings (bali).
Attendants perform such tasks as these;
the cook shall be an attendant stationed at the kitchen.
One who knows the rules for preparing the oblation and is devoted to purity and right conduct—
such Vaikhānasas alone, all of whom seek their goals through these means, one should choose as officiants.
If none of these are available there, one should choose Vaikhānasas as the preceptor and the male attendants, provided they do not belong to other sūtras out of greed for food.
A Brahmin who is not a Vaikhanasa, however, should worship Hari in a temple;
he indeed is called a *devalaka* and is excluded from all ritual acts.
In the absence of those who wear the thread of another [tradition],
however, one should choose attendants who have been initiated, are of virtuous conduct, and follow the procedures prescribed in the scriptures.
The sacrificer should always be devoted to the inner self, contemplating the goal of liberation;
he should be wealthy, capable of renouncing everything, endowed with devotion, and possessed of a serene intellect.
Marked with the insignia of Viṣṇu according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
[he should act] for the sake of the daily worship of the Lord, and especially for the sake of festivals.
Likewise, he should cause the accumulation of wealth to be given away for the sake of other forms of prosperity;
he should await the command of the preceptor, being one who considers the welfare of his kinsmen.
He is devoted to his attendants, compassionate toward his servants,
a seeker of the grace found at sacred fords, and one who shows reverence for the remains of offerings.
Thus, those endowed with these characteristics are fit for the worship of the Ālaya;
then the worshipper, with a tranquil mind, should be devoted to the five times (pañcakāla).
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should recollect Nārāyaṇa,
having performed the purifications and other rites according to the rules prescribed in the Sūtras.

Having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing, having put on clean garments once again, and having applied the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the ritual with [the names of] Keśava and the others; BhS_18.32 //
Having held the purifying garlands of lotus seeds and *tulasī* beads,
and having likewise worn both types of purifiers and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Adorned with an uṣṇīṣa and well-ornamented with the fivefold ornaments,
having completed his daily rituals, he should recite the great mantra and so forth.
Having recited the Aruṇa mantra and thereafter the Nārāyaṇa mantra,
one should bow down and grasp the yantra with both hands.
Placing [the image] upon his arms or his head, endowed with supreme devotion and accompanied by attendants, he should be respectfully attended by the patron.
Accompanied by all musical instruments and adorned with every auspicious ornament,
the wise man should proceed slowly toward the temple.
Having recited "Pratadviṣṇu," one should circumambulate the temple twice in a clockwise direction, moving around it in due order while keeping the God of gods in mind.
One should perform an even number of circumambulations; however, an odd number is for malevolent rites.
Likewise, having circumambulated an odd number of times and bowed down an odd number of times as well.
One should gaze at the rising sun and recite the twelve hymns;
by performing this circumambulation, there shall be no fault from stepping upon the sun's shadow.
Having entered the temple while recollecting the respective mantras, one should then bow to the deities of the door and, with the weapon-mantra, drive away the obstructing spirits.
Having taken hold of the bolt while uttering "Hiraṇyapāṇi," and having firmly joined it to the door-panel while uttering "Divam vīti. (BhS 18.42)
Having opened the door-panel, the wise one should enter within;
having recited "ato devā," he should gaze upon the deity and bow down. (BhS 18.43)
Having summoned an attendant, one should light the lamps in succession;
having uttered the Praṇava mantra, one should perform the ritual there.
Striking him with both hands while uttering "May they be pacified," and so forth,
[one should offer] mirrors, cows, maidens, and auspicious objects such as elephants and horses.
Having stationed the Brahmins learned in the Vedas, as well as dancers and singers,
right there in the pavilion in front of the deity’s face.
Having unveiled the hidden cloth and likewise performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
one should joyfully present it to Hari accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having offered lukewarm cow's milk and fresh butter with sugar to the Lord of Gods, one should then again perform the curtain ceremony.
Having uttered "Bhūḥ prapadye," one should repeatedly bow to the Lord of Gods; with the mantra "Paraṃ raṃ," [one should worship] the Lord of Śrī who is situated upon His bed. (BhS 18.49)
Having uttered, "Thou art the Earth, O Earth," one should place [the mantra] at the seat of the living soul (jīva).
At that time, those who serve Puruṣottama with devotion—BhS 18.50.
Even the gods of the three realms cannot describe the fruit of their merit;
therefore, having respectfully summoned his disciple who was endowed with humility, [he spoke].
The preceptor should instruct him in tasks such as sweeping, saying: "Cleanse," while [he cleans] the inner sanctum and all other areas on every side. (BhS 18.52)
The disciple should indeed sweep with the broom in a clockwise direction,
removing dust and other debris all around until reaching the edge of the enclosure wall.
Having uttered "Āśā'su," one should smear [the ground] with cow dung;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should draw decorative patterns (raṅgavallī).
“O delightful one, one should purify all the vessels with the mantra ‘ā mā vājasya’ according to the prescribed rule. (BhS 18.55)
But for the sake of gathering glory, the disciple, appointed by the worshipper, took up the jar while uttering, "May heaven milk [the earth]. (BhS 18.56)
If a river, a pond, or a well is not available, one should go to another;
having approached the water, one should remember the Jāhnavī, the purifier of the world.
Saying, "I am taking hold of the clarified butter," he should take it with a cloth strainer;
having taken it and purified it by pouring it back and forth, he should then recite the Gāyatrī mantra again.
Having properly decorated a jar and covered its mouth with linen,
one should place it upon an elephant or on the head [of a person], accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having re-entered the ālaya and performed a circumambulation,
one should invoke King Soma in the southern part of the inner sanctum (garbhageha).
Then one should place the water-pot upon a beautiful tripod,
having taken fragrant substances such as cardamom and ushira according to the prescribed rite.
The worshipper should place it into the hand of the priest;
having taken it, the priest should then deposit that water into the full pitcher and consecrate it.
In the absence [of water], one should touch the jar with kuśa or dūrvā grass mixed with tulasī leaves, reciting: "O Waters, you are auspicious" (idam āpaḥ śivāḥ). BhS 18.63.

Having then duly performed the *puṇyāha* ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra, one should sprinkle the ritual materials in sequence with the mantra: "śuci vo havyam. (BhS 18.64)
Having removed the faded flowers [nirmālya], one should purify the pedestal and the flowers while reciting: "May the world perish! I alone am this! // BhS 18.65 //
Having recited "pūtas tasya," one should purify the altar with the *adbhis* mantra;
likewise, the foot-flower of Dhruva [is purified] with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
Having offered [oblations] with the five form-mantras and having prostrated before the deity,
one should adorn Viṣvaksena with the remains of the deity's floral offerings.
Taking any leftover offerings (nirmālya), one should cast them away in a pure place or into water;
and for the sake of worship, one should gather the necessary materials according to one's ability.
Then, having become composed, he should begin the worship of the ritual requisites;
the wise one should place the vessels in their respective locations as is appropriate. (BhS 18.69)
For the purpose of bathing, it should be in the southeast; for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, also in the southwest;
for the purpose of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), it should be in the northwest; and for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*), then in the northeast.
For the sake of purification, one should place this sequence of five vessels in the center:
three feet [of the tripod] set upon a wide copper vessel.
Recalling Lord Hari, one should establish [the fire] with the mantra "agniśśuciḥ" and perform the purification of the vessel, beginning with drying, according to the prescribed rule. (BhS 18.72)
Then, having taken water with a sipping-vessel (uddhariṇī) while reciting the syllable Om,
and having placed a *tulasī* leaf or a flower into it, one should perform the ritual holding (*dhāraṇa*).
Brahmā is said to be at the mouth of the water-pitcher, and Rudra below it;
Varuṇa is to be meditated upon in the water, and in that same manner one should perform the invocation.
Having invoked the moon into the three-footed vessel and the sun into the upper vessel,
one should [invoke] Vasiṣṭha, Soma, the sacrificial components, the moon, and Mandra in their proper sequence.
One should invoke [the deities] into five vessels according to the sequence beginning with the southeast (āgneya) and so forth;
[one should offer] camphor, uśīra, fragrant substances, cardamom, and cloves.
These are declared to be the materials for the bath; one should place them in the bathing vessel:
*viṣṇuparṇa*, lotus petals, *dūrvā* grass, and *śyāmāka* grain.
Having procured the primary substances, one should place them in the water-offering vessel (pādyapātra),
as well as kuśa grass, unbroken rice grains, sesame seeds, vrīhi rice, barley, and mung beans.
One should place priyaṅgu and siddhārtha seeds into the vessel of honor,
followed by elā, uśīra, lavaṅga, and so forth, as well as muktā and kolā, in their proper order.
One should then cast [the remains] into a vessel for rinsing with pure water; thereafter, one should gradually place flowers and perfumes according to what is available.
If these are not available, one should utter that [mantra] and cast in a tulasī leaf;
and with the mantra "dhārā'su," one should fill the vessels with water.
Having recited, "O auspicious waters," and having displayed the *surabhi-mudrā*,
one should perform the consecration of the vessel and carry out the binding of the six directions.
Having recited the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should perform the ritual therein;
one should worship Brahmā in the bell and the Vedas in the sound.
One should worship Ṣaḍāsya on the tongue, and the serpents with the thread; one should also worship Īśa above and Śaṅkhārī at his two sides.
One should install Mahādeva upon the stalk; these are the presiding deities of the bell.
Having placed Vimala upon the tripod to the north, one should place it in the water-vessel (patadgraha).
One should worship Varuṇa in the left side of the conch, the Earth at its base,
all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in the stream, and the Moon within the conch.
One should worship Soma in the water-vessel and the ladle;
having invoked Dharma upon the seat, one should likewise invoke Tvaṣṭṛ upon the strainer.
Having invoked the sun into the upper garment and the moon into the turban,
one should likewise invoke the six-faced deity into the ornament and the moon into the sacrificial thread.
One should invoke Pulla for flowers, Medinī for perfumes and mouth-fresheners, Kāśyapa for unbroken grains (akṣata), and Bṛhaspati for incense. BhS_18.89 //
One should worship Śrī in a lamp, the ancestors (pitṛs) in ghee and sesame oil;
likewise, one should worship the remaining deities in a pillow, an umbrella, and sandals.
One should worship Mārtāṇḍa in the mechanical doll (yantrikā), Soma in the white mustard seed,
Jāhnavī at the tip of the kuśa grass, and the ancestral deities in the sesame seeds.
Having invoked Ravi into the rice, one should invoke the Yajus into the curd;
having invoked the Atharvan into the milk, one should likewise invoke the Ṛc into the honey-mixture.
Having invoked Śarva into the *mātrā*, Divākara into the oblation vessel, Haviṣṇu and Padmagarbha [into their respective vessels], and Niśākara into the drinking vessel; BhS_18.93.
Then one should worship Divākara in the vessels for offerings and the like;
having invoked Jyeṣṭhā into the broom, one should worship Nartaka and Īśvara.
One should worship the Sāmaveda in the singer, Nandīśa in the instrumentalist,
Pāñcajanya in the conch, and the Apsarases among the female dancers.
Having then successively invoked Garuḍa among the attendants,
one should invoke Viṣṇu in the case of materials not specifically mentioned and perform the rite.
Having recollected the presiding deity of each respective substance,
one should worship them with four forms as the possessors of those substances in their proximity.
One should employ [the deity] appropriately at the proper time for each respective rite;
or else, one may invoke [the deity] at that time and employ him in that rite.
Then the worshipper, with a serene mind, having meditated upon himself as Janārdana,
should remain concentrated on the right side of the deity upon a tortoise-seat.
Whether standing before the image or again sitting down,
having meditated according to the rules of meditation and recited the lineage of the masters, ||| BhS_18.100 ||
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other practices according to the rules prescribed in the Yoga scriptures;
having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should then carry out the various ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having performed the placement of the letters from *a* to *kṣa* according to the rules in all the joints [of the body], one should carry out the Brahma-placement (*brahmanyāsa*).
One should touch the heart while reciting, "Brahma, the inner self of Brahma," and having uttered, "Thou art the sky by the skies," one should touch the head. (BhS 18.103)
“O Śikhā, rise up!”—saying this, he should likewise touch the crest-lock;
then, having said, “With the weapons of the gods,” he should bind the armor. (BhS 18.104)
One should perform the binding of the ten directions with the mantra "nārāyaṇāya vidmahe";
then, having said "abhīti sudarśanam," one should place the Sudarśana [seal] on the right.

One should hold a conch in the left hand, saying "O you who are the sun" (*ravipā*); and having said "You are the sun" (*sūryo 'si*) and "You are the moon" (*dro 'si*), one should place them upon the right and left eyes respectively. (BhS 18.106)
The wise man should also place [the syllables] upon the orbs of the sun and the moon:
"Ahuraṇyam," "vidhim," "yajñam," "brahmāṇam," and "devendram. (BhS 18.107)
One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
then, one should place Brahmā in the heart with the mantra "antarasminn ima. (BhS 18.108)
Having restrained the breath and made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should proclaim the lunar day, the day of the week, and so forth;
then the wise one, having likewise resolved upon the seat of the mantra according to the rule, [should proceed].
"Reciting 'pratadviṣṇussavate,' he should likewise say, 'Let there be a seat';
thus he should offer a seat upon one of the flowers, blades of kuśa grass, or at the edge of the pedestal. (BhS 18.110)
Having said, "To those who are superior to all," one should offer a welcome; and having honored the Lord of Gods with the mantra "The mind is the thinker," BhS 18.111.
“One should offer water for the feet at both feet with the mantra ‘trīṇi padā’;
and having offered the water for the mouth while touching it, with the mantra ‘āmā vājasya’. (BhS 18.112)
Having touched the right hand of the deity, one is released from even the most grievous sins;
having recited "śanno devīḥ," one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," he should show him a mirror;
having recited "for the sake of food," he should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
Having prepared a tooth-stick six finger-breadths long, made either of gold, silver, ivory, or udumbara wood, one should practice according to what is available.
“One should perform the purification of the tongue with the mantra ‘idaṃ brahma.
Likewise, one should rinse the mouth and wash it while reciting ‘yan me garbhe’. (BhS 18.116)
Having recited "śanno devī," one should then give water for sipping (ācamana);
having uttered "vicakrame," one should cause the mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa) to be offered.
Having discarded the previous garment and having caused [the deceased] to be clothed in another garment,
one should respectfully perform the veiling over the back of the neck.
Having scattered his hair and being well-established on the left side, the knower of mantras,
having uttered "Uvānahā'va," should place a sandalwood slipper in front.
Having uttered "Bhūḥ prapadye" and bowed to the Lord of the worlds, one should take up the amulet with the mantra "Paraṃ Brahma. (BhS 18.120)
Then, having recited the Svasti-sūkta and saying "pratad viṣṇuḥ," he should firmly establish [the deity] upon the bathing pedestal and offer water for the feet and water for sipping.
Therefore, having anointed the head with oil using the mantras beginning with "deva," one should likewise anoint all the limbs with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
One should cleanse all parts of the body with the mantra "parilikhita," using sour gruel, cold water, and sugar as appropriate. (BhS 18.123)
One should perform the cleansing of the teeth with water infused with *śrīpatra* and *āmalaka*;
one should carry out the purification of the limbs with rice flour, perfumes, and other such substances. (BhS 18.124)
Having thoroughly cleansed [the image] and bathed it with warm water, one should consecrate it with pure waters while reciting the mantra: "The four waters. (BhS 18.125)
Having said, "Homage to Varuṇa," one should sprinkle [the image] with cow's milk;
with the mantra "Bhūrānilaya," one should bathe it with scented water. (BhS 18.126)
“Having recited ‘agnim īḷe,’ one should perform a bath with honey;
[one should perform] the sprinkling of turmeric water with the mantra ‘sīnīvālī. (BhS 18.127)
And upon each of those other substances, there should be a sprinkling of pure water;
then, reciting the verse beginning with "Gandhadvārām," one should likewise do so with scented water.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods of gods preceded by the sounding of musical instruments;
one should bathe him again with pure water while reciting mantras such as those of the four Vedas.
Having said, "O friend Suparṇa," and having wiped away the garment of woven grass,
he discarded his former clothing and likewise donned the other.
One should offer water for the feet and water for sipping according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, having prostrated before the Lord of the Gods, one should offer a handful of flowers.
Having uttered "Bhūr asi bhūḥ," one should place [the offering] at the location of the living being;
having uttered the mantra "Trir deva," one should offer it to the visible sins. (BhS 18.132)
Then, having sprinkled the location of the *dhruva* while reciting the *gāyatrī* mantra,
one should subsequently utter these [words] joined together for the *dhruva* and the *kautuka*.
For the sake of establishing the connection, one should place the *kūrca* at the front of the *kautuka* according to the ritual procedure;
then, having sprinkled the fixed pedestal (*dhruvapīṭha*) with pure water while reciting the *Gāyatrī*, [one should proceed].
Having uttered, "Salutation to Viṣṇu," and recollecting the God of gods,
one should perform the placement of flowers between the feet of Dhruva.
One should then place flowers there, beginning with the east and proceeding in a clockwise order, using the names ending in the dative case: Puruṣa, Satya, and Acyuta. (BhS 18.136)
Having proclaimed "unobstructed" in the four great directions,
one should likewise [proclaim it] in due order in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth.
Kapila, Yajña, Nārāyaṇa, and Puṇya—this is the first enclosure; then follows the second enclosure.
In the very same sequence previously described, one should worship Vārāha, Nārasiṃhaka,
Vāmana, Trivikrama, and thereafter Subhadra.
Having thus addressed the Self as the Ruler, and thereafter as the Upholder of all,
one should worship the Lord of all-knowing ones, who is directed toward external objects.
In the third enclosure, one should worship the respective lords of the directions;
one should likewise perform the worship for the two goddesses using the *mūrti-mantras* of Śrī and Pūmī.
Thus has the deposition of flowers (puṣpanyāsa) on the seat of Dhruva been described;
now, on the seat of Kautuka, it is indeed performed according to the previously stated sequence.
Having invoked Subhadra in the east, and thereafter Hayātmaka, Rāmadeva, Puṇyadeva, and all those who bring happiness; BhS_18.143 //
One should worship Saṃvaha and Suvaha in the first enclosure;
likewise, in the second enclosure, one should worship Mitra, Matri, and then Śiva.
One should worship Viśva, Sanātana, and likewise Sanandana; beyond these, one should worship Sanatkumāra and Sanaka, as well as the Bahirmukhas.
In the third enclosure, one should likewise worship the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Worship beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ" is called *nyāsa*. (BhS 18.146)
One should worship with eleven or eight types of offerings;
therein, one should perform the ritual for the two goddesses according to the rule, as if they were Dhruva and Tārā.
One should worship Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu on the right and left sides of the deity,
and likewise worship Brahmā and Śaṅkara on the side of the wall.
The disciple, as instructed by the Guru, should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite, beginning with the worship of the door, facing these [deities] toward the Lord of Gods.
At each door, one should worship the deities of the doors and the door-keepers,
as well as the guardians of the celestial palaces, the lords of the world, and likewise those who never depart.
Having likewise worshipped the attendants and others, ending with those who have become Viṣṇu, by their respective names with the mantra "bhūrānilaya," [one should proceed].
Having performed the washing of the door, one should invoke Dharma, Jñāna, and Aiśvarya in the right, middle, and left [sections] respectively, and worship them well.
In every case, for the sake of protection, one should worship the peaceful deity on the left side of the door;
then, one should hang a curtain made of linen or similar material at the entrance.

Women, Śūdras, those who have fallen from their status, heretics, revilers of the Vedas, those devoted to other deities, and those afflicted by sinful diseases and the like [should not be invited]. BhS_18.154 //
Those who are accursed, sinful, and censured in the scriptures do not deserve to serve the imperishable Hari at the time of worship.
At that time, the worshiper, having entered into meditative absorption and being well-composed,
becomes Nārāyaṇa in person simply by reciting the Ātmasūkta.
[One should meditate upon] Viṣṇu, the pervasive Self, consisting of indivisible bliss and consciousness,
with a golden luster, his eyes, face, hands, and feet red, and bestowing happiness.
The god is adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, earrings, and bracelets;
he holds a conch and a discus, and is marked by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
He bore the Śrīvatsa mark, possessed mighty arms, had a chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem,
wore garments of peacock feathers, and had a long sacred thread.
The Lord of the World was surrounded by divine weapons, adorned with celestial ornaments, and served by his two consorts and their retinues.
One should meditate upon the flawless Nārāyaṇa as being present within the image;
having established [the deity] in such a way that the image and the self are identical, one should then perform the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having uttered "Suvaḥ," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Bhūḥ," one should place the Vyāhṛtis upon the head, the navel, and the two feet of the image;
this is called the Vyāhṛti-nyāsa.
Then one should place the syllable *ya* on the seat between the two feet;
having placed the syllable *a* on the heart, one should then again place the primordial seed-syllable (*ādi-bīja*).
Having encircled these with the *praṇava*, one should again perform a prostration;
[the vessel] should be joined with flowers, perfumes, and unbroken rice grains, and filled with pure water.
Having raised the vow higher, like a lamp from one [lamp] to another in succession, he should say:
"This is Viṣṇu," and "May the Blessed One come. (BhS 18.165)
One should invoke Hari from the eternal waters of prayer into the *kūrca* grass, he who is of the nature of the *praṇava*, unmanifest, and possesses a divine, auspicious form. (BhS 18.166)
Having taken that [liquid] which pervades it and placed it upon the head of the Kautuka,
the Guru, having poured it down with the Praṇava, should perform the invocation (āvāhana) into the Kūrca.
Having recited the mantra of the embodied form, the wise one should perform the ritual action therein;
likewise, having invoked the two goddesses, he should worship them correctly.

In the same manner, the wise man should perform the invocation according to the prescribed rite during festivals and other occasions; some authorities maintain that the invocation of the portable image (balibera) is performed for the sake of auspiciousness.
Afterwards, having prepared the seat of ornaments according to the rule,
one should offer the seat with the mantra and pay homage to the Lord of Gods.
One should also offer water for the feet and water for sipping with the previously mentioned mantra;
one should present garments such as linen and the like with the *tejovatī* mantra.
Having adorned him with ornaments while reciting the mantra "bhūto bhūteṣu," and having said, "You are the body of Soma," he should cause him to put on the upper garment.
One should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with the eight-syllable mantra;
having recited "Agniṃ dūtam," one should offer the sacred thread (yajñasūtra).
Then, one should worship with flowers and other offerings using the mantra "Tad Viṣṇoḥ," or by reciting the individual form-mantras (mūrti-mantra) beginning with Keśava.
In this way, with one hundred and eight, or one thousand and eight,
or even infinite names, you, Lord Hari, who possess infinite names, are to be worshipped.
Having recited, "tadviprāsa," one should anoint [the disciple] with sandalwood paste;
then, having uttered, "paro mātrayā," one should cause him to smell incense.
One should show the lamp to him with the mantra “viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi,” and offer the water for washing the feet as before with the mantra “trir deva. (BhS 18.177)
In all ritual services, it is traditionally taught that what is dear to Hari is not a base offering;
therefore, the wise man should present a pure gift comparable to honey-cake.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the aforementioned mantra;
then, taking a *droṇa* of rice, or half of that, or even a quarter.
Having taken a bronze vessel filled with rice, sesame seeds, and mouth-freshening fruits,
and having placed it before the deity, [he should proceed].
Then ten other [priests] recited the mantra "Somaṃ rājānam" for the God of gods;
having worshipped the officiating priest with the floral remains (nirmālya) offered by the deities, they then [proceeded].

“Having caused [the devotee] to lick the hand of Hari with the mantra beginning with ‘ghṛtāt parīti,’ it should be given to the worshipper; this is remembered as the ‘taking of the measure’ (mātrādāna). (BhS 18.182)
One should give many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of accomplishing the excellence of the gift;
having accepted it with the mantra "devasya tvā," the worshipper [should do so]. (BhS 18.183)
He may employ it for the sake of his family, for he is the heir to Hari;
however, regarding the consumption of the property of the gods, whatever fault has been declared by the scriptures applies here as well.
For the Vaikhānasas, there is no such defect due to the grace of the God;
having prostrated before the Lord of the gods with mantras originating from the Vedas and other sources.
Having praised him with various hymns, one should scatter a handful of flowers at his feet;
there, one should also offer ten lamps of various forms while reciting the mantra.
Taking a jar-lamp, one should place it before the deity;
[one should also worship] Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Cāmana, and Trivikrama.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite upon the petals, one should worship Lakṣmī in the lamp;
likewise, one should worship Śrī in the wick and Abhava in the smoke.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] and worshipped it in due order with offerings such as flowers and perfumes,
and having recited "śubhrā jyotiḥ," he should take hold of it with both hands.
Performing circumambulation three times, one should cause Hari to be whirled around,
while taking hold of that lamp accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Whether it be a disciple or even a courtesan, having circumambulated the temple,
they should indeed release that lamp behind the leader of the assembly.
From the sight of that lamp, for men there arise longevity, prosperity, and the birth of sons;
of this there is no doubt, for it is indeed the delight of Viṣṇu.
At that time, the preceptor should fan [the image] with various yak-tail whisks;
the fourfold set consisting of the mirror, the chowrie, the parasol, and the fan.
Performing dance, song, and instrumental music while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
he should show these to the Lord and then proceed with hymns of praise according to the sequence of the Vedas.
Likewise, one should cause Acyuta Hari to hear various kinds of hymns;
and whatever has not been specifically mentioned, one should perform it by inferring it from the general principle.
Having placed the respective seed-syllables individually upon the hearts of Śrī and Bhūmi,
one should worship them in sequence with their two specific hymns and the sixteen types of offerings.
And having performed all the aforementioned worship according to the *Uttaracāra*,
one should then formally resolve (*saṃkalpya*) upon the food to be eaten according to the prescribed rule.
Clarified butter, honey, molasses, milk,
and curd combined together in the measure of one prastha is here called the Madhuparka.
“One should offer the honey-preparation with the mantra beginning ‘yanmadhu’;
thereafter, having given water for sipping (ācamana), one should employ the disciple in the ritual task. (BhS 18.199)
“Then, having purified the ground with the *avanīda* mantra, the practitioner of the rite should cause a square mandala to be made there. (BhS 18.200)
Having thoroughly cleansed the sacrificial vessels and worshipped the Sun within them,
one should indeed pour clarified butter over them and then place the oblation therein.
“One should perform the ritual action with the mantra ‘Thou art the underlayer of immortality’ (amṛtopastaraṇam asi);
therein one may include appetizers and the like, as well as molasses, curd, and fruits. (BhS 18.202)
Having placed [the portions] separately in different vessels without mixing them while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
and having sprinkled them with cow's ghee while reciting the mantra "yatte susīme," [he should proceed].
Having placed [the offering] before the deity upon the three-legged stand according to the rule, at the time of offering the oblation, one should not consume it; this is said to be Hari.
Therefore, having abandoned the Vaikhānasas, other Brāhmaṇas who follow different sūtras,
as well as others, must not enter the temple of Viṣṇu at that time.
One should then bolt the door and cause the sound of bells to be made;
one should produce the resonance of musical instruments and the like, for Hari is fond of gentle music.
Then the worshipper, with a serene mind, remembering the God of gods,
should place Tulasī into the vessels of oblation while reciting the eight-syllable mantra.
Having worshipped with flowers, sprinkled [the food] while reciting the Praṇavas, and consecrated it by pouring water around it,
one should touch it with the *Annasūkta* and display the *Surabhi-mudrā*.
Having said, "This is dear to him," one should offer warm oblation;
having said, "The auspicious self-existent one," one should offer a cake. (BhS 18.209)
And other items such as pṛthuka and the like, along with uncooked substances, [should be purified] by means of the *viśvabhaiṣajya* mantra and all else by the eight-syllable mantra.
Having recited "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should offer sweet, cool water as a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa),
and then present water for washing the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamana).
“One should cause the guest to rinse his mouth with the mantra beginning ‘ghṛtāt...’;
then, having recited the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should offer a handful of flowers. (BhS 18.212)
Having sprinkled water around the fire in a perpetual fire-pit or on a hearth,
the wise one should offer oblations of sacrificial porridge and clarified butter with the *mūrti-mantras* in their proper sequence.
Having likewise offered oblations to the Goddesses and others, one should worship Vaiṣṇava deities in due order,
as well as those deities mentioned in the Puṣpanyāsa, and similarly those of the heretics (pāṣaṇḍas).
The best time for the fire sacrifice (homa) is said to be during all three periods of the day; however, the morning alone is the lowest.
The characteristics of a middling fire sacrifice are when it is performed both in the morning and at midday.
One who is unable to maintain the fire without interruption should protect it;
or, having consigned it into his own self, he should lead it forth again and perform sacrifice day after day.
Then, having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) for the journey-seat according to the rules, the wise and learned man,
having sprinkled it with water and adorned it, should take up the chariot or a palanquin with four poles.
Having placed the *balibera* upon it, adorned with all ornaments, one should chant the "Rathantara" [sāman] and perform the ritual there. (BhS 18.218)
Having addressed Hari as the Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and likewise as "the one who is affectionate toward his devotees," he [worshipped] Him with the mantras of His forms.
One should bind [the disciple] firmly with a cord of human hair according to the secret sequence;
having touched his feet with the mantra "Viṣṇus tvām," one should bow repeatedly. (BhS 18.220)
“Having uttered ‘King Soma,’ one should hold the parasol over the head;
saying ‘The Maruts are the Supreme Self,’ one should offer the two chowries on both sides. (BhS 18.221)
“One should fan Hari with fans while reciting the mantra ‘vāyuparī,’ as well as with other great fans provided with divine trappings. (BhS 18.222)
Accompanied by the ringing of bells and the sounding of conchs and kettledrums,
as well as the resonant blasts of bherīs, mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and even kāhalas.
With mṛdaṅga drums and divine musical instruments, accompanied by rhythmic timing and correct pitch,
one should worship Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe, who is free from all affliction.
Having summoned the disciple at that time, and having placed upon him a turban,
an upper garment, and upright flowers, he should sprinkle him with water while reciting the mantra.
The wise one, having placed the vessel for the offering upon his uṣṇīṣa and having adorned it with garlands and other ornaments, should worship it and remember Tārā as if she were a calf.
Having offered the bali-oblation with that very vessel for the bali,
one should everywhere at all the gates perform the placement of flowers as prescribed.
One should sequentially cast the offering toward the eastern and northern limits;
water, flowers, the offering, and water—these are the four constituent parts therein.
Then, having brought the deity, the drivers, proceeding very slowly, should drive that chariot which is beautiful in all its parts.
With body gradually bowed, the disciple should offer the bali in successive order;
having offered the bali, he should go before [the deity], either together with the god or separately.
Then, having led the deity around in due order by way of circumambulation, an offering (bali) should be presented at that time; its sequence shall now be explained.
Then Maṇika and Sandhyā are the first pair of gatekeepers,
and Tāpasa and Siddhida are the second pair of gatekeepers.
One should worship Nyakṣa and Indra in the space between them according to the prescribed rite;
and at the door of the first enclosure, Kiṣkindha and Tīrtha themselves.
One should worship Gaṇeśa and Śeṣa at the door of the second enclosure,
and likewise Śaṅkha and Padma, the two treasures, at the door of the third enclosure.
Likewise, one should worship Tuhiṇa and Balinda in the fourth enclosure,
and in the fifth enclosure, one should worship Khaḍga and Śaṅkha.
In the sixth enclosure, one should worship Avaraṇa, Śaṅkha, Cakra, and Cūḍa;
likewise, one should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa in the seventh enclosure.
One should worship Śrībhūta and Garuḍa in the middle of the steps;
one should properly worship Agni, the protector of the oblation, in the south-eastern direction.
On the right side of the celestial chariot, one should worship Vivasvat and Yama;
and in the southwest, one should worship Varuṇa and Nirṛti.
In the west, one should worship Mitra as well as Varuṇa;
and in the northwest, one should likewise worship Puṣpa, Īśa, and Marut.
In the north, one should worship the doorkeeper and Kubera;
likewise, one should worship Īśāna and the Sun in the northeast.
Having worshipped [the deity] at the site of the elements (bhūtapīṭha), one should likewise worship the wheel, the banner, the conch, the leader of the host, and Akṣahanta.
On the southern side of the pedestal, one should offer the remainder of the *bali* to the spirits, yakṣas, and piśācas with the mantra beginning "ye bhūtāḥ. (BhS 18.242)
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should carry out the rite there,
accompanied by dance, song, and the like, as well as divine hymns of praise.
Having performed three circumambulations and caused the Teacher of the World to turn around,
he placed him in the middle of the stairs and released the binding rope.
Then, with shouts of victory and likewise with mantras, one should offer the water for the feet;
thereafter, having taken up the deity, one should establish him in his own place.
Having recited the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should repeatedly perform prostrations;
one should also offer handfuls of flowers with the twelve, eight, and six-syllable mantras.
Having recited the *puruṣasūkta* and uttering the *praṇava*,
and having offered mouth-freshener, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
Then, having taken water from the *patadgraha* vessel, the worshipper,
becoming self-restrained, should drink it three times and also consume *tulasī*.
Dawn, morning, midday, afternoon,
evening, and midnight are remembered as the six times for worship.
One should perform worship in the morning for the increase of recitation and fire-offerings;
worship at midday is prescribed for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
Worship performed in the evening is for the increase of all crops;
worship performed at the time of dawn is said to be for the increase of progeny and cattle.
The afternoon worship is indeed for the purpose of destroying the Daityas;
the midnight worship is proclaimed for the increase of the four quarters.
Thus, the fruit of worship at six times has been specifically described;
whether it be at six times, three times, twice, or even once. BhS_18.253 //
The worship of the God of gods bestows rewards both in this world and the next;
at the time of the six-fold worship, the wise one should first perform the invocation.
Likewise, at the final hour of worship, one should perform the supreme ritual of dismissal (udvāsana);
during the twilight periods, one should [worship] the Lord of Gods with the eight forms beginning with the seat.
Having performed the full worship, one should likewise offer the oblation (havis), the fire-sacrifice (homa), and the ritual offering (bali);
as well as the placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa), the fire-sacrifice, the worship of the retinue, and the bali-offering.
One should avoid the perpetual procession and festival during the twilight hours;
in other cases of three-times-daily worship, the ritual bathing should indeed take place only in the morning.
He states that at other times, the sprinkling and the worship are performed with a mantra;
likewise, this applies even in the absence of disciples or when there is damage from rain and so forth.
Likewise, in the absence of musical instruments and the like, when the time for the bali offering has arrived,
one should then invoke the deities and place the bali at the entrance.
Then Sūrya, having uttered the mantra, shall fasten the door;
he should act in this manner at midday, at evening, and at every appropriate time.
In the same way, at the proper time, one should open [the door]; the entire worship is as before.
Having purified the flower offered at the door, one should worship it again at the door.
On the fixed seat (dhruvapīṭha), however, the flowers are not to be purified again and again;
without removing those flowers, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) above them.

But at the evening worship, those flower garlands should not be taken from anywhere else; having taken the flowers worshipped during the *kautuka* and other rites according to the rule, the wise one [should proceed]. (BhS 18.263)
Having placed [the image] on the side of the pedestal, one should worship it with ever-new offerings;
then, at the end of the final worship, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one prepares the bed and seat.
Having set aside his garments, garlands, and other ornaments, and having offered a fine cloth,
he worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī, with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings.
Having offered a decoction mixed with all medicinal herbs as well as water to the God of gods, one should provide him with mouth-fresheners.
Having uttered "This is for Viṣṇu," [he should place it] amidst delightful, soft musical instruments,
upon a divine couch provided with a celestial pillow and adorned with divine ornaments.
One should have Hari lie upon a bed that is well-adorned with canopies, beautifully perfumed with divine incenses, and provided with costly coverlets.
Having taken hold of Śrī and Bhūmi with their respective mantras, the Guru should lay them down in the bonds of the deity, while reciting "dhruvanta. (BhS 18.269)
“You have been worshipped and well-praised, O you whose banner is the golden-winged Garuḍa;
O wielder of the discus, O mighty-armed one, dwell as you wish. Om, homage! (BhS 18.270)
Having recited this mantra, endowed with supreme devotion,
one should, in the morning, cause the Śakti invoked [the previous day] to descend into the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Having performed circumambulation and prostration with the mantra,
the preceptor should likewise offer praise with the Puruṣasūkta and the Viṣṇugāyatrī.
And with the mantras of the three pervasive deities, as well as with the mantras beginning with "viṣṇornuka," with the mantras beginning with "ato devā," and with other Vaiṣṇava mantras.
With hymns beginning with the Ekākṣara and others consisting of twelve, eight, and six syllables,
one should repeatedly offer handfuls of flowers and purify the accumulation of faults.
Now I shall explain specifically the worship during festivals and other occasions; the location for Brahmā has already been described as being in front of the *kautuka*. (BhS 18.275)
Then, one should establish the bathing and the festival for the *kautuka* on the two western [sides];
the placement of the *baliberam* is likewise on the northern side of the *kautuka*.

Having established [the deity] either in the contraction of the womb-chamber, or in the portico, or in the intermediate space, one should perform the worship, the bathing, and the festival. (BhS 18.277)
During the bathing festival, one should perform the excellent worship as previously described;
furthermore, one should arrange sixteen services, beginning with the seat (āsana).
One should properly worship Śānta with thirteen ritual offerings,
and likewise worship the Anapāyi gaṇas with nine ritual offerings.
One should worship the deities of the doors, the door-keepers, and likewise the guardians of the world with the eight types of offerings, performing the rites with the root-mantras.
One should worship the other attendants with sixteen forms;
likewise, one should perform the rites for Pākalakṣmī and Dvāralakṣmī.
Likewise, one should perform the rites for Śrīvatsalakṣmī together with the deity;
or else, one should have the installation of an incarnation or the perpetual worship performed.
Then, during the installation of Trivikrama, one should worship the permanent image (dhruvārcā).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
The worship of the Blessed One [is described] hereafter; the worship of the permanent image (dhruvārcā) shall now be fully explained.
One should also purify the flowers and other offerings that have been placed upon the head [of the deity] down to the pedestal.
If there is to be worship of the yogic heroes, one should perform the ritual bath at the three times of day;
or else, one should perform the constant worship on the yoga-pīṭha in the morning and at midday.

In the case of the permanent image (dhruvārcā), one should perform the ritual service (bhoga) specifically at dawn and midday, or even at all three times of the day, after having bathed the image. BhS 19.3.
Having thoroughly purified the garments and other items, and having performed the placement of flowers as before,
one should worship Śiva and the others on the footstool on all sides.
Likewise, the wise one should worship with all [the requisites] such as the seat during the three junctions of the day;
and having worshipped at the end of the first watch (ardhayāma) as before, he should worship again.

One should likewise announce the oblation and whatever has not been previously mentioned, as before; however, one should not perform the invocation and the dismissal—this is the instruction. (BhS 19.6)
Now, at the conclusion of the worship, I shall describe the procedure for the various rites:
the vessel should be made of gold for the highest [grade], and it should be made of silver for the middling.
The inferior copper vessel is also mentioned; thus the vessel is said to be of three kinds:
the best is declared to be three *tālas* in height, while the middling should be two *tālas*.
The inferior [vessel] should have a single palm-tree height; the extent of the vessel is said to be of three kinds, and the middle-of-the-middle is equal to that extent.
In the center of that, one-third [of the area] should be the pericarp, one finger-breadth in height;
surrounding it, one should fashion eight petals with a height equal to that of the pericarp.
The base should have a circumference of two finger-breadths, while its tip should have half that circumference;
the wise one should fashion the tip so that it has the shape of a slightly opened lotus.
One should place therein cooked rice prepared from two *prastha* measures of grain,
having sprinkled it with clarified butter, to a height of eight finger-breadths.
Taking that bowl, which is ten or twelve finger-breadths in height, and placing it before the auspicious knot (kautuka), [he should proceed]. BhS_19.13 //
Taking up the *śakti* out of curiosity, one should worship it with the eight forms, saying both "O Supreme Brahman" and "O Supreme Self. (BhS 19.14)
One should worship the Lord of Yoga, who is affectionate toward his devotees, with the four forms;
one should offer a flower-oblation in the morning and likewise an oblation at midday.
In the evening, one should perform the offering of water and bali as previously instructed,
using either a *kuḍuba* measure of rice or whatever may be available.
Having heard this, one should offer the *arghya* and *bali* oblations with flowers four finger-breadths in length;
at that time, having summoned the disciple, he should be wearing a turban and an upper garment.
Remembering the disciple as Garuḍa, one should indeed lift up the vessel there;
with the mantra "ud u tyaṃ," the disciple should place it upon his head. (BhS 19.18)
Then one should perform a circumambulation accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments,
provided with canopies and umbrellas, and adorned with peacock-feather fans.
Accompanied by incense and lamps, one should slowly perform circumambulations;
having performed three circumambulations, the wise person should enter the temple.
The worshipper should stand within the *bhūtapīṭha* and receive [the deity];
having placed it before the *kautuka*, he should install it with the syllable *oṃ*.
Having first broken off a portion of the bali offering, one should present it to the Lord of the Army;
then, one should cast the remainder, together with water, upon the seat of the spirits (bhūtapīṭha).
If one desires to perform the festival, it is most excellent when done at all three junctions of the day;
it is middling if performed in the evening and morning, and inferior if performed only in the evening.
One should have an offering (bali) or an offering receptacle (balibera) made; for whom is this not so?
Furthermore, the measurement of the height for a deity prepared for the purpose of an offering has been declared.
One should know that the hand of a Mahāvera is twenty-one finger-breadths,
or seventeen finger-breadths, or even twelve finger-breadths.
One should employ three kinds of measurements: superior, middling, and inferior. One-third of the height of the worshipper shall constitute the measure for the best image. BhS_19.26 //
One-tenth of that measure, less one, shall be the medium;
one-tenth of the medium, less one, shall be the inferior.
The width and height of the face of the great primary image is recommended;
one should fashion an image for the sake of the bali offering, and there should be an installation of all [the deities].

One should fashion an image made of gold, silver, or copper, according to whether it is superior, middling, or inferior; for an image fashioned from jewels, there is no fixed measure of weight or volume.
The uṣṇīṣa should be known as a sphere, and the measurement of the head is three mātrās;
the portion from the hairline to the top is equal, and from that junction comes the line for the forehead.
From the suture-line to the end of the jaw, each part should be measured one by one;
the throat should be known as half a finger-breadth, and the neck is said to be half a mātrā.
The mouth should extend from the throat down to the heart and be slightly larger;
the heart and the navel are likewise described, and that which is below them is equal to those.
The thighs are desired to be two mouth-lengths in length and the size of a ball in height; the feet are the measure of a knee, and the knees are the measure of the shanks.
Below the *hikkāsūtra*, however, there should be two arms, two faces, and two eyes;
the forearm and the binding of the face should each be one and a half [units] in length.
The distance from the wrist to the tip of the finger is praised as the measure for the face;
having thus made it four-armed, this is declared to be the measurement.
One should fashion a spherical ball in the shape of a lotus.
Now, I shall describe in detail the method for cooking the sacrificial oblation (havis) according to the rules.
Having cooked [the food], one should also prepare sacrificial offerings according to one's wealth;
whether the offering be small or great, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor.
Having offered it to the Lord of Gods, the wise man should perform the auspicious rite;
for if one does not offer the ghee, that which is auspicious indeed leads to misfortune.
And in the absence of all these, one may likewise use rice grains;
that which is filled with two hundred and twenty-five grains of rice is known as a *śukti*, and by that very measure one should cause [the vessel] to be made.
Two of those are called a *tila*; two *tilas* would be a *prakuñca*. Two of those are declared to be a *prasṛti*, and two *prasṛtis* are a *kuḍuba*.
Two añjalis are declared to be one prastha; two añjalis make one prastha. Two prasthas are declared to be one pātra, and two of those make one āḍhaka.
Four āḍhakas combined are designated as a droṇa;
two droṇas make a khārī, and two khārīs make a bhāra.
An oblation consisting of one *droṇa* of rice is called the best;
half of that is declared the middling, and half of that again would be the lowest.
It is said that the most excellent of the excellent consists of eight *droṇas* of rice;
whatever exceeds that is declared to be the "Great Oblation" (*mahāhavis*) in its entirety.
An oblation prepared with half that amount of rice is called middling;
an oblation prepared with six *droṇas* of rice is considered the highest-middling.
Therefore, that which lacks a *droṇa* is called "inferior"; that which consists of four *droṇas* of rice is said to be "middling-superior. (BhS 19.47)
Where three *droṇas* have been prepared, it is called "middling-middling";
the oblation made with two *droṇas* is said to be "middling-lowest."
Having offered with one *droṇa* of rice, it is called "neither low nor high"; that which measures two *āḍhakas* is said to be "middling. (BhS 19.49)
That which is combined with one āḍhaka is called the Madhusūdhama;
however, for the goddesses, one should provide half an āḍhaka of rice.
Two *prasthas* of cooked rice (*caru*) are prescribed; this is called an *āḍhaka* of sacrificial oblation (*havir*).
A *prastha* combined with a *kuḍuba* shall be the offering (*bali*) for the *piśācas*.
Likewise, the rice grains should be selected as those endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor;
having thoroughly washed the rice grains, one should squeeze out the water again and again.
Having performed the fourfold washing with the mantra "May offspring abide [in me]," he should place the rice grains into the vessel with the mantra "Full of vigor."
Afterwards, one should place it on the hearth with the mantra, "To Viṣṇu, the beloved," and cook the sacrificial oblation until it is steamed with the mantra, "O Lord of Speech. (BhS 19.54)

One should discard food that has the smell or taste of smoke, that is steamed, overcooked, or cold; likewise, one should avoid food infested with hair or insects, as well as that which has been kept overnight.
Mudga and mahāmudga, kūṭastha and rājamāṣaka;
likewise the plantain, the jackfruit, the pumpkin, and the bṛhatī.
Others [offered] bulbs, roots, and fruits rich in pith as side dishes, combined with molasses, curd, and clarified butter. // BhS 19.57 //
Having prepared the oblation, one should offer four parts;
one part above for the presentation, and likewise one part below for the purpose of the fire-oblation and for the bali-offering.
Whatever portion remains in the bowl, having been prepared specifically for worship,
one should offer it in a vessel made of gold, silver, bronze, or copper.
Whatever oblation remains after the fire-ritual and whatever remains after the bali-offering—all that is said by the wise to belong solely to the worshipper. (BhS 19.60)
In the second enclosure, it is said that the kitchen is located in the southeast;
or else, having cooked [the food] in the house of the officiant, one should offer it.
He [prepared] the vessel for the oblation, the vessel for sprinkling water,
and the vessel for offering the guest-water (arghya), which was filled with a kuḍuba measure.
The size of the vessel for the oblation should correspond to the size of the vessel for the bali offering;
and the vessel for the gift of water should be made of bell-metal or even of mother-of-pearl.
Whether made of gold or silver, it should be adorned as beautifully as possible;
likewise, for the offering of betel, it should indeed be made of gold or bell-metal.
And a gift should be given that is equal to the *dhruvānasa*;
for the purpose of invocation, it should be filled to the measure of a *prastha*.
Turbid, infested with worms and moss, devoid of its fibers,
endowed with foul odor, color, and taste, and situated in an impure place.
Water that is defiled by mud or stones, or salt water from the ocean, or water from a stagnant pool, is unfit to be taken; water free from these defects is fit to be taken.
The highest [initiation] is said to be performed with water possessing the three qualities;
the lowest is by means of a river, while the middle one would be the middling [initiation].
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to be that which is infused with uśīra and sandalwood,
and provided with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, and jātiphala.
Water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana) [should be prepared] with uśīra, amaya, and sandalwood;
likewise, water [for other rites] with milk, tips of kuśa grass, barley, white mustard seeds, and rice.
The eightfold water offering (arghya) is said to consist of sesame seeds and rice;
sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron are called "fragrance. // BhS_19.71 //
One, two, three, or even four [verses] should be recited with *karpūra* (camphor),
combined with *uśīra* and sandalwood, mixed with ghee, and drenched in ghee.
That which is mixed with a small amount of camphor is called incense by the wise;
that which is made with cow's ghee is called the supreme lamp.
Indeed, a lamp with a length of four finger-breadths is called a "royal" lamp;
a lamp with a length of six finger-breadths is said to be a "middling" lamp.
The smallest lamp, however, should be two finger-breadths in measure;
it may be made with ghee from a tawny cow and a wick of saffron-colored cloth.
The lamp dear to Viṣṇu is said to bestow all accomplishments;
however, a lamp made with buffalo ghee would be of the nature of tamas.
A lamp made from the oil produced from the seeds of a tree is called a *paiśāca* lamp;
it is also called a *tāmasa* or *paiśāca* lamp, which is unfit for [use]. (BhS 19.77)
The cloth may be made of linen or cotton, or produced from the various parts of the body;
it should be ten cubits in length and two cubits in width.
A garment that is captivating and very smooth is called a *viśeṣa*; the width of the garment is said to be half the measurement of the image's height.
It should have a length eight times its width, be provided with a fringe, and possess the proper characteristics;
it should be made of peacock feathers and be four *tālas* wide.
It should be made facing downwards, and likewise facing upwards;
its staff should measure five cubits, and that is the lowest [standard].
Exceeding twelve finger-breadths in length, whether in the medium or even the superior [grade], such is the peacock-feather fan described; now the characteristics of the parasol are being stated.
The supreme extent of the parasol for the six [deities] is declared;
the middling should be five *tālas*, and the inferior four *tālas*.
The parasol should be made of pearls, and likewise it is beneficial if made of cloth;
one may also make it with cloth or even with palm leaves.
The parasol is said to face downwards, and the staff for the peacock-feather [parasol] should be like a staff;
one should fashion ornaments and the like joined with gold and jewels.
A crown, earrings, a necklace, as well as armlets, bracelets, a waistband, flowers, and indeed anklets; BhS_19.86 //
One should fashion a waist-band, a jeweled necklace, a girdle, a long necklace,
and an ear-flower for the image, as is appropriate.
One should make a fly-whisk from yak-tail hair or even from peacock feathers;
its handle should be one cubit in length, and the size of the hair-fiber should correspond to the length of the handle.
The handle may be made of gold and jewels, or likewise of white copper; or it may be a wooden handle, to which one should attach a peacock feather.
