Thus the *cāmara* has been described; now the *pracchannapaṭa* is being explained: one should have a door curtain made consisting of a combination of linen and cotton.
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the Thousand Streams (sahasradhārā),
using gold, silver, or copper, according to one's own capacity.
The best [stūpa] is sixteen finger-breadths; the middling is twelve finger-breadths;
and the lowest is eight finger-breadths; one should have it made according to one's capacity.
Having properly rotated these fingers like the moon,
the portion raised from the wall is declared to be a *golaka*, especially so.
The circumference of the rim is traditionally said to be eight finger-breadths in width;
the diameter of the handle is equal to its width, while the spherical knob is one barley-corn high.
In the center, one should offer a gem or gold according to one's ability;
one should fashion eight petals well-joined around the pericarp.
One should fashion sixteen petals around the center, thirty-two pericarp sections,
and sixty-four petals on the outermost layer.

Furthermore, one should cause it to be made with a thickness of two barley grains and even a line; it should be provided with a thousand perforations and fashioned according to the prescribed measurements.
The wall should be sixteen, twelve, or eight finger-breadths in length and width;
it should be one cubit in breadth and made level with the interval between two shells.
Having fashioned them in the shape of a lotus and joined them with stalks,
the wise man should skillfully arrange the remainder so that there is an exit for the water.
One should have it fashioned in such a form, endowed with all beauty;
having washed it with the five products of the cow, one should purify it with a cleansing agent.
Having smeared the area in front of the temple with cow dung and having spread a heap of grain,
one should place a cloth upon it.
In the north, one should perform the Vāstuhoma and the Paryagni ritual as before;
there, one should honor the teacher with new garments and finger-rings.
Having meditated upon the lunar mandala in the tantra, one should likewise invoke Padmanidhi in the lotus and Śaṅkhanidhi in the conch, and then worship them.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should again give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
and having performed the purification of the image, one should consecrate it with the mantra itself.
Having worshipped the God of gods, one should present the sacrificial oblation there;
in this manner, indeed, one should cause vessels prepared for the purpose of the deities to be offered.
The evil committed by his body perishes at that very moment;
it pacifies all defects and increases devotion to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the section on the *Prakīrṇādhikāra* within the *Bhṛguprokta-saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the venerable Vaikhānasas.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The Ritual for the Protective Lamp:
Hereafter I shall explain the procedure for the ritual of the protective lamp.
It may be made of gold, or silver, or even copper, according to one's own capacity.
The best [staff] is thirty-two finger-breadths long; the middling is less by one-quarter;
the lowest is twenty finger-breadths; one should have it made perfectly round.
In the eight directions, in the center, or likewise in the four directions; or only the pericarp, or [the design] spread within the pericarp. BhS 20.3.
One should know that half of that is its height; the length of the cheek is six finger-breadths, its circumference is two finger-breadths, and it is one part wide at the top.
Having fashioned a lamp-wick with a width and height equal to half of that [the wick's thickness],
one should collect either rice flour or cow dung [as fuel].
Having placed [the offerings] in their respective locations, one should then combine them in a vessel;
one should cook the *caru* offering as either an *āḍhaka*, or half of that, or even half of a *piṇḍa*.
Having placed turmeric powder mixed with ghee into a vessel, the knower of mantras,
having poured it out and wiped it, makes a firm handful measuring one muṣṭi.
One should collect ten lumps of earth, or half that amount, together with unbroken grains;
then, having filled a water-pot with water mixed with all kinds of fragrances, [one should perform the ritual].
Having placed bundles of kuśa grass, one should also adorn it with sprouts;
it should be provided with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) and accompanied by water for washing the feet and water for sipping (pādya-ācamana).
Having gathered flowers mixed with fragrance, along with incense, lamps, and water for the guest-offering (arghya),
each in separate vessels, one should worship the God of gods.
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and the sound of flutes,
and joined with the resonance of kettledrums, clay drums, and wind instruments.
Accompanied by the sound of hymns and endowed with one's own prayers and sacred verses,
one should hold it over one's own hands, either with female attendants or with devotees.
Having walked slowly in circumambulation, one should approach the temple;
then, having honored the teacher and bowed to the God of gods.
Taking up the protective lamp while reciting "Born for Fortune" (*śriye jāta*),
one should place it upon the head of the image and perform three circumambulations to the right.

Having indeed offered the directional rice-balls and having sprinkled [the area], the knower of mantras should cause [the disciple] to perform circumambulation and prostration with the eight auspicious symbols.

Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; and having offered mouth-perfume, one should indeed praise [the deity] with Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Having touched [the deity] with both hands, one should offer a handful of flowers at the feet using flowers, dūrvā sprouts, and unbroken rice grains, according to the mantra of the deity.
Having gone outside from the inner sanctum (ālaya), one should deposit [the image] beside the pedestal;
this applies to the consecration (kautuka), the offering image (balibera), as well as the ceremonial bath (snāpana) and the festival (utsava).
And likewise at the manifestation and appearance of all things,
having performed it in this very manner and having caused it to revolve, the wise one [should proceed].
The one most skilled in the scriptures should likewise perform the visualization and the circumambulation of Cakravī, Śāmita, and the others, as well as Indra and the rest.
If one should act out of delusion or ignorance, there will be a total loss;
[this applies] always at the end of the evening worship, and at the conclusion of a festival.
In this very manner, the wise should cause it to be made as the most excellent;
it brings about all peace and bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
By destroying poverty and other such misfortunes, one shall obtain all desires.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the palanquins.
One should construct the śikhika and other features according to the rules using finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula);
the enclosure, which is half that in width, is prescribed as the best.
That which is six finger-breadths less than that is proclaimed as the medium; its width should be one and a half quarters [of a finger],
and its length should be double [the width].
There should be a variety of palanquins for those who are superior, inferior, and middling;
one part out of three, or one part out of four, should be allotted.
The thickness should be one-fifth of the width;
thus, each individual projection (vamana) should likewise consist of one-fourth of that [thickness].
The remaining portion is described as being like a lotus, specifically according to the application of the palm-measure;
likewise, the width of the palanquin is one part and indeed another part.
The height of the wall is prescribed to be exactly one-fourth of that;
it may consist of two stories or three stories, and be constructed with small balls and wooden planks.
The height of the *gulikā* at the soles of the feet is equal to the height of the middle upper surface;
it may likewise be one-fourth or even one-ninth [of that].
One finger-breadth and half a finger-breadth, joined with an upper band;
beyond this, I shall explain the sequence of rules for chariots and other vehicles.
It should be five, six, seven, or even eight *tālas* in width and length; its height should be twice that.
It may be provided with a pavilion entrance or even have a gabled roof;
its height should be three times its width, including the lower base.
Having thus calculated the length and width of the parasol according to half its height, the measurement for the palanquin is likewise declared.
The length may be equal to the width, or even half as long, or one-quarter;
the width shall be one-third of that, and the height shall be one-third of the length.
Having prepared a bed made of the same wood as previously described, with a height equal to half its width and a length exceeding half its width; BhS_20.36.
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with every beauty,
the wise one should have it fashioned by artisans according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on the arts.
Having thoroughly purified [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), let the Vāstuhoma sacrifice be offered;
then, having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagni), one should bathe [the image] with water-pots (kalaśa).
One should place it here in a pavilion, or at a water-shed, or upon a sacrificial mound;
having wrapped it in new cloths, one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day to be made.
Having caused the fire-pit for the domestic (aupāsana) fire to be prepared according to the rules,
and having performed the pouring of the oblation (āghāra) as before, one should perform the worship of the water-jar (kumbha).

Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava and the Viṣṇusūkta, as well as to those respective deities with their forms, and having performed the offerings ending with the Vyāhṛtis, the concluding oblation (antahoma) is then sacrificed.
And having likewise invoked the respective deities within those [vehicles] and so forth, having worshipped them duly, and having prostrated before the God of gods; BhS_20.42.
Having worshipped with the offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with the arghya water, one should properly present the sacrificial food,
accompanied by all ornaments and joined with all musical instruments.
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle or similar conveyance and reciting "That toward which Viṣṇu has stepped," one should perform a circumambulation of either the village or the temple.
Having entered the temple, one should install [the deities] each in their respective place;
he who performs this with devotion shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the water-shed pavilion (prapā-maṇḍapa).
The pavilion is to be known as threefold, with a width equal to that of the vimāna.
It may be threefold, being reduced by half, a quarter, or a third;
at its front, it is traditionally taught that there should be a flight of stairs measuring half the length of the main hall.
To the east, however, one should construct a pavilion for the purpose of the ritual bathing;
it should be provided with sixteen pillars or joined with twelve pillars.
Or one should perform it in the northeast; one should prepare it for the purpose of the ritual bath, either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure.
One should properly fashion it to be equal in size to eleven cubits;
thus, it is of three kinds: nine cubits, seven cubits, and five cubits.
In the outer first enclosure, a pavilion is prescribed; one should arrange it for the purpose of viewing the assembly hall, dances, songs, and so forth. (BhS 20.51)
As before, one should perform [the rite] at the front with extensive detail according to one's means;
one should increase the length by two cubits using the hand of the patron.
As before, one should arrange it appropriately with pillars;
in that hall toward the eastern direction, the space for dancing is prescribed.
The width should be nine cubits, or the length should be doubled;
there, one may increase the width by two cubits according to the desire of the patron.
I shall describe the characteristics of the [temple] site and so forth, in accordance with the needs of the patron:
it should be one cubit, half a cubit, or a quarter of a cubit, combined with the appropriate width and length.
Having prepared it in that very manner, the wise man should mark out the foundations for iron and the other materials;
the floor should be one cubit in height, constructed with stones or bricks.
One should construct it with two stories, or properly arrange a single story; having diligently procured pillars made of stone or the heartwood of trees.
Whether circular or square, straight and free from curvature,
he took twenty pillars and held up the outer pillar.
In the center of that, the wise and discerning practitioner should have twelve pillars constructed as before, having determined their height according to the requirements.

One should fashion the Svastika pillar, joined with two *tāla*s in thickness according to the measurement of the pillar; having divided it equally above the capital (*stala*), one should arrange the *vandana* [ornament].
Having placed his foot in the svastika posture upon that very [seat] for the sake of stability,
the wise one should firmly establish the pillar above it.
Or else, the wise one should have a pedestal made two finger-breadths high,
adorned with various ornaments and endowed with various paintings.
Having made the northern [side] equal to that, one should properly join the banner of awakening;
having fixed it above the pillar, one should place the lintel above that.
Above the inner northern part, at the base of the brick-setting,
one should install the upper beam firmly and in due order, as appropriate.
One should have that bilvaka made according to the path, with a lotus-base of appropriate height,
endowed with such characteristics and beautiful to behold.
According to the wish of the patron, it should be constructed together with that particular pavilion,
provided with either sixteen pillars or twelve pillars.
Having prepared it with devotion, one should cause a water-shed (prapā) to be constructed by proper means;
others [should construct] one joined with doors, or even just a pillar, as previously described.
One should install a door there, or otherwise have the remainder executed with skill;
the wise man should have it constructed by artisans according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on craftsmanship.
Upon the completion of the pavilion, one should offer the ritual germs (aṅkura) in due order;
for the sake of purification, one should likewise perform the Vāstu-homa and the Puṇyāha ceremony.
Afterwards, one should feed the brahmins and observe that region;
this should be done at the rising of a lunar mansion and while holding a fixed zodiac sign.
In the center of the pavilion, one should indeed prepare altars of grain;
according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration, one should cause the placement of the ritual jars (kumbha) to be performed.
In the west, one should offer the *āghāra* libation into the *gārhapatya* fire in due order;
there, the *hotṛ* priest should perform the duties of the *hautra* according to the sequence of the *hautra* ritual.
Having invoked each respective deity, one should perform the *juṣṭākāra* oblation;
[one should recite] the Śrīsūkta, the Vaiṣṇava [sūkta], and twenty-one [verses] of the Vaiṣṇava [hymn].
One should offer oblations one by one to Indra and the other world-protectors in their respective order;
one should worship them either upon a grass mat (kūrca) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at each of those locations.
Having offered an abundant amount, or indeed a *droṇa* or even half a *droṇa*,
one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in due order to the teacher, the worshipper, and the others.
Then, one should adorn the water-shed with golden lotuses,
or with flowers, or with lotuses, or with water-lilies, or with other flowers according to one's ability.
Having again adorned the God of gods with garments, garlands, and other offerings,
and having prepared a water-shed, one should lead the Lord of Gods forward by means of meditation alone.
One should install the Lord of Gods there and worship him in due order with water for the feet and other offerings;
one should present a great oblation or an abundant one according to one's capacity. (BhS 20.78)
"Thus, he who performs this with devotion is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous matters in the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Lord belonging to the Śrī Vaikhānasa tradition.
The twentieth chapter.
The twenty-first chapter: Special Worship.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the five days of Viṣṇu:
Śravaṇa, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight, and the twelfth day in both halves of the dark fortnight.
On the full moon day and the new moon day— these five days indeed—
one should plant the sprouts in sequence according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having tied the protective amulet there, one should let it rest during the first part of the night;
then, at the conclusion of the morning twilight worship, one should perform the bathing according to the prescribed sequence.
Having worshipped [it] and offered [the oblation], one should indeed install it in its former place,
especially during the bright fortnight of the month known as Mārgaśīrṣa.
At the conclusion of the morning twilight, having first established the four Vedas in the assembly pavilion, he should always teach them in their proper order.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, which destroys even the greatest sins, one should worship the Lord of the Gods with twenty-seven forms.
Then, on the twelfth day at dawn, having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing,
one should discard old earthen vessels.
Having purified [the image] as appropriate with cleansing, sprinkling, smearing, and so forth,
and having bathed it according to the prescribed ritual sequence for bathing, in accordance with the rules.
Having honored [the deity] with a seat and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa);
then, having given water for drinking and water for sipping (ācamana), one should thereafter offer an aromatic mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa).
Having praised [the deity] with the Puruṣasūkta and having performed a circumambulation according to one's desire,
and having completed the circumambulation of the abode, one should place [the image] in the seat of life.
If the worship throughout the year is deficient regarding the obligatory, occasional, and other rites,
they say that all of it becomes complete when the worship of Dvādaśī is performed.
On the full moon day of Pauṣa, having worshipped the Lord of Gods as described in the Viṣṇupañcadina, one should offer cow's milk.
He too obtains the fruit of a year; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, on the asterism Punarvasu in the month of Māgha, Rāghava himself was born.
Then, having worshipped either Rāma or Viṣṇu therein, and having circumambulated the village and bathed [the deity], one should present [the offering].
I shall explain the ritual of the sesame lotus; listen, O best of sages!
Specifically on the fifth day of the waxing moon in the month of Māgha.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods according to the ritual at the beginning of the night,
and having offered the sacrificial oblations, one should again bind on the protective amulet.
Having caused [the deity] to be shaded as before, one should pass the remainder of the night in due order;
at dawn, having raised the deity, one should bathe him again with water-pots (kalaśas).
Having smeared with cow dung a pavilion, or a peaked roofed structure, or a water-shed, as is appropriate, and having adorned it with five colors; BhS_21.18 //
Having established the Lord of Gods upon that [altar], and having bowed down and offered praise,
[one should place Him] before a heap of grain two cubits in length and breadth.
Having spread out a black antelope skin, one should spread over it a new cloth;
and upon that, having indeed scattered six *droṇas* of sesame seeds.
One should draw a sesame-flower lotus with eight petals, measuring three *droṇas* or even two, and shaped like a mandala according to the proper time. BhS_21.21 //
Having fashioned a golden lotus with three *niṣkas*, half of that, or even just one *niṣka*, one should place it upon a lotus made of sesame seeds.
One should place sixteen full vessels made of *āḍhaka* measures of *śāli* rice upon a heap of *śāli* rice, extending from Indra in the east to Īśāna in the northeast.
Having brought one *aḍhaka* of oil and half that amount of ghee,
and having placed curd in a western vessel, he should bow down to the God of gods.
Having recited the *ātmasūkta*, one should worship with the eight forms;
having prostrated before the God of gods, [one should place it] in the center of the lotus as before.
One should summon the deities of the east and other directions, as well as Puruṣa and the others, with the four forms;
and having worshipped them appropriately with the eleven types of offerings, one should proceed.
Having invoked the deities of the directions beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, one should then worship them.
Furthermore, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta beginning with "ato devā". (BhS 21.27)
Having installed the deity in the image, one should gradually dismiss the others;
then, at that time, the patron should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One who is endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, possessed of the qualities of self-restraint and compassion, dedicated to the complete recitation of the Vedas, and perfect in all his limbs; BhS_21.29 //
At that time, having summoned a Brahmin,
the preceptor, remaining disciplined before the Lord, meditates upon the Lord of Gods in the presence of the God of Gods.
One should indeed offer a sesame-flower lotus to him for the benefit of the entire world;
having praised the deity with hymns, songs, and instrumental music, one should worship him.
Having placed the deity upon a vehicle, fully adorned with all ornaments,
one should circumambulate the temple and install it in the place where the life-force resides.
He who performs this with devotion for Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self,
attains all desires and enjoys the world of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Phālguna, on the full moon day of Phālgunī, having bathed Janārdana together with Śrī, having performed a festival and worshipped him thoroughly, one should present [the offerings].
Likewise, in the month of Caitra, one should perform the Damanaka festival on the very first day,
at the conclusion of the night worship.
Having tied the protective amulet there, one should present it to the Lord of Gods;
having worshipped that garment according to one's desire, one should offer milk-rice.
On the right side of the deity, one should place a garland of *damanaka* flowers;
then, at dawn, having awakened the deity and bathed him, one should likewise worship him.
One should offer [the oblation] to the Deity with devotion, using the flower mantra;
one should offer it to all the members of the retinue using their respective mantras and forms.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise and established [the deity] in the assembly pavilion,
and having worshipped and offered [oblations], one should then present mouth-fresheners.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should indeed bathe [the deity] and worship him;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, however, one should bathe the God and cause new garments to be offered.
That man shall indeed obtain the fruit of a year;
the offering of the guest-water (arghya) to the deity during the month of Āṣāḍha is highly praised.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, especially under the asterism of Śravaṇā,
the wise one should perform the festive bathing and other rites as previously described.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the Jayantī festival:
the auspicious Jayantī is the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
This lunar day, conjoined with Rohiṇī, should be known as the remover of all sins;
on it was born the Lord of the World out of a desire to protect the world.
At the time of the moon's rising, at midnight, by means of his own play,
having diligently worshipped Kṛṣṇa on that very day, [one should proceed].
He who causes a festival for Viṣṇu to be celebrated shall attain residence in the same world as Him;
whether the eighth lunar day is joined with the Rohiṇī asterism or not, it is so regarded by the wise.
The seventh lunar day (tithi) should always be accepted as unbroken;
even if the eighth tithi exists for only a single digit (kalā) at the time of sunrise, [the seventh remains valid].
The entire day should be known as the lunar day (tithi) that extends across the midnight;
it is to be avoided when pierced by the Nāga [tithi], just as the Nandā [tithi] is avoided when conjoined with Śravaṇa.
Likewise, one should avoid the eighth day when it is overlapped by the previous [lunar day], even if it is conjoined with its own asterism;
rather, the eighth day that is not overlapped should be accepted, and one should observe the fast on that most meritorious day.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, joined with Rohiṇī,
[is auspicious] for up to one *ghaṭikā* before or after midnight, as previously described.
She is called Jayantī, the destroyer of all sins;
therefore, it should be performed on the ninth or the seventh day prior to that day.
On the fifth or even the sixth day,
the ritual offering of the sprouts should take place on the preceding evening, at the conclusion of the night worship.
Having tied the protective amulet there, one should have Hari lie upon that bed,
especially on that lunar day at midnight, while he is in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, joined with Śrī, Janārdana, the Lord of the World who has been born into this world to remove the burden of the earth, should offer a handful of flowers.
Thus, while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
one should meditate upon the God and circumambulate the pavilion, which is adorned with all ornaments.
Either in front, or in the middle, or in a decorated assembly hall,
having placed the God of gods upon a seat in its center and having prostrated before him, [one should proceed].
Having filled jars with oil and turmeric powder,
one should place them there upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worship the God of gods.
Having performed anointing with oil, one should perform rubbing with powder;
[one should offer] water from a river, scented water, water with flowers, and water with unbroken grains.
Having collected water with *kuśa* grass, one should arrange five jars;
then, with the mantras beginning with "ato devā," one should bathe Puruṣottama.

Having worshipped the God of gods with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with arghya, and having prostrated, one should offer cow’s milk while reciting the mantra "Hiraṇyagarbha."
Only after offering mouth-perfume and performing a prostration should one proceed;
otherwise, that milk which has been offered will result in the birth of a son who is like the son of a barren woman.
Having drunk it, she gives birth to a son who is long-lived and endowed with strength;
likewise, having taken ghee, oil, and mouth-perfume, [she attains these same results].
Having shown the God to the brahmins, let him be given away;
having adorned the God of gods, [let him be given] to the devotees whose hearts are seized with devotion.
Just as it is for the sacrificer, so too should the wise perform that which brings pleasure,
accompanied by all musical instruments and endowed with all ornaments.
One should perform a circumambulation of either the village or the temple;
having entered the temple, the wise person should bathe [the deity] with water-pots.
Having given the teacher’s fee along with water in the presence of the deity,
and having indeed offered an abundance of food, one should further present mouth-fresheners.
In this very manner, one should perform the festival every year;
this bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as proclaimed by the sages.
Alternatively, on another day, the wise one should cause a festival to be held;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇavas should perform the oblation whenever there is an omission in the ritual of mantras.
In the year following [the previous one], having prostrated before the God of gods,
he performed a purification bath with twenty-five jars [filled] by those of pure mind.
Having performed the *śāntihoma* sacrifice, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
one should hold a festival twice as grand and give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's own capacity.
On the twelfth lunar day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise in Bhādrapada,
[one should perform worship] for the sake of pacifying any faults incurred during the annual worship of Keśava.
In this month, the special rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) to Hari especially pacifies all defects and bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
In this month, one should not undertake the supreme Śravaṇa vow;
yet by fasting for three years and three months, one attains great fruit.
Then, in the month of Āśvayuja, under the asterism of Aśvinī, one should bathe the Lord of Gods;
the offering of the arghya water to the God of Gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is highly recommended.
Now, therefore, the characteristics of the offering of a lamp to the Kṛttikās are described:
on the full moon day of Kārttika, whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is current, [that is the time for the rite].

The lunar mansion at that time shall be the same as the lunar mansion [at the time of the eclipse]; there is no need to wait for a specific time. At the moment of the sun's setting, one should perform the lighting of the lamps.
In the presence of the deity, one should prepare a great lamp with abundant oil upon a pillar that is equal in height to the temple or even taller.
One should procure a lamp-post three feet high or half that height,
made of bamboo, or even of *kramuka*, *tāla*, or coconut wood.
When combined with madhūka, tintriṇīka, and other such heartwood trees,
and accompanied by one hundred and eight lamps, it is called the most excellent of the excellent.
They know the sequence of the middle lamp to be one hundred in number;
likewise, the highest and lowest lamps would be ninety-two.
The medium-superior [type] is said to be eighty-four;
likewise, the medium-medium is said to be seventy-six. BhS_21.81 //
The lamp of middling-inferior quality is recorded as being sixty-eight;
they say that the lamp of inferior-superior quality is sixty in number.
One should prepare fifty-two lamps for the lowest and middle [grades];
this very lowest-of-the-low grade consists of forty lamps.
For those who are unable, one should provide a lamp there according to one's capacity;
it should indeed be placed within the hollow of the staff, sequentially in the four directions.
To the east of the seat of the elements (bhūtapīṭha), the location for the lamp is prescribed; it is illustrated in the Śruti as "resembling the interior of a lotus bud. (BhS 21.85)
Therefore, with every effort, one should fashion a lotus endowed with its proper characteristics;
it should be equal in width and length, measuring four *tāla*s in size.
One should fashion a square measuring one finger-breadth in height;
right there, one should arrange a horizontal lotus made of rice grains, provided with eight petals.
In the center of that, at the height of a palm tree, is a perfectly circular base with a pericarp, one finger-breadth in elevation; right there on top of it, [one should place] grains of rice.
When there is a lotus in full bloom, one should spread a new cloth over it;
having placed a flower upon that, one should fashion a lotus maṇḍala.
Having worshipped the Vasus on the petals, one should worship Dharma in the center;
and one should construct a very beautiful water-shed facing the temple.
Or one should fashion a lotus maṇḍala in the assembly pavilion,
made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's means.
Having carefully collected a shallow bowl filled to the brim with a *prastha* measure [of oil], the wise one should add a small amount of camphor and provide it with a cotton wick.
Having taken cow’s ghee, the preceptor— his mind serene and wearing a new lower garment and upper shawl— should place it in the center of a lotus.
One should perform the kindling of the lamp with the mantra "śriyai jāta" and, having meditated upon Śrī in the center of a lotus in the western direction, one should invoke her. (BhS 21.94)
Having worshipped with the eleven ritual offerings while remaining composed, one should meditate upon the Goddess Śrī in the mind while reciting the Śrīsūkta.
Taking lamps in both hands, especially by the apsarases, and taking other lamps accompanied by showers of water; BhS_21.96.
Accompanied by the sound of songs and provided with dance and instrumental music,
one should then circumambulate [the image] and cause it to enter the inner sanctum.
The best of mantra-knowers, having brought the God of Gods, should place him on the right side of the deity and station him within the mandala at the crossroads.
One should perform the ten modes of service and worship according to the prescribed ritual;
the wise one should kindle the lamps with the mantra beginning with "śriye jāta."
In the inner sanctum, on the staircase, in the temple, in the front pavilion, on the temple spire, at the neck, and even at the base; BhS 21.100.
And likewise everywhere on the walls, in the bathing hall,
in the place where the heaps of flowers were kept, at the gate, and in the assembly pavilion.
Furthermore, in all other places as well, one should gradually kindle lamps by binding cotton wick to a clay bowl and filling it with ghee.
Then one should perform the kindling with the very same mantra previously mentioned,
having made a great effort to proclaim it through dance, song, instrumental music, and the like.
Having propitiated the presiding deity of that lamp situated on the vessel to the west of the sacrificial pedestal, one should place the lamp in the pavilion.
Having uttered "śubhrājyoti," one should place other items on the tip of the staff;
having offered many kinds of things to the God, especially flattened rice and the like.
Having circumambulated the village while adorned with all ornaments, one should offer abundant foodstuffs mixed with molasses and a great sacrificial oblation.
Furthermore, having taken up the deity once more, one should establish it in the locus of the living soul;
that [deity], having obtained the fruit of a year, shall go to the supreme state.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the propitiation during the eclipses of the sun and moon—
the correct ritual for the worship of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
During an eclipse of the sun for four watches, and during an eclipse of the moon for three watches,
the deities and the ancestors do not partake of the offerings to gods (havya) or the offerings to ancestors (kavya).
The great seers do not abandon the worship of Hari even in the state of *ālaya*;
having set aside the offering of oblations, one should perform every form of worship.
But while the eclipse is occurring, one should bathe Puruṣottama;
having obtained the fruit of ten million sacrifices, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
"One should perform the ritual bathing on the following day when [the moon or sun] has been eclipsed;
likewise, one should do so when there is an eclipse at sunrise," thus said Śātātapa.
When an eclipse occurs at any time, one should perform a ritual bath;
likewise during an eclipse, a planetary transit, the "elephant's shadow" (hasticchāyā), the equinoxes, and so forth.
The beginnings of the Yugas and other such times are proclaimed as meritorious occasions;
the wise have declared that abstention [from meat] is prescribed during festivals, just as in the case of the offering of oblations.
One should perform the daily worship and the festival before the ritual bathing;
having bathed Hṛṣīkeśa, the offering of oblations is highly recommended.
One should always perform the purification of the dwelling site during lunar and solar eclipses;
having discarded old vessels, one should procure others.
The purification of cloths is desired by lifting them with the tips of kusha grass;
and for uncooked items, one does not accept what is cooked.
They do not speak of an eclipse when it is invisible;
likewise, for one who is initiated or for anyone else, there should be a ritual bath upon contact with and release from [the sun or moon].
For as long as the time from beginning to end may last, one should proclaim Hari;
remaining silent, pure, and wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one should perform japa and other such rites.
By wearing a cloth that has been struck by the wind seven times while still damp, one incurs no fault;
during the eclipse, service to the Blessed One destroys all inauspiciousness.
One who desires [merit] should indeed offer grains according to one's ability in the temple of Hari;
that becomes infinite where Ananta is present, for Hari himself is the witness. (BhS 21.121)
Having first offered an abundance [of food], one should eat immediately thereafter;
one may perform a śrāddha at night during an eclipse, for that does not cause any fault.
But when the stated time has been corrupted, its very departure occurs;
those who know the scriptures understand that in such a contrary case, there is great fault.
A śrāddha ceremony is not prescribed after midnight, even in times of distress;
those who are under ritual impurity must always bathe, and they too may perform acts of giving.
For them, neither recitation nor austerity serves for liberation when the sun,
in due time, passes from one zodiacal sign into another.
At that time, it would be a meritorious occasion for performing ablutions and other rites;
twenty [days] prior to the Kaṭaka [conjunction], and twenty [days] after the Makara [conjunction].
It is declared that those ghaṭikās are meritorious; there, one should act as in the case of an eclipse, when the sun’s transit occurs at the time of sunset or during the twilight.
The time for merit is said to be in the forenoon;
it is also recorded as being after the afternoon, when the sun has half-set, and likewise when it has half-risen.
The three ghaṭīs before and after [noon] are proclaimed as the twilight periods;
even during an eclipse, one should indeed perform the avabhṛtha bath for Hari on such an occasion.
One should abandon the entire night during a lunar eclipse and a full day and night during a solar eclipse; at such auspicious times, one should never perform the lamp festival of Hari.
Who indeed would not offer a lamp after midnight during an eclipse?
It is taught that offering a lamp on an unblemished festival day brings auspiciousness.
Even during the lunar eclipse, the lamp-offering should not be made if it is not the full moon;
a lamp offered on a non-parvan day destroys previously accumulated merit.
During the lunar months and asterisms other than those [prohibited], and likewise on the five days of Viṣṇu,
midday is declared to be the time for the worship of the God.
"In rites for specific desires, however, the worship should take place at an auspicious moment; one should not perform it otherwise.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra* as proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The twenty-first chapter in the Miscellaneous Section of the Saṃhitā.

Now, therefore, follows the ritual bathing: the bathhouse should be situated in front, or to the north, or specifically to the northeast; it may be either a water-shed or a pavilion. (BhS 22.1)
It was covered by a canopy above, draped and well-adorned,
with pillars wrapped in cloths, fine silk, and woven fabrics.
It is adorned with strings of pearls and provided with full water-jars;
it consists of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as sovereignty and its presiding deity.
One should install the archways in sequence with mantras beginning with the four Vedas;
on both sides, they should be provided with plantain trees and areca palms.
Having stretched six lines from the eastern end to the northern end,
one should arrange twenty-five squares of equal dimensions.
Having left the central Brahma-pada, one should designate eight [squares] around the half of the practice area;
four squares starting from the east should be arranged for the purpose of the doors.
One should bring the remaining twelve parts for the purpose of depositing the substances;
in the center, a hollow should be made according to the procedure for the *aupāsana* fire.
Having made a depression in the center measuring one palm in depth,
one should place a slab made of bilva wood in the middle of that pit.
A pedestal measuring more than that, four finger-breadths on all sides,
having been set aside in the center, should be installed in sequence, accompanied by the two Vedas.
Then, one should go toward the north along a purifying path;
outside the pavilion, in a clean spot, one should have a water reservoir excavated.
Having covered it with plantain leaves, or else with lotus petals, or with turmeric leaves, or with betel-nut leaves; BhS_22.11 //
With the mantra beginning with "atodevā," one should purify the *kuśa* grass; having prepared it to the extent of the depth of a pit, one should collect it. (BhS 22.12)
A broom (*kūrca*) for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) should be one cubit (*hastamātra*) in length;
however, the broom for the purpose of sweeping (*mārjana*) is traditionally recorded as being six finger-breadths long.
One should prepare the vessel for the flask, measuring five, eight, or twelve finger-breadths in length, according to the number of flasks required.
One should prepare a three-tiered altar with rice, paddy, and sesame seeds;
it is taught that the rice should be half the amount of the paddy, and the sesame seeds half the amount of that.
The wise one should arrange the row such that the best [seat] is said to be one *droṇa*, the middle one half of that, and the lowest one *āḍhaka*. // BhS_22.16 //
Having thoroughly burned the unbroken jars and having carefully collected them,
the measure for the shallow bowls (śarāva) is declared to be one kuḍuba.
Taking up water-jars of six *prasthas*, a *karaka* vessel, a *kumbha*, and a *droṇa*,
as well as the ritual pitchers (*kalaśas*) with the mantra "To the God thee," he should proceed.
Having wound threads around the jars to the extent of a barley-corn's interval, and having especially prostrated before the Lord of Gods during the first part of the night; BhS_22.19.
Having worshipped thoroughly and offered a mouth-freshener,
he should then bind the *apratisara* amulet according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having prepared the bed along with its pillows as before,
one should lay the deity upon the bed and provide an upper covering.
One should pass the remainder of the night in due order with dances, songs, and instrumental music.
Then, at dawn, the righteous preceptor, accompanied by the patron, [should proceed].
Having established [the vessel] in the middle of the pit, one should properly place the *kūrca* grasses in sequence;
there, one should also worship Jayā and the others, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
One should first worship Paṅktīśa between Nīla and Vāruṇa;
having worshipped him thoroughly, one should also worship Viṣvaksena between Soma and Īśāna.
Having worshipped the world-protectors with two, ten, or three planetary offerings, one should take earth from the bank of a river, from a field of crops, or from the shore of a lake. BhS 22.25.
And likewise, having taken [the substance] at the root of *darbha* grass, on an elephant’s tusk, on a cow’s horn, in the dwelling of a crab, and in the center of an anthill; BhS_22.26.
Having obtained the permission of the goddess Earth and having brought those [plants] individually,
one should dry them in the sun and then reduce them to ashes by means of Viśvāmitra.
Having filled separate bowls with earth,
one should place them in order from Indra to Īśāna, following the direction of circumambulation.
“One should first apply earth with the mantra ‘udutya’;
then, one should apply a single application of soft earth in the northeast.”
One should make [the sacrificial post] eight finger-breadths in height, square in all respects, using either aśvattha, palāśa, bilva, or khadira wood.
The base is said to be six finger-breadths [in width] and the top likewise six finger-breadths;

in this way, one should arrange the Kālacakra for the purpose of the festival.
Likewise, one should fashion the shaft beneath the wheel to be twelve finger-breadths long;
the handle should be twice the length of the wheel, and the seat should be made of khadira wood.
Alternatively, one should have the edict made here by sacrificial trees;
one should fashion a wooden board six finger-breadths in length and breadth.
Whether circular or square, and provided with hanging garlands,
one should join it with a height of three finger-breadths above the coping.
Below that, however, one should cause a tāṭī (fillet) together with a *kumbhalambaka* (pendant pot) to be made, with a height of eight finger-breadths; such is the instruction. (BhS 23.27)
Having made it hollow inside,
and having joined it at the top or the bottom of the handle with a hard staff, [one makes] a board, a fruit, or a lotus.
"One should have a creeper made even wider than the terrace; this is the instruction.
The lotus, however, should be six finger-breadths in length and one additional finger-breadth in width."
Upon the pinnacle, two lions should move on both sides, carrying the wheel along as they proceed there. BhS 23.30.
The measurement for those two is prescribed as five finger-breadths;
one should fashion it with the middle of the staff, and at the base of the staff, it should be six finger-breadths.
The pedestal should be six finger-breadths in height, or four finger-breadths;
it may be circular or square, and adorned with petals and filaments like a lotus.
The length is proclaimed to be sixteen finger-breadths, and the width is likewise declared;
in the center of the pericarp, the stalk is joined with a length of eight finger-breadths.
Having joined it with a bamboo staff, one should bind it with the eight-fold binding;
one should make it very firm like a necklace, straight and well-aligned.
Having done this, one should correctly perform the placement according to the path;
one should practice the thousand-petaled wheel in the form of a person.
One should visualize [the deity] with a reddish-blue complexion, measuring nine tālas in height,
possessing two arms, wearing a bound crown, and having a cakra upon his head.
One should worship the Sudarśana discus, likewise the thousand-petaled [lotus],
and the one called Anapāyin, with the mantras of their respective forms.
One should worship Kālacakra— the hundred-streamed, the crusher of all asuras,
and the remover of all obstacles.
I shall proclaim the Kālacakra, which destroys all asuras;
it may be thirty-six finger-breadths, or fifty-six, or one hundred and eight.
The measurement of its width and length—whether superior, inferior, or middling—should be taken according to the *mānāṅgula* (measurement-finger); the lathe-wood should be circular.
There are one thousand spokes, or eight hundred, or three hundred, or sixty;
joined in sequence, they are classified as superior, inferior, and middling.
Likewise, there should be twenty-four, sixteen, or twelve flames;
it should be joined with a circular band measuring ten, seven, or five finger-breadths.
One should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) as a lotus with a portion having the radiance of a wheel;
for that [pedestal], one should join the lotus without the staff and other [ornaments].
This great wheel, which destroys all misfortunes, has been described;
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall now declare the method for the installation of the wheel.
Having offered the sprouts, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
likewise, having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one performs the consecration of the five products of the cow (gavya).
Having thus prepared the sacrificial hall, one should adorn it with archways;
and in its center, one should construct a bed-altar measuring one and a half units in both length and width.
Having prepared that altar as a square with its fourth part elevated,
one should place the Āhavanīya fire-pit in the east, just like the Aupāsana fire-pit.
Then, having prepared a bathing altar in the east, the wise one should take the consecrated discus and perform the ritual ablution.
Having completed the fire ritual as previously described, one should again prepare the water-pot (kumbha);
the pot should be placed upon a pedestal of grain facing the wheel (cakra).
Having thus renounced, the wise preceptor should contemplate that which is desired;
then, having circumambulated the village, he should likewise place it within the hall.

Having meditated upon the Lord of the Mandala in the center of the heart-lotus—two-armed, with palms joined in reverence, red in appearance, and wearing garments of a similar hue—and having properly completed the ritual of fulfillment; BhS_23.51.
Therefore, having invoked [the deity] into the pitcher and worshipped it as previously described,
one should then bathe that wheel on the altar using the water-pitchers.

Having purified the face and other parts with the *samala* mantras, and having placed the jar upon the grain-seat (*dhānyapīṭha*) in due order, one should then tie the protective cord (*pratisara*) around it.
Having thus caused [the deity] to lie down and having properly praised the *hautra* ritual,
they declare the limbs of the wheel to be the limbs of the sacrifice and the mantras of the forms.
Thereafter, having strewn grass around the fire, one should offer oblations with mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu,
beginning with the verse addressed to Bhūmānana, followed by the Gāyatrī.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and passed the remainder of the night,
he should bathe at dawn and, taking up the previously mentioned wheel as before, [proceed].
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should likewise place the water-pot specifically on a prepared seat on the southern side of the pavilion.
Then, having placed the jewel, one should establish it with the previously mentioned mantra;
having properly applied the wheel-mantras and applied the seed-syllables as before.
Having likewise invoked the Śakti from the pitcher, one should worship her with the seat and other offerings;
then, having offered milk-rice and other foods, one should properly worship the Guru.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra-saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Regarding the festival: hereafter I shall proclaim the sequence of the festival for the Lord of Gods.
It bestows rain upon the entire world, grants peace, and provides nourishment for all.
To grant victory to kings, to cause the destruction of enemies,
and for the sake of pacifying disease and famine, the wise man should cause a festival to be held.
Festivals are traditionally said to be of three kinds: those based on time, those based on faith, and those based on specific purposes;
one should observe them every year in whichever month one chooses.
And at one time, there may indeed be a festival of the season;
however, that which is performed with faith on a desired day in a desired month [is superior]. (BhS 24.4)
That, however, should be known as a festival of faith; therefore, it is a superior festival of time, [to be held] during occasions that cause fear, such as droughts and the like.
That which is performed there for the sake of pacification is known as the *nimittotsava* (auspicious festival).
On the day of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), one should perform the *saṃvatsarakara* rite toward the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
This is to be known as the Kālotsava, proclaimed for the sake of peace,
for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, and indeed for the advancement of kings.
One should perform auspicious rites for oneself and one's sons on the aforementioned occasions, as well as on the king’s birthday and on whatever day his festival of faith occurs.
The cessation of the emergence of wonders and so forth is the occasional festival;
if there is to be a festival in a village or similar place, one should perform it in this very sequence.
For the sake of pacifying all suffering and affliction, one should first perform a festival for Kālī,
and then for the other cruel deities and the assembly of virtuous spirits.
Thereafter, for the sake of pacification, one should perform the festival of Śaṅkara as prescribed by the Teacher;
and for the sake of pacifying the three classes of spirits, one should perform it through the gentle path in the sacred sites.
Furthermore, one should perform the festival of the Fort (Durgotsava) joined with Cakraseneśa,
[offering it] in every way to all the gods and even to all the sages.
And for the sake of the peace of the ancestors, the planets, and their wives in every respect, as well as for the twice-born and all people everywhere.
Thereafter, for the sake of nourishment, one should perform the festival of the Lord of Devas in due order;
otherwise, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of all.
Therefore, a wise person should especially avoid that [place] from a village,
and also during the equinoxes, solstices, the full moon, the installation of deities, and on the day of the constellation of the founder.
On the days of a planetary eclipse, on the lunar mansions of Āsana and Nakṣatra, on the five days of Viṣṇu,
and on the final day of a festival— one should consecrate a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) on these occasions.
One of these should be chosen according to the desire of the sacrificer,
on the occasion of the equinoxes, the solstices, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
One should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha-snāna) at those specific times and not otherwise;
on other lunar mansions, however, it may be done in the forenoon or at midday when endowed with auspicious qualities.
If there are two festival days for a sacred site within the same month,
the ancestral tradition holds that the festival occurs on the latter of those two days.
If that very [time] is pierced by the sun due to the transits and so forth, it should be avoided; likewise, what was previously described as praiseworthy [is now rejected].
If a lunar day (tithi) should extend across two days, and the same occurs on the subsequent day,
that intercalary month (adhimāsa) must be excluded from the rites for Hari’s seasonal festivals.
The conjunction of a Sunday with the Arka constellation (Pūrvaphalgunī) is always highly praised;
the conjunction of the twelfth lunar day with the Śravaṇa constellation bestows the fruits of all ritual actions.
And the yogas should be highly auspicious, known as Siddha, Amṛta, and Vara;
and on the following day, the lunar mansion should be connected with two lunar days (tithis).
If [the moonrise] should occur on the following day for as long as ten nāḍikās,
one should perform the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) after having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) on the previous day, provided it was deficient [on that day].
The highest [period] is three weeks; the middling should be fourteen days;
or nine days, or seven days—this is declared to be the lowest.
Having first performed three days of festive meals, one should make a proclamation;
on the middle day there should be twice that amount, and on the lowest festive day, [the same as] the beginning.
Alternatively, on the twenty-first day prior to the avabhṛtha bath,
having performed the hoisting of the banner, one should carry out the entire festival.
Bathing is most excellent during an eclipse of Rāhu and at the transits of the sun, even at night;
having completed the ritual at midday, if it occurs at night, the wise one should perform it in its entirety.
Having spent that time in diversion, one should perform the rites at that sacred ford for three fortnights,
or thirteen days, or eleven days, in succession.
One should perform it for nine days, or seven days, or again for five days;
or for three days, two days, or even for just one day.
One should not raise the banner on the sixth day and especially so at the beginning of a festival;
rather, one should have it proclaimed according to the prescribed rule from the first day of the festival onwards.
One should spend the time until the day of the proclamation for the offering of the seed-sprouts;
thereafter, I shall describe the flagstaffs for the Brahmins and others in their proper order. (BhS 24.32)
Having brought bamboo, the *jāti* tree, the *campaka*, and likewise the *kramuka* for the purpose of a flagstaff, one may use the *kramuka* for all [the Buddhas].
Or one may have it made from other auspicious trees; for what [trees] are not suitable?
Furthermore, the staff of the banner, the most excellent kind, should be twenty-four finger-breadths in circumference.
Therefore, the middle flagstaff is two finger-breadths shorter than that;
with a circumference of twenty finger-breadths, it is called the inferior staff.
Having taken hold of the straight flagpole according to its available length and without crooking it, one should make it as tall as the celestial palace.
One should make the vimāna increasingly larger by one-quarter, or half, or one-and-a-half times, or even one-and-three-quarters; it should gradually taper from the base to the top.
If a bamboo staff is to be taken up, it should be four finger-breadths long,
six finger-breadths in circumference, and well-proportioned.
Leaving two *yamas* in the middle of that, one should place a firm band in its center;
its length is two *tālas*, and its width is one *yama*.
The height is prescribed as one part, or it may be made of sacrificial wood; having divided that into four parts, one should discard two parts at the base and two at the top.
In the middle, however, two parts should be made, joined with two apertures;
having applied three segments in order from the base, the middle, and the tip.
One should perform the washing with the root mantra and the sprinkling with those specific mantras;
furthermore, one should place a *kūrca* (bundle) consisting of ten blades of *darbha* grass at the front.
Encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass, provided with a staff and a leaf of the *udumbara* tree,
it should have a circumference equal to the middle finger and a length twice that of the staff.
Having attached the rope to the tip of the staff, one should tie it right there;
then, having cleared a space of four tālas behind the leader of the herd.
Having caused a pit to be dug at the site of the flagpole to a depth of three *tālas* and having firmly leveled the ground,
one should worship it and cast jewels and seeds therein.
Having erected the banner there with the banner-mantra, the knower of mantras,
having gazed upon the God of gods, should place the staff at the front of that [altar].
One should make the flagstaff straight and have it made firm right there;
its height at the base should be three *tālas*, and its width should be one and a half times that.
Above that, one should place a firm, new cloth made of pure cotton, measuring one *ratni* in size, provided with eight petals and a pericarp. (BhS 24.48)
The best cloth is sixteen cubits, the middling is fifteen cubits, and the lowest is fourteen cubits; thus the cloth is said to be of three kinds.
Having understood that the tip, the foot, the face, and likewise the back are respectively five, four, three, and two *tālas* in width; BhS_24.50.
One should make the cloth four parts; one part shall be the head, two parts the place for the tail-feathers, and one part is said to be the tail.
One should properly apply the staff, including its tip and base;
in its middle, one should draw the Lord of the World (Viśa), adorned with five colors.

In the case of a stationary image (dhruvabera), the measurement up to the neck is the highest of the high; that up to the end [of the body] is the lowest of the low; and between those two, there are eight divisions ending at the navel.
The measurement of a single *magadhamāna* is said to be ninefold;
one should examine six auspicious signs on the staff of the banner and the *vīśa*.
Especially under a lunar mansion favorable to the patron,
[the image] should measure nine and a half *tālas* or even nine *tālas*.
With the body bent excessively and possessing three distinct curves,
one should contract the left leg and extend the right.
Slightly contracted, with the heels and sides raised from the seat,
joined by two wings, and adorned with a basket-shaped crown.
Dark blue, white, black, red, and likewise yellow—
with these five colors, which are appropriate and beautiful.
The wise one should form the gesture of Garuḍa with palms joined and gaze slightly upward;
he is adorned with the eight nāgas, and the serpent Ananta is upon his left hand.
Vāsuki is the sacrificial thread, Takṣaka is the waist-string,
Karkoṭaka is the necklace, and Padma is on the right ear.
He should place a great lotus on the left ear and a conch on the head in sequence;
a pill in the right hand and all the ornaments in sequence.
Above the head, a beautiful white parasol should be placed,
and on both sides, it should be joined with two fly-whisks.
On both sides of the feet, it should be provided with two lamps; and having specifically drawn a full water-pot between those two, // BhS_24.63 //
Having specifically painted a conch and a discus beneath it,
and having adorned it with pearl necklaces and the like, one should depict plantain trees on both sides.
On the very same day, having performed the opening of the eyes,
[one should do so] in front of the temple, in a water-shed, or in a pavilion.
Having adorned it with five colors using canopies and pillar-wrappings, and having prepared a heap of rice, one should properly place that cloth-painting upon it.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire;
after causing the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the northeast, at the fire-pit, having prepared the seat according to the rules and having performed the *āghāra* oblation according to the ritual, the Vaiṣṇava oblation is then duly offered.
Having recited that mantra, one should perform the opening of the eyes with gold-colored powder placed in a golden vessel, especially using golden tūlikā-brushes.
Then, having performed the ancillary oblations (aṅgahoma), he should cause [the deity] to be beheld by those worthy of seeing him;
and having offered oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta as well as the Puruṣasūktas.
Having offered oblations ending with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, he should then take up the water-pot,
wrap it with a thread, provide it with a *kūrca* grass-bundle, and include unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and the Gāyatrī of Garuḍa, and muttering in sequence the mantras beginning with "iṣe tvorje tvā" and "āpa undantu," [he should proceed]. (BhS 24.72)
Then, being composed, he should touch that water with the *kūrca* while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta* and the Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Then one should perform the sprinkling with water using the tips of *kuśa* grass;
[one should sprinkle] with the verses beginning with "The waters are golden-colored" (*apo hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*) and with the three verses beginning with "Pavamāna."
Having recited "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye" and the Puruṣasūkta along with the Vaiṣṇava hymns,
one should sprinkle [the site] for the sake of purification and cause the proclamation of "puṇyāha" (an auspicious day) to be made.
Having sprinkled water around the fire, one should subsequently offer oblations with that mantra;
at the conclusion of the evening worship, however, one should perform the worship of the jar.
Having sprinkled [the site] with seven water-jars and tied on a protective cord (apratisara),
one should then spread out the five grains, beginning with those born from eggs, together with cloth.
One should likewise cause [the sacrificer] to lie down on the bed with his head toward the east;
at that time, having praised the office of the Hotṛ, the Hotṛ indeed performs the duties according to the sequence of the Hotṛ's ritual.
One should perform the invocation of his form with the mantra of Vainateya;
having invoked him with the mantras of the forms, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and sacrifice.
“Let the ‘Śatadhāra’ hymn, which is proclaimed as a protective mantra, be recited;
likewise, let the Vaiṣṇava hymn consisting of twelve verses be well-offered.”
Having performed the ritual up to the *vyāhṛtis* and having passed the remainder of the night,
one should place [the drum] upon a bherī drum in the southeast and invoke Nandikeśvara.
Again, at dawn, having performed the ritual bath according to the dharma,
when the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has arrived, one should place the seed-syllable within the heart.
Having invoked the Śakti from the pitcher and worshipped her according to the prescribed rite,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, and having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly, one should present [the offering].
Having kindled the fire, one should offer oblations ten times each in sequence with those mantras;
having caused the concluding oblation to be recited, and having worshipped [the deity], one should present the offering.
Having smeared the cloth and subsequently adorned it with five colors,
and having decorated it with incense and lamps, one should prepare an offering of cooked rice.
Having made it square and even, with a width of one part,
half a *śāli* grain is said to be the measure for rice, and half of that should be taken for sesame.
Having placed the discus on the west, situated upon the seat of grain, and likewise Viṣvaksena on its northern side; BhS_24.87.
Having firmly established Garuḍa facing west upon a seat of grain,
and having placed the drum at his side, one should properly set down the staff.
Having thoroughly worshipped the God of gods, one should then worship him twice as much;
it is taught that the sacrificial oblation for the two goddesses should likewise be double.
One should arrange the wheels and other implements separately, and likewise the seats and so forth individually;
having thus worshipped Nandīśvara, one should offer oblations of sacrificial food.
The preceptor, taking up his staff and uttering "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," and having recited the mantra "Upa śvāsaya," should strike the drum. (BhS 24.91)
The proponent, having become pure and adorned with garments, garlands, and so forth,
and being learned in the scriptures, should take up a drum accompanied by all musical instruments.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should strike the front of the wheel with *droṇas*,
half-*droṇas*, or *āḍhakas* of rice.
Having cooked [the food], one should place the supreme bali offering into the pit,
taking with it mung beans, niṣpāva beans, tilva seeds, parched grain, and cakes.
Having carefully placed it in a vessel, the disciple should carry it on his head,
having first saluted the banner and taken up that which is well-adorned.
Having placed [the image] upon a chariot or a palanquin with mantras and auspicious rites,
and having again gathered flowers and an offering in a vessel, one should follow behind it.
Then the preceptor, having gone before, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, should lead those immeasurable lords of the world like a protector.
To the deities such as Brahmā and others residing in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) in their respective order,
and to the gatekeepers and the guardians of the temple at the doors.
One should offer oblations to the other retinues in their respective places;
having gone outside the dwelling, one should proclaim it throughout the entire village.
In the center, one should move that which is without movement, performing [the rites] from Brahmā to Īśāna;
in whichever direction the abode may be, one should cast the bali offering starting from that direction.
One should perform the festive circumambulation in a clockwise direction;
having gone to the village, one should especially do so at every junction.
Having meditated and understood the presiding deities, the mantra-practitioner should invoke them upon the ground as before;
having worshipped them up to the offering of water (arghya), he should present the food in his fist while reciting their names.
At the junction, having taken that junction, [he offers] to the "Beings" (bhūta) in the east;
to the "Gods" (deva) in the south; and to the "Rākṣasas" in the west.
Then, further north from the Nāgas, one should again offer water in the upward direction with the wheel [of mantras], using the mantra beginning with "Ye bhūtāḥ. (BhS 24.104)
One should offer flowers, a bali-oblation, and likewise incense in the vicinity of the wheel;
or one may offer the bali-oblation in whichever direction the celestial palace (vimāna) of Brahmā and the other gods resides.
Or else, one should perform the bali offering for the lords of the directions in their proper order;
if the pavilion is situated in the west, one should offer the bali beginning with Varuṇa.
Alternatively, if [the ritual] is performed in the middle of a village, one should first offer the *brahmabali* and then cast the *bhūtabali* for the guardians of the directions.
If a junction (saṃdhi) occurs specifically on the Great Path (mahāvīthī) between two lords of the directions, one should offer an oblation (bali) there to the spirits (bhūta).
If one, out of delusion or due to the nature of the work, should perform a joint that falls within the interior of a joint, a failure will certainly occur. (BhS 24.109)
One should draw the eastern end first, then the western end, and a single row of staffs;
there, one should fashion the wheels and so forth, and then perform the offering (bali) starting from the west.
Likewise, one should offer the bali-offering to Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Vāyu in the west;
and one should cast the bali-offering in the middle, together with Dhātṛ, Yama, and Kubera.
One should offer [the oblation] to Indra, Vāyu, and the Rudras in the east, and then in sequence;
if there is a single path ending in the north, one should cast the offering starting from the south.
And likewise, one should offer the bali-oblation to Yama, Nila, and Anala in the south and the center, and to Brahma, Varuna, and Sakra in the north.
One should offer oblations (bali) to the gods and others in sequence within the pavilion;
if there is a temple (vimāna), one should offer them around it, or else in the courtyard.
Having first offered the bali-oblation, the wise one should again recite the previously mentioned mantra for each [deity] and proclaim it in both prose and verse.

In cities and other such places, however, the wise man, having praised [the teaching] with prose, should cause it to be proclaimed by means of drums and the like, while reciting the respective mantra in a low voice.
“May the Blessed Viṣṇu, Hari, the lord of all worlds,
together with Brahmā and Īśa, be pleased and grant us favor during this festival.”
The gods, all the sages, the ancestors, the planetary deities, and others—
all who have gone to the world of Viṣṇu and all those dwelling in the Nānā worlds— [are present].
May all other deities, together with their entire retinues,
come here respectfully to this sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
"Having taken the sacrificial offering and the bali, may [the deities], bestowers of auspiciousness, partake [of them].
Having said this, he should again proclaim [this] at the junction facing the wheel.
Furthermore, the proclaimer should announce Brahmā and the others with their respective rhythmic beats;
and having thus offered the bali-oblation, he should perform a circumambulation in a clockwise direction.
Having recited the Śākuna hymn, he should enter the temple again;
he should also offer the remnants of the bali-oblation upon the *bhūtapīṭha* with the mantra "To all beings."
Then one should throw the offering and the remaining water into the vicinity of the wheel;
having performed the circumambulation of the temple with the banner and other imperishable symbols.
Furthermore, the wise one, knowing the mantra, should place the peaceful wheel back in its proper position;
having entered the site of the banner, the knower of mantras should take up the banner.
With the mantra “svasti dā,” the wise man should bind it with a cord, facing either eastward or northward. (BhS 24.125)
Thereafter, one should join it to the tip of the staff, equipped with a conch and a kāhala trumpet;
having bound it firmly again, one should then mutter the mantra "bhūr asi" while applying oil.
After consecrating the banner with mantras, one should worship it with a seat and other offerings;
thereafter, one should have the proclamation of an auspicious day made, and offer green-gram rice to the banner.
Having offered mouth-perfume, one should also cause him to perform a prostration;
at that time, food made of mung beans is offered to Garuḍa.
Women desiring sons should eat that with devotion,
so that they may give birth to one who is long-lived, strong, healthy, self-controlled, and endowed with auspicious marks.
The preceptor, endowed with meditative concentration, should certainly please Viśva with hymns of praise so that she may give birth to a son who is wise and illustrious. (BhS 24.130)
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Lord of Birds; obeisance to you whose body is the Veda;
obeisance to Tārkṣya, the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, possessed of immeasurable splendor. (BhS 24.131)
Homage to you, O Garuḍa, the death of all the lords of serpents;
O Vainateya, mighty-armed one, of great strength, sovereign of birds!
O Lord of Birds, homage be to you, who uprooted the Kalpaka tree,
who brought back the vessel of nectar, and who liberated your mother from slavery.
Homage to you, the conqueror of the lords of gods and asuras, who are unassailable even by the lords of nāgas;
homage to you, whose support is that upon which all this world rests.
He whose two wings are the Bṛhat-sāman and the Rathantara,
whose two eyes are the Gāyatrī and the Trivṛt-sāman, and who is himself the head.
Homage to Him whose self is the *stoma*, who is perfected in the limbs of the *vāmadevya* chant;
homage to the Lord of the vital breaths and other winds, whose self is Garuḍa.
O Lord of Birds, O destroyer of enemies, in battle you have cast off the armor of the asuras by means of the abundance of wind from the waves of your flapping wings.
Established upon this cloth, salutations to you whose form is the Praṇava;
O Lord of Birds, being invoked, bring about the accomplishment of our rites.
"Remove our faults and bring forth virtues in every way;
destroy all obstacles and take me also into yourself."
Having thus offered praise, one should recite the Gāruḍa mantra with a one-pointed mind,
especially while keeping it in mind throughout the duration of the flag's hoisting.
Whether three times a day, twice, once, or even at a single time,
having properly offered the sacrificial oblation with the twenty-seven forms [of the mantra], ||| BhS_24.141 ||
Having worshipped the banner, one should afterwards offer a bali-oblation to the spirits at night, [reciting]:
"Victory! O highly exalted, auspicious banner! Thus [one addresses] the banner.
Likewise, one should place Indra and the others at the base of the banner, Brahmā on the staff, and the Sun, Moon, and Fire on the three crossbars; Sudarśana is placed on the shaft.
Then one should worship the three forms [of the deity] upon the bracelet, the armlet, and the cord;
likewise, Brahmā upon the bell and Sarasvatī upon the ring of *darbha* grass.
Having invoked [the deity] in this sequence, one should perform worship with their respective mantras,
beginning from the hoisting of the banner until the day before the festival begins.
In the evening and in the morning, at the conclusion of the worship, the disciple and the teacher should likewise offer an oblation facing the mandala, as in the rite of hoisting the banner.
The wise one should always, and especially at night, offer the bali-oblation to the spirits until the end of the sacred ford on every night,
except for the two days of Viśākhā and Maitra.
The wise man should carry the alms-bowl itself for the sake of protecting his strength,
remaining constantly composed until the raising of the flag.
Whether three times a day, twice a day, or even once a day,
having worshipped according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should present [the offering].
And who among those villagers there do not perform the hoisting of the banner even at night, starting from the day the festival begins?
Those who are preoccupied with other tasks should not go to another assembly;
or if they do go, they should return to the sacred site (tīrtha) without fail.
But in that village on the outer path, all the people likewise did not show such persistence toward those staying nearby as had been recorded [before].
The deities who are to be invoked for the sake of festivals have been correctly proclaimed;
now the locations for all those beginning with the gods shall be described.
Indra and the others are stationed in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
likewise are the eleven Rudras and the twelve suns as well.
The Vasus shall be eight, as well as Oṃkāra and Vaṣaṭkṛta;
these are the thirty-three gods declared by Brahmā in the past.
Some wise ones say that the Aśvins are also there;
the northeastern quarter is said to be the station of the thirty-three deities.
Furthermore, others should also be constructed specifically on the banks of rivers,
to the south of the Bhūtapīṭha of the eighteen classes.
The gods and all the sages, the ancestors, the Daityas and Dānavas,
the Asuras, the Gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases.
Yakṣas and rākṣasas, nāgas, bhūtas, and piśācas,
as well as hosts of drought-bringers and hosts of those who bring immortal nectar.
The mothers are indeed the Rohiṇīs, known as the eighteen Sūryās;
these eighteen groups are declared to be the divine origins.
One should worship the other deities not mentioned here at the side of Indra;
and one should worship the wives of the gods at the respective sides of those [deities].
To Skanda, Vighna, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Sarasvatī,
one should offer the bali-oblation in their temple, or on the northern part of the enclosure wall.
In the place mentioned in the *Parivāra*, one should likewise worship Rohiṇī, the Mothers, and those seven wives of the sages together with the sages themselves. (BhS 24.163)
