One should worship the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Cāraṇas, and Devas in the great directions.
Furthermore, at each juncture, one should offer an oblation to the spirits (bhūta), the yakṣas, the piśācas, as well as to the rākṣasas and the nāgas.
In the middle of the courtyard of the royal palace, one should worship Indra;
on his right side, however, one should worship Jaya, Śrī, and Kīrti.
Then, for the sake of the festival, one should especially procure the necessary materials,
such as chariots, palanquins, and likewise mechanical swings and the like.
Having had [the lamps] fashioned according to the instructions of the artisans, and having taken up other lamps as well as musical instruments such as kettledrums, conchs, and trumpets, [he set out].
One should bring palm-leaf fans, other banners, umbrellas, chowries, and peacock-feather fans,
as well as dancers and other singers, just as previously described.
Having beautifully adorned the inner chamber and decorated it with archways and other ornaments,
he should summon his attendants and inform them of their respective duties.
One who is learned in the treatises on the arts should cause all types of pavilions, water-stalls, and so forth, as well as places for seating and dancing, to be constructed in every respect.
With the mantra "ava dhūta," pure Brahmins learned in the Vedas should especially purify the streets of the village in a pleasing manner.
Having uttered "The seven directions," one should sprinkle auspicious substances such as cow-products everywhere, smear the ground, and scatter rice grains. (BhS 24.173)
One should decorate the courtyard of the house with plantains, betel-nut trees, water-jars, and the like; one should especially beautify it on all sides with canopies and other auspicious items.
All the inhabitants of that village, adorned and intent on nothing else,
should— setting aside astrological omens and the like— meditate upon Hari with their minds.

O wise ones, one who resides within the boundary of that village should not perform occasional (naimittika) or optional (kāmya) rites at other sacred sites, except for the performance of obligatory daily duties (nityakarman).
When the festival of Viṣṇu has commenced within the dwellings according to the gentle path,
it is the injunction that one should not perform the festival of another deity there.
During this festival of the gods, in this sacrifice, and especially within its precincts, one should prepare the northern altar; once it has begun, one should not perform other rites.
If total destruction were to occur, the doer and the sustainer would perish;
therefore, a wise person should avoid those who have vomited [their impurities] at the edge of sacred fords.
Seven or five days prior to the day of the festival and other such occasions,
having bathed the Lord of the Gods, one should perform the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on miscellaneous matters, in the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter:
the ritual for festivals (*utsavavidhi*).
Now I shall describe the procedure for the festival of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
prior to the day of its commencement, the patron, filled with joy, [should act as follows].
Having thus chosen a preceptor endowed with the previously mentioned qualities—
one for the sake of twofold service and one for the worship of the water-jar (kumbha)— BhS_25.2 //
For the purpose of the fire-oblation, for the offering of food-bali, and likewise for the worship of the site,
he should select five seekers of alms as many attendants.
Having approached the teacher and honored him according to the prescribed rule, one should request him with humility, saying: "Please perform this rite for me. (BhS 25.4)
The teacher, together with his disciples, having shaved off their hair and so forth,
and having bathed according to the rules for bathing, should put on washed garments in accordance with the prescribed ritual.

Having properly worn the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other rites, and having likewise performed the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) as well as the libations to the gods and sages (devarṣitarpaṇa); BhS_25.6 //
Having entered the sanctuary and prostrated before the Lord of Gods, one should recite the twelve hymns, as well as those dedicated to Nārāyaṇa and Aruṇa. (BhS 25.7)
Having especially worshipped the deity,
the righteous sacrificer, having completed his daily rites, should present his request to him.
Having entered the temple, one should then perform the rite for an auspicious day according to the procedure for the honey-mixture (madhuparka) as prescribed in the Śrī Vaikhānasa Sūtra.
Then, having honored the preceptor and the officiating priests according to the prescribed rite,
one should likewise adorn them with perfumes and other offerings, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth.
With a new upper garment and so forth, as well as the five-fold ornaments,
I shall describe the five-fold ornamentation and how one should perform it with vigilance.
An earring ornament weighing ten niṣkas each,
a bracelet, an armlet, and a finger-ring, each measuring six niṣkas.
The waist-band, possessing the proper characteristics, should be enriched with twenty-one gold coins;
separately, the neck-ornament should be of a measurement equal to half that portion.
One should have the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) made with a measurement of eight *niṣkas*;
according to this rule, one should provide for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) half of what is given to the preceptor (*guru*).
The teacher, having sprinkled himself with water, as well as the patron and the officiating priests,
should then consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and respectfully offer it to those seeking its benefits.
One should especially give it to the sacrificer preceded by the mantra;
then, having established the fire upon a lotus and having sprinkled water around the purifier, [one should proceed].
The preceptor should offer oblations with clarified butter using the four hymns beginning with "yad devāḥ," and he should worship the sacrificial fire with the Vaiśvānara hymn.
Having thus exhausted their evil, they then become worthy of [receiving] the ritual;
therefore, the Kūśmāṇḍa-homa is taught as the destroyer of all sins.

At that time, all those who have been initiated, having first performed the ritual with the mantras and having tied the protective cord (pratisara) on their hands, should then perform the rite as well.
From that time forward, they all had clean teeth and nails;
they ate sacrificial food (haviṣya), were self-controlled, and bathed at the three times of day.
They should have their senses conquered, sleep on the ground,
refrain from conversing with women or Śūdras, and be solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
As long as the initiation remains valid, these [initiates] are considered pure;
even during birth-impurity or death-impurity, no ritual impurity is prescribed for them.
Now I shall describe the procedure for taking the earth for the sake of the seed-sprout:
having worshipped the peaceful wheel and having also offered the oblations.
Taking Viṣvaksena and placing him upon a vehicle like a protector, the preceptor should go in front, uttering the mantra: "May Viṣṇu protect me."
Accompanied by the preceptor, they should follow behind the wheel,
carrying a mirror, a golden vase, full jars, auspicious sprouts, and so forth.
Placing all objects such as the three banners and so forth in front,
those seeking wealth will find total prosperity in the east, but there will be a loss of grain in the southeast.
In the south there shall be the destruction of people; in the southwest, the loss of wealth;
in the west, drought; and in the northwest, royal wrath.
In the north there shall be abundance of sons, and in the northeast it will be a giver of happiness;
in the midst of these directions, one should take auspicious and pure earth.
The teacher, equipped with the necessary implements and accompanied by his disciples, having gone toward a certain direction,
should go to a delightful grove near a village temple.
On the bank of a river or a pond, without overstepping the boundary,
one should take earth from a pure spot after propitiating the deity of the ground with mantras.
The wise man should place the two Viśāmitas and the disc facing east;
having smeared the ground while facing east himself, he should draw a circular shape.
There, having sprinkled the site while reciting "Dadhi krāvṇa," and having drawn the form of the earth while saying "Bhūmir bhūmnā," [one should proceed]. (BhS 25.32)
Having worshipped that goddess Mahī, who lies with her face turned upward in the northeast and whose crown is placed [there], one should perform the sprinkling with ritual ablutions.
One should worship with the eleven services using the mūrti-mantras,
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited while pronouncing the names of the earth and the other elements.
Having worshipped the remainder [of the clay] in the spade, which has been well-adorned with garments and other offerings,
one should apply it to the forehead— which destroys all defects— and to the two arms— which bestows great happiness.
One may never take earth from her two breasts (indicating the increase of age), nor from her belly (indicating all prosperity), nor from her lower parts. BhS 25.36.
Having thus resolved with his mind, he then spoke to the earth and the other elements, while mentally recollecting the Boar-form [of Viṣṇu], with the mantra: "I shall dig you up. (BhS 25.37)
Having obtained permission from the goddess Earth, the wise man should dig into the ground with both hands and a spade to a depth of one palm-span.
Having removed all that [impurity], one should take away the clay beneath it;
having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, one should perform the ritual action there.
Having placed it well within the vessel, one should place it on the head as before;
afterwards, having dismissed the Goddess, one should fill that [vessel] with water.
Having borne [the image] upon his head, and having circumambulated the village from the east toward the Cakra and Śānti shrines, he should approach the temple.
Likewise, one should offer sprouts on the eastern and northern sides,
having consecrated the wheels and other implements and properly presented the sacrificial oblation.
Having established [the deities] each in their own respective place, one should thereafter commence the sacrifice,
either facing the *alaya* or to the south, in a pleasant location.
One should practice between Yama and Agni, or in the portion belonging to Agni;
or else in the northeast, or according to some, likewise in the space between Soma and Īśāna.
One should construct the sacrificial hall according to the procedure prescribed for consecration,
and in the middle row thereof, one should have an altar made according to the measurement of the altar.
For the consecration and other rites, the wise one should likewise arrange five fires in sequence, measuring half a cubit or one cubit in height, during the highest festival.
The wise one should arrange the three sacrificial fires in the central pavilion in due order;
however, if it is an inferior assembly, the intelligent one should arrange them as before.

In that [ritual] where the establishment of the three fires is primary, one should likewise establish the Gārhapatya as the principal fire for both of the other two, namely the Sabhya and the Āvasathya.
Just as in a ground sacrifice, the most excellent guru should purify everything everywhere according to the ritual rules, having taken up the deity and the two goddesses at the bathing pit.
One should especially install [the deity] with the mantra "paraṃ raṃha," having bathed the supreme Hari according to the method prescribed for the daily bath.
Having placed a seat upon a suitable spot, one should spread a cloth over it;
then, having taken up the deity and the two goddesses, one should adorn them with white garments.
One should also adorn him with ornaments such as earrings, armlets, and necklaces;
having decorated him with white garlands and white fragrant ointments.
Having put on a sacred thread and an upper garment, and having prostrated before the deity,
the supreme guide should perform the services and other rites as one would for a king.
The wise one, having taken up nine jars according to the previously mentioned procedure, should likewise wrap them with thread while reciting the mantra, "Indraṃ naro na... (RV 8.96.1). BhS 25.54.
Having spread the aforementioned grains upon the altar, the knower of mantras,
having divided it into nine squares with four lines, should arrange the jars.
Having filled the jars with water, one should place within each jar separately auspicious items such as bundles of *kuśa* grass, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), weapons, and gems.
Having likewise placed [the materials] while chanting the Gāyatrī, one should especially deposit them into the central jar;
the sacrificial ladles and other implements should also be [placed] at a distance of two finger-breadths, as before.
Having performed the rite with the *hānaka* mantra, one should deposit them while reciting the *Viṣṇusūkta*,
wrapping each of them individually within a pair of cloths.
Having first placed the *vīśa* facing west upon the altar to the east,
one should then place the discus facing north to the south.
One should place Paṅktīśa, facing east, upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or alternatively facing west, north,
or south for the rite of pacification.
In the absence of the Garuḍa and other [deities], having placed water-pots in their respective locations here and there, one should meditate upon them in their midst and invoke them in due order.
As long as the conclusion of the ritual bath has not been reached, the wise one should especially worship the attendants according to the rules with water-pots every morning and evening.
Thereafter, standing facing north on the southern side of the altar, one should perform the *āghāra* libation according to the rules in the fire-pit of the assembly hall.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should practice meditation as before;
within the central vessel of the primary [element], one should meditate upon Viṣṇu and the two goddesses together with their lineage.
The practitioner of mantras should invoke Dhruva and the others in due order, starting from the east:
Puruṣa, Kapila, Satya, Yajña, and Acyuta.
Then one should worship the meritorious Nārāyaṇa and Aniruddha—
him who is golden-hued, with a red face and red eyes, the bringer of happiness.
Wearing a crown, necklaces, armlets, and a long sacred thread, his chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem; he bore the Śrīvatsa mark and possessed four arms.
With his right hand he bestows fearlessness upon his devotees,
while with his other left hand he rests it upon his own hip.
With his two other hands, he holds the supreme conch and discus;
he is Viṣṇu, clad in peacock feathers, whose form is the Praṇava.
Resembling molten gold, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
she was adorned above her forehead by three crests of flowers.
With her left hand ending in a lotus, her thick breasts bound by a bodice, her other arm extended, and her face resembling the bright moon; BhS_25.71 //
[She] who has the Śrīvatsa marked at the end of her seed-syllable, who was born from the Uttara constellation in the month of Phālguna,
who stands on the right side of Viṣṇu, and who is borne by a vehicle drawn by swans.
On his left side is the Earth, dark-complexioned and adorned with all ornaments;
she was born under the constellation Revatī in the month of Vaiśākha, and she holds a lotus in her right hand.
With one hand extended and the other drawn back, her face resembling the bright moon,
she is mounted upon a great cātaka bird and endowed with the first syllable of the word "Lakṣmī."
The person is facing east, radiant, wearing yellow garments, four-armed,
bearing a conch and a discus, glorious, and adorned with all ornaments.
In the east is Hari, the granter of boons and the giver of fearlessness, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi;
he is Kapila, facing east, of brilliant luster, wearing red garments, and endowed with eight arms.
With his right hand alone, like a single hand, he bestows fearlessness upon his devotees;
with his other hands he holds a discus, a sword, and a plow, and he is adorned with all ornaments.
And with his other left hand he rested upon his own hip;
with the remaining hands he held a conch and a bow-staff, his form being most beautiful.
In the southeastern direction is Hari, joined with the Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī;
he faces south, is glorious, has the luster of collyrium, and possesses four arms.
Bearing the conch and the discus, gentle, adorned with all ornaments,
bestowing boons and fearlessness, virtuous, clad in red garments, and possessing large jaws.
Accompanied by the two goddesses Dhṛti and Pauṣṇī,
the Lord Yajña faces the western direction from the southern quarter, possessing the luster of molten gold.
Seven cubits tall, with four horns, clad in red garments, and having two heads;
[he holds] a conch, a discus, a vessel of clarified butter, a *sruk*, a *sruva*, an *upabhṛt*, and a *juhū* ladle.
The god who bears three feet, joined with Svāhā and Svadhā, resides in the southwest;
he is the Imperishable One (Acyuta), facing the western direction, golden-hued, and four-armed.
The glorious one, bearing the conch and the discus, adorned with all ornaments,
the bestower of boons and fearlessness, the witness, the giver of the fruits of all actions.
Joined with the earth and the purifier (water), in the western direction, Nārāyaṇa has a dark blue garment,
a western face, the luster of crystal, and four arms.
The glorious one, bearing the conch and the discus, adorned with all ornaments,
the bestower of boons and the giver of fearlessness, clad in dark blue garments and marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Joined with Kamalā and Ilā, the Lord of the worlds, Aniruddha, faces the north; he has four arms and the luster of coral. (BhS 25.87)
Seated upon the lap of Ananta, Hari wears garments of flowers;
he is the glorious one, bearing the conch and the discus, and adorned with all ornaments.
Holding the earth, which bestows great joy, in his left hand while holding [the gesture of] generosity in his right,
the God, the giver of boons and the dispeller of fear, bestows all accomplishments in the northern direction.
He is meritorious, facing the east, glorious, resembling the young sun;
he has the Śrīvatsa on his chest, possesses eternal splendor, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Four-armed, marked with the conch, the discus, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness,
he is beautifully adorned with a white upper garment, a sacred thread, and other ornaments.
Having invoked these deities— Indra, Dharaṇīnātha, and Puṇyapuruṣa in the northeast— and having worshipped them with the eight forms, [one should proceed].
One should worship Viśāna, Sāyi, Paṅktīśa, and Śānta in the directions in due order;
[one should worship] the Lord in the morning and evening together with these [deities], excluding Viśāna and the others, without the water-pots (kumbhas).
Some say that one should worship [the fire] after having established it upon the altar; others say that,
following the praise of the Hotṛ,
the Hotṛ should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire behind [the altar].
Then, having invoked the deities residing in that temple according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter and perform worship in that same sequence.
Having sprinkled water around the fire, one should subsequently offer oblations to Viṣṇu in due order,
specifically on the western side of the altar or, preferably, in the northwest.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there,
the preceptor, together with the patron, should spread out the birds and other [offerings] after bowing to the deity.
Having cast down a handful of flowers while reciting "pra tad viṣṇuḥ," he should take the Lord of Gods together with his two goddesses and place them upon the sacrificial mound.
Having established [the image] facing east, one should worship it with the eight forms,
especially in the absence of a festival image or during the ritual bathing.
If the ritual bathing is not available, one should perform it during the consecration;
however, if the two goddesses are not present at the consecration, one should not perform it in that manner.
The wise one should not heed constant deficiencies in the rites of emission and inhalation; rather, he should perform the festival and the daily worship according to the proper sequence.
If one should perform it with constant deficiency, total destruction will certainly occur;
however, if the wise person performs the bathing during the middle of the festival, [it is auspicious].
If the occasion for a ceremonial bath has arrived, one should perform the bathing ritual during the festival;
even in the absence of a bathing image, if it is during a festival, one should perform the bathing ritual.
In this context, during the ritual bathing and the consecration ceremony, one should not perform the festival without [the proper rite];
one should certainly avoid confusion, for it would be improper to practice both in such a manner.
But if, while a festival is underway, a ceremonial bathing should take place during the period of curiosity,
one should perform both rites at the time prescribed for them.
But in the case of an action already begun in the past, no fault would arise from this;
if there is a desire for austerity, one should act as if performing many rites in a single fire.
In the home, one should constantly maintain the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*) as if they were established without the need for formal re-establishment (*āropaṇa*);
however, on the occasion of bathing and festival rites, this should be done daily with the *kautuka* thread.
If there should be an ascent upon a tree, that rite should be performed as before;
having invoked [the deity] at the beginning of the rite, one should likewise dismiss [him] at the conclusion of the rite in the evening.
The invocation into the vessel (pātrāvāhana) should be performed daily, especially at the beginning of worship;
the dismissal (visarga) occurs at the end of the evening worship, while in the case of a ritual image (kautuka), it may be done as appropriate.

In the same way, at the conclusion of the festive initiation (utsava-dīkṣā), the wise one, having invoked [the deity] from the Dhruva [level], should not perform the dismissal (visarga) in the interim; rather, he should perform it at the very end of the initiation.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should especially cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made;
moreover, a golden amulet should be placed upon rice in a golden vessel.
Having performed the ritual renunciation as before, the wise one should bind [the thread] on the right hand;
having properly bound the jars, the two goddesses, the wheels, and so forth, he should worship them.
Having sprinkled water around the fire, one should subsequently offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, and the Śrīsūkta and Bhūsūkta.
The presiding deity of the daily twilight, the presiding deities of the lunar day, the weekday, and the asterism,
as well as the presiding deity of the month and the presiding deity of the year.
Then, one should offer oblations to those residing in the Ālaya by means of the forms in sequence;
it should end with the *vyāhṛtis* for the principal deity, and thereafter in the Āhavanīya fire.
And likewise, one should recite the Nṛsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymn in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
At the domestic fire (āvasathya), one should worship with the Mahīsūkta and the Ekākṣara mantra;
then, in the Paiṇḍarīka fire, one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn beginning with "vato devā."
The Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, that which is endowed with the "Yad devā" hymn and so forth, as well as the mantras pertaining to the Supreme Self, and those belonging to Brahmā, Indra, and Varuṇa.
One should offer one hundred and eight white lotuses soaked in ghee with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī for the pacification of all defects. (BhS 25.119)
Alternatively, having established the single fire (ekāgni), one should offer oblations, even the lowest of the low;
and one should perform the assembly hall fire-offering (sabhya-homa) as previously described, according to the Vaiṣṇava and other injunctions.
Now, the presiding deities of festivals will be explained in detail: those of Brahmā, the Ṛṣis, Rudra, Indra, Soma, and Viṣṇu. (BhS 25.121)
In the ninth-day rite, there are the offerings to all the gods, to Yama, and to Varuṇa;
as well as those to Agni, Prajāpati, Kubera, and Viṣṇu.
And [the hymns] dedicated to Śrī, Kaumāra, Āditya, and Raudra;
likewise those dedicated to Durgā, Indra, Yama, Viṣṇu, and Skanda. BhS 25.123.
The northeast and the north are said to be presided over by the lunar days (tithis);
one should offer oblations at each respective gate with the mantras appropriate for the lords of those gates.
Likewise, the wise man should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite to the deities of the lunar mansions;
at the three junctions of the day, he should sacrifice to Indra, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati in succession.
The presiding deity of the lunar mansion that governs a month is called the "deity of the month.
These are [the months] belonging to Yama, Viṣṇu, Soma, Brahmā, and likewise Bṛhaspati.
The lunar, the Aindra, the Vāruṇa, the Śeṣa, the Āgneya, the Āditya, the Bhautika, the Māruta, the one presided over by Bhṛgu, the second Vāruṇa, and the Vaighna; BhS 25.127.
The Raudra, the Kauberaka, the Tvāṣṭra, the Maitra, and the Kaumāra;
likewise the Sāvitrī, that which has Śrī as its deity, and that which has Gaurī as its deity.
The wise one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite to Āditya, to the Pitṛs, to Aditi as the deity, and to Yoga as the deity.
The [mantras] dedicated to Indra and Prajāpati, as well as those to Mitra and Aryaman;
likewise those with Bhūta, Śrī, and Yama as deities, and those dedicated to Bhṛgu and Vṛṣa.
One should indeed offer oblations to Kaubera and Vāyu among the Karaṇas; and with the mantra "To the gods and to the ancestors," one should offer on both the bright and dark fortnights.
One should offer oblations to the Sun and the Moon in sequence during the two solstices;
one should offer oblations to "Madhu" and "Mādhava" in sequence during the seasons.
Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Śūlin, Vighneśa, the seven sages (ṛṣis), the eight lords of the worlds, and the five elements beginning with Viśvaṃbhara; // BhS_25.133 //
The eight Vasus, the seven Rohiṇīs, Śrī, Caṇḍikā, Guha, Sūrya, Soma, Cirañjīvī, Kāśī, Vīra, and Purandara.
Cakra, Śānta, Guru, Bhauma, Budha, Śukra, and Śanaiścara; Haviḥpāla, Anasta, Gaṅgā, and Jyeṣṭhā are the Mothers.
These lords of the year are to be understood in sequence starting from Prabhava;
likewise [are determined] the presiding deities of festivals, as well as the deities of the lunar days, weekdays, and constellations.
One should offer oblations consisting merely of the four deities; what else could it be?
[The wood of] the Palāśa, Bilva, Śamī, Nyagrodha, and likewise Udumbara [should be used]. (BhS 25.137)
These trees—the Ashvattha, Khadira, Plaksha, and Brahmavriksha—are to be taken respectively for sacrificial fuel; or else, one may take leaves from only the Ashvattha tree.
The lotus, the bilva leaf, the karavīra, the kumuda,
as well as the nandyāvarta, the tulasī, and likewise the land-lotus.
These flowers—viṣṇukrāntā and rāvinde—are used in successive order; however, if they are unavailable, one may use tulasī, karavīra, or a lotus.
Mudga beans, niṣpāvaka beans, kuluttha beans, and māṣa beans,
as well as sesame seeds, cakes, parched grain, barley, and groats, in due order.
The materials for the bali-offering have been described; however, if none of these are available, one should use mung beans.
In this very manner, one should perform the fire-oblation twice a day.
At the conclusion of the morning twilight and at the conclusion of the evening worship,
having performed the fire-oblation, one should present the bali offering and perform the festival twice a day.
I shall describe the festival procession of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
it takes place especially in the evening and morning at the conclusion of the offering of oblations to Bali.
Having adorned the God of gods with garments and auspicious ornaments,
as well as with fragrant flower garlands and captivating perfumes.
Whether in a chariot, or in a palanquin, or likewise on the shoulder of a porter; or in an elephant, a horse, a swing, or any other well-adorned vehicle.
“Having established the deity immovably with the mantra ‘I am indeed this,’ and having worshipped him with the eightfold offerings as well as parched grain, cakes, and so forth... (BhS 25.147)
Having offered prepared foods mixed with jaggery, and having given mouth-fresheners accompanied by musical instruments and all kinds of ornaments, ||| BhS_25.148 |||
It was accompanied by female slaves and musicians provided with dance and song,
and joined by Brahmins learned in the Vedas, all proceeding very slowly.
It was provided with banners, parasols, sunshades, and likewise with archways,
as well as all other accumulated marks of beauty.
He was being fanned especially by maidservants on both sides with yak-tail whisks held in their hands, as well as by the most excellent devotees.
O twice-born ones, let the brahmins who have mastered the Vedas carry the god on a palanquin, accompanied by many lofty lamps abundantly sprinkled with ghee and other offerings.
Everywhere, he should cause it to be illuminated by more than a thousand Brahmins— those who have mastered the three Vedas and are devoted to silent recitation and praise.
It was well-served by dancers and singers,
as well as by musicians playing the lute and other instruments, and by bards and others.
Accompanied by those skilled in songs beginning with the note ṣaḍja, experts in the playing of musical instruments,
and those reciting bright hymns in prose, verse, and mixed meter.

Indeed, [he was surrounded] by Tāṇḍikas, as well as by those who prattle, those skilled in the art of debate, those devoted to discourses on reality, and by logicians who know the meaning of words and phrases.
By the Mīmāṃsakas, the ritualists, the Vedic scholars, those learned in Sāṃkhya, the knowers of Yoga, the experts in the Purāṇas, the grammarians, and the knowers of reality; BhS_25.157 //
And by groups of astrologers, each desiring to defeat the other,
the object of knowledge is established in many ways according to the methods prescribed in their respective treatises.
By the learned, who speak aloud, who are devoted to the five times, and who, being of a sattvic nature, proclaim the majesty of Vāsudeva; BhS_25.159 //
By people standing in front of, behind, and to the sides of the Lord, who were intent on displaying every kind of proficiency in the scriptures.

With an army rich in the fourfold forces [of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry] in all directions, and with the city walls on both sides of the god [Indra] stained red with lac-dyed staffs; BhS_25.161.
Where there were various colorful wooden figures in the shape of birds scattered here and there,
as well as mechanical contraptions in the form of deities and machines in the likeness of elephants and other animals.
Accompanied by women mounted on various vehicles as described by Bharata,
they displayed a wonderful dance through many kinds of movements.
It was followed by agitated people using writing instruments, those mounted on three-wheeled vehicles, and others with various other machines, all making repeated journeys back and forth.
One should slowly lead the Lord of the World, accompanied by as many as one is able;
beginning from the first enclosure, this constitutes the circumambulation.
Then the Master, having ascended the vehicle together with the King,
should sit there meditating upon Hari for the sake of protecting the God of Gods.
And likewise, the priest, seated properly, should perform the worship correctly;
especially so when mounting the lordly elephant, he should worship the God of gods.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods with garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth as was appropriate, he first placed him [on the elephant] and took hold of the goad with his hand.
The preceptor himself, without haste, should sit upon the back of the elephant;
the priest, taking up the parasol, should likewise hold it over the deity.
Placing a stream of water in front, one should perform a circumambulation;
one should circumambulate the village by the same path along which the offering was made.
At that time, the devotees and the people devoted to the Lord, seeing the God approaching, rose up again and again in the courtyard of their own houses to welcome him.
Having prostrated, they should present many various kinds of offerings:
leaves, flowers, fruits, betel nuts, and even betel-leaf.

And at that time, children, the elderly, and the infirm should especially perform the offering of the lustral waving (nīrājanā) and other rites according to their ability and inclination, along with the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
When the God, who is himself beyond the supreme and accessible only through manifold austerities, has come to the door of his own abode out of compassion for his devotees;
What deluded soul does not rejoice [in this], and what atonement could there be for him who,
having accepted it at that time, takes hold of wealth that is uncooked?
Having first offered the invocation, one should perform what is dear to the Blessed One;
among the offerings there, the worshipper shall take half as his share.
The worshipper himself should take the betel leaf, the flower, the areca nut, the sacrificial fee, and so forth—the entire property of the worshipper. (BhS 25.177)
At that time, to those who have arrived and are bowed in devotion,
the Guru should, with faith, place the sandals of the Blessed One upon their heads.
When held upon the head by mortals, no fault from touch is found;
one should not carry the sandals of Viṣṇu away, having set them far from his presence.
The teacher of householders should not lead her as far as the threshold of the house-door;
however, it is permitted for women to wear sandals within the royal palace.
One should lead her, accompanied by a lamp, without crossing the threshold;
then, with lamps and other such items, as well as with royal regalia.
The sandal of Viṣṇu should not be carried away, for it is the very presence of Hari;
indeed, a worshipper must never bypass its proximity.
One should go to the houses of householders for the sake of receiving offerings;
nor, being distracted by other tasks, should one bypass the five cubits [of distance].
This would be the most excellent form of service, since Hari is thereby honored;
having thus performed the circumambulation, one should return toward the temple.

Having placed the Lord of Gods at the front of the gopura, facing toward the deity, and having worshipped him in due order with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, one should offer parched grain and other foods.
Having performed the circumambulation of the sacred site (dhāma), and having re-entered the temple,
one should lower the Lord of Gods and install him in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa).
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, and having presented mouth-perfume, one should release the protective thread and bathe the Lord with pure waters.
Having wiped it with a cloth for cleaning and adorned it as before,
having again tied the protective thread (kautuka), one should subsequently present the sacrificial oblation (havis).
One should perform royal services for him, for he is indeed the king, the lord of the world;
and one should provide him with much diversion through dance, song, and other such means.
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, one should install [the deity] in its former place;
this is declared to be what should be performed on the first day at evening.
From the second day onwards, every evening and morning,
at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform double the worship and offer the oblation.
Having propitiated the Kumbha deities, one should perform the worship of the Dhvaja deity;
having offered the fire-oblation and the sacrificial offering, one should likewise conduct the festival.
On the third day, in the forenoon, there shall be the festival of Garuḍa;
but on the sixth day, at midday, [one should worship] Hari together with the two goddesses.
Having placed [the deity] in the center of the seat and worshipped it with the eight forms,
one should take water and saffron and likewise perform the festival.
Having offered new garments and other gifts, and having presented parched grains,
and having given betel and water for rinsing the mouth, one should worship the Lord like a king.

On the morning of the seventh day, at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the adoration of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) and choose seven officiating priests (ṛtvij), with the preceptor (ācārya) at their head.
Having meditated upon them as being like the Seven Sages, one should offer gold, a cow, clarified butter,
jars of rice-water and the like, as well as the tips of dūrvā grass and betel nut.
One should give abundant gifts to those Brahmins individually;
and especially at evening, one should offer black fragrant unguents.
Having immediately bound on a protective amulet, one should prepare a sacrificial mound before the deity,
taking black aloe-wood and accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should place [the image] upon a sacrificial mound;
having performed the rite for an auspicious day according to the rules, one should then invoke Śrī there.
Having prepared the fragrances according to the rules and having worshipped Hari,
the Guru should then smear all his limbs with the mantra beginning with "gandhadvāram."
In the same manner, the Guru should perform the rites for the Goddesses and others with their respective mantras according to the prescribed rule;
he should then, out of devotion alone, cause the remaining fragrant paste to be given to the devotees.
By wearing that fragrance, all prosperities shall accrue to men;
at the conclusion of the evening worship, one should perform the chariot procession.
When the eighth day has arrived and the morning festival is concluded,
one should adorn the Lord of Gods and perform the hunting festival.

At midday, a wise person should perform the festival of water-sports for the God of gods on the bank of a river or similar body of water, having established a water-station according to the prescribed rite.
Having adorned the pavilion for water-sports with canopies and other ornaments,
[one should construct] a bathing-pool half the length and half the width of the [main] image, and one *adhyardha* (one and a half) times the height of the image.
Then, having placed a solid, seamless iron water-vat and filled it with river water,
[he should do so] with the mantra beginning with "dhārāsu."
One should perfume it with cardamom, sandalwood, and camphor,
as well as with saffron, white water-lilies, ketakī flowers, uśīra, and agallochum.
Having spread out new cloths with the mantra "I know," while saying, "A holy ford, auspicious, meritorious, the abode of the gods. (BhS 25.209)
Having invoked the presiding deity, one should worship with the eight forms upon a seat covered with an upper cloth in the western half of the pavilion.
Having established the God of gods and reciting the Śakuna-sūkta,
he should adorn him beautifully with new garments, upper cloths, and other ornaments.

Having worshipped [the deity] with water for the feet and other offerings, the preceptor, together with the Sthāpakas, should bow to the God of gods with the mantra beginning, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ. (BhS 25.212)

Having respectfully taken up the deity with the mantra “paraṃ raṃha,” and having placed him in a wooden vat filled with water with the mantra “pratad viṣṇu stavate,” [one should proceed]. (BhS 25.213)
Having invoked Indra and the others, as well as Jaya and the others, within the maṇḍala prepared with rice grains,
the Guru should worship them all around the water-vat.
Reciting the three sections beginning with the mantra "apo hi ṣṭhā," and having said "idam āpaḥ śivāḥ," he recites "āpo vā idaṃ sarvam. (BhS 25.215)
Having consecrated a wooden water-vat with mantras, bowed down to the God of gods, and recited the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Vaiṣṇava hymns; BhS_25.216 //
Reciting the mantra beginning with "iṣe tvorje tvā" and also "bhūrānilaya," he should smear the Lord Hari with water in a large water-vat, placing Him with his head toward the east.
"May he consent for half a watch, or even for two watches;
then, having extracted [the essence] again with the mantra *paraṃ raṃ ha*, [one should proceed]. (BhS 25.218)
Having adorned [the Lord] with garments and other ornaments as is appropriate, and having worshipped him thoroughly,
one should place the Lord of Gods upon a vehicle and proceed to either a village or his own residence.
Having led [the horse] clockwise in due order, fully adorned with all ornaments,
he did not take hold of the halter as it was brought into the village street.
Having entered the inner sanctum again and established [the image] in the pavilion of worship,
one should anoint the deity with fragrant oil and bathe him as before.
Having established [the image] in the place of the living soul and having worshipped it thoroughly, one should offer [it];
at the end of the festival on that night, [one should offer] Hari together with the Goddess.
Then, having tied the protective cord (pratisara) according to the prescribed rite for consecration,
the preceptor should have [the image] laid upon the bed according to the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
At dawn, having awakened the deity, one should worship him with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with the arghya libation;
on that day of pilgrimage, in the morning, one should perform the morning festival with gold and other such gifts.
Having prepared the oblation and worshipped the deity in the assembly pavilion,
one should place Garuḍa in front, and the Discus itself to the right.
The wise one should also place the Amita [image] above the seat of grain;
he should perform the daily worship and the offering of oblations at the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Having diligently discarded previously worn garments and ornaments,
and having put on other clothes, one should adorn oneself with ornaments as is appropriate.
Having worshipped the Lord and the deities of the wheel and other [emblems] with the eightfold offerings,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of rice grains, two cubits in length and breadth.
Having placed the mortar and pestle together with a cloth,
the wise man should worship their presiding deities, Brahmā and Īśa, respectively.
Having taken turmeric into the vessel and having likewise worshipped Sinīvālī,
one should place the turmeric into the mortar with that same mantra.
Having taken up the pestle with Vaiṣṇava mantras, the preceptor,
having recited the Viṣṇusūkta, should strike it [the grain] slightly.
Or, having been ground into powder by devotees or temple maidservants,
it should be placed specifically into one, two, or even three water-jars.
Having taken a māḍhaka measure of vādaila perfumed with fragrances,
and having covered it with lids, one should place it upon a leveled mound of earth.
Having covered [the vessel] with a new cloth, one should worship Soma in the oil;
one should also worship Sinīvālī in its powder, as well as the discus and other [emblems].
Having worshipped the deity and caused the auspicious day to be proclaimed, the Vaiṣṇava preceptor,
having poured that oil upon the head with the mantra "vedāham," [should proceed].
Having bathed the [deities] such as Cakrin with turmeric powder, one should then bathe them;
by wearing the remains of that [powder], the devotee is liberated from all sins.
Then, having placed the deity upon a vehicle together with the discus and other implements,
and having performed this powder festival, one should then perform the ritual of the sacred ford.
If a natural pool dug by the gods should exist there, that site is praised as a sacred ford (tīrtha);
having established [the image] on the bank of a river or similar water, either together with the two goddesses or without them.
Having established the wheel and the other [emblems] as before, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front;
with the ritual substance, one should fill the previously unprepared jars while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having placed a white mustard seed in the center, there should be water with unbroken rice grains in the east;
there should be scented water in the south, and water with *kuśa* grass in the west.
The Guru should place the water for recitation in the northern direction and in the intermediate directions,
and having arranged the subsidiary ablutions (upasnāna) in sequence, he should assign their presiding deities.
The Ādityas, the Apsarases, and likewise his preceptor Kāśyapa;
the seasons and the Maruts, as well as the sages and Takṣaka.
One should invoke and worship the mantras and the vidyādharas in their proper sequence, using the mantra "pūtas tv asi" and also "imā oṣadhayaḥ. (BhS 25.243)
With the verses “abhi tvā śūra,” “catvāri,” and “pūtaḥ kṣīreṇa,” he was bathed in succession with five jars containing those respective substances. (BhS 25.244)
Having recited, "The four waters," one should perform the secondary ablution (upasnāna);
and having sprinkled [the deity] with the remaining water from the jar while focusing on the discus, one should proceed.
Having entered the water there, he should worship Varuṇa in due order;
taking the discus with both hands, he should be accompanied by his devotees.
The preceptor should first cast the wheel into the sacred water (tīrtha) for the purpose of creation; standing firmly in the midst of the water there, with the water reaching up to his navel.
Having established the deity Cakra in his heart and holding it firmly with both hands, he should recite "ye te śatam" while facing either the east or the north. (BhS 25.248)
Then the Guru should immerse the discus accompanied by all musical instruments;
and all the people, having bathed in that sacred ford, shall be cleansed of their sins.
They would obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
then, having established the supreme wheel upon a seat on the bank, [he spoke].
One should perform the ritual bath of purification (avabhṛtha-snāna) according to the procedure prescribed for the pure bath;
then, having discarded the garments and other items, one should adorn the deity with different [robes].
Having gathered the materials for the nasal and bath offerings right there according to the ritual,
the Guru should bathe the Lord of Gods, the Master, together with the two Goddesses as before.
Having adorned [the deity] with special ornaments, one should perform the worship ending with the offering of water (arghya);
thereafter, taking up the deity together with all the ornaments, [one should proceed].
Having recited the Śākuna hymn and led [the bird] around the village clockwise,
he should then enter the temple and place it in the assembly pavilion.

Having worshipped [the disciple] with water for the feet and other offerings, he should teach him the Vedas in due order; repeatedly offering handfuls of flowers, he should establish [the disciple] in the station of the individual soul (jīva).
Having taken up the wheel and the other [emblems] and installed them in their respective places,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited and then perform the sprinkling with consecrated waters.
Having completed the daily worship, one should especially offer the oblation;
having entered the sacrificial hall and offered into the fires that which belongs to Viṣṇu.
Taking the Śakti from the pitcher, one should deposit it into the permanent image (dhruvabera);
then, having performed the concluding oblation and having transferred the fire into the perpetual sacrificial pit (nityakuṇḍa).
On that night, at the conclusion of the regular fire-oblation (nityahoma), having offered the bali as before,
one should afterwards offer the bali consisting of pure food, prepared without the use of the cakra.
One should perform the bali offering everywhere according to the very same path previously described—at a shrine, at a water-station, at a crossroads, or at the foot of a tree. (BhS 25.260)
One should deposit [the remains] in a pond, a spring, near a well, a large reservoir, or an anthill;
or in a cremation ground, in front of another deity, or at the ends of streets.
Having entered the sanctuary again and bathed in the presence of the fire,
he should reach the base of the banner accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
One should perform the descent of the banner while reciting the mantra of the banner;
then, taking hold of that banner, one should indeed proceed in a clockwise direction.
Having circumambulated the temple and then entered the interior once more,
one should place a handful of flowers at the feet of the deity and offer them.
Having recited the mantra of forgiveness, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Regarding the declaration of the fruit:
he who thus performs the festival of Viṣṇu with devotion and respect [attains this].
With his soul purified of all sins and having attained all desires,
he eventually ascends a celestial chariot and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Next, I shall explain the flower sacrifice, which brings happiness.
On the second day, one should perform the flower sacrifice at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
It is threefold, providing peace, providing nourishment, and providing the fulfillment of desires;
these are proclaimed as the times for the morning, midday, and afternoon respectively.
Whether this [rite] be deficient or excessive, it serves indeed to pacify faults;
it may be performed in a pavilion for worship or even in a bathing hall.
Having smeared [the ground] and protected it, one should make it four cubits on each of the four sides;
having laid out twenty-five squares with six lines running east and north.
In the center, on various spots, there is a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp,
made either of jewels, grains, and so forth, or of rice, paddy, and sesame seeds.
Outside of those [enclosures], one should worship Vīśa at the front of the squares;
likewise, having worshipped Cakra in the south, one should worship Paṅktīśa in the west.
Having worshipped Śānta in the north, the wise one should collect the articles of worship and place them individually in each of the remaining positions.
On the eight petals of the lotus, upon pieces of gold,
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) on cloths according to their respective directions.
Upon the pericarp fashioned from three gold *niṣkas*,
the solar disk shines there, as does the lunar disk.
Upon that golden form, one should worship the mandala of fire;
having placed a seat there, [one should worship] within the lotus situated therein.
Having installed the deity there, one should perform the festival for as long as the day lasts,
worshipping it thoroughly with twenty-seven forms.
There, at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer various handfuls of flowers:
the lotus, tulasī, bilva, karavīra, and the utpala.
One should take these in sequence: the *nandyāvarta*, the *kumuda*, the *apāmārga*, as well as the *viṣṇukrāntā*, the *dūrvā*, and the *cakra*.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests,
[should perform worship] accompanied by dances, songs, instrumental music, and hymns from the four Vedas.
The Supreme beyond the supreme, the further shore, more secret than the secret, the Guru,
the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, and likewise that which consists of twelve syllables.
Then, while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one hundred and eight times,
they should devotedly offer handfuls of flowers at the feet of the God of gods.
Then, one should perform the five-fire rite, or the three-fire rite, or even the Paiṇḍarīka rite,
surrounding the deity in successive order, beginning with the highest.
In the excellent assembly pit (sabhyakuṇḍa) and in the central Āhavanīya fire,
one should perform the praise of the Hotṛ priest to the deities residing in that temple.
Having invoked [the deity] and prepared the clarified butter (ājya), one should offer oblations in that sequence;
having especially offered the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] and the Viṣṇu-sūkta correctly.
Then, one should worship the Nṛsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymn in the Āhavanīya fire;
in the Dakṣiṇa fire, one should worship the Viṣṇusūkta and the Śrīsūkta in due order.
Then, one should offer oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with a Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī;
furthermore, into the Āvasathya fire, one should offer the hymn beginning with the single-syllable [Om].
Let it be offered with clarified butter, with fuel-sticks, and with various specific oblations;
this is declared to be the highest [form], while the middling shall now be explained.
According to the available measurements, or according to half of the dimensions previously stated,
one should have images and so forth made for the deities of the lotus-maṇḍala of Hari.
"At the conclusion of the daily worship, having offered pure food, one should offer the five oblations at the end of all the worship; so said the Elder. (BhS 25.290)
One should cause the sound of the four Vedas and so forth to resound in the four directions; then the best of those who know mantras should perform the lotus-homa sacrifice in due order.

Having first worshipped [the deities] up to the end of all the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) according to the sequence of the deposition of flowers (puṣpanyāsa), one should thereafter perform the worship as prescribed in the Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga).
Having prepared various kinds of food and sacrificial offerings according to what is available,
and having presented them with mouth-fresheners at the end, one should cast the *parivāra-bali* (the offering for the retinue).

Thus has the middle [method] been explained; now I shall speak again of the inferior one, which is performed without the distinctions of directions and so forth, and without separate offerings of gold.
Having caused the deity to enter the maṇḍala and worshipped according to the ritual procedure,
one should then offer the five oblations that have been prescribed.
One should offer a handful of flowers with the mantras recited throughout the entire day;
likewise, one should worship [the deity] as far as the knees, as far as the thighs, and as far as the hips.
From the navel to the breasts, it sets externally according to the wheel;
from the neck to the forehead, it sets at the crown of the head according to the wheel.
At the conclusion of each respective worship, one should properly offer the oblation;
this is recorded as the expiation for faults arising from festivals that were not recognized.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the flower sacrifice;
likewise, one should perform the twelvefold propitiation according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, one should duly give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him;
specifically, one should give a fee of twenty-one niṣkas to the preceptor.
And for all those seeking objects, that same amount should be given individually;
having especially given cows and land, one should propitiate the teacher.
The preceptor, with a well-pleased mind, having completed the final oblation in all the fires in due order and having bowed to the God of gods, [should proceed].
Having installed the Lord of Gods in the place of the living soul (jīvasthāna), one should worship him properly;
one should also feed the Brahmins and bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The festival of the flower-sacrifice for the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, has been proclaimed;
however, in the performance of rites such as those for pacification (śāntika), one should first perform the rite of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Thus, he who performs this flower sacrifice dear to Hari with devotion,
having attained all desires and having obtained all sovereignty, [attains the supreme state].
Having conquered all enemies and being endowed with progeny and cattle,
he shall at the end ascend a celestial chariot and attain union with Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the section on the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the examination of the ground and so forth;
one should perform the expiation when there is deficiency, excess, or conflict. (BhS 26.1)
The transgression is generally indicated, and the mind is its prevention;
this is declared to be *prāyaścitta* (expiation), which one should perform for the successful fulfillment of ritual action.
One who does not perform expiation when a fault exists perishes;
therefore, one should with every effort perform atonement with diligence.
Furthermore, the manifestation of an ālaya and whatever rituals such as worship are performed therein become fruitless if they transgress this treatise.
To pacify those very faults, one should perform all the rites again in their proper sequence, preceded by the Great Peace (mahāśānti), exactly as prescribed in the scriptures.
Whatever action is performed by following one's own whims, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, such an act does not yield the stated fruit; on the contrary, it becomes a source of harm.
Crafts, astrology, architecture, and other such traditional sciences (āgamas) may indeed be authoritative to the extent that they do not contradict this [teaching]. (BhS 26.7)
The Lotus-born One, having first composed this Vaikhānasa scripture— which is independent of other scriptures and is a compendium of the meaning of all scriptures— [declared it].
Whether out of delusion or ignorance, whoever, following other treatises, should disparage this teaching regarding the points of doubt; BhS_26.9.
He goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings;
therefore, having expelled that fool, one should practice correctly according to what is taught in the scriptures.
When he should go to the outer gate to thoroughly examine the ground,
if an obstacle should fall [upon him], the wise one should perform an expiatory oblation.
One should recite the Vaiṣṇava and Vighna mantras hundreds of times and perform the rite again;
upon seeing something unpleasant, the wise person should recite the Saura mantra and offer oblations as previously described.
But when harsh words are heard, one should likewise recite the Brāhma and Sārasvata [mantras];
so too during a quarrel at that time, or when there is the flow of blood.
And in cases such as fire-burns and the like, one should employ the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] combined with the Saumya,
as well as the Vaiṣvaksena, the Saudarśana, and the Gāruḍa.
Having meditated upon the deity, one should offer oblations into the worldly fire and thereafter perform the ritual;
however, at the time of examining the ground, if there should be a depletion of soil, [one must act accordingly].
A wise person should likewise offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the two oblations for expiation (mindāhutī),
once the ground has already been examined by other means.

Having established the *aupāsana* fire, one should offer oblations ten times each to Viṣṇu with the *vyāhṛtis* as the conclusion; thereafter, one should perform the ritual acts according to the mantras.
If, however, there is a loss of limb or injury during the plowing, one should offer oblations to Rudra and Brahmā for the pacification of the fault; thereafter, one should bring another bull.
However, if the construction of the sacrificial hall and other structures is performed with trees other than those prescribed for sacrifice,
or if it is deficient in its measurements, one should likewise offer oblations to Viṣṇu.
The preceptor should perform the Saumya, Āgneya, and Prājāpatya rites;
likewise, the Vāruṇa rite when there is a break in the cord, and the Śrī rite when there is a break in the furrow.
If there is a discrepancy regarding the donor, the wise one should offer oblations with the Jyeṣṭhā mantra;
if there is a discrepancy regarding the seer (ṛṣi), he should offer with the Vāyavya mantra, and likewise with the Vāsava mantra for a Kṣiṇī.
In the eastern direction, one should place an elephant; in the south, a goad joined with the *vyāhṛtis*;
and [in the other directions], skull-bones, ash, charcoal, hair, anthills, and potsherds.
If [the deities] are seen at the time of plowing, one should remove them without delay;
having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform oblations in sequence to the gentle and the fiery deities.
If, in that worship, the rites for Śānta, Viśāna, and Pāyin are deficient, one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and again perform the worship dedicated to each respective deity.
If the sowing of seeds has failed, one should indeed offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava;
having offered to Saumya and Vāyavya, one should sow the seeds once again.
If the offering of cows is deficient, one should, being well-composed, offer an immeasurable Vaiṣṇava oblation and recite the Gāruḍa Cakra-mantra ten times.
Having brought loads of straw, one should offer them to the herds of cattle;
when the offerings to the deities of the quarters and the *bali* are deficient, one should perform the oblation preceded by that mantra.
Having offered oblations in sequence to Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Aindra, Yāmya, Vāruṇa, and Kaubera, one should present the bali offering there.
In the event of the failure of the Brahma-padmakriyā, one should offer oblations to the deities of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Varuṇa,
and the Earth, and then perform the rite once again.

But if the demarcation of the directions is deficient, one should again offer oblations to the deities of the directions, to Viṣṇu, and to Sūrya; thereafter, one should perform the determination of the directions.
When the ground is excavated for the sake of a celestial mansion, if gravel, thorns, clods of earth, or similar obstacles are encountered there, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava and Brāhma rites.
One should offer oblations to the deities presiding over the five elements and to the Vyāhṛtis in their proper order,
in the event that the measurement of the stone or the brick is either deficient or excessive.
Having offered oblations according to the rules with the Vaiṣṇava hymn and the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should perform the rite;
however, in the event of an inversion in the placement [of mantras], one should offer oblations to the deities of the directions and to Viṣṇu.
Having performed the oblation and acted according to what was stated, one should recite the mantras beginning with the Vedas;
however, if the placement of the jewels has been omitted, one should offer oblations to their respective presiding deities.
Then, having offered oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should perform the deposition of jewels;
however, if the deposition of the embryo has been omitted, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite consisting of the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having offered oblations to the deity Śrībhūmi, one should again perform the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa);
however, if the measurements are deficient, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite consisting of the Viṣṇu-sūkta.

One should worship and perform the rites according to the rules for the solar, lunar, and fiery [deities] at the time of preparing the ritual substances and when establishing them, even if they are mixed together.
When perversion has occurred, one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava in due order; having offered to each respective presiding deity, one should perform the rite according to the rules.
In the case of a placement where no specific location has been mentioned, one should offer oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta and the Puruṣasūkta;
one should install those deities whose presiding divinities are Śrī and Bhūmi in their respective places.
On a stone slab of immeasurable size, or likewise on the head of a brick and so forth,
the wise man should perform the expiation by means of the first rite for bricks, according to the prescribed ritual.
Regarding the pinnacle-pin and its base,
when they are of improper measure or when the prescribed woods cannot be obtained, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu in a fire kindled with gentle fuel.
Having offered oblations to the deities of the earth according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should then proceed with the work of plastering once the temple has been constructed.
One should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta,
and the hymns dedicated to Śrī and Bhūmi according to the prescribed rite, and then begin again.
Having offered oblations to Āgneya and Bhūmidaivata, one should perform the ritual task;
if there is a deficiency in the sanctum, the door-panels, or other parts, one should also offer oblations to the six deities beginning with Dhātṛ.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava and Śrīmahī mantras, one should have it constructed again;
for if the enclosure wall and gatehouse are deficient, the fault will be very great.
The lineage will perish, enemies will increase, wealth will be lost, and there will be great fear; for one who lacks peace, a great calamity will arise and the family will surely be destroyed.
If the site is devoid of the true *pīṭhas*, there will be a depletion of wealth, grain, and lifespan;
[one should construct] wells, gardens, sacrificial sheds, large halls, flower beds, and orchards.
Likewise, there was a hall for bathing and drinking, as well as an assembly pavilion; and similarly, pavilions were constructed for dance, song, and water-stations.
A great fault would arise, and what has been done would become as if undone;
therefore, a wise person should cause [the rite] to be performed with every effort according to their ability.

Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta, as well as those dedicated to Śrī and Bhūmi, and likewise those dedicated to their respective deities; BhS_26.50.
One should perform it exactly as described and should not practice stinginess regarding the funds;
beginning from the first brick up to the end at the ritual stake of the stūpa pinnacle.
And this shall be the expiation for all faults not previously mentioned;
[it should be performed] in a pleasing place either to the east or to the south of the ālaya.
Having established [the image] in a pure place, one should offer oblations into the fire of lotuses in due order:
the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.

In the subsidiary fire-offering (aṅga-homa), oblations are offered to the deities presiding over the various parts of the temple, from the pinnacle (sthūpī) down to the base (upāna), according to their names.
One should offer oblations beginning with "Dadbhyaḥ svāhā," and one should cause the Brāhma, Raudra, Vināyaka,
Āgneya, Durgāsūkta, and Prājāpatya mantras to be sacrificed.

But if, once the temple has been completed, out of greed for wealth or other such motives, one installs the portable image (kautuka) without having first established the permanent image (dhruvabera); BhS_26.56 //
"O King, this would be a malevolent rite leading to the destruction of the kingdom;
therefore, to avoid that fault, you should perform a great propitiatory rite."
Having properly honored the Vaiṣṇavas, one should feed many Brāhmaṇas;
and having prostrated before the God of gods with the words "Forgive me," one should [offer] the auspicious thread (*kautuka*).
Having installed the *dhruvabera* (permanent image) in the inner sanctum (*bālālaya*), one should perform the ritual;
or else, having fashioned the *dhruvārcābera*, one should perform the installation.
Upon the completion of the temple, however, after one month has passed there,
if the installation of the Dhruva-linga has not been performed, one should then offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava.
Likewise, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, as well as those dedicated to Rudra, Indra, Agni,
Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and the deities Śrī and Bhū.
Having performed the peace-offering according to the prescribed rite, one should give the teacher's fee;
and having fed the Brahmins, one should indeed honor the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having installed the permanent image according to the ritual procedure, one should worship it properly;
thus, when two months have passed, the expiation shall be twofold.
In three months, however, it becomes triple; likewise, it continues until a year has passed.
But when a year has elapsed, the fault becomes even greater.

Having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) for seven days by means of oblations in the lotus-fire according to the rules, one should afterwards feed the Brahmins; thus one should perform everything according to the prescribed ritual.

Some sages indeed maintain that this should be practiced for seven days within the seven-year period, beginning from the first day; others hold that it should be performed until the end of those seven days.
From this point forward, one should again perform the consecration beginning with the plowing;
however, in the event of a loss of limbs prior to the preliminary consecration in water, this applies to the Dhruva fire.
One should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta,
as well as those dedicated to Śrī and Bhūmi, and likewise those beginning with "dadbhyaḥ svāhā."
One should give the teacher’s fee and properly examine the image;
if it is fit for rejoining, one should join it and perform the ritual work once again.
If capable, one should bring a new image and perform the consecration of the stone, even if it has already been fashioned by a craftsman.
Having taken up that image, one should indeed perform the propitiatory rite with Vaiṣṇava mantras;
then, having covered that image in the ground, one should perform the Vāstuhoma.
Having diligently purified the image with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow,
and having gone around as before, one should offer the bali-oblation and worship the deity.
Afterward, having performed the rite with mantras according to the rule, the wise one should install [the image] prior to the preliminary consecration of the water and before the ceremonial bathing.
If there should be a deficiency in the limbs of the deity, the Goddess, or others,
one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
The Śrīsūkta, the Mahīsūkta, the Brāhma, and likewise the Raudra; the mantra of the two sages and the respective mantras of others—let these be well-offered.
One should reconcile with one who is worthy of reconciliation; one should abandon according to the rule one who is unworthy.
Or, having reconciled with another, one should bring him back and perform the rite of re-initiation once more.
But when a great image has been installed and remains unconsecrated for more than a month,
one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite and likewise recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta over a fire of lotus-wood.
Having offered the Puruṣasūkta, as well as those dedicated to Śrī and Bhū, and having offered oblations to Brahmā, Rudra, and the Pārṣadas, one should perform the ritual task.
In two months it becomes double; in three months it becomes triple;
at the end of a year it shall be thus; at the end of that, one should establish it again.
In the twelfth year from that time, having again performed activities such as plowing and so forth,
and having carried out other tasks such as the collection of stones, one should perform the consecration ceremony.
Now I shall speak: one should perform the re-consecration at the beginning of the plowing and other rites;
first, one should clear away the grasses, shrubs, creepers, and so forth from the temple site.
One who is diligent toward his teacher should perform, in due order, the procedure for casting stones, bricks, and wood,
and having completed the application of plaster, paint, and so forth.
To the north of the Ālaya, one should perform the Vāstu-homa according to the ritual procedure;
the learned man should cause the declaration of "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) to be recited and likewise have the circumambulation with fire (Paryagni) performed.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then performed the plowing,
the wise one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila) with rice grains facing toward the temple.
Having worshipped Śānta, Anapāyin, and Viśva, one should offer [the oblation];
having fashioned a plow out of gold, one should [offer it] throughout the inner sanctum and all other parts.
Having taken [the seeds] in his right hand with the mantras beginning with "Viṣṇornuka," and having drawn them out as prescribed,
the preceptor should collect the seeds.
Having sprinkled water on the Soma and worshipped it while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
he should then consecrate the seeds while reciting the mantra "Somaṃ rājānam."
One should perform the sowing everywhere and gather grasses such as dūrvā;
having spread those dūrvā grasses over [the area], one should then recite the Gaudānika Sūkta.
Having recited [the mantra] and offered them to the herds of cattle, one should cause them to be given;
and having thoroughly purified the abode, one should present the bali offering to Brahmā and the other deities.
Having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru) with rice and ghee using either one drona or half a drona of grain,
one should first offer water, then flowers, the offering (bali), and finally water again.
One should purify the abode once again, preceded by a peace-offering (śānti-homa);
and having performed the homa for each respective consecration, one should then perform the ritual acts.
Having established the sacrificial fire-pit for the sake of the first brick, the wise man [should recite] the Vaiṣṇava [hymn],
the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
Concentrated and meditating upon the deity, one should offer oblations to the presiding deity of the site;
then, touching the area where the first brick is to be placed, one should recite the Vedic mantras beginning with the syllable Om.
Having performed the internal sprinkling and having sprinkled the fire again,
one should resolve upon the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta for the purpose of depositing the embryo.
One should likewise offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Śrīsūkta, and the Mahīsūkta; one should also offer to the deity of the region and with the mantra "To the Nāga King."
Having said, "From all jewels," and also "From all minerals," having said "From all seeds," and also "From all metals. (BhS 26.96)

Then one should offer oblations to the rivers, to the netherworlds, and to the nāgas; thereafter, one should offer oblations in sequence to the elephants of the directions and to Viṣṇu, ending each with "svāhā. (BhS 26.97)
Then, having worshipped Medinī at the southern end of the right side of the inner door, one should recite the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Then, having recited the mantras for Medinī and the others, the wise one should touch each respective limb;
having performed the internal sprinkling, he should carry out the ritual action therein.
If the embryo is lost, having thus offered oblations and performed the rites, one should establish it again;
for the sake of other bricks, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta.
Having offered the Puruṣasūkta, the wise one should perform oblations according to the prescribed rule,
while reciting the mantras beginning with the Vedas that have the guardians of the celestial chariots as their deities.
Furthermore, while reciting the Viṣṇusūkta, one should perform the ritual touching (abhimarśana) above the vimāna and likewise below the pinnacle-stake (sthūpikīla).
Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] around the fire on the *dhruva* altar— which is devoid of measurement—
and having offered oblations as in the rite for establishing the *dhruva*, one should recite the mantras prescribed for the depositing of jewels.

The wise one should diligently recite the *Atharvaśīrṣa* and the *Atharvaśānti* hymns, and having performed the protective rites (*kautuka*) and so forth, he should then carry out the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
If the fixed [image] is lost, one should have another made from superior materials;
or else, having prepared it as before, one should install it according to the ritual rules without delay.
If the tooth-relic has been uprooted by men, bulls, deer, or other animals,
one should take it while its parts are intact and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the sake of purification.
Having performed the ritual consecration in water at that site according to the rule, the wise one,
having also performed the placement of jewels, should perform the consecration once again.
If a stone image has been stolen from another temple and its consecration ritual remains uncompleted,
one should properly bury it in the ground.
Having brought [the image] according to the prescribed rule and having performed its consecration, one should carry out the ritual installation;
likewise, one should perform the rite for the pedestal that was previously fashioned by the artisan.

Since an image that has been installed according to the rules, in its proper place, and free from defects must not be moved— otherwise it would bring about the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
To pacify those defects, one should perform oblations in a lotus-fire in the proper sequence;
for seven days, one should perform a great propitiation and feed Brahmins.
One should give gold, cows, and land, and perform the rite of consecration again,
[if it was performed] by preceptors, officiating priests, or those who have fallen from their vows who were ignorant of the ritual rules.
Having recognized that the image has been installed,
the wise one, knowing the ritual, should likewise cause it to be moved according to the rules and then have it reinstalled without delay.
If an image that has been consecrated by those who know the ritual rules is moved out of ignorance,
one should perform a pacification rite according to the prescribed procedure and have it consecrated again by those who know the ritual rules.
Whether by the currents of rivers, lakes, or the ocean, or by a whirlwind,
that celestial chariot— whether it be mobile or even fixed— may be set in motion there by fate.
Having covered that image on the ground and having constructed a new temple,
one should install the image immovably according to the very path prescribed in the scriptures.
But on that ground which is free from danger, one should practice on a nearby spot,
