or in a village and the like, or in a secluded and very delightful place.
Having made the celestial chariot very firm, having placed the god there together with all his attendants, and having established him according to the prescribed rite, one should worship him.
But in the absence of villages and such, one should then build a pavilion in a spacious area beyond a fine of a hundred [coins], establish it there, and worship it.
Having conquered another kingdom and its ruler, and having diligently seized a [Buddha] image,
if he should wish to install it in his own kingdom, he should do so by establishing a village [for its maintenance].
Having installed the image in that temple according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it;
provided that, if the temple is not of human origin, there is a human-sized shrine in its vicinity.
If one wishes to perform it then, one should do so within another enclosure;
having constructed the enclosure and the image and so forth, even without performing the purification of the ground and other preliminary rites. (BhS 26.122)

Having installed [the image], one should worship it; the fruit thereof is equal to the worship at the primary shrine (mūlasthāna), even if performed in a temple or a bathing hall through negligence or by fate.
In the assembly hall, as well as in the kitchen and its surrounding walls,
in the cow-pen, the bathhouse, the drinking-water shed, and so forth, when these are defiled by fire.
When [a person] has been suddenly struck by a great wind,
or likewise by lightning and so forth, one should offer oblations into the fire of the lotus with the supreme self-mantra, beginning with the syllable *IṂ*.
If [the ritual] is interrupted, one should perform the Mindā-hutis, the Āgneya, and likewise the Vyāhṛtis;
having again prepared a new [offering], one should cause it to be established in due order.
At the time of taking up the stone, or likewise when taking up the wood,
if there is a reversal in the ritual actions, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn dedicated to Viṣṇu.
The wise one should offer the *mindāhuti* oblations and, having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblations at their conclusion, perform the final oblation if there has been a breach [in the ritual],
if the doorposts or the serpent-ornaments (*bhuvaṅga*) and so forth are deficient in measurement, or if the fire is defiled.
When it has become old or infested with worms, the wise man should discard it;
having fetched another [vessel] and joined it according to the prescribed rule, he should proceed as before.
In the perpetual fire, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava, Saumya, and Āgneya rites for the sake of pacification,
or else for the purpose of depositing the embryo (garbhanyāsa) or for the purpose of depositing the pedestal (pīṭhanyāsa).
But if even gems are not available, one should place gold there;
one should offer oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, for that shall be the expiation.
Among the elements, mercury is the foremost; let that be the vow for the attainment of stainless merit.
Having cast mercury therein, there is atonement for both the Brahma and Raudra sins.
One should place either barley as a substitute for seeds or mung beans there;
the expiation for that is to offer oblations to Vāyu and Viṣṇu.
In the construction of a fixed pillar, in the act of taking up the trident,
or in its installation or misplacement, [one should employ] the Brahma, Raudra, and Vaiṣṇava [mantras].
Having offered oblations up to the end of the *vāha* according to the ritual rule, one should then join [the deity] again;
for in a measureless celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the image is devoid of measurement.
If that [rite] was performed out of ignorance, it will cause the destruction of the king and the kingdom;
therefore, to pacify its fault, the wise one should perform a great propitiatory sacrifice (mahāśānti).
One should again install that celestial chariot and that image according to the prescribed rules;
however, if the measurement of the spikes (śūla) specified for those respective images is deficient, [the rite must be redone].
Having completed the Vaiṣṇava and the Pauruṣa Sūkta,
and having performed the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma) with the mantra "dadbhyaḥ svāhā," one should then re-establish [the deity].
When the oil, powder, decoction, and so forth are deficient, or when there is a reversal in their application;
likewise, in the case of binding with ropes, the eightfold bindings, and the plastering with sugar.
Likewise, in the application of clay, in the act of covering with cloth,
or in the case of ornaments and so forth, when the sequence is neglected or when there is a transgression regarding the colors and other such elements.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Raudra, Āgneya, the lords of the great elements, Prājāpatya, and the Vyāhṛtis, one should perform the ritual according to the prescribed rules.
One should not have a large image made that is half-painted or fashioned from clay;
rather, it should be made of gold, silver, copper, stone, or wood.

One should fashion an image with all its characteristic marks from precious materials or from variously colored [metals]; furthermore, it may be an artificial one, even if not explicitly mentioned, provided it is subsequently coated with a suitable color.
Having washed the sacrificial vessel with water for drying and wiped it clean,
one should offer oblations into the lotus-fire with the Vaiṣṇava hymns and the Viṣṇu-sūkta, as well as the Jaya and other offerings.
Thereafter, one should apply anointment with the colors as previously described, according to what is appropriate;
likewise, the permanent image (dhruvabera) may be made of plaster mixed with lime or fashioned from bricks.
Or if it is made from malevolent substances, or established through malevolent rites—
having quickly abandoned that, one should likewise [offer] a Vaiṣṇava oblation in a lotus-fire.
The Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, and likewise those dedicated to Śrī and Bhū; as well as those for the gods and others, such as the Brāhma, Raudra, Pāvaka, and Vāruṇa hymns.
Having offered oblations for the mantras of all deities, for the supreme Self alone, and for this Great Peace which destroys all defects; BhS_26.148.
Thereafter, having consecrated it according to the rules and having installed the image, one should worship it;
[the image may be made] from round metals such as brass and the like, or from whatever materials have not been specifically mentioned.
A consecrated image made for the purpose of sorcery may lead to harmful results;
to pacify that fault, one should perform a great rite of propitiation in a fire of lotuses.
Having fashioned the image with all its characteristic marks according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should again install it; he should have it made standing or, alternatively, seated.
One should not approach [the deity] while it is lying down; one should worship it as it stands.
However, when the image is free from defects and is being worshipped during the preliminary consecration (kautuka) and other rites, [this rule does not apply].
One should not bring in a *bimba* fashioned from superior materials,
nor should one abandon one made from inferior materials even while it is being worshipped.
When the marriage-thread and other such items have been worshipped— even if they appear deformed or devoid of color—
one should offer the power of Dhruva, as if joined with the *jharjhura* and other musical instruments.
Having renovated the image and purified it once more, one should install it again;
provided that the festive image being worshipped has not been taken away by kings or others by chance.
Having performed the purification of that site and having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) as previously described,
one should place therein a jewel, gold, or even a tuft of grass (kūrca).

Having invoked the deity at that time according to the prescribed rite— either from the Pole Star, from the heart, or from the solar disc— one should thereafter [install] the image (bera) according to the rule.
One may perform the consecration using either the original substance or even a superior substance;
without waiting for the [specific] time, one should carry out the consecration as before.
Having taken up a Vaiṣṇava image that is deficient in the application of beeswax,
one should perform the *śānti* oblation and then again perform the oblations for Rudra, Saura, and Pāvaka.
If a fixed image or a portable one (kautuka) has been installed in another temple,
and one wishes to install it in yet another temple, the wise practitioner should perform a great propitiatory fire-offering (mahāśānti-homa).
Having thoroughly honored the Vaiṣṇavas, one should feed many Brahmins;
having installed [the deity] at each respective site according to the rule, one should perform worship.
If the temple of a village or similar place is destroyed,
one should transfer the image located therein to another temple and worship it as is appropriate.
When the assembly of seats has been prepared and the image is gradually lowered,
death, loss of wealth, or increase [of prosperity] shall occur starting from the south [and proceeding clockwise].
In the *stunda* division, there is loss of sons;
in the *uraśchidra*, the destruction of grain and the loss of wealth; and in the *kṛśa*, a man shall suffer emaciation.
If [the mark] is too thick, there is a great disease; if it is too long, there is a lack of longevity;
if it is too short, one encounters famine; and when there is an excess or deficiency [in its proportions], misfortune arises.
There may be a deficiency in other ancillary parts; one should perform that which is correctly prescribed by the scriptures.
This applies prior to the installation of Dhruva and likewise before the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).

I shall now declare the expiation for those [offenses] not previously mentioned: with Kapila-ghee, one should offer oblations into a fire of lotuses while reciting the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
One should offer oblations with the mantras dedicated to Śrī and Bhū, and again with the vyāhṛtis;
one should perform each respective rite again, for otherwise it would be fruitless.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, on miscellaneous matters, in the section on the *Prakīrṇa-adhikāra* of the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the venerable Vaikhānasas.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter: Expiation (*Prāyaścitta*).
If the selection of the preceptor, the officiating priests, or especially the worshipper is deficient as prescribed, one should perform a propitiatory rite according to the rules.
Then, one should perform the great pacification (mahāśānti) by offering oblations ten times into the fire of the lotus;
having performed the selection as prescribed, one should subsequently carry out the ritual action.
But at the time of offering the seed-syllables, or during the worship of Brahmā and the other deities,
or even when the presentation of the sacrificial oblation is deficient, one should perform a rite of pacification.
Having offered oblations to its presiding deity and to Viṣṇu, and having performed worship, one should present [the offering].
However, if the rite of sowing sprouts has been omitted, one should offer to Viṣṇu the Viṣṇusūkta.
One should likewise offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Brāhmaṇa hymns, and the Vyāhṛtis;
then, having again performed the rite of germinating seeds (aṅkura), one should subsequently carry out the ritual action.

If, after performing the offering of the sprouts, one does not subsequently carry out the ritual action, there will be destruction of the king and the kingdom; therefore, one should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti).
“Having prostrated with the words ‘Forgive me,’ one should perform the rite again;
however, if [the fault] occurs before the opening of the eyes during the act of assembling the pedestal.”
And in the event that jewels are not obtained, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the Brāhma hymn, the Saumya hymn, and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered gold many times, one should deposit it in those respective locations;
this applies at the time of opening the eyes, even when cows and other such items are unavailable.
Having taken up substances for the vision [of the deity] according to what is available,
one should offer oblations to each respective presiding deity of those substances, as well as to Vaiṣṇava, in due order.
Having prepared each respective substance, one should again present it according to the rules,
whether during the opening of the eyes or at the rising of Rāhu or Saturn.
If the constellation Andhaka occurs and the "uncovering of the eyes" (akṣimocana) rite is performed, total destruction will result; therefore, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta.

Having offered oblations with the mantras of the nine planets and others, one should perform the rite of opening the eyes; this is done when the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of substances such as the five products of the cow has been omitted.
Having offered oblations for the Vaiṣṇava, the Ṛṣi, and likewise the Viṣṇu-sūkta,
one should perform the preliminary consecration in the water for three days or even for a single day.
Having offered oblations to the presiding deity of each respective region, to Viṣṇu with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and to Śrī and Bhū as prescribed, one should perform [the rite] once again.
If one does not purify the image after the opening of the eyes of the permanent icon (dhruvabera),
or even if it is done incorrectly, one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should again perform the Puruṣasūkta, the Raudra, the Ārṣa, and the Vāruṇa hymns,
quickly observing the fire-pits that have been prepared according to improper rites.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the rites pertaining to Brahmā, Soma, and Agni;
this applies even when the sacrificial grass-bunches (kūrca) and other items, as well as the vessels for clarified butter (ājya), the dipping-spoon (sruva), and so forth, are of no fixed measure.
One should offer the oblations of self-reproach, the Sāvitra,
and the Vyāhṛtis into the five fires according to their respective places, after the sprinkling and the drawing of lines have been performed.
If fire produced by friction is unavailable, one should obtain it from the teacher's house,
or else fetch it from the home of a Vedic scholar and perform the ritual with that fire.
Having established the Gārhapatya fire, the wise man should offer the Āghāra libations;
he should sacrifice to Vaiṣṇava, to the deity Earth, and to Agni in their proper sequence.
Having increased that fire and having established it in the Dakṣiṇāgni,
one should thereafter establish it in the Āhavanīya fire, and after that in the Āvasathya fire.

One should perform the ritual leading [the fire] in this manner, sequentially, into the assembly hall and the lotus-fire; however, if the leading is performed in reverse order or devoid of the respective mantras, [it is ineffective].
Having offered oblations into the Vaiṣṇava, Pāvaka, Brāhma, and Saumya fires, one should perform [the rite] again;
and in those respective fires, prior to the Āghāra offering and also in between them.
If one should not go, or if one should go, one should perform the expiation by offering oblations in sequence to the respective guardian deity of that direction, to Viṣṇu, and to Agni.
If the churned fire has been produced but subsequently extinguished through negligence,

or if it has gone out before the initial leading forward (*praṇayana*), or if all the fires have gone out, one should perform the pacification rite (*śānti*) as prescribed, reciting the *Agni-sūkta* a thousand times.
One should cook a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with two *prastha* measures of a single type of rice, using cow’s butter that has been processed over a common (worldly) fire.
At the time of consecration, one should then perform the consecration of that fire with mantras;
furthermore, if a fly or the like should fall into the vessel of clarified butter or the sacrificial oblation (caru), [one should act accordingly].
Having discarded that [fire] and taken up another, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the Prājāpatya and Vaiṣṇava fires;
however, if fresh butter is not available, one should do so again [with what is at hand].
Having removed that defect with *darbha* grass, having kindled and purified [the fire], one should perform [the rite];
but if the consecrated fire is lost, one should recite: "This is your womb. (BhS 27.30)
And one should place fuel upon those ashes as is appropriate;
having cast it into the worldly fire according to the ritual rule with the mantra, "Awake! (udbuddhyasva).

In the event of an interruption, or when the *mindāhuti* offerings, the *vaiṣṇava* offering, or the *vyāhṛti* offerings preceded by those are omitted; or when the materials for the encircling (*paristaraṇa*) and other items are burnt, split, or lost—[one should perform the following].
Then, having again joined that [mantra] preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
the wise one should offer the oblation to Agni, the two Mindā offerings, and the Vaiṣṇava oblation.
If no vessel is specified, one should take the *sruva* ladle as the vessel for the act of oblation;
if no specific sacrificial material is specified, one should use clarified butter or a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with clarified butter.
If the substance is lacking in the required measure, one should indeed offer twenty oblations of ghee prepared according to the Kapila method to Viṣṇu, and only thereafter perform the ritual action.
When no expiation has been prescribed, or when it is performed in the hearth-fire or even the perpetual fire;
when there is an omission of ritual acts, a transposition, or even a confusion of mantras.
One should offer oblations in sequence, beginning with the Vaiṣṇava mantra and the Vyāhṛtis, ending with the Vyāhṛtis;
if the Puṇyāha rite is omitted, one should recite the Puṇyāha mantras twelve times.
If the Vāstuhoma is omitted, however, one should offer those mantras ten times each;
if no specific expiation has been mentioned, then the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] should be used.
Having offered oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta and the Puruṣasūkta, one should perform the rite;
as substitutes for gems, one may use gold, and likewise mercury for metals.
Among seeds, barley is prescribed; in the absence of the former, the latter is traditionally accepted.
Having taken up the vow for the jewels, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymns and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Next, one should take up the ritual application (praṇidhi) for the elements belonging to the deities of the directions and to Viṣṇu, as well as that for the seeds belonging to Vāyu and Viṣṇu.
Twenty times each, for the sake of pacifying defects,
[one should perform this] when the bladder is deficient in its characteristics or when it has been damaged by cutting and so forth.
Having abandoned that [garment] and having obtained another, whether it be dedicated to Śrī, to Viṣṇu,
or among those found from eggs and so forth, one should take up a garment for each [deity].
Having offered oblations to Viṣṇu and to Śrī and Bhū as deities, one should perform the ritual;
furthermore, in the case of archways and other structures lacking the prescribed measurements, there shall be no transgression.
The wise one should offer twenty oblations to the presiding deities of each individual door;
if the darbha rope is missing, he should indeed offer oblations to the Ṛṣis and to Viṣṇu.
If the water-pot is deficient in size, or likewise possessed of defects,
or if it is lacking in its two cloths and its color-marks, Hari does not dwell therein.
Having carefully deposited those [offerings], one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn,
the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the Brāhma hymn, the mantras of the sages, and [oblations] into the fire.
One should offer oblations ten times and provide a meal for the Brahmins;
one should give a sacrificial fee to the teacher, and it will certainly become fruitful.
When the broken jar has been restored, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn,
the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the Brāhma, the Aindra, the Āgneya, and the Ṛṣi hymns.
Having performed the oblation twenty times, one should give the teacher’s fee;
and having fed the Brahmins and honored the Vaiṣṇavas.
The wise one, having procured another jar, should perform the consecration as before;
however, if the consecrated jar is touched by fallen chickens or similar creatures, [the rite must be redone].
Having removed that [impurity] and taken up the noble [mantras], one should accomplish it as before;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
One should worship one hundred and eight [offerings] dedicated to Brahmā, Sūrya, and Agni;
one should give the teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā) and worship the Vaiṣṇavas—this is the procedure.
Likewise, if the image is defiled by touch, one should perform a ritual bath according to the scriptures;
having performed the previously mentioned expiation, one should thereafter carry out the rite.
But in the event that the *sruk* and other implements are unavailable, one should offer the oblation with the *sruva* alone;
and if the sacrificial pit has been touched by dogs, cocks, or similar creatures, one should remove each such contaminant.
Having prepared the sacrificial pit as before and having performed the foundational oblation (āghāra) according to the rule,
one should perform the root-homa consisting of five oblations to Agni, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa.
One should offer oblations by the hundreds and provide food for the Brahmins;
in the absence of sacrificial fuel, one should take wood from the Palāśa or the Vaṭa tree.
Having offered oblations to Agni, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, one should perform the necessary rites;
likewise, having taken up sacrificial grass, kuśa, or fuel-sticks that have been kept for a month.
One should likewise offer oblations to Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, and Agni, as well as to Āditya; in this way, there will be the pacification of faults.
If curd or milk— whether from a goat, a buffalo, or even [other sources]— has been taken,
one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Āgneya, and Saura mantras, as well as the Vyāhṛtis.
Having brought earth or likewise sand from an unspecified location for the purpose of the fire-pit, one should indeed offer oblations to Varuṇa and Viṣṇu in the Vaiṣṇava rite.
One should discard that fuel which is moist, smoky, foul-smelling, smeared with plaster, thorny, or infested with insects when throwing it into the fire.

Having cast other [substances] into the fire, one should offer oblations of the Āgneya, Vaiṣṇava, and Vyāhṛti mantras upon garments and other articles, upon Darbha grass, at a water-station, or even upon a heap of grain.
When [the vessel] has been burnt by fire, one should offer oblations ten times each for the Brahma, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Āgneya, and Vaiṣṇava [mantras].

But in the case of the reversal of the arrangement of the vase-deposit (kalaśanyāsa), one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and to Paṅktīśa as the presiding deity, and thereafter perform the rite according to the scripture.
During the snapping and overturning of the bell, the wise one should offer oblations according to the ritual rules, reciting the five Vāruṇa mantras and the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
If there is a reversal regarding the bed, one should offer oblations ten times each for the Vaiṣṇava, Śrī, Mahī, and Manu mantras during the ritual bath and the laying out of the bed.
Whether the praise of the *hautra* office be inferior or erroneous,
one should there offer oblations to Brahmā, to the mantras of the Lord of Munis, and also to the assembly of attendants.
If the invocation and other rites of worship are performed in reverse order or omitted,
one should offer ten oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Brāhma hymn, and the Raudra hymn.
When all the aforementioned oblations have been performed, or when they have been omitted or performed erroneously,
one should offer [oblations] into the lotus-fire with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
One should rescue the deity even if he is lying down at an improper time, even without mantras;
having offered oblations dedicated to Śrī and Bhūmi, one should cause him to lie down four times.
If one's study is deficient, one should perform the Sārasvata sacrifice one hundred and eight times;
having offered the oblations, one should then practice according to the scriptures as an expiation.

One should accept [the offerings] according to what is obtained; if there is no obtainment, one should have all performed by the sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) through a single ritual procedure (tantra). This is remembered as the rule of the scripture.
Likewise, for those performing consecrations, festivals, or other auspicious rites, as well as for the preceptor and the officiating priests performing the *puraścaryā* observance; BhS_27.74 //
For those who have been initiated, no impurity is proclaimed until the ritual bath;
yet those who, out of delusion, observe impurity fall into a foul hell.
Whether they be those already consecrated or others,
the teacher may take hold of them, even while employing such actions as scolding them for their faults and so forth.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the Brāhma, and the Sārasvata hymns, and having obtained their permission, one should proceed.
When the time for the teacher’s fee has passed, one should indeed offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and separately offer the sage-mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should give the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and should not harbor greed for wealth;
if the gift of food to the Brahmins is deficient, one should perform a rite of pacification (śānti).
A three-day great propitiation (mahāśānti) wards off those defects;
a sacrifice performed with meager fees destroys [the rite], whereas one with proper fees bestows its fruit.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the life-force of the sacrifice; therefore, one should protect it with effort.
This [fee] should be understood as being for the immediate occasion; one should cause the land to be given later.
Having specifically assigned land for the worshipper’s share of the offerings and for the sake of his family,
one should perform the Mahāśānti rite.
But the divine abode does not increase for one whose conduct is free from conceptual construction;
for it is through the practitioner’s vow that the king and his kingdom prosper.
Therefore, one should act with composure so that the worship is not neglected;
even in times of dire distress, one must not let this worship fall into disuse.
Whenever worship is interrupted by any cause whatsoever, one should consider it a fault; this offense is like a fresh wound.

Therefore, through the inheritance of land and other stable gifts, the worshipper, having firmly established his authority, should proceed with reverence in the performance of worship hereafter. (BhS 27.86)

Because the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and so forth occurs when worship is neglected, therefore the inhabitants of that village, as well as those belonging to the kingdom, [should perform it]. The king too, even though he belongs to the kingdom, [must do so].
For the sake of worshipping the Blessed One, they should perform service with great effort;
for the worshipper becomes one whose offenses are fresh regarding transgressions.
Seeing him emaciated by his lack of livelihood, the king and the village dwellers should act so that he is as comfortable as the deity and as honored as the priest.
Even if they receive a greater livelihood than before, those who are envious should not harbor suspicion;
rather, they should employ their own abilities as is appropriate for the sake of his happiness.
But if the installation is not performed according to the rules and no worshiper is appointed, that worship shall become demonic; the performer will certainly not obtain the fruit.
If, having bypassed the family designated by the deity for the worshiper,
one should instead cause the worship to be performed by another, [there is a fault].
Both the one who performs [the act] and the one who causes it to be performed go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, with every effort, one should observe what is prescribed in the scriptures.
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what belongs to the afternoon;
for death does not wait—therefore, one must gather the accumulation of dharma.
One who has renounced worldly wealth should never be attached to wealth even when it exists;
one should act according to one's ability and should not covet further riches.
In the absence of amulets and the like, one should place gold dedicated to Viṣṇu;
[one should recite] the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, and the Vāyavya hymn dedicated to the Lord of the northern direction.
O assembly member, if the internal oblation is deficient, the wise man, being composed, should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Pāvaka, and likewise the Vyāhṛtis ten times each.
But if the taking of the fire has been omitted, having performed the previously mentioned expiation,
one should fetch fire from the house of a Vedic scholar and perform the rites beginning with the Āghāra oblation.
From that time forward, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) and carry it out;
for one should invoke [the deity] in the Dhruva vessel and so forth, as well as in the four [vessels] beginning with the Kautuka.
If, through negligence, the invocation of them was performed at the Kumbha-tīrtha,
one should quickly bathe them with pure water while reciting the "iṣetva" mantra and others.
Having honored the Lord of Gods, the Vaiṣṇava, one should offer the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
one should then offer the Puruṣa-sūkta and again invoke [the deity] starting with Dhruva.
Now, the expiation for the failure of daily worship shall be declared:
[if it occurs] from sunrise until midday, or even until sunset.
If the opening of the door fails, or if the perpetual fire in the Great Mouth is deficient,
one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava, to the deities beginning with Dhātṛ, and likewise to the Doorkeeper.
Having prostrated before the God of gods, one should quickly open the door;
or else, when the opening of the door-panel has been performed by others without mantras.

One should offer the previously mentioned oblations and recite the twelve hymns for peace when the purificatory sprinklings and other rites have been omitted, or when the floral offerings have not been cleared away.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, and Śānta,
the Guru should once again perform everything correctly with the mantra alone.
If water is unavailable, one should perform the rite using a substitute substance;
if the bathing of the deity is omitted, one should offer an oblation to Varuṇa in the Vaiṣṇava ritual.
“One should cause the animal to bathe with the mantras beginning with ‘apo hi ṣṭha’; thus there shall be atonement.
One should always perform this bathing for the animals as prescribed for the daily worship. (BhS 27.108)
If bathing is impossible, one should sprinkle [the image] with water from kusha grass while reciting the mantra;
having removed the clothes and other garments, one should offer a washed cloth.
If daily bathing is impossible, some indeed say that one should bathe the Lord of the gods on the five days of Viṣṇu.

Having purified the floral remains (nirmālya) on the permanent seat (dhruvapīṭha), one should again perform the ritual placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa); thus there shall be the daily worship (nityārcana) at the Dhruva.
If one performs the worship of the *kautuka* (protective thread) without the ritual placement of flowers (*puṣpanyāsa*),
one should likewise recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
And having offered oblations, one should perform the Viṣṇugāyatrī and the placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa) in due order;
however, for one who lacks the connection to the *kūrca*, there is the Vaiṣṇava sage-mantra.
Having offered oblations and cast away the *kūrca* grass, one should thereafter perform the remaining rites;
however, if the worship of Dhātṛ and the others has been omitted, one must perform that specific deity’s rite along with the Vaiṣṇava rite.
Having offered oblations, he should likewise worship the Dhātṛs and the other members of the assembly in their proper order;
and in the event of any reversal in the ritual services, he should seek forgiveness by bowing down.
Having obtained permission, one should worship the deity even when the physical form is deficient;
having recited the mantra of that deity, and especially the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Furthermore, one should worship with all the forms using those very same offerings;
however, when the aforementioned substances are unavailable, one may use flowers, water, or unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having taken all of that and meditated upon it, one should worship the deity;
whether at the time of worship, at another time, or when [the image] has been defiled by mice and the like.
Or even if the lamp has been extinguished by the wind, one should diligently rekindle it incessantly,
doubling the light of the solar, lunar, and fiery lamps.
Having likewise offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation, one should perform the worship again;
for at that time, if all the lamps should go out, the fault is very great.
Having bathed the deity with pure water and consecrated him with kuśa-water,
and having offered the previously mentioned expiation, one should perform double the worship.
Even if one among many lamps is extinguished, it does not cause a fault;
in the event of a lapse in the mantras, one should perform the rite with the Mūrti-mantra together with the Praṇava.
At the time of worship, if the curtain is missing, one should offer oblations to Prajāpati and to Viṣṇu,
and having mended the cloth, one should worship again.
By those who revile the Vedas, by heretics, by people afflicted with sinful diseases, by those born in inverse orders, by barbarians, and indeed by those of the lowest castes; BhS_27.124 //
At that time, having offered oblations into the fire for Viṣṇu and for Brahmā,
and having offered oblations for Rudra and Pāvaka, one should then worship the Vyāhṛtis.
If the death of a human being should occur outside the enclosure at a distance of fifty *daṇḍas*, one should remove [the body] and then worship Hari.
One should not perform worship or the offering of oblations before that;
rather, one should carry out the rites for the *dhruva* and *kautuka* [vessels] up to the conclusion of the placement of flowers (*puṣpanyāsa*).
If the time has passed, one should offer oblations for peace and perform worship twice as much;
if the worship at the first appointed time was omitted, one should perform it twice as much at the second.
On the third day, one should perform three times the rites for a single-day fast, excluding the *iḍā*;
likewise, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta.
On the second day, the merit for the deity Śrībhūmi becomes twofold;
on the third day, it becomes threefold; and one should continue in this manner until the end of the twelfth day.
In the past, with reference to the twelve causes,
[he recited] the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Puruṣasūkta into the fire of worship.
Having offered oblations according to one's ability into the fire for the deities of the assembly in the Ālaya,
and having bathed the Lord of Devas with water-pots and worshipped him, one should present the sacrificial offering.
For one month, the preceptor should perform the worship with inferior materials facing the temple;
he should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta in the sacrificial fire of the assembly hall.
Having offered oblations to Śrī, the Earth, and all the deities,
one should bathe Hari with eight and forty jars.

One should offer the sacrificial oblation with special care; likewise, on the second [day] it should be doubled, and on the third it should be tripled, increasing it in this manner throughout the year.
And in the past year, for seven days on the day of the lotus-fire (thirteen), having indeed performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) and having completed the worship of Viṣṇu; BhS_27.136.
Having fed the Brahmins and having bathed the Lord of the Gods once more with one hundred and eight jars, he should then perform the ritual of re-consecration (punarabhiṣeka).
However, during the preliminary consecration of the eyes and again during the ritual of the ceremonial bath,
one should perform all other rites as before, omitting the remaining actions.
When the sacrificial oblation is lacking, all the people dwelling in that village and those nearby shall be afflicted by hunger,
thirst, and the like, and they may even fall ill.
Therefore, one should offer the sacrificial oblation with extreme care;
if the oblation is deficient at the first time, it shall become double at the second.
On the third day, once one day has passed, one should perform the triple-fold rite;
likewise, one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Śrī, Mahī, the mantras, and the Mūrti.
Having bathed the deity with pure water, one should offer an abundance of food,
including side dishes, as well as raw, cold, and even stale offerings.
Not placed in another vessel, with remnants remaining, stepped over, uncovered, drained, altered, and defiled by sight. BhS 27.143.
If one should offer the sacrificial oblation (havis) that has not been sprinkled with water, nor touched, nor grasped, nor sealed,
then [one should recite] the Vaiṣṇava [mantras], the Śrī-sūkta, and the Mahī-sūkta.
One should offer oblations ten times each for the fire-god, the water-god, and the wind-god;
having performed this twice over, one should present abundant offerings.
Having offered what has been touched by the *āśu* [mudrā] and having bathed the deity with mantras,
one should recite the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] and the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī thirty-three times in succession.
One should perform the propitiatory rite according to the prescribed rule and also sprinkle [the area] with consecrated waters;
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, one should offer double the usual worship and oblation.
When the sacrificial oblation has been offered, mixed with rice, charcoal, and husks, and combined with sugar and other ingredients, by means of the eight-syllable mantra.
Having praised [Viṣṇu] with Vaiṣṇava mantras and with the Gāyatrī dedicated to Viṣṇu,
one should request forgiveness by showing respect with the words "Forgive me," bowing down, and making a formal entreaty.
If the offered oblation has been defiled by insects such as flies or even by hair and the like,
one should bathe Hari with pure water.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and those dedicated to Śrī and Bhū, one should then present double that number.
And when that great oblation was thus prepared, it was then defiled;
immediately thereafter, however, [the portion] merely sufficient for human consumption was removed.

Having sprinkled [the deity] with ashes, water, kusha grass, and with the mantras "Hiraṇyavarṇa" and "Pavamāna," and having properly worshipped the deity, one should take hold of that [offering] and present it.
If one offers a side-dish or an oblation that has been cooked before sunrise while it is still lukewarm during the morning worship, one incurs a fault.
One should likewise offer in the evening that which was prepared before sunset; however, betel-leaf that is unrefined, or which is smeared with substances or contains hair, should be avoided.

Having offered that which has been touched by a living being, having performed the consecration with the *Śrīmahī* mantra of the Vaiṣṇavas and having offered it into the fire, one should offer fresh betel-leaf again.
Indeed, it is exactly the same regarding other auxiliary limbs of worship and other ritual objects;
when they are defiled or deficient, their respective presiding deities [are likewise affected].
Having offered the Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should again worship with other [substances];
and in the absence of all these, he should take up flowers and water.
Having resolved upon a substitute and having recollected each [deity], one should perform the worship;
however, if the daily fire-oblation is omitted, one should offer oblations ten times to Viṣṇu.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the aforementioned oblation twice over.
For those unable to maintain the sacred fire, [the rite is performed] while reciting the mantra "vayante yo'ni."

Having placed the fuel-sticks upon the fire from the sacrificial pit, and having established it in the worldly fire, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should offer oblations daily in sequence with the mantra "Upāvaroha".
Because the strength of gods, sages, and men increases from him, he is therefore called Bali; for that reason, he worships Hari every day.

Having invoked [the deity] into the aforementioned three substances, the preceptor should worship them at the three times of day and thus cause [the image] to be carried around; if he is unable to perform the supreme rite, he should do this instead.
Having placed the bali and the kavya exclusively into the vessel as described, one should then set down the bali-image upon it exactly as prescribed.
Carrying the bowl upon his head— either three times, twice, or even once—
he should then circumambulate the temple of the gods, keeping it to his right.
Then, having set aside the offerings for Bali, one should place them upon a palanquin or the like, or upon an elephant,
and cause them to be circumambulated according to the prescribed ritual.
If the morning circumambulation is omitted, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Soma, and Prajāpati; and likewise if the prescribed circumambulation is omitted.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Gāruḍa, one should perform the circumambulation with the bali-offerings;
if the morning bali is deficient, one should perform double the bali at midday.
Likewise, one should perform it three times at the low noon and at night;
however, when the *bali* offering on a single day is deficient, or in the case of the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) or the great mouth (*mahānana*).
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and likewise to the deities of the directions, one should then perform circumambulations.
If the temple is devoid of ornaments, the wise man should worship the deity Śrī;
likewise, if an umbrella, peacock feathers, or other such items are unavailable, he should offer oblations to Varuṇa.
In the absence of yak-tail whisks and other such items, an oblation to Vāyu is offered;
and in the absence of lamps, one should worship the triad ending with the Vyāhṛtis as an oblation to Agni.
On the second day, one should perform double [the penance], and on the sixth day, triple;
this should continue until the end of the twelfth day, after which, when the twelfth day has passed, [the rule changes].
Having established the domestic fire (aupāsana), one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn,
the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the hymns dedicated to Śrī and Bhūmi, and likewise the Brāhma hymn.
Having offered oblations with the mantra of the directional deity Raudra, one should perform the circumambulation;
but when the measurement has elapsed, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta into the lotus-fire.
Having offered the Nṛsūkta, the Pāramātmīka, the syllable Oṃ and others,
as well as the mantras of the assembly deities into the fire, one should perform the circumambulation.
In two months one should double [the penance], in three months one should perform it triple;
one should increase it up to the end of a year, and when a year has passed, one should do so again.
Having properly prepared the assembly hall, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta, facing either toward the gods or toward the southern pillar.
Having offered oblations to the deities of Śrī and Bhūmi, as well as to all the deities,
and having honored the preceptor, one should perform the removal of the sacrificial offerings (bali).
If the food-offering falls to the ground, or if it is broken or spoiled, one should perform the offering again as before;
having offered the oblation, one should likewise recite the Vaiṣṇava and Gāruḍa mantras.
Then, according to the ritual rule, one should perform a circumambulation to the right;
however, if an obstacle should arise at the time of offering the oblation, then—
Having offered oblations to Saura, Saumya, and Vaiṣṇava, one should then perform [the rite] again;
in the absence of a vessel, one should take a vessel for the sacrificial offering and offer it to Vaiṣṇava.
If the food lacks the proper measure or strength, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu and Prajāpati; however, if the sacrificial offering is defiled by a fault, one should perform an expiation.
But in the case of the food-offering (annabali) performed during a circumambulation without an invocation,
one should likewise recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
Having offered oblations to the deity Śrībhūmi according to the prescribed rite, one should perform circumambulation;
and when the offering has been presented to Śānta according to the rite in the section on the foremost bali-offering.
Having offered the Vaiṣṇava Mūrtimantra ten times each in sequence,
and having presented [the offering] to Viṣvaksena, one should offer the mouth-perfume (mukhavāsana).
Furthermore, one should then have the offering of the oblation (bali) performed according to the prescribed rite;
however, if the offering of the oblation has not been made, one should first sip the water from the feet of Hari.
Having partaken of the prasāda, one should worship again with double the intensity;
while the worship is underway, it should continue until the offering of the oblation (havis) is complete.
Whether it be the gift of a holy site or the acceptance of sandals, if performed otherwise than prescribed, it is inauspicious; one should perform a peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma) to rectify it.

If, at the conclusion of the worship, someone other than the worshipper should drink from another sacred water-vessel or take the *prasāda* before him, that worship shall become fruitless. (BhS 27.190)
Having likewise performed the great propitiation (mahāśānti) with oblations, one should again perform worship;
thereafter, [offer] water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), flowers, milk, and then fragrance.
In this [rite], one should offer all sacrificial oblations as well as betel leaves;
whatever has been offered to the Deity, that one should give to Agni and the Aṅghricakra.
Since the officiant is traditionally held to be Hari himself in embodied form,
one should first worship the priest in every rite of the daily obligatory duty.
Furthermore, if a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin ever worships Lord Hari in His temple, he should likewise honor the Ācārya, the Marcaka, or the Naimittika. (BhS 27.194)
To disrespect that deity is to commit a supreme offense;
the sacrificer shall meet with ruin, and the kingdom and its people shall perish.
If one should act otherwise out of ignorance or delusion,
having honored [the image] twice as much, one should perform another [act of worship] twice as much.
Whether he is impure or of improper conduct, a father who is always pure like a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) overlooks the accumulation of faults committed by his sons without hesitation.
For the Blessed One is the father; the sons of Viṣṇu are the worshippers of Hari.
Therefore, one who desires to live a long life should not be angry with them.
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation based on ritual bathing;
bathing is of three kinds: daily, occasional, and optional. (BhS 27.199)
The ritual bath on the equinoxes and at the two solstices is declared to be obligatory; that which is performed during lunar or solar eclipses is remembered as being occasional.
In the remaining cases, that which is called *snapana* is proclaimed as being for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*).
However, when the daily *snāpana* is omitted, the *vaiṣṇava* [mantra] and the *viṣṇusūkta* [are to be used].
One should again offer oblations ten times with the Puruṣasūkta and the Vāruṇa hymns;
one should perform the ritual bathing according to the rules as the expiation for the daily failure to bathe.
If the seizing or the bathing is deficient, one should perform expiation as before;
and in the case of a rite for a specific desire, having performed [the preliminary] as before, one should consecrate [the disciple] with pure waters.
Otherwise, there is great fault and the sacrificer perishes;
[the altar] should be in front of the temple or to the north, in a pleasing location.
The bathing hall in the northeast is the best; that in the west would be middling;
and likewise, that in the south is proclaimed as the lowest.
In the corners beginning with the southeast, one should likewise perform the Vaiṣṇava bath;
one should offer oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, and the mantras of the lords of the directions.

One should subsequently cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed; this is the expiation for the transgression when the time of twilight has arrived, as well as in the case of a ritual bath prompted by a specific occasion.
Having completed the occasional rite (naimittika), one should perform the daily worship (nityapūjā);
otherwise, the wise person should mutter a Vaiṣṇava mantra one hundred times.
In the first part of the night, during the *pratisara* rite, and likewise when lying down on one's bed,
one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the *Śrīmahī* mantras, and likewise the *Saudarśana* mantra.
Having abandoned the consecration of the bed, one should again bind the protective amulet (kautuka);
however, when this amulet is to be applied to the image (emabera), it should be done without the bed.
Having tied the protective amulet (pratisara), one should immediately perform the ritual bathing correctly;
however, if the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) has been omitted, one should likewise perform the Vaiṣṇava bathing.
Having offered oblations to Saumya, Śrī-Bhūmi-daivatyam, and Vighna, one should perform the consecration;
some say that one should first perform the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and then bathe [the image].
If the number in the row is deficient or excessive, or even if there is a pit for bathing,
one should worship Vaiṣṇava, Bhūmidaivatyā, and the mantra of Paṅktīśa.
In the case of inferior worship of Śānta and others, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite and the Śānta rite;
and in the case of inferior worship of Paṅktīśa, one should perform his mantra and the rites beginning with Jaya.

If the worship of Indra and the other deities has been omitted, one should indeed offer oblations with that Vaiṣṇava mantra; and when the water-pots (kalaśas) are deficient in measure, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava and Vāyudevatya mantras.
One should offer oblations to Agni when the earth is deficient; in that case, one should also offer oblations to Viṣṇu.
One should offer oblations to the Earth-deity in all types of earth; this is the rule.
In the case of immeasurable mountains, one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Pāvaka;
and in the case of grains, the wise man should likewise offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Vāyavya.
When the sprouts have failed, one should likewise offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Gāruḍa, as well as the vyāhṛtis; then one should provide the necessary materials again as appropriate.

In the case of those lacking caste or those who are dishonored, one should indeed offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Aindra deities during auspicious rites; one should perform them as is appropriate and also gather the necessary materials.
If the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are devoid of mantra, or if the ritual application is deficient,
one should indeed offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava and Raudra deities, properly joining them with the mantra alone.
In the case of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances that lack the stated measurements,
one should first [sprinkle] water upon the primary items, and likewise recite the mantra of the presiding deity of each substance.
Having offered oblations together with the Vaiṣṇava mantra itself, one should perform the consumption or the sprinkling wherever it is enjoined in this scripture. (BhS 27.222)
This same procedure is to be understood for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in all cases;
however, if the consecrated jar is broken, one should take another and proceed as before.
Having filled and worshipped [the vessels], one should then offer oblations ten times to Viṣṇu;
when the water-jars have been exchanged, one should likewise bathe [the deity] with that very clarified butter.
Having offered oblations to Viṣṇu and to the deity of the materials, and having purified it once more,
one should bathe it with pure water and then install it again according to the prescribed rule.

But once the ritual placement of the jars has been performed, if they are touched by dogs, crows, and the like, or even by those who are untouchable, the remaining rites should be accomplished as before.
Having performed the *śānti* rites and offerings with Vaiṣṇava mantras, one should carry out the task;
however, if worms, insects, or the like fall [into it], one should discard that particular substance.
Taking another substance, one should offer it to the deity Viṣṇu;
if gems are not obtained, having offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation, one should cast gold [into the fire].
In the event that clothing is not obtained, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu and to Śrī;
if the prescribed bathing ritual has somehow been deficient, one should perform the bathing again.
Alternatively, one should have a pure ablution performed according to the prescribed rite.
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation for festivals.

Their distinctions according to time and so forth, as well as their characteristics, have been explained previously; some [practices] prioritize the lunar day (tithi), while others prioritize the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
They imagine a final ablution that brings an end to suffering,
whether it occurs at a fixed time when [the cause] has not yet been performed, or likewise at an unfixed time when it has been performed.
There is great fault in performing a festival at an improper time; one should perform an expiation for that.
Prior to the festival, one should carry out a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) for six days.
Having informed the Lord of the Gods, one should then perform the festival of Kāla;
otherwise, an action performed would undoubtedly be as if unperformed.
If one does not perform the festival in another month as well,
this very same procedure is prescribed when it is performed in the following year.
Thus it shall be for three years; after that, especially, having performed a great propitiation (*mahāśānti*) for seven days, one should perform a festival.
At the end of these twelve years, there is a re-establishment;
for the deity who is the presiding divinity of the festival does not delight therein [otherwise].
In whichever temple Viṣṇu is first installed,
all subsequent work therein should be carried out by that very same preceptor and officiating priest.

In the absence of those, however, his sons, grandsons, or others born of that lineage, or those appointed by him, or his own kinsmen, should perform it; in the absence of all preceding ones, others may do so.
If it is performed otherwise, the sacrificer perishes;
when the festival days have been omitted, one should perform the expiation.
One should increase the Vaiṣṇava duty and never diminish it;
if, however, one fails due to negligence or incapacity, one should offer prayers to Hari.
Having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti), one should diligently perform the remaining rites;
this very procedure applies to the rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), which bestows the increase of well-being.
But when the avabhṛtha bath has been performed by chance through an exchange, one should act as if it were un-intended; in that case, the previously mentioned expiation applies.

Whether through negligence or intentionally, when those [rites] for various times and festivals have not been performed according to the scriptures, one should perform them again collectively (tantra) as prescribed.
Or again, at the proper time, one should perform the avabhṛtha bath subtly by means of a mantra;
for the avabhṛtha is the end of the sacrifice, and there should be no festival immediately following it.
One should perform the festival rites as previously described;
one should conduct the daily festival for Hari, being ever-prosperous and always auspicious.
The god Hari Nārāyaṇa is not capable of being worshipped by the gods when the preceptor, the sacrificer, or another person acting as a worshipper is the object of that worship.
If it has been lost, one should immediately choose another [astrological moment] and perform the rite;
for human effort does not allow destiny to obstruct its task.
Having honored the Lord of Gods, he who has attained the Great Peace in the Lotus [Realm] is worthy of the Brahma-sacrifice; his body is said to be purified. (BhS 27.249)
All those seeking the ritual objects (padārthin) are said to be preceded by their guru;
however, this applies when the seeker of the object has departed for another village during the course of the initiation.

When [the body] is defiled by the fault of touching the untouchable, by drinking liquor and the like, or by other unspecified defects, or when purity and so forth are impossible due to disease; BhS_27.251 //
Or likewise for one who follows a corpse, or for one who is fit for contact with a corpse and so forth;
and for one who carries [the corpse], or burns it, or eats at a funeral rite (*śrāddha*) for the deceased.

If there should be a fault regarding the officiant of a śrāddha, or one who eats the remnants of a śrāddha, or a guest at it, then one should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) according to the prescribed rule.
There is no fault for the performer of the *śrāddha* in that case, for he would indeed be the giver;
[but] the mouth is scorched by another's food, and the hands are scorched by accepting gifts.
One whose mind is consumed by other men’s wives incurs the curse of a Brahmin; how could this happen in the Kali age?
One should not perform another initiation during the course of an initiation, except for the initiation of the womb (garbhadīkṣā).
But when the sacrificer is incapacitated, there should be a consecrated man;
whether he has a wife or not, he should be one who possesses a wife once he is consecrated.
If this auspicious occasion should occur while the husband and wife are performing a sacrifice,
or if the preceptor is without a sacred fire or without a wife, he should not initiate him.
One should show respect toward others who occupy a position according to their capacity;
however, when there is a deficiency among them, those [other monks] do not become faulty at all.
The one-year period of impurity and other such impurities do not apply;
however, that which was prescribed for the death of a mother or father applies again in the case of a funeral rite (abhyudaya).
If the festival is performed without the hoisting of the banner, it is fruitless;
therefore, having first hoisted the banner, one should conduct the festival.
If, after raising the banner, one does not perform the festival—whether out of ignorance or greed for wealth—one may perform it in another month. (BhS 27.261)
If one does not perform it in the second month, however, the performer will perish;
therefore, having offered an expiation-oblation into the fire of lotuses, one should perform the festival.
The Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, and the Gāruḍa;
likewise the Dhvāja, the Śānta, the Cakra, and the deity of the festival.
Having offered oblations ending with the *vyāhṛtis* and having worshipped the Vaiṣṇavas, one should perform the rite;
I shall now describe the characteristics of the banner and the measurement by which it should be made.
One should design it in five ways: equal to the vimāna, or greater by one-quarter or one-half, or less by one-quarter or one-half.
Those known as Jaya, Śrī, Kīrti, Vijaya, and Maṅgala are proclaimed [as auspicious];
one should not perform [a rite] with half [the required materials], for that would be a state of having no other recourse.
Therefore, it should not be inferior, but rather superior according to one's capacity; it should be straight, not crooked, unconnected with anything else, and secured by pins and the like.
Having taken an excellent, unbroken piece of smooth and captivating wood,
one should divide it into fourteen parts and have the rosary made from them.
Leaving aside one part at the front, one should construct three girdles there;
furthermore, the length of those girdles should be equal to that same part.
One should make it three *tāla*s in width, or indeed as wide as a staff;
the space between them should be equal, and one should make three cross-pieces (*yaṣṭikā*).
One should place two staffs in front and one is prescribed behind;
however, in all cases, one should provide a full hundred small bells without exception.
Thereafter, the wise one should divide the remainder into three or four parts for the banner:
an octagon, a hexagon, a square, and a circle.
Starting from the base, one should fashion the banner in four parts;
however, if it is made in three parts, one should not make it six-sided, but should perform the remaining procedure as prescribed.
Having divided the first portion into three parts, some perform it in this manner:
they say the "peak" (śikhara) is the head, and the peak should consist of half [of that].
Having recovered a pinnacle that has fallen through negligence, one should restore it according to the prescribed rite;
or, if the image is cracked or broken, one should act as previously stated.

But when a mountain peak has been occupied even once by birds such as vultures and the like, or if excrement and so forth have been deposited there, or if one has dwelt there continuously; BhS 27.276.
Having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire;
this very procedure is prescribed for temples, spires, and the like.
At the base of the banner, one should construct a charming altar with bricks, joined with a pedestal, a foot-base, and a stone slab.
A person who wishes to live long should not even occupy that [place], let alone descend into the abode and so forth. (BhS 27.279)
The celestial chariot (vimāna) should be in the form of Viṣṇu; one should not step over its feet or other parts.
First, one should perform the circumambulation of the abode, and there one should offer salutations to the three goddesses.
One should not step over the shadow of a banner, nor that of a gate-tower, a celestial palace, a wall, or a temple, except by way of circumambulation.
Having indeed transgressed [the rule] through negligence, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
[visualizing] the vision of Śiva, the vision of Viṣṇu, and the gaze from the side of Durgā.
The wise say that the gaze directed upward at Vighneśa is sharp;
for as long as the shadow extends, for so long does the ground of defects persist.
Having abandoned the ground of faults, one should establish one's dwelling;
through such renunciation, there will be the flourishing of prosperity, whereas otherwise, the opposite occurs.
Just as there may be a difference [in distance] caused by paths such as those for chariots (*radhya*), that does not constitute a fault;
or alternatively, they say that after leaving the area up to the limit of a hundred *daṇḍas*, one finds a suitable dwelling.
Some wise ones say that it is as high as the height of a tree, or the back of a mountain, or even a cloud, and some say it is even greater than that.
Some always desire a banner where one [person] indeed [stands] among those who do not fall;
however, the supreme sages do not accept the performance of rituals such as ascending it there.
Having erected the festive banner, they perform the ritual there;
however, some wise ones say that there should be only one banner everywhere.
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation regarding the flagstaff when the firm flag,
due to negligence or by means of wind and so forth, has fallen to the ground.
Whether it is unbroken or broken, one should cast the banner there once again;
if it is unbroken, one should take that banner and perform the carving with the mantra.
Having performed the ritual of acceptance (*adhivāsana*) and so forth, the wise one should install it in that place.
When the banner is broken, it must not be kept; one should discard it in water according to the prescribed rite.
Then, taking another banner, one should set it up without delay;
if it has been intentionally felled by thieves or others, the procedure is as previously described.
In that case, the artisans should again perform additional carving;
one should make it like an unbroken banner, doing the rest without haste as before.
For a banner that is not utilized for its proper purpose must indeed be abandoned;
by giving away that which has become defective, there shall never again be its acceptance.
Alternatively, having firmly grasped a great foundation, one should proceed;
having set aside the defective portion, one should again mark out the measurement.
Whether it be a measuring-standard or a non-measuring-standard, one should not join it with another piece of wood;
one should have it extended [with its own kind]. This is the universal rule.
One should fashion armor and other such items from copper or other metals;
having constructed a small temple, one should perform the ritual there.
One should keep the banner exactly as it stands and never move it;
if the banner is burnt, one should discard it and procure another.
If the banner is touched by those of the lowest castes, one should then perform a great propitiatory rite;
if they have approached its vicinity, one should perform a thousand oblations.
When [the banner] has fallen, or likewise by way of transgression, or similarly upon the top of the flagpole and upon the girdles, all of that should be renewed according to the rule.
Having fixed it to the flagpole, one should perform the consecration once again;
likewise, if the flag moves or if it is broken through negligence.
One should perform the prescribed expiation for a banner that is broken or not broken;
this very same rule is declared for all other staffs in every respect.
If, due to the falling of lightning or other such calamities,
the deity within the temple has perished while the flagstaff remains standing, then the propitiation of the flagstaff must be performed.
Furthermore, having made it his abode, he should propitiate that very banner for three years,
observing it in a temple that has not been constructed.
In such a place, the deity does not take delight; therefore, a wise person should abandon that banner.
Alternatively, one may install it anywhere else and worship it there.
Now I shall describe the location for the flagstaff as determined by the scriptures:
having divided the space between the pedestal and the gateway into five parts.
Having set aside one-fourth from the base (pīṭha), the placement of the banner (dhvaja) occurs in the fifth part;
at that junction, it should be auspicious, so that one may perform the ritual according to the tradition.
If the banner should be outside the enclosure, one should act according to the scriptures;
and if it is placed in an unstated location, one should likewise act according to the scriptures.
If one is unable [to do so], one should instead construct another rampart in due order;
one should make it visible to the sight of the gods and ensure the banner is clearly perceived.
And when the interior is enclosed by other buildings or even by gate-towers (gopura) and the like, one should nevertheless create an opening within the range of vision.
If [the site] is destroyed, moved, or lowered by falling trees and the like,
one should diligently perform that same rite as before within three months.
If a flagstaff has been damaged by worms, birds, or the like within its hollow interior,
one should subsequently construct a new shrine for the deity, level the site, and worship it once again.

When the raising of the flagpole has been performed by means of rope-tying and other such methods, there should be no construction of a small shrine (bālālaya) there; rather, one should perform the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi).
One should sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while the dhvaja-mantra is being offered as oblation.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of worship for the rite of expiation (niṣkṛti).
Wherever the banner has been destroyed or even damaged according to the prescribed rule,
one should again perform the auspicious bamboo-banner rite, beginning with the re-consecration and ending with the final installation.
Alternatively, the wise one should have a banner made of gold, silver, and so forth;
having erected it to the height of a palm tree, he should install it in the inner sanctum and worship it.
One should perform all that, beginning with the ritual acceptance (*adhivāsa*), as prescribed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The bamboo staff (*veṇudaṇḍa*) should be immovable; it may be movable within the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*).
On all occasions such as festivals and the like, one should employ the bamboo staff (veṇudaṇḍa);
for the "moving staff" and the "bamboo staff" constitute two types of festivals.
But when a festival or similar occasion has commenced, this procedure applies even if the aforementioned fault occurs:
having carefully released Garuḍa from the flagpole, one should remain composed. (BhS 27.319)
Having led [the image] into the sacrificial hall and established it there, one should worship it;
having installed the bamboo staff, one should immediately apply [the ritual] to it.
One should likewise perform the Mahāśānti rite and offer a thousand oblations;
[one should recite] the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇudaivatyam, the Gāruḍa, and the Dhvāja [mantras].
One should worship the Sudarśana and one hundred and eight Kūṣmāṇḍas;
likewise, the wheel-mark should appear everywhere on the lamp-post.
One should not place a lamp upon a banner; the lamp-stand should be separate.
By placing a lamp there [on the banner], one does not obtain the imperishable fruit.
Having placed a lamp upon the banner, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava deity a hundred times;
they shall declare that the lowering of the lamp from the banner is for times of distress.
If a banner equipped with a lamp is lost, one should perform expiation as before;
likewise, if the hoisting of the banner is performed when the consecration of the Vīśa has been omitted.
Having offered oblations ten times each to the Vaiṣṇava [mantra], the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, the Dhvaja [mantra], and the Gāruḍa [mantra], one should perform the consecration once again.
Likewise, for the omission of the worship of Dhvajadeva, Cakra, Śānta, Nandīśa,
and Vaiṣṇava, one should perform the rite accompanied by their respective presiding deities.
Having performed the fire-oblation and worshipped once again, one should thereafter carry out the ritual action;
even when the beating of the drum is omitted, one should likewise recite the Raudra mantra and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered the Mahāvyāhṛtis, one should perform the striking of the drum;
this applies everywhere in worship and other rites wherever the sounding of the bell occurs.
This very rule has been proclaimed: one should perform the expiation when Garuḍa has been mounted [but not yet released], or when the offering has been deficient.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava, Dhvaṃsamatra, and Gāruḍa mantras,
one should present the offering twice as much and request forgiveness, saying, "Forgive me."

In the case of a deficiency regarding the *mudga* grain offering, one should likewise perform the Vaiṣṇava, Vāyudevatya, Āgneya, those beginning with the syllable *Iṃ*, the Gāruḍa, and the Dhvāja rites.
Having offered [the oblation] with great effort many times, one should present the *maudgika* [dish];
even when damage from rain, wind, or heat occurs properly.
And likewise when it is defiled by excrement and the like, or when birds repeatedly or even once alight upon it,
or when the rope and so forth snap, or even when it falls through negligence.
When the cloth has been intentionally cast down, or planted out of season, or touched by Śūdras and others of the anuloma classes, or when it has reached the top of the flagpole; ||| BhS_27.335 |||
Having purified the impure and leveled what was uneven,
the Guru should offer oblations six times to the presiding deity of the festival.
The Gāruḍa mantra and the Dhvaja mantra, along with the Sahasra, should be offered;
then the remainder should be completed, and one should not act contrarily.
If the cloth is burned through negligence or intentionally, one should procure another;
having performed the previously mentioned propitiatory rite, one should perform the consecration once again.
One should perform the descent and the dismissal with the mantra;
however, if the descent is omitted, the dismissal shall be performed with the mantra alone.
Then one should perform the remaining rites; if one is unable to descend [from the seat], one should take up a large cloth and perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite.
Taking up another [vow], he should perform the remainder of the ritual;
likewise, in the case of a low [offense], he should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite at the commencement of a festival or during a ceremonial bath.
The Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Nṛ-sūkta, and the Vāruṇa-sūkta are offered;
it is recorded that the rite of atonement consists of being consecrated with pure waters.
But if the binding of the protective thread (kautuka) is deficient, one should offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Śānta,
and Saudarśana, and then bind the protective thread once again.
In the sacrificial hall, whether the altar-pot is deficient or even excessive,
the wise man should offer oblations to the Vaiṣṇava fire and the deity of the earth.
If arches are not available, one should offer oblations to the guardian deities;
if the garland of darbha grass is deficient, one should perform the rite for the ṛṣis and then perform the other rites.
But if it is devoid of ornaments, one should likewise offer oblations to Śrī as the presiding deity;
and having presented the morning bali, the same applies when the daily festival is deficient.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, Śānta, and Īśa, as well as to the deity of the festival,
one should perform the evening festival and cause it to be conducted in sequence with double the usual intensity.
If the festival is deficient in the evening, one should perform a double celebration in the morning;
if it is a single-time festival, one should offer the bali-oblation at two times.
One should perform the festival in the evening; even if the time has passed, this is the prescribed rule.
Having invoked the deities of the directions, one should worship them on the first day.
The offering of the bali should proceed clockwise from the east to the northeast;
however, in the invocation of the deities, there may be a reversal or an exchange of order.
Having performed the expiation previously mentioned, one should offer twice the amount of the *bali* offering;
however, the offering of the *bali* to Brahmā and the lords of the directions is a daily rite (*naityika*).
Having performed atonement for non-giving, the offering should be sixfold as previously stated;
it may be offered to the deities of crossroads, to trees and the like, or according to one's desire.
If there is a transposition prior to the first invocation, the previous expiation applies;
otherwise, the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi) comes first, after which the sacrificial offering (bali) is given.
Those streets become pure; they become pure again at the proper time.
If the purification of the site has not been performed, one should offer the bali-oblation upon the streets.

Having performed the previously mentioned rite of peace (śānti), there is again the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi) and the offering of oblations (bali); however, if the site is already pure within, one should not perform the circumambulation of the oblations.
After lifting up the corpse, the ritual of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) should take place;
offering oblations at an improper time increases the gratification of the asuras.
If the offering is given at the wrong time, the offering at the proper time shall be threefold;
for that is the place for the circumambulation of the offering, indeed for the circumambulation of the deity.
The conduct of the Lord is not otherwise than a swift sprinkling;
for they do not declare this to be a fault during a festival of faith, since it is indeed different [from ordinary conduct].
In cases of the expansion or contraction of a site, as well as when the boundaries of a village are being determined,
one should obtain the permission of the Lord of Gods and perform a ceremonial bath with one hundred and eight jars.
Having established the boundary and determined it with certainty, one should then perform the ritual;
one should hold a festival at night and perform the ceremonial bath with a thousand jars.
Having performed the invocation of the deities, one should likewise carry out the festival;
because the strength of the gods and others increases thereby, it is known as the Bali.
An offering is said not to be fit for consumption by wicked beings such as dogs and pigs;
the crow is declared a consumer of offerings, while cows and other such creatures are pure animals.
If it is done incorrectly, there is great fault; one should cause a hundred oblations to be offered with those mantras.
A Śūdra should not eat the remains of the offering; the worshipper is the one who partakes of the remains of the offering.
If [the substance] is thrown away without the mantra of power, or if it is consumed in a condensed form or devoid of the prescribed ritual,
one should perform the previously mentioned expiation for such acts as consuming it in a state of non-conformity and so forth.

When the *bali* has been left overnight, when it is excessively hot, or likewise when it has not been offered; or when it is offered before or after the proper time; or when it is seen by Śūdras and others during the *bali*— [in these cases, the rite is defective].
Having performed the expiation previously mentioned, the sacrificial offering (bali) is doubled everywhere;
in whatever place the invocation of the deities was previously performed, from that point [the rite proceeds].
In that very place, the offering of the bali should be made until the dismissal takes place;
the mandala, the water, and the kūrca are said to be the support for the invocation.
For the offering of the bali-oblation on the streets, the pedestal should be made of stone or other materials;
