the bali-offering must be kept secret, so that those who are non-Vedic do not see it.
One should conceal that same [image] at the proper time with curtains and the like;
however, when the offering of oblations is omitted, one should [conceal] the Vaiṣṇava protector of the oblation.
Having performed the oblation, one should then perform an expiation and offer a bali-offering again;
likewise, if the bali-substance or the vessel falls upon the ground.
If [the vessel] is broken or lost, one should offer the previously mentioned oblation and bring forth another;
having indeed performed the offering of the bali, one should then cast it upon the seat of the spirits (bhūtapīṭha).
If no specific place is mentioned for the remainder of the offering, one should mentally offer it;
[reciting] the Vaiṣṇava, the Akṣamānu, the Vaiṣvaksena, and the Gāruḍa [mantras].

Having offered the *saudarśana* oblation, one should cast the *bali* upon the seat of the spirits (*bhūtapīṭha*). This should be done whenever the presentation of the sacrificial food is deficient, and when the worship is performed with double the usual intensity.
Having performed the Vaiṣṇava oblation for peace and likewise having worshipped, one should present the offering;
however, if the prescribed oblation is deficient, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite consisting of the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having offered the Nṛsūkta thirty-three times,
one should offer again for the sake of the Cakravins, Īśas, and Amitas, or even for those residing in the water-pot.
When the worship of the gods is deficient, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta,
the two peaceful mantras, the Gāruḍa, and the Ākrama.
Having offered oblations and worshipped once more, one should especially present offerings;
if the ornaments of the deity are deficient, one should perform the rites dedicated to Śrī and Viṣṇu.
Having obtained the ornaments for the face, the preceptor should adorn [the disciple] according to the prescribed rites;
among the substances used for the ornaments, there should be resin, sandalwood, and excellent flowers.
Having discarded that and taken up another substance, having washed it with mantras and sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), it is called an ornament.
If the dance or the song is deficient, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu or to Rudra; likewise, if the hymn of praise is deficient, one should offer oblations to Brahmā and then to Sarasvatī.
When surrounded by groups of devotees, one should likewise perform the rite for Varuṇa;
when it is deficient, the rite for Viṣṇu, whose deity is Peace; and likewise when the peacock feathers and other items are lacking.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantra and then with the Haviḥ-kṣama mantra;
this is done when the deity does not proceed from the vehicle to the sacrificial hall at the appointed time.
Wherever the deity has been consecrated, there should be daily worship;
as in the case of perpetual worship previously described, there is no deviation from that rule.
Upon seeing that the deity has returned, one should perform another festival;
and at the end of the day, one should perform the festival prescribed for that specific time.
One should also perform the past festival here according to the tantra;
if, through vigilance, that day should be spent [in observance], it shall be so.
One should not abandon [the festival] and should instead perform the celebration appropriate for that time;
if one should be negligent in this matter, the atonement is indeed that which was previously stated.
Having been initiated with garments, garlands, and ornaments offered to the five fires, one whose self is purified should act constantly; however, in the contrary case, one incurs fault.
If, however, there is the loss of the garment that is an auxiliary to the initiation, or likewise of the *pratisara*, there is great fault therein; therefore, one should bring another again.
Having offered a thousand oblations of the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should then perform a rite of pacification;
until the initiation is completed, there is the undertaking of the ancillaries of the initiation.
"In the end, the incapacity directed toward that [object] will naturally diminish;
or else, one might effect liberation," so indeed some say. (BhS 27.390)
In that regard, the wise declare the time for the *pūrṇāhuti* [offering];
at the conclusion of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), that initiation (*dīkṣā*) shall be joined with a festival.
There is no confusion of initiations there, even if two [rites] occur in one place;
yet, if the preceptors and others quarrel with one another during the sacrifice, [confusion occurs].
In this matter, there would be great harm, for the Guru is the guarantor here;
and the great seers have declared that the word of a Guru is equal to the command of a king.
While one who has been initiated is present, one should not allow another to enter there;
for when a single task is to be performed, the association of two teachers is not appropriate.
If, through negligence or intentionally, blood flows during a quarrel,
or if wounds should occur, one should dismiss that person and have it performed by another.
However, initiation shall not take place for him; rather, one should perform a great rite of pacification (mahāśānti).
For he indeed becomes initiated through the previous ritual procedure.
As long as the transition of impurity occurs while one is already impure, one becomes impure again; having undertaken another [period], one should observe the remainder as previously prescribed.
If the feeding of Brahmins is deficient at the beginning, the middle, or the end,
one should perform the Trivākya Mahāśānti oblation and then provide the meal for the Brahmins.
One should indeed cause the worship of the Vaiṣṇavas to be performed twice as much;
for when worshipped, the Vaiṣṇava instantly and repeatedly purifies one from sins.
If the deity is mounted by non-Vaiṣṇavas or heretics, it causes double the misfortune;
to pacify that fault, one should perform the ablution with a thousand jars.
Worship performed by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava destroys previously accumulated merit;
however, if the deity has fallen from the vehicle, one should quickly lift it up with respect.
Having obtained his permission with the words "Forgive me," and having been consecrated by those pure ones,
he [recited] the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Nṛ-sūkta, in their proper sequence.
Having offered oblations to the presiding deity of the day, one should perform the festival;
this applies individually for Cakrin, Vīśākha, Amita, and the others, in the absence of their respective images.
Having invoked [the deities] with mantras into vessels containing rice upon mats,
and having recollected their respective forms, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered oblations to each respective deity, one should thereafter perform the festival;
likewise, in the event of their falling, one should extract them and proceed as before.
Having bathed it, one should perform oblations for the respective deities as well as for Viṣṇu;
likewise, when the image has fallen from its vehicle, or is deficient in limbs, or when there is a gravity of fault.
Having performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) in the fire of the lotus for the pacification of that fault,
one should then, according to the ritual, deposit that power (*śakti*) into the permanent image (*dhruvabera*).
Having appropriately adorned either a ceremonial image, a bathing image, or a bali-image, one should invoke [the deity] according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed the worship thoroughly, one should conduct the festival; there must be no transgression in that regard.
However, if another image is unavailable, one may use a gem or likewise gold.
Having deposited [the deity] in a vessel, having invoked it, and having worshipped it day after day,
and having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) with oblations, one should perform the festival once again.
Furthermore, if the image has a missing limb, one should restore it according to the rules of rejoining;
having thus restored it, one should perform the consecration once again at the crossroads.
Upon the fall of cows and other such animals, the deity is Śrī and Viṣṇu;
but upon the fall of musicians, the deities are Brahmā and Rudra.
But when teachers and others fall or are shaken in that manner,
or likewise when banners and the like are brought down, [the expiation] is the Ārṣabha or the Vaiṣṇava rite.
One should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rite for the deities of Indra, Varuṇa,
and Vāyu when there are rain showers, a whirlwind, or when struck by a flash of lightning.
One should not perform a festival at an improper time; however, if one does so, it should be dedicated to Viṣṇu, reciting the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, and those hymns whose deities are Śrī and Bhū.
One should perform a festival after making an offering; however, if the opposite occurs, it causes harm.
Likewise, when rain showers enter between the streets, or during thunder and the crashing of lightning.
When there is especially the touch of wind carrying grass and dust,
or when accompanied by the sound of quarreling, the knower of mantras should bathe the deity.
Having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, the deities of the directions, Vāruṇa, and Vāyudevatya,
as well as to the gods and others, one should perform the festival once again.
In times of strife, when blood is shed, during a conflagration, or even at a festival—
one should likewise employ the Vaiṣṇava, the Agnidevatya, the Brāhma, and the Raudra [mantras].
One should offer oblations to the deity presiding over that day and pray to Hari;
likewise, if death occurs within the interior of the temple due to weapons or other causes, one should do the same.
Having quickly abandoned that very thing, one should likewise offer it as an oblation into the fire of the lotus;
especially so for the great propitiation (mahāśānti) and the presiding deity of that day.
If [the image] is damaged on the street or elsewhere, one should quickly remove it,
perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), and then conduct the festival once again.
Furthermore, if one should perform a festival again after [the lapse of] a nāḍikā, provided that a corpse remains within eighty daṇḍas of the temple, [then it is not a transgression]. BhS 27.423.
One should not hold a festival there; if one should do so, it will perish.
Having abandoned that [festival] immediately, one should perform the penance as prescribed.
Having offered the great peace-offering and to the attendants, one should perform a festival; this is the procedure for a *lagara*, and it is prescribed for a village as well.
One should perform the festival with the Antaśsava itself for the prosperity of the village, from the time the flagstaff is hoisted until the day of the Tīrtha arrives. (BhS 27.426)
If one should perform any other auspicious rite or even a malevolent incantation (*ābhicārika*),
then for the very purpose of pacifying that fault, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the *Viṣṇusūkta*.
Having offered the *Nṛsūkta* and the *Pārṣada*, one should feed the Brahmins during the first part of the night, provided the binding of the *kautuka* has not yet been performed.
Or, upon the bed, having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava, to Śrī and Bhū as deities,
and to Saudarśana, one should perform the remaining rites as prescribed.
If the time for bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) has passed or if it is deficient, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava,
Vāruṇa, and Skanda rites, and having offered oblations, perform what has been prescribed.
If the lowering of the banner is deficient, or if it occurs during that very night,
the Guru, having offered oblations to the Gāruḍa and Vaiṣṇava [mantras], should pray to the Lord of Devas.
But when the descent-rite is performed, especially if the *bali* offering is deficient,
one should thoroughly worship the deity of the banner, the Vaiṣṇava, with the *Viṣṇu-sūkta*.
Then, having specifically offered oblations with the mantras of the deities residing in that abode and having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should cause the banner to descend.
At the conclusion of the festival, when the ritual immersion is omitted, one should cause the Vaiṣṇava hymn,
the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the Jayādīni, and the mantras of the [divine] forms to be offered as oblations.
Regarding the faults not mentioned here, this expiation should be performed:
the Vaiṣṇava [hymn], the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Nṛsūkta.
The Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, which destroys the life-force of all sins,
is thus recited twenty-eight times, or one hundred and eight times if one is capable.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Miscellaneous Section," in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now, the expiation for touching those who are untouchable will be declared;
[it applies] in the case of snakes, mice, frogs, cats, mongooses, and the like.
When they have entered the inner sanctum and discharged excrement, urine, or other waste,
that area should be cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise with the *abliṅga* verses.
One should recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra and the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one hundred and eight times while standing firm during the discharge of feces,
urine, and other bodily wastes.
Having quickly wiped it with a cloth and cleansed it with *kuśa* grass,
[he should recite] the verses beginning with "The waters are golden-colored" and "Driving away evil."
Having sprinkled [the image], one should worship the deity; otherwise, one who acts contrarily would be at fault.
According to the rule, one should touch the images with these very [substances] and bathe them with pure water.

If a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a washerman, or those of the lowest castes should enter the first enclosure, or if they should enter the place of the image, or the assembly of the faithful; BhS_28.6 //

Then, once he has entered and touched [the site], having kindled a fire with wood from the Darbha tree, performed the Vāstuyajña oblation, and sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); ||| BhS_28.7 |||

Having performed the rite for an auspicious day at the end, one should then offer oblations into the perpetual fire (nityāgni) with the mantra of the Gatekeeper and the Vaiṣṇava mantra of the Door-keeper.
But in the case of a dwelling, purification occurs in every respect through sweeping, smearing with cow dung, sprinkling, and the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyajña). BhS 28.9.

When these images of the deity have been seen, one should bathe Hari according to the prescribed rite with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then bathe him with pure water; thus one becomes purified.
Having sprinkled [the site] with ritual sprinklings (prokṣaṇa) and offered oblations as before, one should then perform worship;
likewise, when these [deities] have entered within the interior of the monastery.
Furthermore, if food touched by such [impurity] is inadvertently offered,
one must specifically purify that substance according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should then carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire;
having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having bathed the deity with water-pitchers and then offered oblations into the perpetual fire,
[he should recite] the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Nṛ-sūkta, and the Raudra hymn.
Then, one should recite the *Brahma-sūkta* from the *Śrī-mahī-sūkta* and feed the Brahmins;
this should be done especially after touching the images, such as those of Dhruva and others.
Having performed the purification as before, one should then have the Vāstuhoma sacrifice performed;
thereafter, one should purify the site by means of the circumambulation with fire and the five products of the cow.

Then, having bathed the deity with water-pots according to the ritual procedure over a fire of lotuses, and having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) with oblations, one should perform the consecration once again.
Then, having offered the oblation that has been touched by Śūdras and others born in the natural order (anuloma),
one should reverently bathe the deity with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using pure water.
Afterwards, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made and offer double the amount;
[this applies even] in the case of those who have committed great sins, as well as Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, and others.
But when [the spirit] has entered the *ālaya*, touched it, and made itself known,
one should perform a great propitiation for seven days by offering oblations into a fire of lotuses according to the ritual injunctions.
Having bathed the deity with water-pitchers, one should perform the re-consecration;
and again, whether in the permanent image (*dhruvabera*), or in other images within the temple.
When [the body] has been touched, having performed purification as before and likewise doubling [the rites],
one should offer a great propitiatory oblation (mahatī śānti) and bathe the Lord with ritual jars.
One should perform the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration;
likewise in the event of a fall [from the path], in the case of a heretic, or one initiated by another tantra.
Once one has entered the inner sanctum and performed the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi),
having offered a great propitiatory oblation (śānti), one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once again.
When these [beings] are constantly present in the first enclosure as described, or especially when they have moved into the second enclosure after a month has passed; BhS_28.25 //
Having performed a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) for one month according to the prescribed rules,
and having again carried out the plowing and other preparatory rites, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) once more.

Likewise, when a year has passed, having omitted the invocation and other such rites, and having well-protected the marriage-thread and so forth throughout the inner sanctum and all else; BhS_28.27 //
One should especially cause the cows to dwell [there], particularly after a month has passed;
having performed purification everywhere, one should then offer oblations for three months.
Having thus performed the great propitiation (mahāśānti), one should again carry out the rites such as plowing;
then, having conceived the foundation of the temple, one should first perform the purification of the image.
Having bathed Lord Hari with one thousand and eighty jars, according to his means, by means of the preliminary consecration with water and other rites; BhS_28.30.
Having fed the Brahmins and indeed having honored the Vaiṣṇavas,
he then duly installed the Lord of Gods in the temple for children.
Having renovated the temple everywhere,
especially by performing the great consecration, one should worship the God of gods.
Upon touching those who have come into contact with these [outcasts], the expiation is the same as for one who has touched a woman recently delivered;
and upon touching those who have come into contact with them, purification occurs through bathing and other such means.
Furthermore, no fault is declared for those who come into contact with such [food],
nor when offering oblations that have been touched by a twice-born person lacking the sacred fire, just as in the case of [the impurity of] uncooked meat.
Having performed a great propitiatory rite for one day, having bathed [the image] with waters,
and having had the declaration of an auspicious day recited, one should worship it as before.
Furthermore, when the images or the festoons and so forth have been touched, or if the fixed [image] is affected,
one should again perform a great propitiatory rite as before and re-install it.
Once he has entered the monastery, he should act appropriately in all matters; having understood the gravity or the lightness of each situation, he should carry out everything with due consideration.
If creatures such as insects, birds, or similar beings enter into the interior of the monastery,
or if they touch the sacred images, one should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) as before.
Having thoroughly purified [the site] with the five products of the cow and having consecrated it with pure waters,
one should sprinkle it with ritual sprinklings and offer oblations to Viṣṇu in the perpetual fire or on the hearth.
Having thoroughly cleansed the images and other objects situated near them as before,
and having bathed them with pure water, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite and carry out the prescribed fire-oblation (*homa*).
In the previously mentioned places, if there is cutting or beating of dogs and the like, or even of humans, or if blood flows, or likewise if death occurs; BhS_28.41 //
Having removed those [impurities] and performed the purification of that place according to the rules,
and having indeed offered the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should bathe [the image] with seven jars.
Then, for the purpose of pacifying those defects, one should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti); having worshipped the deity as before, one should properly offer the oblation.
Once it has been produced, having performed the *paryagni* rite outside the *ālaya* as before,
one should bathe the deity with pure water and perform the *śānti* oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Having honored the Vaiṣṇavas, one should worship them properly as before;
and upon seeing the corpse of the Lord of Gods, one should bathe Hari with water-pitchers.
Then one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣa hymn;
furthermore, [one should place them] at the mouths of the elephants, horses, and cattle in the first enclosure.
Having removed any remains of those who have died there, having dug up such a spot, and having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and sprinkled [the site] with pure water; BhS_28.47.
The ritualist should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta,
and the Pauruṣa hymn in cases of perspiration, the flow of blood, weeping, and likewise in idle chatter.
When laughter is seen, when the great drum sounds, and when smoke and other signs arise spontaneously,
having established the fire of Viṣṇu within the lotus facing toward the ālaya, one should then proceed.
Having offered oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, the Ṛṅkāras, and the Pāramātmika hymns,
he should bathe the Lord of Gods in succession with seven jars.
Having worshipped thoroughly, offered the oblation, and respectfully fed the Brahmins,
and having honored the Vaiṣṇavas well, one should give the Ācārya a sacrificial fee.
When grass, an anthill, or an insect has appeared there, as before,
one should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite by making oblations and also feed the Brahmins.
Having installed the deity in a new temple, one should perform the rite of renovation;
likewise, when a celestial mansion (vimāna) has been forcibly broken or has fallen, one should act according to the prescribed rule.

Having performed the *śānti* rite for three months, having carried out the plowing and other preparatory rites, having consecrated the site for the temple of the Child [Kṛṣṇa], and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the waters; ||| BhS_28.54 |||
Having indeed performed the purification of the image and bathed Hari with jars [of water] numbering one hundred and eighty thousand, according to the extent of one's wealth;
Having fed the Brahmins and indeed having honored the Vaiṣṇavas,
one should install the deity in the children’s chamber after renovating the temple and its surroundings.
In all cases, one should perform the re-consecration without distinction,
especially when [the image] has been struck by lightning or covered by flies and the like.
Having bathed the deity with water-pitchers and performed a special worship, having offered abundant food and performed the fire-oblation according to the ritual for peace; BhS_28.58 //
Having fed the Brahmins, one should perform the re-consecration;
this applies when the pillar of the stūpa situated atop the temple has been destroyed.
Having performed the rite like that of the celestial chariot (vimāna-kalpa), one should again perform the reconnection;
likewise, upon seeing a second sun in the sky, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite.
Having offered oblations ten times to Saura and having especially worshipped him,
[one should likewise offer] to Vaiṣṇava, to the deity of the direction (Digdaivatyam), and to Āgneya when there is a conflagration of the quarters.
In the case of a shower of stones, one should perform the Vāruṇa and Vaiṣṇava rites thirty-three times each;
likewise when there is an untimely appearance of the moon, or during its waning, or at the new moon.
And during a great portent, having performed a great propitiatory rite according to the rules,
one should especially worship the deity and then feed the brahmins.
Whether inside the dwelling or specifically on the outer wall,
and likewise upon seeing a red woman, one should thoroughly purify that place.
Having especially worshipped the deity, one should properly present the oblation;
likewise, when the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) or the portable image (*kautuka*) and so forth have been touched, the procedure prescribed for the permanent image should be performed.
Having performed purification and the ritual consecration with water, one should install [the image] once again;
however, if snakes or other creatures are seen within the sanctum, one should remove them.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and sprinkled it with the five products of the cow,
and having established the *aupāsana* fire, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite for peace.
Having caused the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce an auspicious day, one should then feed them;
but in the case of death from a snake or similar cause, one should remove that [impurity] from there and smear [the ground].
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow and performed the purification of the ground (vāstuśuddhi),
one should then bathe the deity with twenty-four water-pots (kalaśa).
Having bathed the deity with pure water and performed a great rite of pacification,
and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, one should perform a special worship.

But when [the image] has died outside the temple, having removed it as before and sprinkled it with ritual ablutions (prokṣaṇa), one should indeed offer oblations to the deities of the directions and to Viṣṇu.

If a snake dies in a place for cooking, at a city gate, or similar locations, one should remove it, smear the area with cow dung, and perform the daily fire sacrifice, especially that dedicated to Viṣṇu.
One should perform the rite by offering oblations ten times to the presiding deity of that very spot,
whether inside the temple precinct or even within the enclosure of the serpent-shrine.
In the event of a great wind, a lack of rain, or an affliction by enemies, thieves, and the like,
one should consecrate the deity with water-pots and perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.

Having purified [the site] according to the rules with fire circumambulation and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, as well as the Vaiṣṇava hymns and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having offered oblations with the Nṛsūkta, the Śrīmahī mantras, and especially those dedicated to Brahmā, Rudra, and Prajāpati, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule.
Now I shall explain in detail the specific rite for protection against fear,
when one is beset by thieves, enemies, or the armies of a foreign foe.
And one should arrange for the disappearance of the iron images by digging a deep pit in a pure and well-concealed place.
Having filled the pit with sand and strewn kusha grass over it,
one should worship the Earth Goddess within the pit and sprinkle it while reciting the mantra "apo hi ṣṭhā."
Having entered the temple, the preceptor, together with the patron, should bow down to the God of gods,
worship him, and pay him due honor.
“O Lord Janārdana, as long as there may be fear, you should lie down there together with Hari and Śyāmā,” [he spoke] this excellent mantra. (BhS 28.82)
Having informed the Śakti residing in the image, one should install it within the permanent image (dhruvabera);
however, in the absence of an image, one should install it in the heart according to the prescribed rite.
Having said, "Go to the highest speed," the one who moves through the four crossroads took [the image] from the pedestal;
then, with the mantra "Pratadviṣṇu stavate," he placed it in a pit and protected it.
Having said, "This is for Viṣṇu," he should then cause [the body] to lie with the head toward the east;
meanwhile, the pit should first be diligently filled with either sand or earth.
One should make the pit secure, very firm, and well-guarded;
then, having gone inside and bowed to the God of gods, [one should proceed].
Having grasped a *kūrca* (grass-bundle) woven from fifteen *darbha* blades,
twelve finger-breadths in length, and having placed it in the seat of life (*jīvasthāna*).
Having taken [the deity] from the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should perform the worship with its tufts of grass;
this applies especially to the child-image (bālālaya) and the worship-seat (arcāpīṭha).
Having deposited the *kūrca* from the heart and having established it in the *praṇidhi*,
one should indeed remember the syllables mentally, conceiving the *kūrca* as being like the [divine] image (*bimba*).
Having consecrated [the deity] at each respective place, having performed the ritual renunciation (*sannyāsa*), and having invoked [the deity], one should worship;
when the time for bathing and other rites arrives, the wise one should perform the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*).
After one month, however, one should remove that beard and have another installed;
at the proper time, having extracted the image, one should then purify it with sour liquids and other such substances.
If an untouchable person has been touched at the conclusion of the Puṇyāha rite, one must perform the preliminary rites without delay,
beginning with the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa).
Either facing the Ālaya, or to the south, in a delightful place, having established a fire of lotuses at a water-stall, in a pavilion, or on a mound; BhS_28.93.
Having offered the Vāstuhoma sacrifice to the north of that,
and having performed the circumambulation with fire near the image, one should purify it with the five products of the cow.

In the western part of the lotus-fire [mandala], having constructed [a mound] made of grain, with a width exceeding half a bimba, a height of one-eighth [of its width], and rising as high as desired; BhS_28.95.
Having spread five garments over the enchanting altar,
he bathed [the image] with fourteen divine jars.
At the conclusion of the auspicious day, having tied the protective thread (pratisara) according to the prescribed ritual,
one should lay the images, together with the Goddess, upon an auspicious bed.
The lying down of the incarnations (avatāras), however, is prescribed separately;
having sprinkled [the site], one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the lotus-fire (*padmāgni*).
Of the Lord of Gods and the Goddess, and of their host of incarnations, [there is the vow] toward the south,
and likewise toward the north for the attendants.
Having invoked [the deity] and performed the offering of the oblation, one should offer oblations of clarified butter in sequence:
the Vaiṣṇava [mantra], the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Puruṣasūkta.
One should offer the Gāyatrī, the Vaiṣṇavī, the twelve-syllable mantra, the Prājāpatya, and the two Mindā oblations when [the ritual] has been interrupted. BhS 28.101.
This is called the *śāntihoma*; others have declared it the *mahāśānti*.
When six months have elapsed, one should especially perform the *śānti* oblation.
One should offer oblations into the fire for Vaiṣṇava rites with parched grain flour, fried rice, sesame seeds, and cakes mixed with clarified butter;
the ritual procedure is that one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta for each of these a hundred times.
In the absence of lotuses, one should offer white or red *bilva* leaves soaked in clarified butter with the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī; likewise, one should perform the oblation.
And at the end, one should offer oblations to all the deities and finally to the Supreme Self;
the wise call this the "Great Peace" (mahāśānti) homa.
Thereafter, having specifically offered one hundred and eight oblations for each of the respective mantras of the [various] incarnations separately, he should then pass the night.
Having bathed at dawn, having bowed to the Lord of Gods with the *praṇava*, and having awakened Him and paid homage, [one should say]: "O Ocean of Compassion, forgive me."
Having repeatedly and with devotion prayed thus: "For hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and incalculable numbers of offenses committed," BhS_28.108.
Having removed old garments, garlands, and so forth, and having adorned [the image] with others,
one should recite the Śākuna Sūkta accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Placing the stream of water in front, the preceptor should go ahead;
the installers, having lifted up the deity, should perform a circumambulation of the temple.
Having entered within, they should establish [the deity] as before;
the Guru, having touched the feet of the Lord, should recite the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta.
Having recited the *puruṣasūkta* and the *ātmasūkta*, and having meditated according to the prescribed rule,
one should fix the power of contemplation upon the *dhruva* or the heart.
Having performed the arrangement of the syllables, one should then carry out the invocation;
one should likewise summon the deities residing in that abode and others as well.
Afterward, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; then he should perform what was previously prescribed.
The patron (*yajamāna*), being pure in soul, should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Afterward, having strewn grass around the fire, one should perform the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma);
one should then conduct the festival and the ceremonial bathing according to the extent of one's means.
If one is unable, one should perform the ritual bathing; everything else is as before.
If the worship with the *kūrca* grass and other items is deficient, one should then perform the expiation for that.
And thus, O dear one, when this has passed, one should perform the installation again;
others say that for a specific incarnation, one should perform it separately.
Furthermore, if there is a re-consecration of those [images], some perform the respective fire-offerings;
in this way, there shall be protection from fear, expiation, and the attainment of all siddhis.
Now, O wise ones, I shall explain in detail once more the restoration of a child-like temple (bālālaya),
when the great image or the pavilion has fallen or become decayed.
If a limb is broken or missing, or if [the image] is destroyed by fire or lightning;
if there is a loss of color, a displacement from its pedestal, or if the interior of the shrine is otherwise altered; BhS_28.120.
In the event of the destruction of the pedestal, the inner sanctum, and so forth; or upon entry by those who are untouchable;
or when there is a desire to install [the deity] on a higher place—one should construct a temple for Bāla-Hari.
When the abode of the foolish is being honored, when it has become a crowded place,
when it is presided over by outcasts, and when the site is destroyed by lakes and the like.
But otherwise, having performed all the activities such as plowing in a suitable location according to the previously mentioned method, one should respectfully bring forth the image.
Having performed the consecration right there, one should then construct the primary temple,
as well as the external structures of the celestial mansion (vimāna) and its various limbs and sub-limbs, in case of damage.
When there is a breach caused by flies, grass, anthills, trees, or the like—
except in the case of a child's dwelling— one should take up the Śakti weapon and travel by means of a celestial chariot.
Then, having again superimposed the deities of the limbs upon the *dhruva* [pole star],
one should perform once more the consecration as described for celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
Without having performed the installation of the deity, especially in the case of a great image, one should not occupy the temple; this rule is prescribed for all instances.

In the event of the simultaneous destruction of both the celestial palace (vimāna) and the fixed pole star (dhruva), the expiation for that consists of installing the Kautuka and other [images], while omitting the formal invocation (prārthanā).
Having prepared a temporary dwelling for the child according to the prescribed rite, one should perform worship there;
even if the [proper] time has passed, no fault is incurred by doing so at that time.
In whichever limb there may be a loss, there the construction of a small shrine (bālālaya) should take place;
having performed its consecration as prescribed, one should perform that [rite] once again.
And when there is destruction of the auspicious knots (kautuka) and so forth, or when it is certainly possessed of defects,
as well as when the celestial chariot (vimāna) is likewise corrupted, one should construct the children's abode (bālālaya) once again.
Having obtained a wooden image according to one's means and with pride,
one should then install it according to the procedure taught for the original temple.
Having consecrated the auspicious thread (*kautuka*) and the other items, one should install and worship them in due order;
however, in the absence of the *kautuka* and others, or when the wooden [image] is possessed of defects, [one should proceed otherwise].
Having collected its image and having installed a wooden one,
one should duly abandon that former image and [re-install it] again in the original temple.
Having installed the primary image according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it;
now I shall describe the arrangement of the subsidiary shrine in relation to the primary shrine.
To the south of the central line, likewise in the first enclosure,
or in the second enclosure, or in a delightful pavilion and so forth— BhS 28.136.
Wherever there is space, one should construct a hall for novices (bālāgāra) right there; beyond the second enclosure, no hall for novices is to be constructed.
The width is prescribed as beginning from one cubit up to three cubits;
the height should be one and a half times, or three-quarters, or twice that [of the width].
Having divided the height into five parts, one part is for the base;
two parts are for the height of the wall, and two parts are considered for the pinnacle.
The wise one should have another [shrine] made of clay, covered with grass and free from cracks;
its wall-width should be equal to that of the original temple.
Having doubled and then quadrupled [the measurement] according to the prescribed rule, that which remains should be known as the *nālīgṛha*; that indeed is the *taruṇālaya*.
If, in the pavilions and so forth, there is a connection with the wall as is appropriate,
it may have a portico with the pavilion, or it may be without one at the front.
In a combined [mandala], one should make it equal, or three-quarters, or even half;
or it may extend from east to west, or from south to north.
Or one may construct a symmetrical young house according to the rules stated in the treatises on architecture;
having then divided the inner sanctum into twenty-five parts.
In the center is the single Brahma-pada, and around it are eight divine (daivika) squares;
surrounding those are sixteen other human (mānuṣa) squares.
If one installs the *kautuka* in the Brahmāsthāna, it shall be excellent;
if installed in the Daiva or Mānuṣa [sections], it shall be middling or inferior.
One should always install the three images for the bathing ceremony and so forth;
however, they should be placed only in the two final positions, as a change of location is not recommended.
In the location of the vital breath (prāṇa), there should be a beautiful pedestal with three tiers;
it should be as long as available, and likewise endowed with its proper width and height.
Or, having removed the deposit of jewels from its extensive display of wealth,
the wise man should do as before at the front of the Ālaya or at the front of the Bālāgāra.
Having constructed the sacrificial hall and having erected the archways and other structures, he should,
with good servants, procure the necessary materials and appoint the officiating priests in due order.
Having prepared a beautiful bed-altar in the middle of the hall—
specifically one that is square, lacking feet, or especially lacking half [of its usual size].
Having established that wall, one should likewise determine its height to be equal to a quarter of its width,
measuring five, three, or one [unit], just as before.

Then, having purified the child’s chamber and the sacrificial hall according to the ritual procedure with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow, one should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day to be made.
Having offered the *āghāra* oblation into the fire-pits and kindled the primary fire,
he should recite the Gāyatrī, the Vaiṣṇavī, and the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇu-sūkta.
The Pauruṣa-sūkta beginning with the single syllable (Om), the Śrī-sūkta, the Bhū-sūkta, and the Vāruṇa-sūkta— these five mantras, as well as the Jayas, the Abhyātānas, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛts.

Having offered the intermediate oblations, which are characterized by interrupted supernatural power and associated with Vaiṣṇava rites, one should immediately offer each oblation with its respective mantra.
One should offer one hundred and eight white lotuses, Viṣṇu-gāyatrī verses, and bilva leaves smeared with ghee; this destroys all defects. (BhS 28.157)
At the conclusion of the night worship, having diligently worshipped the deity and offered the sacrificial oblation,
one should join that Śakti with the *kautuka* and other [protective] items.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a large stone and brought the water-pot as before, one should wrap it with a thread while reciting the mantra: "śucī vo havyam. (BhS 28.159)
Having washed [the vessel] and performed the purification, one should fill it with water while reciting the mantra "In the streams," and touch it while reciting "O Waters, you are auspicious."
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments, one should place the nine gems and other items therein;
having recited the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should perform the ritual action there.
Then, having entered the interior and placed the water-jar upon a mandala of grain before the deity,
he should sit before the deity facing north.
Composed in meditation, while reciting the mantra and meditating upon Hari, he should pray:
"This house of yours is unworthy; having quickly demolished this dilapidated structure, [let it be renewed]. (BhS 28.163)
"O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, please remain here for a short time while we prepare the new [image] and perform its consecration."
"O Lord of the World, please grant your favor in this house!
Having spoken thus, he then respectfully set a limit of one, two, or three years.
Having invoked the deity together with the Goddess and the others into the water within the pitcher,
the preceptor, holding the pitcher upon his head, should proceed in front.
Thereafter, the officiating priests, having taken the image from the bathing pit,
shall install it in the sacrificial hall with exactly fourteen [mantras].
Having bathed [the image] with water-pots, adorned it with garments and other ornaments, and worshipped it thoroughly,
one should then prepare five couches upon a heap of grain on the sacrificial altar.
Then, having spread out garments and tied a protective cord (pratisara),
one should cause [the deceased] to lie down in that same manner and again provide a covering from above.
Having sprinkled water around the principal fire, one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* verses;
having performed the invocations (*āvāhana*) and other rites, one should offer oblations into the fires as before.

Having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle in the principal fire, one should [recite] the Vaiṣṇava [mantra], the Gāyatrī, the Vaiṣṇava [hymn], the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta. (BhS 28.171)
Having offered oblations three times with the hymn beginning with "Ekākṣara," as well as that which has Śrī and Bhū as its deities, and also the mantra of the assembly of all deities; BhS_28.172.
Having performed the oblation and dispelled [obstacles] according to the ritual rule, he should remain composed for the remainder of the night;
then, having bathed at dawn and bowed to the Lord of Gods with the *pramava* mantra, [he should proceed].
Having awakened [the deity], the sacrificer, filled with joy, should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
then the preceptor, having propitiated the fire, likewise performs the sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having formally dismissed the fire according to the rules,
he should carry the jar on his head while reciting the Śākuna Sūkta.
The preceptor should go in front, and immediately after him those with water-jars;
holding the deity with both hands, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Adorned with all ornaments, preceded by a stream of water,
he went around the palace and then entered once more into its interior.
Having left the fixed zodiac sign, especially at an auspicious moment,
one should recite "Pratad viṣṇu" while remembering Hari upon the seat of the vital breath.
Having installed the Lord of Gods, one should then consecrate Śrī and Bhū on his right and left sides respectively, using their respective mantras in due order.

Then, touching the feet of the deity while reciting the Viṣṇusūkta, the preceptor, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the syllables and so forth, should say: "In this [world] is Viṣṇu. (BhS 28.180)
Taking [the water] with the *kūrca* grass from the vessel containing the *śakti*, one should invoke it with the mantra:
"May Viṣṇu come! and then, over the head of the *kautuka* thread, [one should say]: "Invoke Viṣṇu! (BhS 28.181).
“Having offered oblations to the two goddesses Śrī and Hariṇī on the right and left [sides], one should then invoke the deities and also their attendants. (BhS 28.182)
Having established the [deity] on the right for the sake of the protective thread (kautuka) and on the left for the sake of the ritual bathing and so forth,
one should invoke [the deity] and worship it for that duration.

Having performed the *puṇyāha* ceremony together with the architects, having honored the Lord of Gods with seats and other offerings, and having presented the sacrificial oblation and performed the daily fire-sacrifice (*naityika-homa*).
Having offered the bali-oblation, one should perform the circumambulation of the bali-offering;
then, one should cause the ritual bathing, the festival, and so forth to be conducted in sequence, as before.
In the worship of the abode of the Child (Bāla), one should perform the worship of the two permanent deities;
omitting the invocation and the dismissal, one should carry out everything else.
Furthermore, in the rite for the construction of the Bāla-ālaya, one should perform the creation of the kitchen and other structures as described for the Sūla-ālaya; one must not act contrarily.
If there is a lapse in time due to ignorance or greed for wealth,
one should especially worship the Lord with a Vaiṣṇava rite accompanied by propitiatory rites.
Having offered oblations and honored those worthy of worship, the patron as well as the preceptor should pray to the deity and inform him once more of the appointed time limit.
Then, bowing with devotion, one should quickly perform this rite with care; thus one should cause it to be done until the end of twelve years, and thereafter as desired.
There is no joy for me in that; therefore, one should perform what has been prescribed.
If one is unable to do so, then again, [one should go] from the house of a child to the house of a dog.
One should establish [the mind] there through focused intention; otherwise, one acts perversely.
Just as a person is consecrated when passing from one body to another body.
Likewise, upon reaching another location, one should have the installation of Hari performed;
whether in the first or the second [instance], provided that the old shrine has been worshipped and is no longer in ruins.
Or, if it is defiled, having thoroughly purified and properly adorned a delightful place such as a pavilion by some means, one should do so again according to the rule.
Having established the auspicious thread-crosses and other items, one should worship them according to the prescribed ritual;
then, having renovated the child-dwelling (the temple), one should proceed with that very same rite as swiftly as possible.

Having performed the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi) and the rite for an auspicious day (puṇyāha), and having established [the image], one should worship it; but if that [image] is not suitable, then, having placed it elsewhere, one should establish the temple.
Furthermore, having established [the image] by means of the path of installation, one should worship it.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter:
Expiation (*Prāyaścitta*).
Now I shall explain specifically the ritual preparation for the permanent image (dhruvabera), whether it be made of copper, stone, clay, or wood. (BhS 29.1)
The fourfold nature of the eternal [state] has already been explained by me here;
having established the lotus-feet as the seat together with the six mental faculties.
Having fashioned an image of copper according to the prescribed procedure for the consecration rite,
having performed the opening of the eyes, and having completed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), he should install it immovably.
One should install the two goddesses together on every festival day for the sake of purification;
having consecrated them with pure waters and adorned them with ornaments.
Having performed the placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa) for all the assemblies in due order,
one should fashion them as mountains, just as Śātātapa has declared.

Having fashioned a mountain, a fixed [mandala], or likewise a variegated one, or half a variegated one, according to the previously mentioned procedure, and having consecrated it in the supreme manner through that sequence; ||| BhS_29.6 |||
One should certainly perform [the rite] for the goddesses, other gods, and those residing in their abodes,
using that substance while remaining firmly composed in mind for six months.
And likewise, having [placed them] on the eyes, the eyebrows, both lips, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet, on the nails, and also on the crown of the head; BhS_29.8 //
One should smear the ornaments according to the prescribed rule with the respective colors; if they are made of clay or wood, one should smear the deities with that very same material.
One should have it made with those [mantras] residing in the ālaya; otherwise, it will produce contrary results.
Alternatively, one should have the mountain made everywhere devoid of color.
Indeed, on a mountain that is half-painted,
as well as upon the minor limbs and even the subsidiary parts, that would result in an undesirable outcome here.
Then, having brought the power [of the deity] into the temple, one should bring forth the image;
having covered it over the ground, one should likewise imagine the lotus-fire above it.
And having performed a great propitiatory rite (śānti) just as when taking up the stone,
one should have the production of those respective limbs carried out by a carpenter according to the proper method.
If a large limb is deficient in that image, and it cannot be rectified,
one should abandon that image according to the prescribed rite and procure another.
He who abandons a meal fit for a formal agreement becomes indeed a sinner;
everything would be ruined. One should perform the agreement according to one's capacity.
If one is unable to perform both the permanent image (dhruvabera) and the movable image (arcā) as before, then one should establish at least the permanent image alone according to one's capacity.
"Having installed [the image], one should worship it correctly"—thus say some wise ones;
this very procedure is prescribed for the installation of a single *bera*. (BhS 29.17)
If one is unable [to do so], one should certainly install and worship an image (bera), whether it be a mobile image (arcābera) or otherwise, accompanied by the two goddesses or even without them.
In the clay temple, at the station of Brahmā, one should bring forth the permanent image of the deity;
having placed that together with the Goddess, one should especially construct a celestial chariot (vimāna).
If one wishes to construct a stone temple, the deity should resort to a divine [image];
having thus fashioned the vimāna, one should then fashion the kautuka.
Having fashioned a mobile image out of metal, one should perform the rites in the place of the forehead;
however, if it is made of stone, one should install it as an immobile image.
Having installed a small image made of clay in a consecrated pavilion,
one who desires to perform [the rite] should certainly prepare a permanent image and a pavilion made of stone.

Having fashioned a celestial chariot according to the prescribed rules and the measurement of a cubit, and having established the God together with his two goddesses within the divine portion; BhS_29.23 //
Having taken up the image previously worshipped for the rite of the *kautuka*, one should install it to the north of that [main shrine] for the festival and other rites, and worship it.
Previously, while the worship of the stationary image was being performed in an earthen temple,
one may desire to construct a vimāna out of stone or bricks.
Then, for the sake of protecting that image and to prevent contact with craftsmen,
one should construct a sturdy wooden cage as a child-chamber.
Having thoroughly cleared away any splinters below by means of supreme skill, one should again measure [the base] with two cubits, according to the proportions of that image.
Having constructed a palace according to the extent of one's wealth, one should protect it well; its square base should be equal to, half of, one and a half times, or twice the height of the image.
The inferior, the middling, and likewise the superior—these three types have been declared;
having made [the measurement] four parts, three parts, or even half of that.
The remaining interior chamber, as well as the thickness of the walls, should be made;
the procedure for the temple with its pavilion should be carried out as previously described.
In a palace made of stone or brick, at the end of a section or elsewhere, one may have it made mixed; for if one is unable to construct such [an edifice], one may do so.
Furthermore, above the base, one may fashion it again in any desired location using mixed materials; however, one should not allow for greed regarding power.
When there is a certain loss of color due to the accumulation of defects such as cracking and the like,
or even when the defect is slight, one should then consider the incapacity inherent in the fixed image (dhruvabera).
Having invoked [the deity] into the water in the jar, and having taken that jar along with the protective amulet and other items,
one should proceed according to the ritual rules into the pavilion within the courtyard.
Having performed the ritual dismissal (sannyāsa) regarding the auspicious thread and other items, one should invoke [the deity] and worship it;
then, having deposited [the deity] into the water-pot (kumbha) at the proper time, one should perform all the ritual actions.
Two days later, Cāturmukha took another jar;
having drawn the Śakti from that jar, he poured it into the other jar.
One should worship in this manner for three days and perform the purification of the water-pot;
thereafter, having applied the colored pigments and so forth, one should indeed thoroughly cleanse it.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, the Puṇyāha rite, and the Dhruva-śuddhi purification;
then, taking the water-pot and the image, one should enter the interior.
Having properly established the auspicious thread-crosses and other items, and having performed the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and so forth,
one should take the Śakti residing in the water-pot and install her within the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Furthermore, from the Dhruva [pole star], one should worship [the deities] in the kautuka and other [mandalas] while facing downward;
this should be done after a month has passed due to the gravity of the faults, when the appropriate time is required.
Having installed the deity in a house of clay, one should purify that earthen image again;
then, one should purify in sequence an image of wood, and then one of stone, up to the limit of stone.
In the celestial chariot of the nine, six, or five forms, having taken that floor which is joined with defects and having designated it as the place for the child, one should proceed.
Having properly established the auspicious thread and other items, one should worship them correctly according to the rite;
thereafter, having taken up the auspicious thread and others, one should proceed in a faultless lower chamber.
Having established [the image] once more, one should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
Now, I shall describe in due order the procedure for the abandonment of a worn-out image.
If the *dhruva* is devoid of limbs, one must indeed abandon it immediately;
otherwise, there will be great danger for both the performer and the worshipper.
Therefore, with every effort, having thoroughly cleansed the worn-out [image] on all sides,
one should cover it with new cloths and bind it with cords of *kuśa* grass.
Having had the Brahmins carry [the body] across the broad river flowing to the ocean, or having led it to the bank of some other inexhaustible reservoir of water; ||| BhS_29.47 |||
Having constructed a water-shed and established the domestic fire (aupāsana), he, being unwearied,
should offer oblations a hundred times to Viṣṇu at the conclusion of the pouring of the clarified butter (āghāra).

The wise preceptor, having loosened the binding of the cloth and facing either east or north, should perform the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma) ending with the *vyāhṛti*s, reciting "To the teeth, svāhā! and so forth. (BhS 29.49)
Having cast both the Vāruṇa and Vaiṣṇava mantras into that water,
one should bathe while recollecting the Lord of Gods, especially when using a wooden vessel.
Having burned it with fire, one should then cast those ashes into such water,
while reciting the respective mantras of the Goddesses and their retinues, together with the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Then one should cast [the thread] into pure water and subsequently give the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Now, if there is a loss of limbs or other such misfortunes regarding the protective amulet (kautuka) and so forth, that is explained as follows.
The head, the belly, the chest, and the throat are called the major limbs;
indeed, they declare that the feet, the hands, and the arms are the minor limbs.
The wise know the fingers, ears, nose, and so forth to be the minor limbs (pratyaṅga);
the head, the wheel, the pedestal, and the halo are likewise [the major limbs].
The secondary limbs (upāṅgas) were said to begin with ornaments, weapons, and garments;
however, if the secondary limb is deficient there, one should accomplish the *kumbha* as before.

Having invoked that Śakti into the water-pot and joined it with the image as before, and having performed the preliminary rites such as the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa) and the Vāstuhoma sacrifice; ||| BhS_29.56 |||
Having thoroughly purified [the image] with the five products of the cow and especially with water infused with *kuśa* grass,
one should reverently bathe the Śakti residing in the jar with seven jars of water.
Having invoked [the deity] again into the image, one should worship it properly according to the rite;
and if any limb is deficient, one should transfer that power into the great image.
Having extracted the image and sprinkled it with the five products of the cow and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
one should join it with metal of equal quality and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) upon *kuśa* grass and other materials.
Furthermore, one should perform the consecration again by means of the path of re-consecration;
however, if it is deficient in its limbs, one should join it together as is appropriate for joining, just as before.
If one worships otherwise, or if the great limbs are deficient,
one should cover that image on the ground and perform the oblation in sequence above it.
Having omitted the limb-oblation and the great propitiatory rite for that day,
one should lift up the image, wash it with the five products of the cow and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Having heated silver three times in the fire, one should purify it with acidic water;
gold should be heated in the fire twice or once—this is the sequence.
Having fashioned an excellent image with that very same material as before,
and having performed the consecration once again, one should carry out the worship in due order.
Having painted [the deity] on a cloth or a wall, or having worshipped it according to the rules in an image,
one should observe when it has become worn out and then project its power into the solar orb.
Having renovated it and reinstalled [the deity] therein, one should worship it;
and by that same preceptor by whom the initial rites, such as the plowing and so forth, were performed.
If the consecration of Viṣṇu has been performed, one may have others performed by that same [preceptor], as well as daily worship, festivals, and even rites of atonement and so forth. (BhS 29.67)
And in his absence, [the king shall support] his son, grandson, or great-grandson;
or one born of his lineage, or his disciple, or finally, one appointed by him.
In the presence of one's own teacher, one should never choose another teacher;
if one should so choose, there will be great danger for both the kingdom and the king.
The worship would become fruitless and every undertaking would perish;
therefore, with every effort, one should not cause confusion regarding the gurus.
But if a confusion of teachers has occurred through ignorance or greed for wealth,
one should perform the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) in the fire of the lotus-born [Agni] and earnestly pray to the Guru.
Having asked for forgiveness with the words "Please forgive me," and having especially honored him, one should have that task performed by that very person; such is the teaching.
But if an ācārya or others are not available, one should have an image of him painted on a cloth;
then, in his presence, one should likewise choose another suitable ācārya.
If, however, there should be a concurrence of karmas in a single funeral rite,
the sons and other relatives of the deceased, having prostrated before the officiating priest, should perform it according to the prescribed rules.
If that is not obtained, the Guru should have it made according to the Tantra;
having first established it by way of yoga, it should then be worshipped.
If one should perform the installation afterwards together with the two goddesses,
it would result in malevolent magic that brings about the destruction of the king and his kingdom.
Formerly, when that which was joined with the eternal wonder was being worshipped, then,
upon the destruction of both the celestial chariot and the Pole Star, the worship of Dhruva took place in the abode of Brahmā.
Some say that one should place the amulet at the site of the festival;
and one should prepare a seat or, according to one's desire, a bed at that location.
One should perform reclining while on a seat, but one should not cause oneself to stand; likewise, while reclining, one should not sit, but according to the rule, one should cause oneself to stand.
One should perform the festive rite for the bridegroom whether he is standing or seated; likewise, one may perform the rite for the bridegroom while standing or indeed while seated.

One should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the offering of the food-remnants (balibera) to be performed everywhere for the host of deities who have descended and for the fivefold group of images.
If one establishes the rite of *kautuka* through mutual confusion, a greater fault would arise; therefore, one must indeed strive for the pacification of that defect.
Having performed a great propitiatory rite (śānti), one should install [the image] in its proper place;
now I shall specifically describe the ritual procedure for the fivefold propitiatory rite (śāntipañcaka).
Due to the abundance of evil among men and because of specific transgressions, the gods swiftly create wonders; when these are seen, [men are quickly transformed].
One should perform the pacification as prescribed; for if it is contrary, it brings misfortune to the performer, the patron, the king, the kingdom, and the site of the dwelling.
Disturbance arises immediately and destruction certainly occurs;
therefore, within twelve days, one should perform a pacification rite according to the prescribed rules.
In the past, preceded by the twelve causes and the great peace,
one should indeed worship the Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability and give abundant sacrificial fees.
One should undertake a superior rite especially after a month has passed;
having performed a great propitiatory rite for seven days, as well as feeding a hundred Brahmins.
Having fed the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission, one should cause [the rite] to be performed;
when six months have passed, Hari rejoices there.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the pacification (śānti) as prescribed;
for a portent (adbhuta) is of three kinds, distinguished as terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial.
There will be planetary conflicts, divisions, and disturbances within the planetary spheres;
total eclipses, famines, and the impairment of the senses.
Such divine wonders as these they proclaim,
as well as atmospheric phenomena such as the continuous halo surrounding the sun and the moon.
Due to the abundance of other colors,
such a halo appears at night in the sphere of the sky over the abodes of Indra and Dharmarāja.
The falling of thunderbolts and meteors, the sighting of Rāhu’s tail and other such portents, the falling of stars, the appearance of comets, and the sight of smoke from Indra’s banner; BhS_29.94 //
The sight of a city of Gandharvas, its subsequent disappearance, and the appearance of a mock sun, a lotus, or a star are what they declare [to be signs].
Terrestrial signs have been described in many ways according to their division into mobile and fixed;
[one should observe] their production and so forth as being contrary to place, time, nature, and other factors.
Likewise, there is birth specifically among animals such as the spotted deer, snakes, and horses, as well as among cattle, elephants, buffaloes, and other such creatures.
Among worms, insects, moths, birds that scratch for food, and those born from eggs, as well as in the dwellings of those with discolored bodies and clothing, and likewise in their abodes; BhS_29.98.
Furthermore, among the wonders occurring on earth— such as the sight of red women—
and those that are divine or atmospheric, the most excellent of these is this [teaching].
The intestines of humans are the best; those of buffaloes and similar animals are middling; they say that those found in reptiles and such are the lowest.
Weeping, laughing, prattling, flaming, rolling about, perspiration, the flow of blood, and the appearance of worms, insects, and the like.
Explosion at an improper time, smoke, trembling of the limbs,
as well as falling asleep, tasting [non-food], and the appearance of grass or anthills.

If, while in the presence of an image, there should likewise be the sight of women who are lustful, or of heretics, those of inverse caste, those of the lowest castes, or those who have fallen from their status; BhS_29.103 //
When touched by untouchables such as jackals and the like, upon entering [such a place], when a pillar sprouts, or when there is shaking or shifting [of the ground]. BhS 29.104.
Likewise, when moving away, as well as when using a door, a bed, or a seat, or similarly with a wall, weapons, clothing, or the implements for the Agnihotra sacrifice and so forth; BhS 29.105.
And in the celestial palace, in a transformation, in the falling of flies and trees,
in the setting in motion, in approaching, and in leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Furthermore, there is specifically the sight of things being inverted in branches and the like, as well as the oozing of blood and the oozing of water from stationary objects; these are portents among stable things.
O Bhavānī, those [omens] occurring specifically in the inner apartments and on the throne are particularly destructive to the king, the kingdom, and the brahmins.
Śātātapa declared that there is destruction for both the builder and the patron;
this applies to temples built by kings, and especially to those within a royal palace.
On the pedestal, on the base, on the platform, on the neck,
and on the pinnacle— these, O Bhavānī, are the [ornaments] belonging to Kṣatriyas in due order.
Indeed, these acts bring about great calamity for one worthy of consecration, for a crown prince,
and for a consecrated sovereign.
In the first enclosure, there will be great fear for those of the Vaiśya caste who are ministers, as well as for the domestic chaplain and the lords of those mandalas.
Due to the misfortune of the Śūdra caste, in the second enclosure and the others,
there occurs the destruction of crops and the death of livestock such as elephants and horses.
For the domestic priests, it is in the fire-pit; for the twice-born, in the place of Brahmā;
for all others, in a temple of Rudra; and for the king, in his secret chamber.
There shall be misfortune for the wives of army commanders in the abode of Vakratuṇḍa; likewise, for the wives of kings in the abode of Śṛṅkhalā, and for other women in the place of Durgā.
In the Mātṛsthāna [region], there are those of the lowest castes; in Kuberaka, there are medicinal herbs;
and in the abode of the Sun (Bhāskarālaya), there are those who subsist by means of royal vehicles and weapons.
One should also observe the respective enjoyers in other temples,
as well as in the assembly halls, meeting pavilions, and courtyards.
In the kitchen, in the royal residence, especially in the pleasure grounds,
and in the dwellings of the preceptor, the patron, and other seekers of material goods.
The appearance of red women and so forth arising from sacred trees and the like,
as well as anthills and other such signs, grant results according to the specific directions and the paths prescribed for them.
When Mars is situated in the images of deities, their pedestals, or within the sanctum of a temple,
the defects arising therefrom are declared to be of the highest degree.
Furthermore, those born in the gateway pavilion (prākāramukhamaṇḍapa) are the most excellent;
those in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) are middling; and those in the remaining [enclosures] are said to be the lowest.
Likewise, in the royal courtyard, the very best are situated all around; in the courtyards, the superior ones are found, while those within the inner residence are considered middling.
The lowest [type of omen] occurs outside the dwelling; this is known as the gradation [of severity].
For those occurring in the celestial or atmospheric realms, there is no medical treatment; only pacification is desired.
In this case, regarding the terrestrial moving [omens], one should cause the omen and the subject of the omen to dwell in another region, and there perform rites for pacification.
Furthermore, when there is weeping or laughing from the images of the stable [deities],
or likewise when they blaze, one should install the deity in a new temple.
Having placed the Śakti residing in that [liṅga] there according to the prescribed rule,
and having performed the rite of pacification (śānti), one should again perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) and worship in due order.
Upon returning [to consciousness], one should again perform rites for pacification and so forth as before;
and in the event of sweating or the flow of blood, one should perform everything just as in the case of weeping.
Having projected the power (śakti) as before into the arising of worms, insects, moths, and even ants, one should again aim it with skillful means.
One should perform rites for pacification and so forth in cases such as untimely cracking [of images],
as well as upon the pedestal of a statue, and likewise within the interior of a temple.
Having installed the deity in a new temple where anthills or similar growths have appeared,
one should dig out the defect and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow.
Having thoroughly cleansed everything and restored it, one should again perform the ritual bath once the opening has appeared outside the temple and has been made clear.

Having ground [the ingredients] and filled [the vessel] with water from the Marīci and other sources, one should rub it with a stone and prepare sugar; this brings about the peace enjoined by the divine.
Furthermore, when [the thought] has arisen again, one should likewise apply oneself with skillful means;
yet, upon seeing a fly, one should remove it without delay.
Having purified himself, the wise one should then begin the rite of pacification;
likewise, upon touching those who are untouchable, he should perform the rite of pacification.
In cases such as the regrowth of a pillar, one should perform the rite again after rejoining [the parts];
however, for the Lord of Trees (Śiva), peace is achieved only through the prior abandonment of that act performed by force.
When a calamity had arisen in the royal courtyard, he settled the king along with his army in another part of the palace and performed the appropriate rites for pacification.
Having consecrated him, one should again, on an auspicious day, lead him into the kingdom;
this applies to the highest of the high, the high, and the middle [classes].
And for even the lowest person who touches the untouchable, there is, respectively,
a wondrous peace that is first abundant and then great.
Peace and purity—thus peace is said by the wise to be fivefold;
likewise, it is directed toward the Ālaya, or toward the northeast, or the north.
On a mountain peak, on the bank of a lake, or in a pavilion, a water-shed,
or a gabled structure provided with sixteen pillars— highly beautiful.

Having constructed it in the center according to the prescribed rule, measuring four cubits in width and provided with an interior space of equal measure, and joined with ridges and elevated mounds; BhS_29.141.
Having first dug twelve finger-breadths deep, one should then construct a pit as described for the ascetics,
measuring two cubits in length and breadth toward the east.
Having prepared an excellent sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in height,
one should establish the Āhavanīya fire in the four directions starting from the east, in due order.
One should cause the anvāhārya, the āvasathya, and the gārhapatya fires to be established;
likewise, one should prepare the aupāsana sacrificial pits in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Having performed [the preliminary rites] at the gates according to the rule, one should arrange the archways and so forth,
adorned with full water-jars, sprouts, plantain trees, and banners.
Having decorated it with pillars, coverings, and the like, as well as with garlands of *darbha* grass and canopies, according to the extent of one's means.
Having made a heap of grain upon the sacrificial ground,
and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in its center, one should place rice grains in the middle of that [lotus].
Taking a water-pot made of gold, silver, copper, or clay according to one's means, and filled with thirty-two *prastha*s, one should proceed according to the scriptures.
Having encircled it with thread at intervals as far as a barley-corn,
and having wrapped it with a pair of garments and adorned it with ornaments.
There were eight golden auspicious vessels as well as the five weapons,
bearing their characteristic marks and not lacking even by a single finger-breadth.
Precious gems, gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, as well as tin, lead, iron, steel, and magnetite— these indeed have the forms of the planets.
Having poured [the water] and filled it according to the pure ritual procedure,
one should also add camphor, sandalwood, ushira, cloves, cardamom, and so forth.
Having placed other fragrant substances and sprouts of the mango tree and so forth,
one should cover its mouth with a similar lid as if to seal it.
Having selected both the preceptor and the officiating priests according to the scriptural injunctions,
one should honor them with new garments, upper cloths, and ornaments applied to the five limbs of the body.
Having adorned [the site] and offered the *āghāra* oblation into the fire-pits as prescribed,
one should likewise place the Sun in the center, as well as Indra and the others, along with Venus and Mars.

Having meditated upon Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the others— beginning with the Sun, followed by the Moon, Rāhu, Ketu, and Mercury— in a clockwise direction, one should then worship them with offerings.
Having touched [the patient] according to the prescribed rite taught for the sacrifice to the planets, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra ten thousand times, or one thousand plus eight.

Then, having offered oblations of sacrificial wood, cooked rice, and clarified butter, each dedicated to its respective deity, one thousand and eight times in due order into the Vaikhānasa fire; BhS 29.158.
One should daily offer one thousand and eight oblations of bilva leaves soaked in ghee while reciting the eight-syllable mantra, as well as oblations of bilva wood fuel.
