Having offered one thousand and eight oblations with ghee using the eight-syllable mantra,
at the conclusion he should likewise offer ghee with the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, cause it to be proclaimed with dances and songs,
and should daily teach the four Vedas in their proper order according to the directions.
Now, this Kalpasūtra was composed by the Teacher in ancient times;
wherever the private recitation (svādhyāya) is prescribed therein, it should be studied according to the rules.

One should give sacrificial fees to the officiating priests; in this manner one should perform the rite for seven days, whether the defect occurs in the temple, beside the water-jar, or on the sacrificial mound.
Having established and worshipped that deity and offered the great oblation,
one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) before the deity at the conclusion according to the prescribed rule.
According to the prescribed rite, one should hold a festival for nine or seven days;
then, one should bathe the king with the water from the divine and celestial jars.
Having sprinkled that vessel upon the earthen mounds with the remaining water,
the king should sprinkle the monarch and his wife, after having duly honored the preceptor.
One should give gold, cattle, land, and so forth to the officiating priests alone;
one should give abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), for the life-force of the sacrifice is the sacrificial fee.
If there is trouble in Rājagṛha, one should construct a pavilion nearby and perform,
as before, the sacrifice to the planets and the fire-oblation in a Śramaṇaka fire.

Having performed the ritual preparation of the water-pot, one should bathe the Lord with the water from that pot at the end of seven days, according to the sequence prescribed for the final consecration.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and his predecessors, having performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
and having performed the consecration (abhiṣecana) under an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
One should enter the house of the preceptor for the sake of accomplishing Dharma, as instructed by the Guru;
this very rule is declared and approved even for householders.
Because kings act for the sake of others, he (the king) is treated here as the primary subject,
for the purpose of pacifying all-consuming eclipses and other such divine wonders.
According to one's capacity, one should give gold, land, and even cattle to the Brahmins;
likewise, one should especially give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) commensurate with great abundance.
For the sake of ending the drought, having taken up a water-pot as before and having invoked all the sacred fords (tīrthas) into it, he should worship it before Hari.
On the meditation seat, having placed a golden lotus endowed with eight petals upon a golden vessel, one should invoke the deity there.
Having worshipped him and placed the water-pot upon a seat above that,
one should fashion a hole at the base of the pot, about the size of a needle.
One should sprinkle Hari with that stream of water which flows in an uninterrupted form,
using either fuel-sticks of reeds or of palāśa wood.
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of the Pañcavāruṇa mantra into the Śrāmaṇaka fire, and subsequently perform the offerings to the directions as previously described.
The wise man should offer one thousand and eight oblations for each of the five Varuṇa rites with fuel-sticks of vetasa wood, according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oblations separately with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and reed-twigs—one thousand and eight times—reciting the mantra "indraṃ praṇayanta" as well. (BhS 29.181)
Having established the *śrāmaṇa* fire, one should invoke Vajrin upon its southern side;
having worshipped him thoroughly, one should perform the oblation with the mantra beginning, “O you who are accompanied by Śacī.”
Having honored the deity especially, one should perform the ritual bathing and other rites;
thus, having understood the gravity of each respective action according to the prescribed rule.

Having completed the [preparation] day by day according to the ritual procedure in the fire of the ascetic (śrāmaṇa), from the first day until the end of thirty days, one should fill a jar with that [substance] and sprinkle [the site] with it.
At the very end, having bathed the deity and worshipped him thoroughly, one should offer the oblation;
at the conclusion of the rite there will be a great rain, therefore one should perform it with diligence.
Alternatively, one who desires rain, or seeks liberation, or desires cattle, or seeks the pacification of all calamities, especially one who seeks victory; BhS_29.186.
Having reached the bathing hall and having adorned it as before,
and having understood the gravity of the ritual, he prepared water in many ways.
One should first worship the preceptor with diligence, for he is the sustainer;
the preceptor, with a well-pleased mind, [should place] rice grains to the east of the pit.
Having formed a row extending from south to north with wide intervals,
he established the sacrificial pit for the ascetics to the south of the chasm.
Having established the fire and wrapped nine jars with thread,
he should wash them with water and purify them with a bunch of *kuśa* grass at the crossroads.
Having filled [the vessels] with milk, one should indeed place them in sequence by blowing [upon them],
and having arranged them in a row, one should cover them from above in order with lids.
One should cover the pit with cloth after worshipping Hari at the conclusion of the ritual;
having bowed down with the Svasti-sūkta, one should install [the image] in the middle of the pit.
One should perform everything according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure;
then, having taken milk into a vessel wrapped with thread.
With the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the mantras beginning with "ceṣe," the Guru should, in due order,
bathe him with that stream of milk for the sake of liberation.
In the same manner, having sprinkled water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "Viṣṇornuka," "Atodevā," and likewise with the eight-syllable mantra.
One should offer oblations with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one thousand and eight times;
or otherwise, one should perform the ritual rubbing (udvartana) with mantras for as long as it takes for the ceremonial bathing (snapana).
Then, having cleansed it with yellow powder and treated it with sour liquids and the like,
one should bathe it thoroughly with scented water and wipe it dry with a cloth.
Having adorned [the image] with garments and other ornaments and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer oblations such as milk-rice and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
By this, a person shall obtain all desires without exception;
provided that, during the worship of the permanent image, one has bathed it and placed a water-pot before it.
Therefore, having brought [the milk] there, one should bathe [the image] right then due to the aforementioned gravity;
one should arrange for the milk-bath for seven, five, or six days.
In this way, one should perform the consecration with ghee, which yields a corresponding fruit;
Kāśyapa and others proclaim this as a marvelous pacification.
Now, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall proclaim the rite of Prabhūtaśānti;
having caused the pavilions and other structures to be built according to the rule as before, BhS_29.202.
Having performed the Viśā-homa in the ascetic fire (śrāmaṇāgni) as prescribed, and having prepared the vessel (kumbha) as before, especially at the end of seven days; BhS_29.203.
Having collected one hundred and eight, or forty-eight, water-pots, and having worshipped them and performed the consecration; BhS_29.204.

Having especially worshipped the deity, one should offer the oblation; this is the procedure. I shall now describe the sequence for the Great Peaceful Rite (mahāśāntikrama) without the preparation of the ritual water-pot (kumbha).
In the fire of the ascetic, one should offer one thousand and eight oblations, soaked in clarified butter and made with bilva leaves, sequentially with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having performed worship, one should offer the oblation; this shall be a great pacification.
Having offered oblations for one day in the domestic fire according to the prescribed rule, peace is established.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should indeed give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Now I shall describe the procedure for purification; thereafter, one should perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice.
Having offered oblations separately one hundred and eight times with bilva leaves and other materials,
at the conclusion of the auspicious day, one should worship the preceptor and also feed the Brahmins.
One should perform the ritual consecration of the jar with every kind of mental visualization;
then, from that, there shall be universal peace, as well as freedom from the fear of untimely death.
In the case of planetary affliction, great disease, fear of enemy armies, as well as the loss of wealth or kinsmen, famine, and defeat; BhS_29.212 //
In the event of fear from malevolent magic, when oppressed by the three types of suffering,
or when adverse circumstances befall oneself, one should perform the rite of universal pacification.
For seven days or nine days, one should perform oblations separately with the twelve-syllable mantra,
offering one thousand and eight times according to the prescribed ritual sequence.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, on miscellaneous matters, in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra* as proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter:
Expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Now I shall explain specifically the expiation for the commingling of tantras;
one should declare that there is fault in the commingling of a Vaiṣṇava with another tantra. (BhS 30.1)
There will be the destruction of the village, the sacrificer, the king, and the kingdom;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying those evils, one must abandon all intermixture.
One should specifically recite eighty-eight [hymns], namely the Padmāvali, the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣa, the Pāramātmika, and the Oṃkāra. BhS_30.3 //
Having offered one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight oblations, with a view toward the gravity of the fault, one should perform the rite as previously described.
The sages have proclaimed that the Vaiṣṇava scripture is of two kinds:
the Vaikhānasa and the Pañcarātra, which are respectively Vedic and Tantric in nature.
The Vaikhānasa tradition is Vedic, honored by the twice-born who follow the Vedas;
it is proclaimed to be gentle and bestowing fruits both in this world and the next.
Furthermore, the Pañcarātra system of Āgneya is non-Vedic and unreal;
it is honored by those who possess initiation through the five purificatory rites beginning with *tāpa*.
It is said to be inauspicious and to yield results only in the hereafter;
yet it is gentle and should be worshipped everywhere, especially in villages and other such places.
O gentle one, one should not worship Hari in the houses of Brahmins;
likewise, one should worship Āgneya in the house of a Vāstavya and similarly in a smithy.
One should not perform this [rite] on mountains and the like, in forests, or in secluded places; nor indeed in the dwellings of Brahmins or the dwellings of common people.
If there is a confusion between the gentle path of the Vaikhānasas and that of the Āgneyas,
and this is adopted by the Pañcarātra, the king and his kingdom will perish.
To pacify those very faults, one should perform oblations in the fire of lotuses in due order;
one should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti) according to the ritual procedure for seven days or six days.
Then, having bathed [the deity] with one hundred and eight jars,
and having worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, he should indeed honor the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having fed the brahmins according to the previous procedure,
one should perform the installation and the worship according to the ritual rules of the Pañcarātra.
When that [time] has been bypassed by time, one should perform an auspicious entry;
because of its auspiciousness, it will bring prosperity to the king and his kingdom.
Having first performed the great propitiation (mahāśānti) in the fire of the lotus, one should then, in due order,
[construct] the temple and the image according to the Vaikhānasa rite.
Having consecrated it with all the appropriate consecrations, such as plowing and so forth,
and having installed it, from that time forward one should perform everything by means of that alone.
Even in the case of secondary worship, no confusion whatsoever is permitted among the retinues and assemblies of the deities residing in the ālaya.
What indeed shall I say regarding the majesty of this great scripture? Even the three gods, including Indra, and even Ananta himself, are not able to describe it fully.
"Listen, all you sages, to the supreme majesty of the scripture;
I shall proclaim it according to my ability, as it has been understood through the power of the Guru's grace. (BhS 30.20)
In ancient times, the four-faced Brahmā, desiring to create the entire world,
arose after a long period of sleep and proceeded with the work of creation.
When the Creator, his mind overcome by sleep,
forgot the Vedas which are primary for creation, the process of creation did not proceed at all.
Then Brahmā, distressed with anxiety and bewildered as to what ought to be done,
reflected in many ways but found no cause for it within himself.
Whatever could be performed by his own power, the deluded-minded one did it all;
yet he did not find the cause for that, which was simply the forgetting of the Veda.
Having finally abandoned that long-held anxiety, the Lord of Creatures, with a composed mind,
beheld the Puruṣa within the center of his heart-lotus through supreme meditative absorption.
He meditated indeed upon Viṣṇu, who embodies the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
and then Brahmā, his mind intent on Hari, offered praise.
Then he bowed to Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace,
and he worshipped the Lord of Gods with offerings such as water for the feet, using equal portions for each of his limbs.
Then, bowing again and again with his head to the Lord, the Master of the World,
his inner self became stainless through a mere fraction of the Lord’s unfeigned compassion.
Pleased, Brahmā praised Nārāyaṇa, the unborn Lord of the world:
"Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one! Homage to you, O creator of the universe! (BhS 30.29)
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One! O infinite one, consisting of pure consciousness, devoid of the limitations of space and time.
O Supreme Lord, whose nature is truth, knowledge, bliss, and joy; O You whose form is the infinite manifestations consisting of the fivefold, fourfold, and manifold arrays!
O Viṣṇu, O Puruṣa, O Satya, O Acyuta, O Aniruddha, O Lord of the World,
O Leader of the supreme sky which is the abode of the eternally liberated!
O You whose divine and auspicious form is served by Śrī, Bhū, Nīlā, and others;
O Wielder of the conch, discus, mace, and arrow; O Bestower of fearlessness and boons upon Your devotees!
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and bangles, and graced by neck-ornaments and a girdle; BhS_30.34.
Adorned with a magnificent garland of *tulasī* upon his broad chest,
graced by a long, hanging sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and radiant with the *kaustubha* jewel as an ornament.
O inconceivable Lord of all worlds, marked with the Śrīvatsa;
you who are served by divine weapons and beautifully adorned with yellow garments.
O you whose essence of compassion spreads forth eternally, effortlessly, and without interruption;
whose lotus-face is gently smiling, and whose sprout-like lips are sweet!
O one with a golden luster, whose eyes, face, hands, and feet are red and bring happiness; O you of beautiful brows, forehead, and fortunate nose, with lovely elongated eyes! BhS_30.38 //
O you with rounded, thick, and long arms, with a slender waist and a great mouth,
whose lotus-feet have traversed the three worlds through their playful prowess!
O sinless one, you who are the ordainer of knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor—salutations to you, Viṣṇu; salutations again and again to you, the Puruṣa.
Homage again and again to the one whose nature is the eightfold equanimity, the imperishable;
homage to Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose form is unceasing.
Salutations to the one whose nature is consciousness, who possesses an infinite and peaceful form,
the wielder of the bow, the impartial ruler, the independent sovereign, and the supreme authority.
Salutations to the infallible, the changeless, the treasury of splendors;
to the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, who is to be known through the Vedas and who is the knower.

Homage to you whose form is the supreme manifestation; homage to you whose body is the pervasive power! Homage be to you, the inner controller; homage to you, the eternal one whose form is the object of worship.
I have gone for refuge to you, the thousand-headed Puruṣa, the thousand-eyed, stainless one, the thousand-footed protector.
"You are my mother, you are my father, you are my brother, you are my friend;
you are everything, O Soul of All, for everything is established in you."
Having found refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible, infinite ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel of afflictions.
Indeed, there is nothing that should be hidden from you, for nothing remains unknown to you;
you alone are the witness of all embodied beings, pervading everything, you shine forth.
You have no form, no instrument, and for you, O sinless one, there is no cause;
you are the teacher of all worlds, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, O Hari.
O Brahmin, both I and Bhava are born from your grace and anger respectively;
my first birth was mental, O one honored by the twice-born.
O Madhusūdana, this consciousness that has been attained and this state of Brahmanhood that has been acquired— all of it is but a mere fragment of Your glance.
My mind being overcome by darkness, the Vedas have been forgotten by me; it is not possible for me to create a world-order not ordained by the Vedas.
"Be gracious, O Supreme Lord; grant me the alms of the Vedas"—as he was thinking thus, his mind became turbid.
Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā obtained the mass of the Vedas;
he remembered all the Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs and the collection of Upaniṣads.
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras in their entirety, as well as the sixty-four arts and whatever other branches of knowledge there may be.
Because he specifically excavated the Vedas that had disappeared,
that omnipresent Lord is called Brahmā Vikhanas by those who discourse on Brahman.
And that venerable Grandfather is called the Vaikhānasa;
he [established] the entire world in its entirety by means of the path revealed in the Vedas.
Likewise, from the vital breath (prāṇa), from the eye, from the sense of ego (abhimāna), from the vital organ (marman),
from the heart, from the head, from the ear, and from the upward-moving breath (udāna) and the pervasive breath (vyāna).
And from Samāna and Apāna, O best of ṛṣis, these ten were born:
Dakṣa, Marīci, Nīlalohita, and Bhṛgu; and also—

These nine Brahmās indeed would have perished, along with Nīlalohita, due to the loss of the Vedas and out of pride; however, their original form was subsequently reunited.
The sage taught this Vaikhānasa branch to those whom he called by the names Vikhanas and likewise Śātātapa.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
as well as Vasiṣṭha and Dakṣa— these nine are declared to be the Brahmās.
"These nine Brāhmaṇas alone are to be appointed as [the officiants], excluding Nīlalohita. These are the disciples of Vikhanas according to the injunctions of Śruti and Smṛti;
their disciples, moreover, are high-souled sages who perceive the ultimate reality."
Desiring the welfare of the world, they composed treatises following the Vedas;
some indeed composed the Gṛhyasūtras, which consist of both domestic and Vedic rituals.
Some great seers spoke of the Dharmaśāstras, some of the Purāṇas, and others of the Itihāsas as well as the Kalpas.
Some composed grammar, some logic, and others likewise other branches; they produced the entirety of all literature, bound together as various treatises.
The supreme creator, the Lotus-born One, assigned the Ākhaṇḍalī branch of the Tāṇḍava school to his own sūtra, and within it, he established the threefold propitiation.
He assigned that Vaikhānasa branch to his own Sūtra,
having divided it separately according to the distinctions of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas.
In the beginning, however, the Blessed One, the sage Vikhanas, who was Brahmā,
composed this great Sūtra in accordance with the Yajurvedic branch.
In the beginning, middle, and end of that [scripture] which is endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life and is consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti,
the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu resides.
Because it is praised as that which is to be worshipped, it is indeed the best of all Sūtras;
it is the dharma proclaimed in the Vedic Vaikhānasa Sūtra.
All should practice the true Dharma; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
[Yet it is lost] through the abandonment of one's own Sūtra and the taking up of another's Sūtra.
A Brahmin indeed falls immediately if he does not take refuge in the Veda;
however, when he attains the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, that is truly the Veda.
This Vaikhanasa Sutra is independent of other sutras;
this Vaikhanasa Sutra is a compendium of the meaning of all the Vedas.
The Vaiṣṇava [tradition] is declared to be common to all Brahmins,
as well as to the followers of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra, the Āgneya, and the Śrāmaṇaka.
The majesty of the god Nārāyaṇa is not understood [by all],
just as among all the Vedas, the Sāmaveda is praised.
Likewise, among all the sūtras, this sūtra is praised;

These seven Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who know the Gāyatrī are highly purifying;
one obtains the fruit of having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs by [honoring] them.
A twice-born man who recites this sūtra obtains its fruit immediately;

Relying upon this very Sūtra, they all go to that Mādhava;

This Vaiṣṇava thread is indeed supreme, bestowing all accomplishments;

then there are all the vānaprasthas and those twice-born who follow other sūtras.

They should be known as equal to Viṣṇu, the most excellent among all,
among all the Vaikhānasas who are born from the womb of Vaiṣṇavas.
Nārāyaṇa himself bears his own mudrā within the womb;

Those beings who remain steadfast in exclusive devotion do not worship another until the end of their bodies;
these four are proclaimed in the world as the most beloved of Viṣṇu.
The holy fig tree, tawny cows, Tulasī, and Vaiṣṇava twice-born men;

At the conclusion of the worship, at the conclusion of the ritual bathing, and likewise at the end of the festival,

Whatever kind of honor a person may desire before the gods, disregarding a Brahmin who is a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) worshiper, [that honor shall instead go to him].

Six times a day, or three times, or twice, or even once at the proper time,

"It is the teaching that she shall bring about all prosperity for the worlds;

Kings are the crown of the tree; worshippers are its roots.
Therefore, one should not harm the root, for from the root the crown grows.
Kings are the fruit of the tree; worshippers are the flower of the tree.
Therefore, one should not harm the flower, for from the flower the fruit is produced.
The king who does not protect the property of a deity, the property of a Brahmin, or the honor due to a worshiper, is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
The king is the refuge for all who are weak, helpless, children, the elderly, ascetics, and those oppressed by injustice.
The king is both father and mother; the king is the supreme teacher.
The king is considered the protector and the teacher of all living beings.
Just as one quenches a forest fire with water,
so do the Brahmins who proclaim the Vedas find satisfaction in a king, as if filling the ocean itself.
Fire burns with its heat, and the sun burns with its rays;
a king burns with his rod of justice, and a brahmin burns with his wrath.
The Brahmins have anger as their weapon; Hari has the discus as his weapon. Anger is sharper than the discus; therefore, one should not provoke the Brahmins to wrath.
What is burnt by fire may sprout again, and likewise what is scorched by the sun;
but one struck down by the curse of a Brahmin, once slain, shall not sprout again.
Even in times of great distress, the worshipper must not be treated with contempt;
for whatever is spoken by a satisfied priest in the presence of the deity [is authoritative].
That speech is indeed the speech of Hara; for a worshipper is not to be disparaged.
He who angers the worshipper truly incurs the wrath of the God. (BhS 30.114)
He who pleases the Lord of Gods is indeed one who brings satisfaction to the worshipper;
[he offers] fragrance, flowers, as well as garlands, betel, unbroken rice, and so forth.
Furthermore, the favor of the Lord is first due to the worshiper,
as well as to those who know the six auxiliary sciences and who perform sacrifices with the most excellent rites.
A Vaikhānasa purifies the assembly of even a hundred Brahmins at the outset,
for he performs every single action entirely free from desire for fruit.
One should perform [all acts] with the realization that everything is an offering to Brahman; such a person shall indeed be the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
One should not bow to another deity, nor should one worship another deity.
One who constantly worships and meditates upon Nārāyaṇa, the unborn,
through body, mind, and speech— he indeed is called a Vaiṣṇava.
One must never worship before the deity a heretic who is not a Vaiṣṇava and who wears the horizontal sectarian mark (tiryakpuṇḍra); for that indeed constitutes an insult to the Vaiṣṇavas.
For those devoted to Viṣṇu, the Vaiṣṇavas who are dear to the Blessed One, are indeed to be honored;
however, the worship of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava in their presence is most dreadful.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid from afar those who are not Vaiṣṇavas,
who regard Puruṣottama with a merely ordinary disposition.
Those who do not accept the command along with Rudra and the others should also be known as non-Vaiṣṇavas;
among men, Brāhmaṇas are the best, and among Brāhmaṇas, the wise.
Among those who possess wisdom, they alone are truly the doers;
and among those doers, they are indeed the knowers of Brahman who are devoted to the assembly of people.
Among all devotees of Viṣṇu everywhere, the Vaikhānasas are remembered as the most excellent;
therefore, having first honored a Vaikhānasa twice-born man with devotion, [one should proceed].
Then, having honored a devotee of Viṣṇu according to the sequence of their castes,
one should honor the assembly at the proper time, and other twice-born men should also be fed.
Women who are devotees of Viṣṇu and take refuge in the Vaiṣṇavas should be honored according to the prescribed rule;
for one should reflect that the creative power of Viṣṇu is not common to all.
Through austerities, meditations, and concentrations over thousands of other births,
devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises in those men whose sins have been exhausted.
For Viṣṇu cannot be truly known, praised, or even seen by those who are not devotees; O fools, how indeed could they ever enter him?
Purified by being permeated with devotion to Him, those men whose minds are fixed on Him indeed become Bhāgavatas and enter into Viṣṇu.
When the accumulation of sins gathered through the cycle of many births has been exhausted,
the mind of men becomes directed toward Govinda.
That man who feels hatred toward Govinda and reviles the twice-born and the Vedas—
one should know him to have arisen from a portion of the asuras.
Delight in heretical sects and an inclination toward rationalist arguments arise from the illusory power of Viṣṇu for those fallen, evil-minded men.
When the evil of men has been destroyed, then faith becomes unshakable toward the gods, the twice-born, the Viṣṭi, and the Lord of Sacrifice.
Just as when the accumulation of sins among men has been almost entirely exhausted,
those men become devotees of the Blessed One (bhāgavata), intent upon the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
For men wandering here in this saṃsāra, which is difficult to traverse due to karma,
Janārdana— purchased through devotion— is indeed the sole hand to hold.
He who is free from malice toward living beings in deed, thought, and word,
and who is devoted in spirit to Govinda Viṣṇu— he indeed is a Bhāgavata.
He who always bows down to the Brahmins and the Vedas, and who does not covet the wealth or property of others, is remembered as a Bhāgavata.
He who knows Hari to be all the gods and Keśava to be all the worlds,
yet does not consider himself to be superior to them— he indeed is remembered as a Bhāgavata.
Gods, humans, or others, beasts, birds, and ants; trees, stones, wood, and so forth; earth, water, fire, air, and the directions.
That meritorious soul who does not perceive himself as distinct from Janārdana, the Lord of gods— he indeed is remembered as a Bhāgavata.
"Everything that has been and everything that exists in the future is the portion of the Blessed One"—
he who truly understands this is indeed remembered as a Bhāgavata.
When he is meditated upon with a spirit of devotion as the Blessed Lord, he removes the fear of worldly existence; such a person is remembered as a Bhāgavata.
He who does not commit any evil toward any living being by deed, thought, or word is remembered as a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
He who, independent of external objects, performs the service of the Blessed One with devotion and with a sincere disposition— he indeed should be known as a *bhāgavata*.
He whose enemies are very affectionate and do not behave with indifference—
he who sees all this as such is indeed a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Neither by well-performed austerity in this world nor by sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees do men attain that goal which the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) reach.
Even Śatakratu, the king of the gods, is looked down upon by the devotees of the Lord who have fallen from yoga;
how much more so those who have reached the further shore of yoga?
For the sake of completing the sacrifice, for the sake of the Lord of Sacrifice, and for his gratification, he strives;
indeed, he is remembered as a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
He who has fixed his disposition upon Viṣṇu with his whole being and with devotion,
because of his being disciplined and having accomplished all that was to be done, is indeed remembered as a Bhāgavata.
For those observing vows, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, is undoubtedly worthy of worship;
likewise, women have no deity other than their own husbands.
For a householder who is a husband, Hari is the Lord of Sacrifice to be worshipped;
for the forest-dwellers (vaikhānasas), Madhusūdana is to be propitiated through austerities.
Vāsudeva is to be meditated upon by the high-souled wandering mendicants;
likewise, Viṣṇu is the ultimate refuge for all those belonging to the stages of life.
The Blessed Lord Hari is not so pleased by gifts or by austerities as He is satisfied by one who follows the conduct prescribed for their social class and stage of life.

By a person who follows the conduct prescribed for their social class (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama), Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, is propitiated; there is no other path that causes him satisfaction.
Regarding the faults not mentioned here, the expiation shall now be declared:
having established the Paiṇḍarīka fire and having sprinkled water around the sacred fire, [one should perform the rite].
Likewise, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra six times, the Vyāhṛtis four times,
the eight-syllable mantra eight times, and the twelve-syllable mantra likewise [eight times].
Having offered oblations twelve times with the Viṣṇusūkta and the Pauruṣasūkta,
one should offer the Ekākṣarādi-sūkta and the two Śrī-bhū-sūktas.
Having bathed the deity and worshipped him, one should properly present the sacrificial offering;
by this rite, auspicious peace is attained there.
Furthermore, together with the repeated oblations for the defects of the *hāda*,
one should specifically perform the eighty-eight [oblations] beginning with the syllable *Iṃ* dedicated to the Supreme Self (*pāramātmika*).
Having offered oblations to all the deities with eight hundred jars,
and having bathed and worshipped the Lord, one should properly present the sacrificial food.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter:
The Threefold Sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
Now I shall state the summary of the penances mentioned therein:
namely, sprinkling with water and likewise light sprinkling.
The great sprinkling (mahāsaṃprokṣaṇa) and so forth—thus penance is recorded as being threefold;
it should be applied when the occasion arises, having understood its gravity or lightness.
One should perform an immediate sprinkling according to the procedure to be described;
no restriction regarding time is prescribed for the ritual of sprinkling.
One should not observe the month, lunar mansion, lunar day, weekday, and so forth;
therefore, when an occasion arises, one should immediately perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
When there is a cause for consideration of place, time, and so forth, there is respect [to be shown], whether toward many images or toward a single one, whether stationary or mobile. (BhS 31.5)
When worship is omitted, when the time has passed, in cases of reversal, when there is worship with stale offerings, or when what has already been offered is offered again; BhS_31.6 //
Even on a single day, if worship is omitted, if the daily bathing is neglected, if the offerings and fire-oblations are missing, and if the daily festival is abandoned; BhS_31.7 //
When something impure has entered within the enclosure due to negligence, or when there is the arrival of those who are untouchable, such as Caṇḍālas and others, having entered therein—
Upon the entrance of dogs, cocks, boars, camels, or donkeys;
or by a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, or likewise by heretics and the like.

If [the site] is entered by those who have fallen from the *kuṇḍa-gola* vow, by Turuṣkas and others, or if it is touched by other thread-owners or twice-born [brahmins], whether through delusion or even out of ignorance; BhS 31.10.

When the reflection is struck by a great wind, when it is drenched by drops of rain, when there is a flow of feces, urine, or blood, and during sexual intercourse; in these cases [the image is not to be used].
When such signs appear, one should perform the sprinkling with water;
for it is certain that Hari does not dwell in an image that has not been consecrated by sprinkling.
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the image, one should worship it after performing a formal sprinkling;
however, when an excess of defects arises, one should perform a brief sprinkling.

During a disturbance in the kingdom, in times of famine, when the Tantras are corrupted by confusion, or when they are perverted by Śūdras, those born of mixed castes, or even by wandering heretics; BhS_31.14 //

If a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, those who have fallen from their status, or those guilty of mortal sins, or even Caṇḍālas and the like, should enter the inner sanctum, especially so.

If [the corpse] has been entered by charioteers, or by those born from pots or eggs, or likewise by temple-priests and the like, or by dogs, cocks, boars, and so forth, or by donkeys and the like; BhS_31.16 //
Likewise, when an owl, a vulture, a crow, or similar creatures enter the interior of the house,
or when Turuṣkas and others enter, or even when semen and blood [are discharged].
Or if there is the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth; or in the inner sanctum or the half-pavilion;
or if, after six days, the worship has been neglected and the lamps are absent. (BhS 31.18)
After one night has passed, when the deity is staying in another village,
during a fire, a lightning strike, or in the inner chamber or the lower pavilion.
If an image has been praised by one who is not a follower of the Buddha, or touched intentionally by others,
one should perform a light sprinkling with other faults that have not been mentioned.
When the great omen has occurred, one should perform the great consecration according to the rule,
beginning from the twelfth day until the end of the year.
In the case of inferior worship, whether it be the daily or the occasional rite;
when the ritual action is deficient, or when there is an inversion, or when the monthly festivals and so forth are deficient—BhS 31.22.

Even when daily ablutions are neglected, when the giving of alms to one's mother and others is omitted, when offerings and fire-sacrifices are abandoned, and when a confusion of scriptural injunctions has occurred; BhS_31.23 //
In such inferior cases, if through negligence [the offense occurs] at the end of the year,
it concerns the assemblies, their retinues, and those who depend on or frequent the monastery.

But when the raising of the banner has been performed, and after the seasonal festivals and other rites have been completed, should the death of a Brahmin or others occur, especially in a temple; BhS_31.25 //

If one dies with the faces of a donkey, a horse, a hyena, a camel, a horse, or a pig; or if there is the destruction of elephants and other wild animals; or if [this occurs] through negligence in a temple; [these are causes for rebirth as a preta].
Especially upon the death of those of the lowest castes, such as Caṇḍālas and others,
or by Śūdras, or by those born in the natural order (ānuloma), or by heretics, outcasts, and the like.
When the image of Viṣṇu has been touched by thieves such as Turuṣkas, or by Caṇḍālas and others who are defiled by great sins; ||| BhS_31.28 |||
Whether there is a crash of a thunderbolt upon a celestial palace, or even the falling of great meteors,
or a rain of blood, and especially a rain of stones—
When the image has been moved by an earthquake, when an anthill has formed around it,
or when its foundation has become loose— especially in the case of the eightfold binding.
When a pillar or similar support has decayed and fallen, when a temple has been defiled, when there is contact with fire regarding the image, or likewise upon the birth of a human being; BhS_31.31 //
Furthermore, in all cases of construction work, such as for the inner sanctum and so forth, or when worms, insects, and the like are seen in the images or in the inner sanctum; BhS 31.32.
Especially in laughing, weeping, and speaking,
as well as in the appearance of sweat or blood, there occurs a deterioration of the complexion.
Whether in a celestial chariot, in a pavilion, or anywhere else belonging to Hari, or when these various defects have arisen in the temple of the deity; ||| BhS_31.34 |||
Indeed, during famine, civil unrest in the kingdom, or when ill omens appear;
or during bad dreams, earthquakes, or threats from foreign kings and the like.
When the image has been buried in the earth and then unearthed, or if it has remained for a long time in another temple,
or if three nights have passed while the deity remains in another village.
When worship is performed by those initiated as Kuṇḍas, Golakas, Sūtas, and others,
whatever unmentioned misdeeds and extraordinary evils are committed, [they are purified].
But having seen the sacrificer, those people in his vicinity,
the inhabitants of the village, the forest-dwellers, the king, and the kingdom with great effort—
Having understood through devotion that the fruit arises from defects according to the procedure taught in the scriptures,
one should perform the great consecration (mahāsaṃprokṣaṇa) for the removal of great defects.
In all cases of great transgressions, a great rite of pacification is performed;
however, this does not apply to an image previously consecrated for ordinary reasons.
There may, however, be a re-consecration; therefore, one should perform a great sprinkling (mahāsaṃprokṣaṇa) for both the rite of great sprinkling and the installation of a new [image].
The sages, such as Kāśyapa and others, have declared that the difference is very slight;
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall now proclaim the ritual for sprinkling with water.
Permitted by the patron, the preceptor, having bathed according to the prescribed rules,
should proceed either toward the front of the temple or to its right, in a pleasant spot.
On a pure mound of sand, having quickly performed the rites beginning with the declaration of an auspicious day and the fire-ritual (agnimukha),
and at the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, one should [prepare] whatever ground is free from defects.
Having consecrated the image according to the ritual with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow, the wise one should then bathe it with water-jars while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
Having placed five jars upon a heap of grain measuring six *droṇas*,
and having wrapped them with a pair of garments, one should deposit the images within them.
Having decorated separate jars with coconut leaves, mango leaves, and so forth,
one should recite the five hymns (*pañcasūkta*) and likewise the five propitiations (*pañcaśānti*).
Having invoked [the deity] with the five forms and worshipped him thoroughly with the eight manifestations,
the wise one should thereafter strew grass around the fire and offer oblations with the five hymns.
Thereafter, one should offer eighty-eight oblations of *iṅguda* and other substances,
together with the five Varuṇa mantras and the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Afterwards, having dismissed the fire, he should give a sacrificial fee to the teacher,
consisting of gold weighing no less than a niṣka, as well as garments, ornaments, and earrings.
Thereafter, having sprinkled [the area] with water from the ritual jar while reciting the mantra,
and having presented abundant offerings, one should then perform the daily worship.
By this method, defects are destroyed without a doubt;
and Aṅgiras has said that the presence of the deity will abide within that image.
This much alone is declared to be the procedure for the sprinkling with water;
the preceptor should indeed perform a brief sprinkling by means of the patron.

"Prior to the day of commencement" (ārambhadinād adhaḥ) means on the day preceding the actual start of the ritual. The phrase "two or three days" (dviyahe vā triyahe vā) indicates that the *aṅkurārpaṇa*—the ritual sowing of seeds to produce auspicious sprouts—should be performed at least two days before the main ceremony. This practice is intended to ensure an auspicious beginning and to ward off obstacles. The mention of both two and three days allows for flexibility based on the specific requirements of the ritual calendar.
