On the following day, having performed the Vāstu-homa in the domestic fire (aupāsana-agni) and having purified [the site] on all sides with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while circumambulating it with fire; BhS_31.55.
And having consecrated the Lord of Gods with one hundred and eight handfuls of water,
he should cause the materials, the site, and the furnishings to be sprinkled according to the prescribed ritual.
Thereafter, having approached the lotus-fire and performed the foundational rite (ādhāra) according to the rules,
the Guru, endowed with meditative concentration, should then properly perform the worship of the jar (kumbhapūjā).
Having brought thirty-two beautiful jars filled to the brim,
and having wrapped them with thread, one should fill them with water while reciting the mantra.
Having wrapped six heaps of grain, each weighing one bhāra, upon the altar in sequence with a pair of cloths, one should place the images within them.
There, one should carefully place nine gems, each weighing three *niṣkas*, into the jar;
or, in the absence of gems, gold may be placed for each one.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, with coconut fruits and mango sprouts, likewise with the five weapons, with archways, and with the eight auspicious symbols; BhS_31.61 //
Having adorned those jars and touched them with the *kūrca* grass, the wise preceptor [recites] the five hymns (*pañcasūkta*),
the five pacifications (*pañcaśānti*), and then the twelve hymns (*dvādaśasūkta*).
Having recited the Sārasvata and other hymns, the Dik-sūkta, the Pañca-vāruṇa, the Svasti-sūkta, and likewise the Auṣadhi-sūkta; BhS_31.63.
Having invoked [the deity] with the nine forms, together with the two goddesses and the attendants,
and having properly worshipped him with the thirty-two manifestations, one should present the offering.
Having approached the Paiṇḍarīka fire and having sprinkled water around the sacred fire,
one should offer oblations with the five hymns and with the three all-pervading mantras.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations, or indeed twenty-eight;
thereafter, one should offer eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable *riṃ*.
Having offered the oblation to Dhātṛ and others, the root oblation, and the five Vāruṇa oblations, as well as the Kūṣmāṇḍa oblation and the five Vāruṇa oblations; BhS_31.67 //
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with lotuses or bilva leaves while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should subsequently dismiss the fire.
Afterwards, having been honored by the teacher with garments, ornaments, and earrings,
he should take the water-pot upon his head and proceed to the village or the monastery.
Then, having circumambulated clockwise in the presence of the God of gods,
one should take that water with a blade of kūrca grass and sprinkle it with the five forms.
One should sprinkle the entire temple with the mantra "śucī vo havya," worship it thoroughly with ritual offerings, and bow down, saying, "Forgive me. (BhS 31.71)
One should offer a great oblation or an abundant one to the Lord of Gods,
and feed a thousand Brahmins together with the preceptor.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor consisting of five niṣkas of gold,
and one should also bestow desirable land adorned with rows of ripening crops.
Then, having performed the tenfold gift, one should carry out the daily worship;
he who thus performs the brief consecration of Hari with devotion.
One attains the presence of Viṣṇu, and the pacification of faults arises;
there shall be prosperity for the king and the kingdom, and it becomes a source of nourishment for the world.
Indeed, I have proclaimed this concise rite of sprinkling,
which was likewise enjoined by the sages beginning with Kāśyapa.
I shall explain the specific details regarding the ritual of the Great Consecration (mahāsaṃprokṣaṇa):
it is devoid of the preliminary water-soaking (jalādhivāsa) and excludes the rite of opening the eyes (netronmīlana).
One should perform everything according to the previously stated procedure for consecration;
likewise for the sharpening of the eyes, especially in cases of visual defects.
One should perform the ritual immersion in water and then the opening of the eyes;
this specific procedure for the performance of the Great Peace (mahāśānti) is proclaimed here.
Having consecrated all the mobile images with the preliminary rite of *adhivāsa* and sprinkled them according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity as before.
When the great auspicious moment has arrived, the learned preceptor, requested by the patron,
shall perform the installation on the day prescribed for it, together with officiating priests endowed with the proper characteristics.
Adorned with garments and ornaments as previously described,
one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts on the day following the sprinkling and other preliminary rites.
Having also well-provided the ritual materials and entered the sacrificial hall, which is adorned with garlands of plantain and betel-nut trees, as well as banners and other ornaments; BhS_31.83.
In the middle of that [area], one should construct an altar for the purpose of the bed according to the prescribed rules;
and on its eastern side, an altar for the water-pot (kumbha) with its proper characteristics.
One should have fire-pits constructed all around and a lotus pond made;
and having thoroughly cleansed the temple with scrubbing, sprinkling, and smearing.
The preceptor, with a well-pleased mind, being repeatedly requested by the sacrificer,
bathes according to the rules for bathing and recites the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times.
Having recited the twelve hymns, he should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed;
then, having performed the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice in either the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), the Guru—
Having purified [the site] on all sides with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow,
one should perform the foundational oblation (āghāra) in the sacrificial pits, beginning with the Gārhapatya, in their proper sequence.
Having wrapped twenty-five jars, which have the appearance of ripe bimba fruits,
with a threefold thread, one should purify them and fumigate them thoroughly.
Having taken divine water according to the mantra and having brought it with care,
he filled [the vessel] with pure waters using coconut and mango sprouts.
Having thus adorned it with tufts of grass, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and so forth, or with barley or rice, one should place twelve *bhārakas* upon the altar.
Having spread them out and established [the images] upon them, one should wrap each separately with a cloth;
there, golden images made from five niṣkas each should be placed individually.
One should cast forms such as elephants and tortoises, as well as the nine gems and so forth,
into the central and other jars according to the sequence of the wheels by means of the path of meditation.
The Guru should invoke, by means of the mantra according to the sequence of the nine forms,
Indra and the other lords of the eight directions into the jars situated beneath the altar.
Having invoked [the deity] and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present [the oblation],
having bathed [the image] with a thousand jars according to the procedure prescribed for the ceremonial bathing (snāpana).
Having bound a golden marriage-thread (kautuka) according to the prescribed rite for consecration,
and having sprinkled the bed-altar (śayyāvedi), one should arrange five couches (pañcatalpa).
With six bhāras each of śāli rice, vrīhi rice,
and barley, and half as much of that in paddy, and likewise half as much of that in sesame seeds.
Having spread layers upon layers, one should arrange skins, cloth, and so forth; one should place the festive image upon the bed on the altar as previously described.

One should perform the consecration of the *kūrca* for a fixed duration according to the sequence; one should cause [the student] to study the Vedas in the various directions, for the Śruti declares: "The East is the seat of the Ṛg-veda. (BhS 31.99)
In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) such as the Gārhapatya and others,
he should have the priests perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rules for installation, preceded by the respective deities.
Having approached the fire in the assembly hall of the guru and having sprinkled water around the sacrificial fire,
he should recite the five hymns in their proper order, preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra of the three pervasive deities, again with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, and likewise with the vyāhṛtis; BhS_31.102 //
Then, having approached the fire of the lotus, together with the five hymns,
he should perform the root-homa beginning with Dhātṛ, conjoined with the five Vāruṇa mantras.
Then, having recited three times the mantras prescribed for the great pacification, one should perform the fire offering;
having approached the altar of the pitcher, one should worship it with the eight forms.
Having touched those jars with the *kūrca* grass together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
the Guru should indeed recite the *ātmasūkta*, and thereafter the five hymns (*pañcasūkta*).

Furthermore, after the fivefold pacification, one should recite the Svasti-sūkta, the Durga-sūkta, the Rātri-sūkta, the Ekākṣara-sūkta, and the sūktas dedicated to the eight guardians of the directions.
Having recited the two verses beginning with "āpo hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and the Pāvamānī hymns, as well as the twelve Sūktas, he should then [offer oblations] into the Sabhya fire in due order.
One should perform the entire praise of the *hautra* as before,
following the sequence of the four forms together with a thousand oblations.

“Having offered oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* mantras beginning with ‘yad devā ādya’—which belong to all the deities—as well as with parched grains and sesame seeds, for the sake of pacifying faults; (BhS 31.109)
Having offered oblations into the fire-pits as before with cakes while chanting the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, one hundred and eight times, or likewise twenty-eight times; BhS 31.110.
Then, having performed the sprinkling, especially over the white lotus,
one should [offer] lotuses or bilva leaves with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
One should diligently offer one thousand and eight oblations, having soaked them in ghee,
using the supreme ātman-mantras beginning with the syllable *riṃ*.
Then, having offered eighty-eight oblations preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
he should offer them for the destruction of that fault and for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
Having abandoned the sabhyāgni and the pauṇḍarīkāgni, one should perform the internal oblation (antahomaka) in the other fires.
The preceptor should spend the remainder of the night with dance, song, instrumental music, and the like;
then, having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rule, he should perform the ritual bathing with water-jars.
Having bathed [the deity] with five hymns accompanied by the fivefold pacification (pañcaśānti),
and having subsequently adorned the deity with fine garments, ornaments, and so forth.
When the auspicious moment has arrived, the preceptor, taking a water-pot, [should perform the rite] with fragrant flowers and perfumes that are pleasing to the eye and the mind.
Reciting the Svastisūkta, having circumambulated the village or the temple,
he should place the water-pot before the deity upon a seat of grain.
Then, having honored the guru according to his capacity, the sacrificer should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) just described, which are dear to the Blessed One.
The patron, having properly honored the preceptor with garments, bright ornaments, and especially earrings, as well as with cattle, land, and other gifts; BhS_31.120.
One should give twenty-one niṣkas as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, and likewise to the officiating priests; thus the blessed Lord Hari becomes well-pleased.
The preceptor, having subsequently invoked [the deity] and worshipped it with the eight forms,
should offer the great oblation consisting of milk-rice and cakes upon the sacrificial altar.
Having offered [the food] with clarified butter and various condiments, one should present mouth-perfume;
then, having offered a handful of flowers and prostrated with the words "May there be exhaustion [of defilements]," one should bow.
One should feed a thousand Brahmins for the sake of peace;
specifically, the tenfold gift will bring delight to the gods.
Thus, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) after twelve years;
thereafter, due to the rite of re-consecration (sthāpana), there is no other atonement required.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform everything as prescribed in the scriptures;
he who thus performs the three sprinklings for Viṣṇu with devotion [attains the highest goal].
Having attained the fruit of consecration, one shall reach the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the section on miscellaneous topics within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the sacred scripture of the Lord according to the illustrious Vaikhānasa tradition.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter: Miscellaneous Matters.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequence of festivals for Jyeṣṭhā;
when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism.
This shall be a special offering for Viṣṇu alone; one should procure fragrant oil.
O best of sages, listen as I describe the procedure for the oil. BhS_32.2 //
Having prepared the sacrificial hall, fully equipped with all ornaments,
he should cause the Sabhya and the Paiṇḍarīka fires to be established according to their defining characteristics.
On the day preceding that day, or on the third, the fifth,
or even on the seventh day, one should perform the ritual of planting the seed-sprouts.
Having performed the libation according to the rule, this supreme rite for all purposes should then be carried out on the ground to the north of the altar, using a cloth.
It should be four tālas in height and equal in width and depth;
within that depression, one should place a vessel with a capacity of two droṇas.
With the mantra "Bhūḥ pratiṣṭhā," one should carefully place the vessel in a low spot;
likewise, [one may use] sandalwood, agallochum, and deodar.
And whatever fragrant substances here are fit for the gods,
having collected guggulu among them, one should grind them together repeatedly.
One should place those substances in a vessel while reciting the Viṣṇugāyatrī;
then, having covered it with a shallow bowl, one should smear it all over with clay.
One should place cow-dung and wood upon it and cook it over a gentle fire until the emergence of oil occurs.
The wise one should cook the collected oil for that length of time,
having indeed removed from it those substances that have been perfumed.
One should place the fragrant oil vessel upon a seat made of grain and wrap it with a thread using the very same mantra mentioned previously.
Having likewise worshipped the ancestors, Soma, and the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati),
one should then worship [the deity] in that oil according to the rule, up to the offering of the *arghya*.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and likewise the Nara-sūkta,
one should then chant the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one thousand and eight times.
The teacher, having gone quickly to the vicinity of the assembly fire,
[should prepare] a circular mound two tālas wide and four aṅgulas high.
Its shape is fashioned from wood-apple and other materials, resembling the form of a tortoise.
In the consecration and in festivals, in recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
in all rites for the deities as well as in other rituals.
One should take up the tortoise-seat (kūrmapīṭha), for otherwise it would be fruitless;
seated upon the tortoise-seat, one should likewise offer oblations into the sacrificial fire of the assembly hall.
One should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Narasūkta; these belong to all the deities and are indeed supreme in relation to the Self.
Having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the wise one should perform the concluding oblation;
he should then consign the fire into the Praṇidhi or into a conch vessel.
Before applying the oil ointment, one should fetch fire from the perpetual flame (dhruva);
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garlands, garments, earrings, and other such gifts.
Then, having summoned an attendant and honored him as was fitting,
he placed the *uṣṇīṣa* upon the head of that attendant.
One should carefully set down the vessel of fragrant oil,
proceeding very slowly while accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by the sound of the Brahma-voice,
having circumambulated the street, he should place [the offering] before the God.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with offerings up to the *arghya*, and having prostrated before Him,
one should recite in sequence the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Narasūkta.
The preceptor, acting with haste, should likewise smear the deity with oil;
thereafter, he should smear the two goddesses as well, using their respective mantras.
The preceptor, having gone quickly to the vicinity of the festival, should cause all the retinues to be performed with their respective mantras.
One should purify the armor with the mantra "parilikhita";
if the armor is worn out or broken, one should have it well-repaired by a craftsman.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should purify it with water;
and even after performing the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi) as prescribed, one should carry out the expiation (niṣkṛti).
One should likewise join the armor with the mantras beginning with "viṣṇornuka";
having thus made it firm, one should carefully arrange that which was previously described.
Having bathed the deity with a thousand jars according to the prescribed rite,
and having propitiated the deity as before through the performance of the daily worship ritual.
Or one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) produced from a great oblation;
saying "Forgive me," one should again bow down to Puruṣottama. (BhS 32.32)
Then one should cause the sound of the Veda to be proclaimed and give the teacher’s fee;
one should perform this on the day, the fortnight, the month, and likewise every year.
Whatever form one meditates upon, that very form one should apply to the images;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice the protection of the images.
Now I shall describe the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa), specifically the offering of the sacred thread to Hari.
It pacifies all defects, bestows the fruit of all sacrifices,
grants all desires, and is the supreme bringer of universal satisfaction.
For the sake of the prosperity of the entire world and for bestowing peace upon the entire world,
whatever has been performed that is deficient in mantra-rites or lacking in ritual substances— [may it all be perfected].
To pacify those very faults, one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa);
for if the offering of the sacred thread is omitted, whatever worship is performed becomes fruitless.
Disturbance arises there; therefore, one should perform it with diligence, especially during the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Proṣṭhapada.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, or on the day of Viṣṇu (the eleventh),
as well as during the Saṃsarpa month, an intercalary month, or when the lunar date and the day of the week are both empty (śūnya).
One should avoid that day when the tenth and eleventh lunar days are mixed;
rather, the auspicious installation of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should take place on the eleventh lunar day when it is free from defects.
For nine days, or seven days, or five days, or six days,
one should successively choose a preceptor who is endowed with the previously described characteristics.
One should choose the officiating priests (ṛtvij) just as one chooses disciples;
thereafter, on the night preceding that day, the Guru should pray to the Lord of Gods.
Having said, "O powers of the Blessed One," with his body bowed and well-composed,
he quickly worshipped the Lord especially with water for the feet and other offerings.
Having recited the *prārthanāsūkta*,
the teacher, surrounded by his disciples, should begin the study of the Veda around the sacrificial hall.
At the four gateways, starting from the east and proceeding in order,
he himself should perform the study of the four Vedas and the primary mantras along with their Śaktis.
Then, having performed the rite for an auspicious day, one should proceed with the collection of earth;
having caused sprouts to be produced, one should offer an oblation of green gram (*mudga*) rice.
One should perform the *āghāra* oblation according to the rules in the sacrificial pit of the *aupāsana* fire;
and having performed the *vāstuhoma*, one should prepare the products of the cow (*gavya*) according to the prescribed injunctions.
One should purify the yoga-hall with the ritual fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow,
reciting the verse "tamekanemi" and also "āmāvājasya."
Having said, "tantuṃ tanvan," and uttering, "yan me garbhaḥ," as well as with the six Vaiṣṇava mantras and likewise with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī; BhS 32.50.
Having thoroughly sprinkled the purifiers according to the ritual rule with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), while reciting the mantras "That Viṣṇu... and "This Viṣṇu...".
And having bowed down to the purifier with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra from behind; BhS_32.52 //
Taking an excellent golden thread, a middling silver thread, and an inferior cotton thread— all of them free from every defect— BhS_32.53.
An excellent thread should be prepared by auspicious Brahmin women, especially those who are married, or,
if they are unavailable, by young maidens.
One should take one thousand and eight beads according to the measurement of the *biṃba* fruit;
the knots should be the size of a thumb, and with them one should have the rosary made. (BhS 32.55)
The Vanamālā is declared to be most dear to Viṣṇu;
having recited the Viṣṇusūkta, one should then recite the mantra beginning with "aṇoraṇīyān."

Having sprinkled it with turmeric water, one should fumigate it with incense while reciting the mantra "ime dhūpāḥ" and other mantras beginning with "caturveda," and having adorned it with archways and similar decorations.
Having fashioned a fire-pit in the navel, one should perform the libation according to the prescribed rule.
One should construct a bed-altar with a measurement of one and a half times that of the image;
and having prepared a grain-pedestal with sesame, rice, and other grains.
Having spread darbha grass there, one should spread the eggs and other [offerings];
having recited "pratadviṣṇu" and placed the purifier (pavitra) nearby.
Having invoked [the deity] with the five forms, having worshipped and prostrated,
and having recited the *pratisara* mantra, one should present incense, lamps, and so forth.
"Therefore, with the verse beginning 'ato devā' and so forth, the Guru should afterwards pray to the Lord of Devas;
having worshipped him with water for the feet and other offerings, he should present incense, lamps, and the like. (BhS 32.62)

Having bound the protective amulet (pratisara) upon the deity, as well as upon Śrī and Bhūmi, and likewise having bound the protective amulet upon the preceptor and the officiating priests; BhS_32.63.
“Having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, one should prepare a sacred bed;
having covered it with a fine cloth, one should offer flowers and unbroken grains.”
The Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Godāna-sūkta, the Ātman-sūkta,
the Ekākṣara-sūkta and others, and likewise the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta.
The Nṛsūkta, the Rudrasūkta, and likewise the Durgāsūkta;
the Sārasvatasūkta, and after that the Rātrisūkta.
Having recited "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ" and also "Sahasraśīrṣā," and having likewise recited the Śrībhūsūkta, the most excellent preceptor should perform [the rite]. (BhS 32.67)
The recitation of ten hymns is the best;
that of ten hymns is middling, and that of five hymns is the lowest.
Likewise, in the cardinal directions beginning with the east and in the four intermediate directions as well,
there are, in sequence, the peaceful Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), the discus, and likewise the conch shell.
Having summoned the guardians of the celestial chariots and honored them especially,
one should offer them mung-bean rice and perform prostrations repeatedly.
One should worship the wheel that provides all protection upon the purificatory thread;
then, one should offer it with food and present the bali-oblation for the rites of pacification and so forth.
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule,
he should duly praise the office of the Hotṛ priest and then perform the invocation (āvāhana).
Having performed the *juṣṭākāra* rite, one should offer oblations in due order;
one should cause [the fire] to be invoked with the five hymns, each according to its respective deity.
Having extinguished the fire at dawn, the preceptor should pass the remainder of the night;
then, in the morning, the righteous one, having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing, [should proceed].
At the conclusion of the ritual for daily worship, the Guru should pray to the Lord of Gods;
thereafter, he should bathe the Deity with one hundred and eight jars.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods, one should offer incense, lamps, and so forth.
Holding the purifier upon his head with the mantra beginning "audyantaṃ," accompanied by all musical instruments and preceded by a stream of water.
Having walked slowly in a clockwise direction and having placed it before the deity,
one should recite the *Sūrya* mantra over the sprout one hundred times.
The teacher, with a well-pleased mind, having performed the protection of himself,
should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and plant [the blades] beginning with the little finger.
Having reverently worshipped the deity with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with mouth-fresheners,
one should likewise adorn seventeen jars according to the prescribed ritual.
One should place the jars upon the altar after arranging them on a svastika diagram;
and having prepared the bed-altar to the east of that, one should likewise arrange the sabhya fire-pit.
One should prepare a lotus-shaped fire-pit in the southeast and likewise an aupāsana pit in the northeast;
then, in the aupāsana fire-pit, one should perform the āghāra oblation according to the prescribed rule.
And to the north of the bed-altar, having made a mechanical altar (ayantravedi) that is three cubits in length and breadth, square, level, and possessing the proper characteristics; BhS_32.3 //
This yantra is especially beautiful to behold with its five colors;
now I shall proclaim the yantra, O best of sages—listen! (BhS 32.4)
The Sudarśana Yantra, which provides all forms of protection: First, having drawn a hexagon and having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhya) in its center,
[one writes] *oṃ kṣrām*, *hrīm*.
Having written "Śrīm," on both sides of that.
Having written "irm" and "im" as the seed-syllables of sight, and "um" and "ūm" as the seed-syllables of hearing,
Having written the six-syllable mantra of Sudarśana, "sahasrāra-hūm phaṭ," within the six angles,
at the junction of the angles—
Having written "Oṃ haṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ," and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus outside of that,
one should write "Oṃ na ma ssu da r śa nā ya" upon the petals.
At the junction of the petals,
having written "oṃ ja ya ja ya nṛsiṃha," one should draw a circle outside of that and then a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Having written "Oṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya svāhā" in the center,
and having written "Oṃ hūṃ namo bhagavate vajravārāhāya svāhā" at the junctions of the petals,
one should draw two circles above that, and within the space between the two circles, write the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet from 'a' to 'kṣa'.
Above that, having drawn two square enclosures (bhūpura) with four corners,
and having written "oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krom" at the four gates,
one should write the seed-syllables (bīja) of the respective deities of those directions.
Having written the seed-syllables *laṃ raṃ haṃ ṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ śaṃ*,
[one should write] the mantra for the installation of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) from the southeast to the northeast,
and the Gāyatrī of the King of Mantras.
Having written the Gāyatrī of the King of Yantras and having invoked and worshipped it with its respective mantra, one should recite the root mantra of Sudarśana ten thousand times.

Having recited that [mantra] ten times its length, and having recited the King of Mantras ten times its length, one should perform libations (tarpaṇa) ten times its length, fire offerings (homa) ten times its length, and feed Brahmins ten times its length.

The seed-syllable (bīja), the vital breath (prāṇa), the power (śakti), the gaze (dṛṣṭi), subjugation (vaśya) and so forth, as well as the Gāyatrī of the mantra-diagram (yantra), the placement of the seed-syllable, and the seed-syllables of the elements and the guardians of the directions—these are indeed the ten limbs of the diagram.
The Gāyatrī of the diagram:
We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra;
may that Yantra inspire us.
(This is) the Gāyatrī of Sudarśana:
"I bow to the fierce, heroic Mahāviṣṇu, the blazing one whose face is turned in every direction, the terrifying yet auspicious Nṛsiṃha, the death of Death.
In all the indices there, this recitation of the yantra is seen.
In the original manuscript, however, this is seen with the commentary (*mātṛkā*).
Nevertheless, because many manuscript copies (*mātṛkākośa*) have not been found,
its presence here is recorded even though it remains doubtful.
Having spread the sacred grass according to the rule, one should worship the purifier (Agni) in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
Reciting the root mantra, the best of preceptors should perform the fire oblation with one hundred and eight parched grains (lājā) mixed with cakes (apūpa), using the syllable *miśra*. (BhS 32.83)
Then one should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta thirty-two times;
afterwards, having strewn grass around the fire and having prostrated with the words "O Agni, dwell here," [one should proceed].
One should perform this every day; at the conclusion, one should plant the deity.
Having performed the evening twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) and entered the sacrificial hall— BhS_32.85.
Having established the sabhyāgni and the paiṇḍarīkāgni, the preceptor should perform the āghāra oblation;
having offered the śānti-homa in the abjāgni, he should proceed without delay.
Some indeed say that the Mahāśānti-homa may be performed without a water-pot (kumbha);
standing before the altar, one should perform the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other preliminary rites.
Having invoked [the deity] with the nine forms, one should invoke the guardians of the directions in their proper order;
having worshipped them with the eightfold offerings, one should present an offering of mung-bean rice.
Having given water for drinking and water for sipping, one should then offer mouth-perfume;
with the mantra "āpo vā," one should hold the purifying vessel.
Having uttered "Agni in Agni," and having placed the purifier in the fire-pit,
one should fully adorn the fire according to the very measurements of the pit.
Having said, "Pavitrantu," the Guru should place the purifier [upon the head];
then, having offered fuel-sticks into the Sabhya fire and sprinkled water around it according to the rule.
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest according to the rules, the Guru should cause oblations to be offered with fuel-sticks;
then he should invoke, in due order, the deities residing in that temple.
After that, having well-offered the *juṣṭākāra* formula, then the *svāhākāra*,
then the *Viṣṇusūkta*, and after that the *Puruṣasūkta*.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru), parched grains (lāja), and cakes mixed with clarified butter;
thereafter, one should worship [Viṣṇu] one hundred and eight times with Vaiṣṇava mantras.
After that, one should offer the syllables beginning with *iṅkāra* conjoined with the supreme Self;
then, having offered eighty-eight oblations, each dedicated to its respective deity.

Having offered oblations of all the deity-mantras, the five beginning with the Dhātr-mantra, and the Vāruṇa-mantra, as well as the root-homa, and having likewise performed the final sprinkling at the end; BhS_32.96 //
One should recite the four Vedas at the four gates of the sacrificial hall;
however, one should especially chant the eight-syllable mantra in the northeast.
The twelve-syllable mantra, the Gāyatrī, as well as the Vaiṣṇava [mantra],
the Gāyatrī known as Nārāyaṇa, and also that which pertains to the Supreme Self (pāramātmika).
Combined with the three pervasive [mantras] and joined with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
one should then recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra and the five [syllables] beginning with "Yo vā bhūt...".
Having recited the *puṣpāñjali* mantra, the preceptor should place it at the feet of the deity;
he should then pass the remainder of the night with dance, song, instrumental music, and other such performances.
Then at dawn, the righteous-souled one, having bathed and performed the twilight devotions,
entered the sacrificial hall and thereafter prayed to the Lord of Gods.
Having uttered "Bhūr agnaye" and sprinkled the altar and the surrounding area,
one should perform all the rites, such as the worship of the pitcher and the fire-oblation, as previously described.
One should first propitiate the water-pot (kumbha), and immediately thereafter perform the worship of the image (bimba);
afterwards, one should carry out the fire-oblation (homa), and after that, the offering of the sacrificial fee (balidāna).
In this manner, the most excellent of gurus should perform the rite according to the prescribed rule every day;
when the day is completed, he should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the evening.
Therefore, after three days have passed, one should prepare the fire in a fire-pit.
Taking a water-pot upon his head, preceded by a stream of water,
he walked slowly in circumambulation and placed it before the deity.
One should sprinkle [the deity] with water from a jar while reciting the hymns beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇaḥ pavamānaḥ";
having worshipped the deity with water for the feet and other offerings, one should present abundant food.
Having given water for drinking and water for rinsing the mouth, one should then offer an aromatic mouth-freshener;
having recited the mantra of forgiveness, one should repeatedly bow, saying, "Forgive me. (BhS 32.108)
The patron also, being pure in soul, humble with devotion, and composed in mind,
should honor the teacher there with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then, adorned with the five ornaments and likewise with new silk garments,
the preceptor, with a serene mind, should then bestow blessings.
They should receive with reverence that which has been spoken by the Blessed One;
thus one should perform the annual offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Hari every year.
Having become happy in this world, he goes to the supreme goal;
may the Blessed Viṣṇu be pleased—thus is the Prārthanāsūkta recited.
The hymns beginning with “kanikradat” and the mantra “ā pipīhi” are declared to be the Śākuna Sūkta;
having recited “svasti no mimītām,” it is remembered as the Svasti Sūkta. (BhS 32.113)
“The pure are these animals”—thus the *Go-sūkta* is cited;
“*Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ*,” etc., is called the *Aghamarṣaṇa*. (BhS 32.114)
Having recited "aṇoraṇīyān," the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is declared to be performed with the three verses beginning with "apo hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and "pavamāna. (BhS 32.115)
Some, however, have declared that the *prokṣaṇa-sūkta* is optional;
the mantras beginning with "yā jātā" are called the *oṣadhī-sūkta*. (BhS 32.116)
The hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ" is called Pratisara;
the hymn beginning with "ato devāḥ," consisting of six verses, is said to belong to Viṣṇu. (BhS 32.117)
The six mantras beginning with "ato devā" are called the Vaiṣṇava-padas;
the six mantras beginning with "viṣṇornu" are declared to be the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
"The Puruṣa-sūkta beginning with ‘The thousand-headed Puruṣa,’ and the Śrī-sūkta beginning with ‘Golden-hued,’ grant all desires. (BhS 32.119)
The mantras beginning with "bhūmirbhūmnā" are cited as the Bhūmisūkta;
those beginning with "upa śvāsaya" are called the Dundubhīsūkta. (BhS 32.120)
“The hymn beginning with ‘You are Suparṇa, Garuḍa’ is called the Gāruḍa Sūkta;
the hymn beginning with ‘Hiraṇyagarbha’ is extracted as the Brahma Sūkta. (BhS 32.121)
The hymn to Indra is recited here with the verse beginning, "Indraṃ vo viśvatas"; the hymn to Agni is declared to consist of the six verses beginning with, "Agne naya. (BhS 32.122)
The hymn beginning with "āyātu deva" is proclaimed as the Yama-sūkta;
the hymn beginning with "namas te nirṛte" is called the Nairṛta-sūkta. (BhS 32.123)
“*astabhnād dyām ṛṣabha*” is the hymn to Varuṇa;
“*pīvonnāṃ rayivṛdhas sumedhā*” is that to Vāyu. (BhS 32.124)
“From the waters, he vanished,” etc., is called the Kauvera Sūkta; “Praise the renowned one on his seat,” etc., is proclaimed as the Rudra Sūkta. (BhS 32.125)
The hymn beginning with "omāsaś carṣaṇi" is the Sārasvata;
the hymn "viśvajit edhanam" is called the Viśvajit hymn. (BhS 32.126)
The *Rātrisūkta* is cited beginning with "rātrī vyakhyad" (RV 10.127.1), and the *Ṣaḍdurgāsūkta* is said to begin with "jātavedase" (RV 1.99.1). BhS 32.127.
Having recited "ā godānāt," the hymn beginning with "godānam" is declared;
having recited "ekākṣaram," the hymn beginning with "ekākṣara" and so forth is declared. (BhS 32.128)
“‘The self, the self, the supreme,’ and so forth—this is proclaimed as the *Ātmasūkta*. (BhS 32.129)”
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and thereafter the Śrīsūkta and Bhūsūkta— these five are here called the Pañcasūkta.
Others sang the Viṣṇusūkta, the Nṛsūkta, and thereafter the Śrībhūsūkta, as well as the Ekākṣara and other hymns—these are known as the five sūktas. (BhS 32.131)
The Viṣṇu-sūkta, the Nṛ-sūkta, the Śrī-bhū-sūkta, the Vaiṣṇava [hymns], and the Ekākṣara and other sūktas, together with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī; BhS 32.132.
Taken together, these seven constitute what is proclaimed as the Saptasūkta:
the Rudrasūkta, the Dhruvasūkta, and thereafter the Durgāsūkta. (BhS 32.133)
Likewise, the Rātrisūkta, the Sārasvatasūkta in due order, the Viśvajitsūkta, and also the Sahasraśīrṣa; BhS_32.134 //
The Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, the Godāna hymn,
and likewise the Ātmasūkta— these together are declared to be the ten hymns.
Having made ten hymns into five hymns and likewise having condensed them,
it is thus that the designation "five ten-hymn [sections]" is proclaimed.
Henceforth I shall proclaim; listen, O best of sages:
one should perform the daily worship of the mandala, the auspicious day rite, and the ceremonial bathing.
After forty days have passed, for five days he should perform the auspicious rite (*puṇyāha*) according to the rules over rice grains placed upon paddy.

Having taken a new water-pot according to the previously mentioned procedure and having worshipped it, one should perform the recitation of mantras together with Brahmins who are exponents of the Veda.
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and thereafter the Puruṣasūkta;
likewise the Śrīsūkta and the Bhūsūkta, as well as the five Śāntis, each separately.
Having recited [the mantra] four times over and chanted it, one should certainly bathe Acyuta;
likewise, the wise one should bathe the *kautuka* and other items according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered curd-rice, jaggery-rice, and especially milk-rice to the God of gods, one should provide mouth-fresheners.
One should give the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā) as well as to the officiating priests (ṛtvij),
starting from the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) until the final day of the mandala, on each successive day.
In this very manner, one should especially cause it to be made in due order;
however, if one makes only half of the mandala, that is declared to be the medium [size].
At the conclusion of the mandala, one should especially cause the feeding of Brahmins to be performed;
having prepared the sacrificial fire-pit for the assembly, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day recited.
Having offered the libation according to the rules and recited the Vaiṣṇava hymn,
he should then offer the Viṣṇu-hymn accompanied by the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Having recited the Śrībhūsūkta, and thereafter the Pañcaśānti,
one should then sequentially shake off the eighty-eight [impurities] beginning with the syllable *Iṃ*, which relate to the supreme self (*pāramātmika*).
Having recited the eight-syllable mantra as well as the twelve-syllable one,
he should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and the concluding oblation (antahoma) is performed.
One should bathe the fixed image (dhruvabera), endowed with its colors, sequentially with one hundred and eight water-pots; however, one should not bathe it before [the preliminary] rites.
One should perform twelve circumambulations according to the prescribed rite,
having circumambulated the village from left to right while accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having placed [the image] upon the king of birds, one should show it the protective lamp;
having established it well in the place of the life-force (jīva), one should then cause it to perform prostration.
Thus, he who performs the worship of Hari’s mandala with devotion,
having attained all his desires, goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter:
The Greatness of the Incarnation as an Image (*arcāvatāra*).
Now I shall describe in detail the fivefold form of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, according to its divisions such as the Supreme Manifestation (paravyūha) and the others.
Out of compassion for his devotees and for the sake of favoring the worlds,
the God of gods manifests through various emanations, such as the supreme manifestation (paravyūha) and others.
By the first, which is the supreme form called the *vyūha*, and by the other, namely the *vibhava* form that assumes various manifestations; // BhS_33.3 //
Furthermore, Hari is established in five ways: as the inner controller (antaryāmin), as the fourth [form], and likewise as the incarnation in the form of an image (arcāvatāra).
Furthermore, he partakes of that which is incomparable and indescribable,
which nourishes the universe with a splendor equal to ten thousand full moons.
The supreme abode, the supreme light, consisting of all powers,
stainless, free from dualities, free from conceptual constructions, pure, eternal, inconceivable, and everlasting.
Immeasurable, without beginning or end, visible and yet invisible, beyond the reach of the senses;
because of its extreme subtlety, it is indefinable—the omniscient, all-pervading Lord who is both being and non-being.
The beginningless supreme Brahman, devoid of all that is to be abandoned,
is all-pervading, abiding within all beings, and beyond both existence and non-existence.
Adorned with divine weapons— the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus—
he stands upon a cloud in the sky that resembles a thousand suns.
Hari, who possesses four arms, is conceivable as eternally liberated;
he is adorned with his own six attributes, which are neither deficient nor excessive.
His limbs were well-proportioned and symmetrical, and all his members were beautiful;
he was adorned with divine ornaments that shimmered like waves of nectar.
The Lord of the World is served by Śrī, who is eternal and never departing from him.
Furthermore, the fivefold arrangement is proclaimed as being in accordance with the sacred scriptures;
the Lord, through the distinctions of Viṣṇu and the others, abides in a fivefold manner.
Indeed, this person is fivefold and consists of five selves, according to the Śruti;
likewise, it is said that he is purified by his own five qualities.
Viṣṇu is the primordial form of the five,
and his divisions are the four forms beginning with Puruṣa, which possess distinct characteristics.
"Therefore, for the sake of removing the fatigue of Viṣṇu, it is fourfold"—thus says the Śruti.
For this reason, those who know the Vedas declare that Brahman has four quarters.
Through the differentiation of their powers— consisting of one quarter, half, three-quarters, and the whole—
they are respectively endowed with the qualities known as virtue, knowledge, sovereignty, and dispassion.
Therefore, there are four forms; through their respective objects, there are four forms of the primordial deity due to its fourfold nature.
Thus, there are those four forms therein.
Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu—in this sequence;
then Vyāpin and Nārāyaṇa—these are his names in order.
Puruṣa is a portion of Viṣṇu, while Satyaka is a portion of Mahāviṣṇu;
Acyuta is a portion of Sadāviṣṇu, and Aniruddha is a portion of Vyāpin.
The fourfold division by means of the qualities of Brahman, beginning with Dharma, has been declared; the third is called Vibhava, while Viśva is the intermediate one. // BhS 33.21 //
I shall describe the forms of the Great-Souled One as the performers of various actions;
his manifestations are considered to be the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, as well as Hayagrīva and the rest.
This fourth state is said to be the essential nature of the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin). Like the awn of a wild grain, it is slender, yellowish in luster, and subtle in appearance.
"The Supreme Self is situated in the center of that crest," so it is said; thus declared by the Śruti, He resides in the center of the lotus of the heart.
In a great blazing fire with rays of light everywhere, with its flames facing in all directions,
it constantly heats [the body] from the soles of the feet to the top of the head.
And there, the crest is yellowish in appearance, slender like the awn of a grain of wild rice;
and in the middle of that crest, a great light blazes forth.
By the power of his own particular resolve, he shone with the luster of refined gold;
wearing yellow garments, he was gentle, serene, and possessed a pure smile.
Padmākṣa has red eyes, face, hands, and feet;
he is four-armed, holding a wheel, a conch, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness, while his other hand rests upon his hip.
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, mighty-armed, and adorned with all ornaments,
the Self of All dwells in the heart, together with Śrī, Bhūmi, and his attendants.
Causing all beings to revolve by means of His illusory power, as if they were mounted on a machine, He should be known as the Inner Controller, the cause of all causes. (BhS 33.30)
But the nature of the other [form], that of the Arcā (the image), bestows the highest fruit,
because Hari exists there as the Paravyūha and other forms, which are to be enjoyed eternally by the liberated.

Because the self in its state of manifestation has as its sole object of focus that which is proximate at that very moment, and because the inner self is to be meditated upon by means of those purified and perfected through yoga; BhS 33.32.
The unrestricted right of all belongs to the Self alone;
however, because it is the cause of specific devotion, the worship of an image is supreme.
The incarnation in the form of the image is the kinsman of all and is affectionate toward his devotees; regarding this incarnation in the form of the image, I have also spoken thus in brief.
The qualities [of this] cannot be fully described even in hundreds of years;
the wondrous perfection of the body is offered to the Lord.
Formerly fashioned by Brahmā and endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, this tongue will speak in vain, saying "Kṛṣṇa" or "Keśava. (BhS 33.36)
The mind that does not incline toward Him is in vain; what could be more excessive than this?
That is a true tongue which praises Hari, and that is a true mind which is offered to Keśava.
Worship is directed toward that [Brahman]; anything other than that is useless.
The Supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, is mere existence (sattāmātra) and devoid of all qualifications.
Since that which was previously difficult to conceive is now spoken of here for the sake of its attainment:
the mind is unstable, without support, and as flickering as the wind and waves. (BhS 33.39)
Because the unborn Brahman is subtle, it cannot be grasped by one whose nature is subject to grasping;
however, for one who practices correctly and continuously, its power becomes fully augmented.
Even after hundreds of other births, one is born as one who is to be grasped by Brahmā,
provided that no decline is contemplated due to the fault of obstacles.
Just as a yogin who is well-established in yoga falls from the tip of a palm tree,
so too does he reach the supreme Brahman even with great effort.
Through concentration and consciousness arising from practice in previous births,
that Brahman known as Viṣṇu— which is difficult to attain for one whose mind is overcome by sense objects— is realized.
For a person of little strength, this is the means for attaining that [state]:
a beautiful image of Viṣṇu with a serene face and eyes.
Having fashioned an image that brings him joy with gold, silver, and other materials, he should worship it, honor it, bow before it, and meditate upon it. (BhS 33.45)
But one who has cast off all defects enters that very [nature] which is of the form of Brahman.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra-sahitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter:
the five types of sacred sites, beginning with those that are self-manifested (*svayamvyakta*).
Henceforth, I shall explain the arrangement of the five sites;
[therein resides] the God of gods, the mighty-armed Hari Nārāyaṇa himself.
In whatever manner he manifests upon the surface of the earth—
in the form of an archavatāra— for the sake of being easily accessible to his devotees.

The wise have declared that there are five types of sacred sites: those self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), those divine (divya), those attained through spiritual power (siddha), those ancient (paurāṇa), and those created by human effort (pauruṣa).
That is declared to be "self-manifested" (svayaṃvyakta) where this Hari,
for the sake of protecting the world, manifests himself upon the earth by his own will.
In that regard, the ritual installation of the God of Gods is not prescribed by the rules;
nor is there ploughing, nor any such actions as the purification of the image.
Since the Lord of Gods himself dwells together with his image,
he remains duly worshipped for as long a time as one desires on this earth.
Worship at a self-manifested site bestows auspiciousness upon all the world;
there are four such self-manifested sites here upon the earth.
There, we three— including myself— rely upon the supremely auspicious Vaikhānasa scripture to worship the Source of the World.
Marīci worshipped Viṣṇu Keśava on Mandhara,
while Atri worshipped the god Śrīnivāsa, the supreme among all gods, at Śrīnivāsa.
Kāśyapa was in Viṣṇvadhiṣṭhāna, and I too was in the auspicious field of Bhṛgu;
such was the nature of the worship performed and such was the arrangement of the images.
One should not disregard even a slight thought [of devotion] but should practice as previously described;
for it was there that the Lord himself manifested out of compassion for his devotees.
Whatever is to be done there is determined by his command;
nor does he incite Mādhava to act contrary to the scriptures.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice what was performed by the ancients;
for if one acts otherwise, one commits an offense against the gods.
Who on earth is able to describe the majesty of that God, by whose illusory power all are deluded and whose end no one knows?
Whatever is practiced at any time, all of that is indeed scripture;
moreover, there is a distinction therein regarding the observation of penances and the like.
One may commit every kind of negligence; in that regard, the scripture is the authority.
For both Śruti and Smṛti declare these two to be his supreme commands.
Worship at a self-manifested site brings auspiciousness to all the world;
for the Lord of the World has manifested Himself spontaneously within stones and other such materials through identity with them.
He himself, having considered the desires of his devotees, grants them;
for there is no requirement for spiritual practice here, as he is the bestower who manifests spontaneously.
Where Hari indeed manifested himself after being installed by the gods, that place is designated as Vidyasthala; there the divine Lord is proclaimed.
The thirty-three gods are remembered to be as many as thirty-three crores;
all of them, desiring the fruits [of their merit], indeed take refuge in Hari just as others do.
The Lord, that treasury of compassion, bestows [favor] upon them accordingly;
for when those seeking fruits have consecrated Hari in due order, [the Lord acts].
Having worshipped [the deity] and immediately obtained his desired object,
he indeed constructed such a temple for the sake of favoring the world.
Having resolved that he would remain for a long time, they honored him as was fitting;
for a deity residing in a divine abode indeed brings the gods into his presence.
This elixir is said to bring ultimate nourishment and to effect all forms of pacification;
moreover, worship performed at a divine site extends its influence for a hundred yojanas.
It purifies the surrounding region; no doubt is entertained in this matter.
It is said that there are countless divine sites upon the surface of the earth.
For the gods never descend themselves onto the earth during the Kali age to perform the installation of the God of Gods anywhere at all.
O best of beings, in the Kali age, divine places on the surface of the earth will indeed become rare;
many among them will have their worship lost.

Worship performed at divine sites is established by the scriptures; of this there is no doubt. However, the deities in heaven do not perform consecrations and the like that are contrary to the scriptures.
And even in the world of the gods, the deities, having constructed a temple of Viṣṇu and having worshipped the Lord of the World, obtain great fruit.
But the worship that takes place upon the surface of the earth is not at all like that of the gods;
for the earth is declared to be the field of action, whereas the celestial realms are certainly not equal to it.
Whether intentionally performing merit or evil, people will go from this earth to other worlds;
therefore, that region of the earth is superior for all ritual actions.
Then the gods, having installed and worshipped the Lord of Ramā in the form of an incarnate image, themselves crossed over [the ocean] again and again.
Out of compassion, they will deliver all living beings dwelling upon the earth;
therefore, O brahmins, you should always perform sacrifices, give gifts, and repeatedly practice austerities.
They will indeed satisfy the gods for the sake of discharging their debt to them;
for even among humans, the gods remain natural enemies.
By propitiating the Lord, human beings provide assistance;
this very power of worship of Hari is the fruit thus accomplished.
All those of a sattvic nature proceed [toward their goal] and are satisfied with the fruits they have earned for themselves;
they do not even hate their enemies—of this, the gods are the example.
Just as one who is subject to death may dwell in heaven or rely upon the celestial realms,
so too, O son of Aditi, there are no eternal places here on earth.
In all divine places, however, the worship was performed according to the divine Āgama of the Vaikhānasa; for that is recognized as being in accordance with the Śruti.
Whenever the specific causes for which an expiation is appropriate arise in this context, one must certainly perform that which is prescribed in the scriptures;
the rule is not to be performed otherwise.
But those whose minds are devoted to the Supreme Self through austerities previously acquired, having perfected their penance, conceptualize the fruit of their own austerity.
Having installed the God of gods, the Lord of the world, the peerless Nārāyaṇa, in some image and having worshipped him especially; BhS_34.41 //
"Because they will bestow worship here for the sake of reviving the worlds, that region is called 'Saiddha'; the worship performed there is known as Saiddhā."
For perfected ones never display their wondrous power of ascetic success anywhere;
rather, virtuous practitioners perform austerities here desiring to bestow grace upon someone.
O Brahmins, having abandoned the propitiation of Him for whose sake they perform sacrifices, gifts, and other rites, what is it that the Siddhas are doing?
They are perfected, they are great-souled, they are virtuous and ascetic— those who,
having realized that the Lord Hari, the Consort of Śrī, is the fruit of their own actions.
Having established that form, they worship it continuously;
for there is no other cause for attaining liberation than such worship.
But the worship performed at a site of accomplishment is remembered as bringing all-pervading peace;
it purifies the earth for fifty yojanas all around.
Many lands established by the Siddhas were known in the past;
Siddhas will arise and exist upon the surface of the earth.
There will be many sites of accomplishment (siddhasthala), both those that exist now and those yet to come;
these were established by the Siddhas themselves, relying upon the Vaikhānasa scripture which they composed.
In this world, those who worship the Divine generally remain steadfast even when shaken;
for the perfected ones do not perform anything that contravenes the scriptures, even in times of distress.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform all rites at a site inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas), relying upon the Vaikhānasa scripture for all actions.
The Siddhas know the meanings of the scriptures; the Siddhas know the traditional teachings (āgamas);
and the Siddhas indeed worship according to the Vaikhānasa injunctions.

If a region inhabited by perfected ones (siddhas) is worshipped by others out of negligence, the king, however, must investigate it and then [re-establish order] through the Vaikhanasas in due sequence.
Having performed the expiation according to the rule, one should perform the sacrifice quickly;
some call this place *saiddha*, and this is also accepted as *ārṣa*.
Now, the ancient region is described: wherever indeed an ancient legend (paurāṇikī gāthā) may exist, that place is considered an ancient site (purāṇasthala).
In this regard, many places whose authors are unknown are mostly remembered;
these are declared to be the Purāṇas.
In former times there were infinite sacred sites upon the surface of the earth;
however, when the Kali age arrives, they are destroyed in great numbers.
Having circumambulated the ground for a distance of ten yojanas, the ancient site is purified; therein, nothing whatsoever is lost.

All those [shrines] mentioned in the Purāṇas, such as the self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and others, are also [included], since we observe their usage distinguished by categories such as "self-manifested" and so forth. (BhS 34.59)
Their antiquity would be established, and another [text] is called "Paurāṇa";
the installation of the deity in an ancient site is approved by the ritual rules.
But if the image is installed without the prescribed ritual, Hari will not take delight in it; for the elders do not worship an image fashioned contrary to the scriptures.
For in a traditional land, the high-minded ones must demonstrate both the dignity of the sacrificer and the dignity of the purpose.
If one whose self is deluded should see [this], he would go to the Raurava hell;
this alone shall be the distinction, while otherwise he should act like an accomplished adept (siddha).
The worship of ancient sites should be performed according to the path seen in the scriptures; however, if it is carried out through negligence, there shall be no transgression on that account.

O best of men, that person who gives land constantly covered with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and grass does not fall from heaven.
An auspicious and beautiful throne, a parasol, excellent horses, and noble women—these are the signs of the gift of land; this is its fruit, without a doubt.
Āditya, the Vasus, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, Hutāśana,
and the Lord who wields the trident— all these rejoice in the giver of land.
Golden parasols, golden vessels, showers of wealth that grant all desires,
Gandharvas, and Apsarases— these attend those who give land wherever they may be.
This very land was formerly protected by many kings and bestowed upon others by numerous monarchs who were true to their vows.
For whomever the land belongs at any given time, for that person alone is there fruit at that time—
both for him who receives the land and for him who bestows the land.
Both of them, having performed meritorious deeds, are destined for heaven;
yet between the two—giving and protection—the preservation [of what has been given] is superior to giving.
Through giving, one attains heaven; through protection, the imperishable state.
Protecting what has been given by another yields twice the merit of that which one has given oneself.
Having ascended to heaven from this earth, he prospers for eternal years;
and having attained birth once again, he will certainly become a lord of the earth.
Just as the goddess Earth always makes the donor her husband,
so too does a cow, when given with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), make him a lord of men.
Even if he receives from one who has committed evil, the giver of land is purified;
for by giving land, one becomes pure, since the earth is sacred.
"Priyadattā" is indeed her secret and eternal name;
therefore, as you bestow [this gift], it should always be proclaimed with affection for her.
Virtue based on austerity and sacrifice, freedom from greed, truthfulness,
and the worship of gurus and deities— none of these surpasses the giver of land.
Those who are intent on the supreme welfare of their husband, who have renounced their own bodies and are slain in battle,
having gone to the world of Brahmā, do not overstep the giver of the earth.
Just as a mother joyfully nourishes her own son with milk,
so does the earth nourish the donor with all virtues.
By performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which is gained by giving the earth once again.
For the servants of Death, the staffs of punishment, the most dreadful torments of fire,
and the terrible nooses of Varuṇa do not approach the giver of land.
The ancestors dwelling in the world of the Pitṛs and the gods dwelling in the world of the Devas satisfy the donor, O lord of men, when he rules over the earth.
Those men who bestow the earth upon Hari, the witness of the world, shine with splendor like the Ādityas.
A person who provides a livelihood to one who is emaciated, whose servants are emaciated, who is destitute, and who is perishing—
even if he is a Brahmin who has fallen from the sacred fires— attains great prosperity.
The fathers clap their hands and the grandfathers dance, saying:
"A giver of land has been born in our family; he will deliver us all."
He is the benefactor of our lineage, our kinsman, and our teacher;
he is the giver and the valiant one who bestows the earth.
In the beginning, when the worlds were being created by the Self-born One, cows were created for the sake of the growth of all beings; therefore, they are remembered as mothers.
Having given those cows of the sun-like lineage, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
likewise, having given a well-behaved milch cow together with a pillow.
For the sake of pleasing the God of gods, one should give a divine, tawny cow with her calf to a teacher, a worshiper, or to a brahmin.
It is not possible to describe his merit even in hundreds of years,
as numerous as the hairs on the cow and especially those on her calf.
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on that Kapila cow, along with her calf and a bronze milking vessel, she shall yield all desires for him who gives her away.
With golden horns and silver hooves, and endowed with various other qualities of substance,
that cow becomes a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadughā) and approaches the donor.
He who gives a thousand cows adorned with all kinds of jewels,
having attained supreme prosperity and glory, is honored in the heavenly world.
And ten generations of maternal and paternal grandfathers on both sides shall go to the worlds of the virtuous after death, by giving cows according to the prescribed rite.
If one acquires cows through means such as inheritance or acquisition and bestows them [as a gift],
for him too there are inexhaustible worlds both here and in the hereafter.
Or he who, having won wealth at dice, purchases cows and bestows them [as a gift],
shall go to the stainless worlds acquired through the fruit of the gift of cows.
Whoever should give cows with a pure mind, having accepted them,
goes to a place difficult to attain and rejoices together with the immortals.
And he who, having sold himself, gives cows according to the prescribed rule,
goes to the stainless worlds and dwells there happily like a god.
He who, having cast off his body in battle, gives away cows,
obtains those eternal, wish-fulfilling cows which are the price for the sale of his body.
By giving a cow that is worn out, already used, decrepit, and devoid of good character, one enters into darkness; one should not subject a twice-born man to such distress.
One should never give a cow that is unfit for donation—one that is emaciated, vicious, or prone to running away;
for the brahmin who gives such a cow would become as wretched as the animal itself.
One should give to Hari a young, strong, dark bull, the leader of the herd, the lord of cows, adorned with many horns and accompanied by a plow.
The lineage of Brahmins and that of cows are indeed one, though divided into two; on the one side reside the mantras, and on the other resides the sacrificial oblation.
But he who, having approached, gives cows with a pure mind,
is honored in heaven for as many years as there are hairs on those cows.
I shall describe the worlds of the cows, such as they are situated there—
delightful, beautiful, and always yielding all desires.
The worlds of cows are meritorious and indeed destroyers of sin; of this there is no doubt.
There, beings are exceedingly happy and entirely free from all evil.
In the great abode, men free from defilement rejoice;
equal in power to the gods, they delight with hosts of celestial nymphs.
Without a doubt, those Brahmins who are of virtuous conduct, compassionate, and merciful, are praised by the Gandharvas as those who provide refuge for cows.
Those who are compassionate and performers of good deeds rejoice together with the deities,
just as a fish in the water dwells together with the water.
By means of cows, even firmly committed evil karma is utterly dispelled;
they are the mothers of all beings, established for the protection of all creatures.
Cows are the essence of the world, equal to Brahmā, and they remove the fear of sin;
when they are given as a gift in this world, what could possibly remain ungiven here?
Furthermore, songs should always be offered especially to the Lord of Gods and to His ritual acts by those who desire prosperity and abundant fortune.
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee.
This is the ultimate purifier; this is the great means of securing well-being.
Having given [a gift] to those worthy of it, one may rescue ten ancestors, ten descendants in the lineage, and oneself in particular— even if one has committed a hundred sins— from their misfortunes.
We have heard that those people who bestow gold with a pure mind,
the deities bestow everything upon them.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold is the consumer of oblations;
therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities are given.
And in the absence of fire, those who know the authoritative measure of all the gods perform [the rite] with gold in the place of the fire, according to the evidence of Vedic revelation.
He who kindles this fire at the rising of the sun and offers it in honor of the God shall indeed attain all his desires.
The giver of gold obtains all desired objects in the world;
clothed in stainless garments, he wanders here and there.
In a celestial chariot, sun-colored, radiant, and resplendent, he shone,
surrounded by hosts of apsaras and glowing with that brilliance.
Drawn by swans and peacocks, that best of men traveled here and there through heaven in his vehicle that moves at will, wafting divine fragrances.
Therefore, men on earth should give gold according to their own capacity;
by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, he goes to the highest heaven.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world superior to this for the immediate destruction of evil:
he who bestows gold upon a pure vessel of the Veda.
"He is honored in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
Thus has the fruit of the gift of gold been briefly declared by me. (BhS 35.222)
Now I shall explain specifically the fruit resulting from the giving of food to Viṣṇu, to Śrī, to the Earth, and indeed to all the gods.
Because of giving with reverence to supplicants that which remains of what has been felt,
it is not possible to describe its fruit even in hundreds of years.
Nevertheless, although it has been sung at length by the supreme sages,
I shall now proclaim in brief the fruit acquired through the gift of food.
One should call clarified butter "immortality" (amṛta), food offered to the gods "immortality," and one should call the water from the feet of the deity "the sacred ford" (tīrtha) and "immortality."
The gods and the hosts of seers likewise praise food alone;
for the governance of the world, as well as all designations, are established upon food.
A gift equal to food has never existed before, nor will it ever exist in the future;
therefore, human beings especially desire to give food.
In this world, food provides vigor; the vital breaths are established in food.
By food is sustained everything—this entire great universe.
In this world, householders, mendicants, and likewise ascetics depend upon food;
indeed, life-breaths arise from food—this is perceptible, there is no doubt in this matter.
One who desires their own prosperity should give food to a high-souled Brahmin and to a mendicant, even by causing hardship to their own family.
Whoever gives food to a worthy Brahmin who asks for it,
establishes for himself the most excellent treasure for the world beyond.
A householder seeking prosperity should honor an Arhat who has arrived at his home—an elder who is weary from traveling along the road. (BhS 35.233)
Having abandoned arisen anger, being well-behaved and free from envy,
the giver of food attains that which is abundant on earth and whatever happiness exists both here and in the hereafter.
One should not despise a guest who has arrived, nor should one ever turn them away;
even if it be a dog-cooker or a dog, a gift does not go to waste.
Whoever gives unblemished food to one traveling on a journey who is peaceful and has not been seen before, shall attain the great Dharma.
That man who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, the seers, the learned brahmins, and especially guests with food, gains a great fruit of merit.
If one should give food to a seeker— even after having committed a heinous act—
especially to a Brāhmaṇa, that person is not deluded by sin.
Among Brahmins, there is an inexhaustible store of names; among Śūdras, there is great strength.
Furthermore, even for a Śūdra, the gift of food is distinguished as superior for a Brahmin.
When requested for food by a brahmin, one should give it when asked; one should not inquire about his lineage, conduct, sacred study, or native land. (BhS 35.240)
For a king who gives food, trees of food that grant the fruits of all desires arise both in this world and in the next; of this there is no doubt.
For the ancestors hope, just as farmers hope for good rain: "May one of our sons or grandsons provide us with food. (BhS 35.242)
For a Brahmin is a great being; whether one is unwilling or willing, by giving when he personally begs "Give!", one shall obtain merit.
The Brahmin is the supreme intellect among all beings and the first to partake of what is offered;
he is the one whom the learned always approach at home when seeking alms.
They desist even when treated with honor, yet they proceed excessively;
and after death, they constantly obtain birth in a family of great wealth.
Having given food in this world according to the highest place,
a man who constantly gives choice food dwells in heaven, highly honored.
Food is indeed the life-breath of men; everything is established upon food.
The giver of food possesses cattle, sons, wealth, and enjoyments as well.
He becomes possessed of vital breath and likewise endowed with beauty;
the giver of food in this world is called the giver of life, indeed the giver of everything.
Having given food to a Brāhmaṇa guest according to the prescribed rule,
the donor attains happiness and is honored even by the gods.
For the brahmin is said here to be a great being, a field;
whatever seed is sown therein indeed yields great fruit of merit.
The gift that produces immediate joy belongs both to the recipient and the giver; indeed, all other gifts possess fruits that are beyond direct perception.
For from food comes procreation, and from food indeed joy is born;
one should know that wealth and purpose arise from food, and likewise the destruction of disease comes from food.
"Food is indeed wonderful," so said Prajāpati in a former aeon;
"food is the earth, the heavens, and the sky; everything is established in food. (BhS 35.253)
When food is lost, the five elements in the body are broken apart;
even the strength of a strong person perishes here through the lack of food.
Weddings, marriages, and sacrifices for the sake of food likewise cease especially here,
and the Veda is bestowed in this place.
Furthermore, whatever exists here—whether stationary or moving—in all three worlds, food should be given for the sake of dharma by the wise; therefore, this is so.
The strength, vigor, fame, and lifespan of the person who gives food increase accordingly; this is certain in those worlds.
Above the clouds, the Lord of Winds establishes the vital breaths;
and Śakra, filled with joy, rains down that water which resides within the clouds.
The sun draws up the terrestrial juices with its own rays,
and the divine wind rains down those juices heated by the sun.
Just as when water falls from the clouds upon the earth,
then the goddess Earth becomes moistened and nourished.
From that, the crops grow by which the world subsists;
and from that, furthermore, the manifestation of flesh, fat, bone, and semen occurs.
From that semen, living beings come into existence upon the surface of the earth;
for the Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya sacrifices indeed create and nourish that semen.
Thus, from food indeed arise the sun, the wind, and semen;
this alone is remembered as the single aggregate, from which all beings are born.
He who gives food to a seeker who has come to his house bestows life upon living beings and a splendor that is constantly radiant.
Listen with concentrated minds to those worlds which are attained through the gift of food;
the palaces of those great-souled ones shine in heaven.
They possess various forms and shapes resembling stars, are endowed with numerous pillars,
are as white as the lunar disc, and are adorned with networks of tinkling bells.
Having the color of the rising sun, they consist of both the stationary and the moving,
comprising many hundreds of levels and containing various aquatic creatures within them.
Shining with the luster of beryl and the sun, made of gold and silver,
and bearing trees that yield every desired fruit, these dwellings are established within the palaces.
Ponds, pathways, assembly halls, wells, and long reservoirs were everywhere;
moreover, thousands of resounding vehicles were released.
There are mountains consisting of various kinds of food and drink, as well as garments and ornaments;
likewise, there are rivers flowing with milk and mountains of cooked rice.
Those who give food attain palaces with the luster of white clouds and couches radiant with gold; therefore, one should always give food.
One should always give food that has been offered to Viṣṇu;
the sacrificial vessels and other implements should be made of gold, silver, or even copper.
Or whoever might give bell-metal, as well as vessels for the arghya offering and so forth, water-pots, jars, pitchers, and other such utensils; BhS 35.273.
Even without harboring greed for the power [of the reward], the fruit of his merit is great;
he who gives [gifts] made of gold alone obtains the fruit of attaining a form similar [to that of the deity].
Furthermore, if one should give [images] made of silver, one obtains the fruit of proximity;
if one gives those made of copper or bell-metal, he attains the state of being in the same realm.
He who gives various banners endowed with many colors will become the foremost of all and shall be a banner for his lineage.
The canopy may be white, red, black, yellow, or dark green;
it may be made of fine silk, woven cloth, thread, or some other material.
He who gives [a bed] to the God of gods shall go to the station of Viṣṇu;
and he who gives a couch to Hari, complete with pillows and a mattress, [attains the same].
Having reached the realm of Kubera, he rejoices there for a long time;
likewise, he receives a golden parasol adorned with strings of pearls.
One who gives [an image] equipped with a golden staff goes to the world of Indra;
one desiring a kingdom shall become a king, and may even be born as a sovereign ruler of the whole earth.
By the gift of a peacock-feather umbrella, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa;
likewise by giving a fly-whisk with a golden handle and a fan adorned with jewels.
Whoever offers even a single golden staff to Hari, endowed with devotion and according to their capacity, is honored in the world of the gods.
Likewise, he who, out of devotion alone, gives a peacock-feather fan with a golden handle according to his ability to Hari, is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
If a man should cause a celestial palace (vimāna) to be constructed for Viṣṇu, even though it is completely covered [in ornaments],
the fruit of that deed is impossible for all the gods and asuras together to describe.
We have heard that for whoever causes an image of Viṣṇu made of gold to be fashioned with devotion alone, all the fruit thereof is likewise infinite.
Or else, a pavilion or a water-shed, adorned with jewels and pearls,
