provided with golden pendants, and decorated with pillars of gold.
He who, with devotion, offers to Hari an excellent golden throne, shall attain the realm of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the immortals to reach. (BhS 35.287)
Having ascended the lion throne, he shall attain the prosperity of Mahendra;
he should likewise cause golden palanquins and various types of colored cloths to be made.
Having ascended a golden vehicle, he likewise goes to the world of Viṣṇu; or else, being unable [to afford that], he may go by means of large boats, rafts, and the like, or even by palanquins.
He who gives a lion-throne goes to the world of Soma;
and he who gives a bell made of white brass, endowed with a pleasing sound, [attains the same].
That man shall possess a heart-pleasing voice and a melodious tone; he shall be a charming and eloquent speaker.
By the gift of conchs, kettledrums, and other such instruments, he is honored in the world of Śakra.
He who causes proclamations to be made with dances, songs, and instrumental music,
or who causes celestial nymphs to dance, shall attain the world of the Gandharvas.
Whoever worships Hari according to their ability with the sounds of lutes and flutes shall enjoy great sovereignty on this earth and attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Whatever substance a man, filled with joy, may give to Hari,
he should first offer it to the worshippers and especially to his guru.
For the sake of pleasing him and other Brahmins according to the prescribed rules,
one undoubtedly attains abundance of that very same object.
Whatever a man might desire when giving, he shall obtain all of that;
whatever action is performed for his sake, and whatever service is rendered to him.
Whoever performs service to it with faith,
having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, shall attain the state of non-return.
Therefore, having established here a temple for the God of gods,
one should do so with devotion and without any greed for power or wealth.
If one should perform the ritual service in many ways and on a grand scale, that is most excellent;
now I shall describe specifically the fruit of worshipping the Enemy of Madhu.
A man who daily performs circumambulation with devotion in the temple of Viṣṇu, bowing to the Lord of Gods in the evening and the morning and then meditating upon Him; BhS_35.300 //
He who should repeatedly perform prostration shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice;
the specific fruits resulting from particular modes of service will now be explained.
Having performed meditation as an invocation, one shall obtain all desires by mentally contemplating Hari through the path of the eightfold yoga.
Having first reflected with the mind, he whose body is purified and who is high-minded should perform worship of Viṣṇu; there the God will certainly dwell.
Due to the ascetic power of the priest, the excellence of the worship,
the beauty of the image, and its proximity, the presence of Hari is proclaimed.
Having offered a seat to Hari, one attains long-lasting stability;
he who honors Mādhava with a welcome and respectful estimation [is likewise blessed].
Having been approved by all, that man receives a welcome;
he then offers water for the feet and water for sipping to Hari.
He who constantly worships with devotion using auspicious flowers shall be liberated from whatever evil is external or internal. (BhS 35.307)
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot resembling ten million suns,
he went to the world of Viṣṇu and truly rejoices for a long time in the abode of Viṣṇu.
And for that wise person who adorns the Lord of Gods with flower garlands and other offerings, an infinite fruit is proclaimed; for the Blessed Hari is infinite.
By offering campaka, aśoka, punnāga, jasmine, and malaya lotus to the God of Gods, one shall become a refuge for auspicious things.
If one offers damanaka, uśīra, lāmajja, ketakī, and utpala, his auspiciousness shall indeed be unbroken; of this there is no doubt.
The wise man should devoutly offer *tulasī* at the feet of Hari;
having obtained infinite fruit, he rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.
By the gift of fragrant flowers, a person becomes fragrant;
by the gift of many flowers, Hari is indeed pleased in manifold ways.
He indeed finds delight through the gift of many excellent births by offering even once a heap of flowers at the feet of Viṣṇu.
By placing *tulasī* upon the head of the God who is the enemy of Madhu, one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice at every step.
A person who offers a flower to the all-pervading Hari upon all his limbs is liberated from sin and is not defiled by action. (BhS 35.316)
He will always be a thief of desires in all worlds;
yet, by adorning the deity with fruits, he shall obtain the fruit of offering flowers.
One should offer fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and other such substances, smooth and beautiful for every limb, upon the body as is appropriate.
That man goes to the realm of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the immortals to attain—
he who worships Mādhava with flowers gathered by his own hand.
He obtains all the fruits of offering flowers and other such gifts;
among all flowers, however, Tulasī is the one that gives pleasure to Hari.
Wherever the worshiper goes taking a Tulasī leaf,
the God follows him, just as a cow follows her calf with great affection.
Whoever worships the Garuḍa-bannered Lord with Tulasī every day shall be liberated from birth, death, old age, and disease, and attain final liberation.
Jewels, golden flowers, pearls,
and lapis lazuli do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of offering a *tulasī* leaf.
Those who perform the worship of Hari in the Kali age with tender tulasī leaves joined with *sumañjarī* blossoms have achieved their life's purpose.
Whether it be dry or stale wood, or even fresh wood or a *tulasī* leaf,
when used in the worship of Vāsudeva, it becomes a hundred thousand times ten million times more meritorious.
The taking of Tulasī is recommended for the purpose of worshipping Viṣṹṇu;
while withered flowers should be avoided, a Tulasī leaf should not be avoided.
Stale water is to be avoided, but the water of the Ganges is not to be avoided;
other stale [water] is to be avoided, but the lotus flower is not to be avoided.
By worshipping Vāsudeva even with dry or stale wood, roots, earth, and so forth, a person becomes liberated.
The sacred fords beginning with Puṣkara, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
and the gods who dwell in heaven— all abide upon a Tulasī leaf.
Flowers such as the *mālatī* and others boast with pride only so long as the meritorious *tulasī*, the beloved of Viṣṇu, has not been obtained.
By worshipping Govinda even once with Tulasī,
a person becomes a partaker of liberation, free from fear, and becomes an attendant of Kṛṣṇa.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains, nor Śambhu with water from a conch shell;
one should not worship Durgā with dūrvā grass, nor any other deity with tulasī.
If Tulasī leaves are not available, one should worship Hari with [other] leaves;
if leaves are not available, with its stalks; or in the absence of stalks, with pieces of the root.
If water is not available, one who is devoted should worship Hari there with earth;
and for the worship of Hari, Tulasī is the supreme means. (BhS 35.334)
If Tulasī is not available, the utterance of its name is supreme;
the lotus-eyed Lord is satisfied a thousandfold.
Govinda is not so pleased with lotuses, nor with white water-lilies, nor even with golden flowers,
as he is with the leaves of the tulasī.
Those on earth who, having taken up *tulasī* with devotion, always perform the worship of Hari using *tulasī* alone—[they attain all their desires]. (BhS 35.337)
Therefore, there has been no being, nor will there ever be, equal to Tulasī; for wherever the winds are infused with the fragrance of a grove of Tulasī, [there all beings are purified].
The servants of Yama do not roam upon that portion of the earth where those who constantly repeat the names "Tulasī, Tulasī" dwell. (BhS 35.339)
Having reached the world of Viṣṇu, they behold Madhusūdana;
[this occurs] through seeing, hearing, touching, remembering, and even by chanting his praises.
The meritorious Tulasī purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants;
wherever there is a grove of Tulasī, or wherever there is the chanting of Hari’s names.
There alone dwells the glorious Hari, armed with the conch, the discus, and the mace;
he who worships Viṣṇu there with unripe fruits that are like nectar [attains his goal].
By whom can that fruit be described, which arises from the tree of merit?
It is the one who causes the king to smell sandalwood, agallochum, koṣṭha-wood, and other such fragrances.
Having gone to the world of the Sun, he indeed goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
he who offers a lamp made with Kāpila ghee and provided with a firm wick.
One should present to the God of gods a lamp that is pleasing to the sight;
such a bull among men shall never enter the blind hell.
But he who shows a brightly blazing lamp kindled with oil ascends a celestial palace of exceeding radiance and goes beyond darkness.
The man who with devotion shows a carbūra lamp to Hari—
his sins are destroyed and he shall become stainless.
A person who, with devotion, offers the eight-limbed *arghya* to Hari according to the prescribed rite,
goes to the world of the Moon and thereafter attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
He who offers fragrant, auspicious, and purified water for bathing to the Lord of Gods will, by that very act, become free from all impurity.
And then, having reached the world of Varuṇa, he rejoices right there,
wearing clean, soft upper garments made of woven cloth.
Having offered [garments] to the God of gods, one shall attain the auspicious world;
likewise, [one may offer] cotton, linen, silk, or wool.
Having offered even according to one's capacity, one enjoys infinite fruit;
from cotton comes rāṅgava, and from that, kauśeya and also kṣauma.
Excellent clothing has been prescribed here according to one's capacity,
as well as golden ornaments or those made of pearls and gems.
One should offer [an image] to the God of gods; indeed, such a person shall become a lord of the earth.
[The materials may be] Jāmbūnada gold, Śātakuṃbha gold, Hāṭaka gold, or likewise that which comes from bamboo.
Then there is that which comes from horns, that which is produced from oyster shells, and thereafter that which is born of gold;
it is likewise said to be "perfumed by mercury" (rasaviddha) and also "extracted from a mine" (ākarodgata).
Many kinds of gold have been described, each subsequent one superior to the preceding;
and upon them, various types of ships belonging to Hari are especially inlaid with jewels.
The nine planets shall devotedly bestow ornaments upon his friends;
and having enjoyed royal splendor, he goes at the end to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who gives a sacred thread made of golden threads shall become a supreme twice-born man possessed of higher knowledge and attain the world of Brahmā.
He who offers a garland fashioned from many śālagrāma stones to the God of gods attains the presence of Viṣṇu.
Lakṣmī is the most beloved of Viṣṇu, for she is eternal and never-departing;
she is the supreme power (śakti) consisting of all things, conformed to by her own volition.
She is the primordial source of nature and the sovereign mistress of the worlds for the virtuous;
having fashioned an image of Lakṣmī with jewels, pearls, and other gems, [he installed her].
He who, having tied [a garland] upon a string, offers it to the Lord of Gods—
for him the two lords of the world, the divine couple, become pleased.
And by especially placing an offering in the hand of the God of gods, one attains all desires; for the mobile and immobile beings of Hari are thereby gratified.
Clad in spotless garments, white as the moon, he should joyfully offer the *madhuparka* to Hari with devotion, which brings delight to Hari. (BhS 35.364)
Having become the lord of the world of the moon, he shall go to the great abode of Viṣṇu;
by offering oblations into the fire of the deity, he enjoys the fruit of his firm establishment.
Having offered an abundance [of gifts], one likewise obtains the fruit of restoring what is dilapidated;
and by offering milk-rice (pāyasa) with special devotion to Hari, one gains even greater merit.
By offering kṛsara to the Lord, that joyful man brings his ancestors to satisfaction through lakes of milk.
Having offered sweetmeats to the Lord, one attains mountains of molasses and shall enjoy food for a very long time in one's own home. BhS 35.368.
By the gift of mung-bean rice, one obtains a heap of mung beans; by the gift of barley porridge, one certainly becomes free from disease. (BhS 35.369)
By the gift of pure food, offspring become pure in three ways;
by the gift of cakes and such, a man is born intelligent.
Will there not be an accompaniment [of food] by the giving of snacks and the like?
He who would offer fragrant, delicious, and pure water to Hari [shall receive it]. (BhS 35.371)
One fully enjoys half the fruit of the merit of giving sacrificial offerings [of] plantain, coconut, mango, and jackfruit. (BhS 35.372)
And whoever should devoutly offer unripe but pure fruits,
he too shall obtain a fruit equal to one-fourth of the merit from the offering of sacrificial oblations.
It was likewise provided with camphor, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg and other such fruits,
as well as pure, well-ripened citron fruits.
He who offers betel leaf with areca nuts as an oral fragrance attains all sovereignty and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who, having worshipped Bala according to the prescribed rite, performs a circumambulation,
attains the strength of the strong and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whoever serves Bali with devotion shall likewise obtain the fruit of sacrifice;
one should construct a pavilion for the deity, adorned with perfumes and flowers, or provide a water-shed.
Having attained all sovereignty, one shall go to the realm of eternal flowers and fruits;
indeed, after reciting the stories of Viṣṇu and praising him with Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Having heard this, one who meditates on Hari with devotion is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
[these are] these four gentle and meritorious modes of worship of Viṣṇu.
The wise person who causes [this] to be heard with devotion, as well as whoever listens to it,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Now I shall declare the fruit resulting from the performance of festivals and other rites for the Slayer of Madhu:
for those with desires, the fruit is what they desire; for those without desires, it is the supreme state.
The gods will proclaim the festival as the worship of the God of Gods;
however, for human beings in particular, "utsava" is said to mean enthusiasm.
The word *ud* here signifies "excellent," and *sava* is declared to mean "sacrifice";
therefore, because it is the supreme sacrifice, it is designated as a festival (*utsava*).
Therefore, the festival of the gods is superior to sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice;
whoever performs the festival of the God of Gods shall [elevate] his own family.
Carrying Viṣṇu himself across, he goes to the supreme abode;
because it carries one across with ease, it is celebrated as a festival (utsava).
"That sacrifice will surely deliver you, O heroes"—having proclaimed this, those Vedas uttered that festival cry. (BhS 35.386)
Whatever fruit may come from one who performs a thousand horse-sacrifices,
equal to that is the fruit for both him and the one who performs the sacrifice with festivity when they have passed away.
Through the ritual of the festival, those who perform sacrifices obtain the entire fruit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Because he causes all beings to transcend [suffering], it is called a festival (utsava); those mortals who assist in the festival rites of the God [attain great merit].
Through their actions, thoughts, and speech, they too obtain abundant fruit;
whether in a village, a town, or even a city, there shall be a great festival.
Wherever Viṣṇu’s prosperity prevails, there indeed are all blessings;
in whatever region, district, or kingdom there is a festival of Hari.
Therein, there is no fear of untimely death, nor the occurrence of drought;
there is no harm from thieves and the like, nor any encounter with the threefold suffering.
In the Kali age, Dharma shall exist with four feet; therein, it will be as if the first age [Kṛta] had arrived.
The king will be righteous, and the subjects will be devoted to Dharma.
All become happy and free from all suffering when that which is given to those who seek it during a great festival.
Whether it be water, food, or clothing, that [gift] becomes a thousandfold;
likewise, worship with flowers, roots, fruits, and ornaments for the God [yields great merit].
When performed according to one's ability, it leads to eternal infinity; those who serve the God there day and night without weariness [attain this].
Even the gods together with the asuras are not able to describe the fruit of merit for those who perform anointing, sweeping, and likewise the settling of dust. (BhS 35.397)
Those who perform the raising of lamps with water, as well as the acts of shouting and clapping their hands,
go to the world of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the immortals to attain.
Those Brahmins who carry the vehicle go to the station of Brahmā;
and those horses that draw the chariot, they too go to the abode of the gods.
Furthermore, those men who carry the parasol and other insignia rejoice in heaven,
as do the teachers, the worshippers, and likewise the attendants.
Those people who recite there the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas obtain, during the festival of Viṣṇu, whatever they desire.
Free from desire, they abide by the side of the god in the supreme sky;
[this state] brings peace to all and is the highest destroyer of all suffering.
The great propitiation of Vāsudeva brings happiness to the king and his kingdom, increases longevity and health, and is a source of welfare for all subjects.
Having performed this supreme festival of Viṣṇu, all these beings, beginning with the gods,
attain the eternal state that is exceedingly difficult to reach.
Now I shall specifically describe the fruit arising from the great ablution (mahāsnapana),
by which substance one who bathes the Lord of Gods with devotion [obtains that fruit].
That wealth will increase for him, while his inauspicious things shall surely perish;
that wealth of the king and the kingdom will indeed come to full prosperity.
The inauspicious perishes and the auspicious arise for him who constructs a water-shed for the sake of the purification of the divine Viṣṇu.
For him, a house is constructed in heaven by the inhabitants of heaven;
through the bathing with clay, the earth becomes endowed with all kinds of crops.
By the mere circumambulation of a mountain, stability for one's lineage is attained;
by bathing Viṣṇu with grains, an increase in grain is obtained.
From worshipping Viṣṇu with sprouts, there will be an increase in progeny;
from worshipping him with auspicious objects, all auspicious things indeed come to pass.
By bathing [an image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one completely destroys all evil;
by bathing it with ghee, one obtains a fruit greater than that arising from the study of the Sāma Veda.
One should bathe Viṣṇu with milk and go to cows that yield milk;
one should bathe Viṣṇu with honey, and one's speech shall flow like honey.
One should bathe the God with curd; his fame shall become stainless.
From bathing Viṣṇu with scented water, one shall be surrounded by all prosperity.
By bathing [the deity] with unbroken grains (akṣata), one's progeny shall remain unbroken;
by bathing with water and fruit, however, one shall obtain auspicious fruits.
By bathing [the image] with water infused with kuśa grass, one shall attain the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa);
by bathing it with water containing jewels, one shall increase [the power of] gems, jewels, and the like.
By bathing with water that has been consecrated by recitation, one obtains the fruit of all recitations;
likewise, all medicinal herbs become effective through immersion in water consecrated by all medicinal herbs.
By worshipping with meritorious flowers alone, a man becomes possessed of merit;
by offering powders such as *śrīveṣṭaka* and the like, there is an increase in lifespan.
Through anointment with medicinal decoctions and powders, a healthy luster is attained;
and by bathing in the waters of sacred fords, the fruit of pilgrimage is obtained.
Through contact with forest herbs, there shall be constant freedom from disease;
by bathing with turmeric powder, Acyuta becomes pleased.
Through cleansing with all kinds of perfumes, prosperity becomes unshakable;
through cleansing with root-fragrances, one's lineage shall perpetually flourish.
Furthermore, by adorning [the image] with minerals, there will be an increase in mineral wealth;
or by other substances not mentioned, which are used for the rite of bathing.
He who should attend upon the Source of the World obtains an extensive reward;
he who should construct a water-tank and a bathing-seat for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow [attains the same].
He shall be honored by all and shall dwell in the exceedingly exalted seat (pīṭha);
thus, that man who performs the ritual bathing of Viṣṇu according to his ability [attains this].
Having enjoyed for a very long time on earth the fruits obtained here as described,
one finally ascends a golden celestial chariot, surrounded by gods.
Delighted by the dances and songs of the *kinnaras* and *apsarases*,
surrounded by *yakṣas* and *gandharvas*, he was honored with joy.
He who is devoted to the bathing ceremony of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, shall attain the world of Vaikuṇṭha, which is more meritorious than all other worlds.
He too shall serve [the deity] and be liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
And whoever should cause a festival to be held for the Lord of Gods at the conclusion of the ritual bathing, [he likewise attains liberation].
He who especially observes the festival attains an increase in progeny and abundant prosperity;
he too shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice.
Whoever bathes the Lord, the Master of Gods, on the five days of Viṣṇu,
shall possess great prosperity, including cattle, sons, and other such blessings.
Likewise, during eclipses, at the equinoxes, and indeed at the solstices and other such occasions,
as well as on other meritorious days, one should worship the Lord of the World.
Whoever bathes [there] and serves [it] obtains that same fruit;
likewise, he who constructs a Vaiṣṇava temple, endowed with devotion and faith, attains that very result.
If a temple is broken, cracked, or defiled by plasterers and the like,
one who restores it again goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
If one whose image has been stolen by thieves should have another image made and install it with devotion, he goes to the supreme goal. (BhS 35.433)
If the image falls due to negligence, or cracks, or becomes defiled,
he who repairs it and joyfully performs the consecration once again as before [attains merit].
The Lord of Gods will be pleased with him and will grant his desired boon,
especially when his ornaments and other such things have become worn out, decayed, or broken.
The sin of one who,
having observed that vehicles such as chariot parts have indeed become worn out, restores them and offers them [to the deity], is utterly destroyed.
If a person, having made [the recipients] equal, should give those [gifts] with devotion,
or should take them away, the sin committed by that person’s body perishes at that very moment.
But he who, seeing the image of Hari falling, does not honor it with gifts of wealth out of disrespect, for him there are no worlds of the Slayer of Madhu.
He who provides a suitable livelihood for those who are sinking, deprived of their means of subsistence, and seeking refuge at the feet of the Lord, does not approach Yama.
But for one who, endowed with devotion, causes festivals for the gods and other such rites to be performed—
even if they have mostly fallen into disuse— the fruit for him shall be infinite.
O best of beings, the ministers who are the servants of Yama do not [seize] that virtuous person who restores neglected duties in the temple of the deity, for he has already accomplished his purpose.
He who would sacrifice his excellent body for the sake of the gods or for the sake of a Brahmin shall dwell in heaven for fourteen Indras.
He who renounces his entire property for the sake of the gods or for the sake of a Brahmin—
of him the Lord of Gods is pleased, and he attains sovereignty over heaven.
Having seen the causes for expiation arise within his own abode, he who, endowed with faith, approaches the God; ||| BhS_35.444 ||
The Lord of Gods is pleased with him; being delighted, he becomes gracious.
Indeed, all expiations without exception are for the destruction of the flood of sins.
These were taught in a former age by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; indeed, the Guru has now set them in motion without delay for the sake of favoring the world.
Seeing the extremely defiled mental states of men who were despondent,
he who seeks the welfare of the worlds proclaimed the rules for expiation.
No one should fail to perform every action prescribed by the scriptures in its proper sequence;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the rite of expiation.
But he who, having performed the expiation, performs the prescribed rite, shall obtain double the merit; this is considered to be its proper observance.

He who, endowed with devotion and faith, performs or causes to be performed, in due order, the virtuous rites for the Lord of Gods, beginning from the installation and ending with the expiation; ||| BhS_35.450 |||
Even the gods of the thirty-three heavens are unable to describe the fruit of his merit;
having experienced all desires here in this world with happiness for a long time, [he shall attain liberation].
At the end of the body, he immediately becomes one who bears the conch, discus, and mace;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, four-armed, with a dark-complexioned and very beautiful form.
Mounted upon Garuḍa in the sky and honored by all the gods,
he pierced the orb of the sun and entered the orb of the moon.
Then, having descended, he [beheld] all the worlds in their proper order,
situated in truth and within the realm of truth— the origin and dissolution of the world.
Likewise, it is devoid of all particularity, eternally blissful, stainless,
comparable to the tasting of the essence of nectar, and bestowing eternal satisfaction.
One shall enter that supreme, eternal light; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall explain specifically what the fruit is when ritual action is omitted.
But that wise man who, having formed the intention to create an ālaya, is later awakened by another, turns away from that object.
Both of them, after passing away, shall become partakers of suffering in hell:
the doer, the one who causes it to be done, the instigator, and the one who approves.
They say that both good and evil deeds share equally in the fruit;
with the desire to create the abode of the Lord who is the enemy of Madhu, they have built this temple.
But for one who turns back by himself— especially after having resolved to build a temple for the deity— a great calamity shall befall him.
One should choose an ācārya; if one does not, one's purpose perishes.
The ācārya is the constant protector, and the ācārya is remembered as the father.
He who thinks that the Teacher [is responsible] for everything is thinking of the construction of the world's abode by the Lord, the Master of the universe.
But that fool who, out of greed, turns back without having completed [the task],
will suffer the ruin of his prosperity, and the Imperishable One becomes angry with him.
When the consecration has begun, whoever creates an obstacle for any reason whatsoever, his merit shall perish.
If one kills that by which an obstacle would arise, one incurs no fault;
likewise for one who seeks the goal and performs the action prescribed by the scriptures. (BhS 35.465)
A fool would dispute with an artisan, yet there is no fruit for him anywhere; he who disputes against the teacher who seeks his welfare by transgressing the scriptures.
In that case, there would be many inauspicious results; of this there is no doubt—especially when a sacrifice is being performed with the materials prescribed by the scriptures. (BhS 35.467)
He who would not give is a most sinful person and shall not obtain the fruit born of his actions;
likewise, he who, having installed an image of Hari, does not honor the guru.
Furthermore, he shall not obtain even the slightest fruit from those who seek other ritual objects;
rather, he should worship constantly and without interruption at the conclusion of the consecration.
If the sacrificer does not choose an officiating priest, he perishes;
likewise, he must choose an officiating priest, a preceptor, and others who seek their respective positions.
He who, having fixed a time limit, should employ [others] in ritual acts,
would indeed become a slayer of a Brahmin, and his wealth shall perish.
If the patron should perish, the temple residence will go to ruin unless he provides maintenance for the one who performs the worship.
If one who has been removed from his own position should appoint himself as the preceptor or the priest,
or if another person should be appointed there instead, both of them will perish.
Even in the most dire of calamities, one should never under any circumstances appoint another as an officiant,
solely because of a previous dismissal.
For those noble-minded individuals who are born in the lineage of the original worshipper, they are all entitled to perform the ritual worship in due order. (BhS 35.475)
The worship of a deity is inherently an ancestral inheritance;
therefore, if the performance of worship is carried out by others while excluding those born of that [deity's] own lineage, [it is improper].
The killing of a Brahmin shall befall him, and his worship shall become fruitless, he who gives wealth to the priest solely for the sake of a salary. (BhS 35.477)
Nor does Hari take pleasure in any other unstable object;
yet he who, out of greed, delusion, or ignorance, seizes wealth from the one-eyed man [the poor]. (BhS 35.478)
Likewise, if a foolish-minded sacrificer should give only half the wages,
both he and the [artisan] go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
He who, for the sake of wealth, worships Hari even while observing a fixed limit [of time] is known as a *vaidehalaka*,
excluded from all ritual acts.
Without first giving land for the purpose of worship to the worshipper, the patron instead creates a Brāhmaṇa who is a *devalaka*. (BhS 35.481)
For no sin whatsoever committed against a brahmin results in a fruit comparable to that of constructing a temple for the gods.
Having incurred the state of being a slayer of a Brahmin, he perishes without a doubt;
so too does the one who seizes or causes the seizure of land that has been given by a ruler of the Danus.
Among those other servants of his, he who is deluded and shrouded in darkness is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa and dragged from all sides.
Afflicted by suffering, he is born again in hell and among the animal wombs—
he who seizes land given by himself or granted by another.
For sixty thousand years, one is born as a worm in excrement;
protecting what was given by another yields twice the merit of what was given by oneself.
By seizing what was given by another, one's own gift becomes fruitless;
land taken by unjust means is likewise lost through unjust means.
The fire of one who steals, even of a thief, burns the family up to the seventh generation;
one kills five by lying about a maiden, and one kills ten by lying about a cow.

One kills a hundred horses by speaking falsely regarding a horse; one kills a thousand men by speaking falsely regarding a man; and by speaking falsely regarding gold, one kills both those born and those yet unborn. (BhS 35.489)
Falsehood destroys everything regarding one's land; therefore, one should never speak a lie.
[For there are those] dwelling in the parched, hollow trees of the waterless forests of the Vindhya mountains.
Those who seize the property of the gods or of Brahmins are reborn as black serpents;
[this is expiated] by a thousand tanks and a hundred horse-sacrifices.
A usurper of land is not purified even by the gift of ten million cows;
the same applies to the property of a Brahmin, the killing of a Brahmin, and whatever wealth belongs to a poor man.
One would cause even one's teacher, friend, or wealth to fall from heaven;
therefore, one should not set one's mind upon the property of a Brahmin, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Those burnt by fire sprout again, but one burnt by Brahman does not grow.
They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison.

Poison kills only the one who consumes it alone, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons; the property of a Brahmin, when consumed out of friendship, burns the family unto the seventh generation.
By means of *vikrama*, however, a man may digest ten ancestors and ten descendants of those who consume it,
as well as iron filings, various powders, or even poison.
What man in the three worlds could ever digest the property of a Brahmin?
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brahmin [is lost].
On account of that evil, in the next world he lives on the leftovers of vultures,
due to the destruction of the property of the gods and the theft of the property of Brahmins.
Families fall into a state of non-nobility by the neglect of Brahmins;
a single cow is equal to a thousand [other gifts], and a bull is equal to ten cows.
A vehicle is equal to ten oxen; a horse is equal to ten vehicles;
a maiden is equal to ten horses; and she is equal to the gift of land.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years;
both the one who seizes it and the one who consents to its seizure shall dwell in hell for that same duration.
When a field is seized, it destroys the family up to the seventh generation, as the Brahmins weep, shedding tears while wretched and despairing.
Having seized land from the virtuous, one finds no land anywhere;
for by giving land to the virtuous, one obtains the most excellent land.
Because he is the one who makes the vow for the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World,
that virtuous Brāhmaṇa is declared to be a god and a great being.
Therefore, a wise person should not have any suspicion regarding the livelihood offered to that [deity];
nor should one seize or even covet land offered by its worshiper.
What more need be said? There can be no atonement for him; the destiny of that evil-minded one cannot even be described in words.
That person of evil deeds dies immediately and is born again and again; no refuge whatsoever can be found for him.
One should act according to the will of the Lord and never seize the property of a Brahmin;
those who enjoy temples, pavilions, and other such structures belong to the Enemy of Kaiṭabha.
Those of deluded minds, having passed away, dwell in the hells without respite;
they are surely reborn again and again in low births.
That evil-minded man who steals ornaments, umbrellas, garments, and so forth,
is dragged into the hells with his neck bound by nooses.
Those who, out of delusion, seize the mounts and vehicles belonging to Vaiṣṇavas dwell for a long time within the belly of the Maṅgāra hell.
After passing away, they are born yet again in the wombs of donkeys, camels, and the like;
so too are substances such as sandalwood and fragrant flowers [reborn in lower states]. (BhS 35.512)
Do they go to their own realms of Viṣṇu, or do they undergo the torments of Yama?
Having experienced those, they are born again and again as musk-rats.
Those who take away sandals, shoes, seats, or vehicles,
having dwelt in the hells, are born into the family of serpents.
Those who, having seized wealth such as cattle, land, gold, and clothing— which is the property of Viṣṇu—
enjoy it for themselves, fall into hells that are difficult to escape.
Having dwelt there, those who have seized the property of gods or Brahmins are born again even after death in the wombs of dogs and other such creatures,
as well as in all the hells.
Those of deluded intellect undergo torments in the hells of Yama,
such as the breaking and cutting of an image of Vāsudeva.
Those of evil mind who strive in such things as sexual dalliance and the like go,
in due course, to all the most dreadful hells.
Even for other transgressions, whether gross or subtle,
men who have committed them are cooked in hell after death, partaking of suffering.
Now, regarding the daily worship of the Lord of Gods, especially when there is a deficiency in the ritual services and so forth, this shall be the fruit of that sin.
If the seat is lacking, there will be the destruction of Dharma;
if there is no welcome, there will be loss of intelligence; and if there is no inference [of the guest's needs], there will be muteness.
If the sandals are lacking, lameness will surely arise;
if the water for the feet is lacking, there will be great disease as well as suffering.
By neglecting the cleansing of the teeth, one is born with diseased teeth;
by neglecting betel, one suffers enmity; and by neglecting oil, one suffers leprosy.
If the cleansing of the hair is deficient, a disease of the throat will arise;
and likewise if the bathing substances are lacking, or if the bath itself is omitted.
Consumption (rājayakṣmā) shall be the disease for one who is most sinful and very cruel;
wind-disease (vātaroga) occurs for one lacking a head-cloth, and dropsy (jalodara) for one lacking a garment. BhS 35.525.
If one is deprived of an upper garment, there is heart disease; if deprived of the sacrificial thread, fear of being burned by fire and weak digestion arise.
If it lacks fragrance, there will be leprosy; if it lacks ornaments, there is great fear;
if it lacks flowers, there will be loss as well as the arising of phlegm.
Worship with flowers brought by a Śūdra, or purchased by purchase—even if they come from a forest, a house, or bought from a marketplace—is fruitless. (BhS 35.528)
Flowers that have not been requested, even if they are obtained and suitable, are not fit for worship;
likewise, those that are stale or defiled by insects.
Worship performed with faded flowers, those touched by the untouchable, those that are foul-smelling, those trodden upon by feet, or those gathered from outcaste dwellings, shall be fruitless.
A flower gathered by oneself is said to be the best; one from the forest is middling;
one purchased is inferior; and that which belongs to another is the lowest of the low.
Some say that one should not offer a flower brought by hand, brought on a cloth, one that has fallen of its own accord, or one grown in another's garden. (BhS 35.532)
On Sundays and Fridays, on the anniversaries of the Manus, and on the anniversaries of the Yugas,
one should not take a *tulasī* leaf after midday.
Those who pluck Tulasī on the day of the sun’s transit, at the end of the fortnights, on the twelfth lunar days, at night, or during the two twilights, they cut off the head of Hari.
One should not pluck a tulasī leaf on the days of the sun or Mars, on the twelfth lunar day, on the five parvan days, on the Nandā tithis, or when the moon is in the Śravaṇa nakṣatra.
One should not accept food that is infested with hair or insects, discarded, decayed, or stale; nor should one take what has wilted leaves or is tainted by worms.
One should avoid anything scented by a spider if it appears beautiful;
one should not pluck a flower grown on land, but one may cut one grown in water.
One should never worship the Lord with prohibited things that cause suffering;
one should not worship the Lord with dry flowers, nor with those fallen upon the ground.
One should avoid flowers that are withered, those remaining from previous offerings, those that are unwholesome, those that do not bloom, and those that have a putrid or foul odor.
But those twice-born ones who take flowers after having performed their ablutions—
the deities do not accept them, nor do human beings accept them.
The ancestors do not accept that; it turns to ashes like wood.
Having performed one's midday bath, however, one should not gather flowers.
Enraged by them, Viṣṇu bestows inexhaustible suffering upon them because of that anger;
whereas he who worships the Lord Hari with offerings intended for other deities [receives a different fate].
But by that very same sin, that man is born as a frog;
thereafter, he goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
The man who smells the fragrance of flowers or offerings intended for the deities will be born with a foul odor and as one afflicted by leprosy.
Indeed, for two births, the deluded man falls into the state of a Śūdra,
like a flower not strung on a thread or rice unmixed with oil.
All the water, even if it were ten million *avālukas* in volume, would become stale;
through offerings made with these, all ritual actions immediately become fruitless.
If the mirror is lacking, there will be cataracts;
if the incense is lacking, deafness; and if the lamp is lacking, one will fall into blindness. (BhS 35.547)
If the *arghya* offering is omitted for the deity, his lineage becomes censured;
and if the *madhuparka* is omitted, he will suffer from diabetes mellitus.
If the offering of the *mātrā* is omitted, there will be total destruction;
if the protective rite (*rakṣā*) and the lustration (*nīrājana*) are omitted, there will be an obstruction by the *rāṅgasas*.
If the study of the Vedas is neglected, the performance of rituals will certainly cease;
if the offering of oblations is neglected, famine will certainly occur. (BhS 35.550)
If the condiment is lacking, there will be poverty for the village dwellers;
likewise, if the coconut fruit is deficient, or if the milk and other ingredients are deficient, [the same result follows].
O Lord, when various kinds of food and drink as well as the sacrificial oblation are deficient, there will certainly be the destruction of all crops and a famine. (BhS 35.552)
For the sacrificer of that village, there will especially be misfortune;
here, when the sequence of application is deficient, even worship itself perishes.
If the curtain is removed at the improper time, the performer himself perishes;
if the worship of the door is omitted, thieves and others will enter.
If the worship of the gatekeepers is deficient, there will be calamities such as theft and the like;
likewise, if the worship of Śānti and the [other] Ever-present Ones is deficient.
There will undoubtedly be the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and everyone else;
even for the sacrificer, there will be affliction from foreign kings and other such calamities.
Furthermore, there will likewise be affliction from evil diseases and the like, and there will be great loss caused by snakes, scorpions, spiders, and so forth. (BhS 35.557)
If the offering of flowers is neglected, deficient, or devoid of mantras,
there will be hostility toward the king among those living in that village.
Either beside or especially to the south of the Bhūta-pīṭha,
[one should perform the rite] from the Bhūtas down to the Nāgas, provided it is free from offerings and worship.

All the planetary spirits, such as the Śākinīs and others, will undoubtedly enter [the practitioner] if the worship of the Illustrious Goddess is neglected; furthermore, there will be a loss of prosperity.
If the worship of Hariṇī is omitted, the site will be destroyed;
likewise if the fire-worship is neglected, deficient, or devoid of mantra.
If the offering of food or the clarified butter is deficient, there may arise a confusion of castes,
the loss of the system of castes and stages of life, and calamity shall befall the Brahmins.
If the god is deprived of drinking water, there will be drought;
if he is deprived of mouth-perfume, however, there will be hatred from the people.
If the offering materials are lacking, if [the rite] is deficient, or if it is devoid of mantras,
there will be a loss of strength for people and a downfall for the ancestors.
If one is devoid of a handful of flowers, royal wrath will arise;
if one is devoid of prostration and praise, death will occur instantly.
If meditation is lacking, it destroys one's family; if the ritual deposit (nyāsa) is lacking, misfortune shall arise;
but if breath control (prāṇāyāma) is lacking, there will be fear of enemy armies.
If one is devoid of purity and proper conduct, there is the destruction of cattle, children, and so forth;
if one is devoid of the installation of the image, his wife perishes.
If one fails to perform the circumambulation, that man becomes a sinner;
therefore, at the conclusion of the daily worship, it is for the pleasure of both the worshipper and the preceptor.
But if it is devoid of the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), that worship shall be fruitless;
there will be fear for the kingdom, for the patron, and even for the king. (BhS 35.569)
But if [the rite] is deficient, in the act of giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) by the cooks and others,
the loss of cattle and vehicles will occur for the people in that village.
If the morning worship is omitted, there shall be drought in that village;
the ritual activities of the Brahmins will decline, and all their undertakings will come to naught.
If the midday worship is omitted, there will be turmoil in the kingdom;
if the evening worship is omitted, it will affect that village and the patron.
There will be loss of wealth and loss of subjects, without a doubt;
when the twilight worship is neglected, there will be a failure of ritual action.
If the five-day festival of Viṣṇu is deficient in bathing and worship,
or especially if it lacks a festival, fear will come upon the patron.
If the monthly worship is neglected, there will be hatred toward one's brother;
likewise when the solstices are neglected, as well as the rites prescribed therein.
There will be a loss of fame for the village and for the patron;
likewise, on another day mentioned for the ritual bathing, if the bathing is omitted.
Furthermore, if [the festival] is performed at the wrong time, there will likewise be fear of emaciation;
and if it is devoid of constant festivities, the people will become joyless.
If another substance for worship is lacking, a fault will arise;
however, if the prescribed occasion has arrived, one should not fail to bathe Mādhava.
Indeed, no one at all is able to describe the fruit of his evil deeds;
there will certainly be a great calamity everywhere for both the king and the kingdom.
If the water-shed is deficient, there will be the destruction of the house; if the decoration is deficient, there will be loss;
and if the clay is deficient, there will be the destruction of the crops—of this there is no doubt.
When the mountains have perished, his stability is lost;
likewise, when the grains have perished, there occurs the destruction of the harvest.
If there is an absence of sprouts, a loss of progeny will occur;
furthermore, when auspicious rites are deficient, misfortune shall befall him.
If the five products of the cow are omitted, one incurs the sin of killing a cow;
if clarified butter is omitted, there is loss of intellect; and if milk is omitted, it results in a short life.
If honey is lacking, there is a great disease; if curd is lacking, there is a fever;
and if milk is lacking, his fame indeed becomes tarnished. (BhS 35.584)
If it is devoid of scented water, a foul odor arises intensely;
if it is devoid of unbroken rice and water, injury befalls him.
If it is devoid of fruit and water, his life is fruitless;
and if it is devoid of kusha grass and water, his spiritual luster shall not increase.
When the water containing jewels is lacking, there will be the destruction of wealth and grain;
and in the absence of medicinal herbs, there will be the affliction of disease.
If one is devoid of the preliminary bath, the family becomes defiled;
if there is an absence of warm water, the body shall become hot with fever.
If one is devoid of meritorious flowers, that person is born as a wicked man;
furthermore, in the absence of powdered nutmeg and other such substances, misfortune shall arise.
If the powder is deficient in astringent decoctions, a person will be devoid of luster;
if forest herbs are unavailable, it is certain that one will become ill. (BhS 35.590)
If it is deficient in turmeric powder, the man becomes bereft of fortune;
if it is devoid of the root-fragrance, old age certainly ensues.
Even when there is an absence of the elements, a man is born with the elements;
he is deprived of mats, garments, upper robes, and ornaments.
The destruction of one's merit certainly occurs; Lord Ramāpati is not pleased with the teacher, the officiating priests, and likewise with others who seek such positions.
If the offering of the sacrificial fee is deficient, there will be total ruin;
if the oblation for the deity is deficient, the ritual bathing will be fruitless.

The Lord is not pleased when the festival at the conclusion of the ritual bathing is omitted; nor is He pleased by a man who, having seen or heard that the temple of the Blessed One is dilapidated, [fails to repair it].
If those rites are omitted, he will certainly become a hater of the gods;
so too shall all the inhabitants of that village, as well as the king and another wealthy man.
Having quickly leveled everything, one should perform it again as before;
otherwise, if one should act differently, the king's kingdom will perish.
A person should recognize this bridge of Dharma as common to all;
it must always be protected, for within it lies the stability of the worlds.
But when the occasion for expiation has arisen, he who is dull-witted and performs or causes another to perform a subsequent rite without having first performed the atonement— BhS 35.599.
Out of greed, delusion, or ignorance, and by disregarding the teaching,
that person who acts in hostility toward the Blessed One’s instruction shall become a sinner.
Since a lapse is inevitable for heedless human beings, the ancients prescribed a means of atonement; therefore, one should never transgress even slightly.
Even by the gods beginning with Brahmā, the worship of Hari is difficult to accomplish;
yet the expiation prescribed by the ancients for that [negligence] shall never fail to reach its goal.
If one performs the obligatory, occasional, or optional rites without having first performed the appropriate expiation for a transgression,
that [performance] shall be as if it were not done at all.
Therefore, when the occasion arises, one should immediately perform the expiation;
thus has been briefly declared the fruit based upon the yoga of action.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter: On Transgressions.
Likewise, thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu have been proclaimed;
among them, traveling to the house of the Blessed One by means of vehicles or even on sandals.
Not attending festivals and other celebrations for the gods, not bowing down before them, bowing with only one hand, and circumambulating them [in the wrong direction]—these are [faults]. (BhS 36.2)

Prostrating before the Blessed One while one is impure from eating remnants, stretching out one's feet in his presence, or sitting in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) likewise [constitute offenses]. BhS 36.3.
Sleeping, eating, idle chatter, speaking loudly, vain talk, weeping and the like, and quarreling; // BhS_36.4 //
Repression and indulgence toward women, speaking with intentional innuendo, uttering vulgar speech, and even the emission of downward wind [flatus]. BhS 36.5.

Covering oneself with a blanket, censuring what is excellent, praising others, using figurative expressions when one has the capacity [to speak directly], and eating food that has not been offered. BhS 36.6.
Not offering fruits and other items that have grown in their respective seasons;
and giving away what remains after it has been assigned for use as condiments and the like.
Turning one's back on one's own seat, saluting others, remaining silent toward the guru, praising oneself, and likewise disparaging the deities; BhS_36.8 //
One should avoid such various kinds of misconduct; for there exist endless other forms of misconduct arising from negligence.
“‘Forgive me’—this very request is a faultless atonement that brings no harm;
otherwise, if one acts [wrongly] either through negligence or through intentional knowledge,” BhS 36.10.
He goes to the terrible hells, which are constantly and exceedingly dreadful,
which cause one's heart to break at the mere thought of them.
There are thirty-two hells;
indeed, those thirty-two hells are proclaimed by the teachers of Brahman:
Raurava, Dhvānta, Śīta, Uṣṇa, Tāpa, Ambuja, and Mahāmbuja.
Kālasūtra is indeed the eighth; these are renowned as the hells:
Sūcyagra, Kālakhaḍga, Kṣuradhārā, and Cabarīṣaka.
Some say that in the eight hells there are the great burning of heated coals and intense heat; they are terrifying, filled with loud noises, and fearsome.
The [hells] of Lakṣāpralepa, Māṃsāda, Nirucchvāsa, and Socchvāsa;
and those of Yugma, Adri, Śālmalī, Loha, Pradīpa, Kṣudh, and Pipāsā.
A mass of worms and kings are also proclaimed [as its features],
as well as an iron pillar, excrement and urine, and likewise the Vaitaraṇī river.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, Raurava,
Mahāpadānugāmin, and the one called Rājarājeśvara.
In the thirty-three compartments, half is made of earth and half is made of iron;
in their midst are the terrible hells, situated mostly in darkness.
There are twenty-eight crores of these various divisions of hells;
he is established as the lord of these terrible hells.
Renowned as Kūśmāṇḍa, possessing the brilliance of the sun at the time of universal dissolution,
he has a terrifying face, is filled with rage, and has round, hollow eyes.
Surrounded by many such beings with hammers in their hands,
these wicked men are cooked within them according to their own karma.
Those who have abandoned the rites of atonement, who are arrogant and turned away from their own duty, undergo various tortures until the exhaustion of their sins.
Thieves who delight in the dharma of others fall into the fires of hell;
those who have committed the great sins remain in the fires of hell for an eon.

For a manvantara, those mortals who are great sinners— those who steal the property of the gods or of Brahmins— and those who commit secondary sins against the gods, the gods of gods, or the sacrificial fires [suffer].
Those who revile the twice-born, cows, gurus, and the Dharma spend a day of Brahmā as mortals;
others, the lowest of men, spend half of that period.
Those wicked ones who are devoid of dharma and addicted to gambling, women, and sensual pleasures, remain in the terrible hell in accordance with their own sins.
Those lowest of men who are fools and do not listen to the weightiness of the Dharma spoken by the virtuous fall into those terrible hells.
"And they say that even what is beyond the senses was seen by them and reported back;
likewise, those overcome by lust and greed act like cats in their conduct."
Those who are most wicked, devoid of virtuous action, devoted solely to the tongue and the genitals, intent on censuring ascetics, and defilers of sacred fields, holy fords, and the like.
Bound by their sins, those mortals fall into them helplessly;
having experienced here the lifespan ordained for mortals by the Self-Existent One.
Having encountered some sign, they are liberated from their bodies;
yet they obtain again a divine state of torment born of their own karma.
Endowed with qualities corresponding to those [past actions], it bestows the experience of pleasure and pain;
thus the wicked are cooked in the fires of hell until their evil karma is exhausted.
Just as metals are blown in a fire until they are reduced to dross by the application of *āmalaka*,
so too are all beings— however many there may be— in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, everywhere.
There are exactly as many terrible fires of hell below;
twenty-eight crores of hells are said to exist beneath the earth.
Beneath the seventh level, situated in a terrible darkness,
is the first abyss called Ghora, which is located at the base of the Ghoratala.
Atighorā, Mahāghorā, and Ghoraghorā as the fifth;
the sixth is named Taralatārā, and the seventh is Bhayāvahā.
The eighth is Kālarātrī, and the ninth is Bhayotkaṭā;
the tenth is Tadadhaścaṇḍā, and below that even further is Mahācaṇḍā.
Another is Caṇḍakolāhalā, and another is Pracaṇḍā, presiding over the hells;
there is Padmā, Padmavatī, Bhīmā, and Bhīmabhīṣaṇanāyakā.
Karālā, Vikarālā, Vajrā, and Viṃśatikā are remembered;
[the shapes] are triangular, pentagonal, very long, and perfectly circular.
The seventh is Saptabhūmā and the eighth is Dīptāyāmā; thus these ten million terrible hells have been declared by name.
These are indeed twenty-eight hells, consisting of the torments of the wicked;
they should be understood in sequence as having five leaders each.
Learn now their names individually for all these millions:
Raurava is the first among them, where embodied beings wail.
Mahāraurava is where even the great ones weep;
Tamaḥ, Śīta, and Uṣṇa—these five are remembered as the primary [hells].
Sughora, Asrutapastīkṣṇa, Padmasaṃjīvana, Śata, Mahāmāṃsa, Viloma, Subhīma, and Kaṭaṅkaṭa.
Tīvraveṣī, Karāla, Vikarāla, Prakampana,
Mahāpadma, Supadma, Kālavaktra, and Garjana.
Sūcīmukha, Sunemi, Khādaka, Suprapīḍana,
Kuṃbhīpāka, Supāka, and the exceedingly dreadful Cakraka.
There is a forest of burning heaps of coals, as well as rivers of blood and pus;
and there is the Great Saṃvartaka bird with a sharp iron beak. BhS 36.47.
The intensely heated lotus, the excellent destroyer, the putrid flesh,
the molten tin, the inhalation, the breathless, the very long, and the deceptive śālmalī tree.
They were terrifying, possessing great roar and power, and of excellent manifestation;
O Śalya, they had the faces of bears, rams, wolves, lions, tigers, and elephants.
They have the faces of dogs, pigs, kings, buffaloes, donkeys, rams, and horses;
they have the mouths of planetary spirits, crocodiles, and sea-monsters; and they have the faces of snakes, tortoises, and crows.
Kṛdhra, ulūka, jalūkā, śārdūla, kapin,
karkaṭa, gandhaka, pūtivaktra, raktākṣa, and pūtimṛttika.
There is smoke from grain-husks, fire from chaff, and likewise heaps of worms;
there is filth that cannot be remedied, and the consumption of blood and food.
Lālābhakṣa, Abhakṣa, the fierce Sarvabhakṣa,
Jaṅkaṭa, Suvilāsa, Vikaṭa, and Kaṭapūtana.
Ambarīṣa, Kaṭāha, the agonizing Vaitaraṇī river,
the bed of intensely heated iron, and the Ekapāda-taptaka.
The terrible Asitālavana forest, where bones are crushed and broken;
the Tilā, Atasī, and Kṣu mills; and the torment of the kūṭapāśa.
The Great Baking Oven, the Small Baking Oven, the slab made of heated iron,
that which is called the Mountain with Razor Edges, and likewise the Mountain of Excrement.
They are cast into wells of urine and excrement, or into pits of caustic lye; they are subjected to the machine of the pestle and mortar, or crushed by slabs of stone and ploughshares.
The thicket of palm leaves and swords, the great pavilion of mosquitoes,
the deluder, the breaking of bones, the heat, the trident, and the iron ball.
It is full of much suffering, great suffering, defilement, impurity, and stain;
it is like deadly poison, formless yet appearing as beautiful form, and follows after darkness.
Ekapāda, Tripāda, Tīvravīci, and Rantima—
these twenty-eight are traditionally taught as five successive groups.
In successive order, there are five leaders for each of the ten million [beings]; and from Raurava onwards, there is one hundred [hells] of equal strength in every respect.
The mandala of the great hells consists of forty [hells] plus more;
therein, sinful men are cooked according to their respective karma.
Men are severely bound by their hands with a heated chain and subjected to various tortures until their karma is exhausted.
This [earth] is easily traversed by those who are not servants of Yama due to its great branches and boughs;
yet when shaken with extreme velocity, they go a yojana unconscious.
Then, for those situated in the intermediate space, a hundred loads of iron are bound to their feet by the mighty messengers of Yama.
Severely beaten by that great burden,
people remain silent and overwhelmed, recounting their own past deeds.
Then, those evildoers are struck by their terrible servants with heated iron rods, red-hot like fire and covered in thorns.
Then they are smeared all over repeatedly with blazing caustic, especially that of fire, and again with molten copper.
With their limbs wounded and mangled by the extremely smeared iron [wheel], they have their bodies reconstructed again, beginning from the head and proceeding in order down to the feet.
They are cooked like eggplants in a cauldron of boiling oil,
and likewise in a pit filled with excrement and in a mass of worms.
Are they thrown into a pond filled with fat, blood, and pus? Furthermore, they are devoured by fierce worms and by crows with iron beaks.
They are cooked like sacrificial porridge in heaps of blazing coals by dogs, gadflies, fierce wolves, and deformed tigers, as well as by men.
Men are impaled upon sharp spikes by their own sinful deeds,
and are then crushed by terrible mountain-presses produced by their own past actions.
In the hell called Cakraka, men are crushed like sesame seeds and are cooked in many ways within intensely heated iron vessels.
Furthermore, having repeatedly bound all their sense organs in cauldrons filled with oil that is intensely heated, they undergo torments through their evil deeds.
Terrible afflictions arise individually within the body as a result of that [sin];
for those who hear the censure of Hari, their ears are filled [with impurity].
Furthermore, [they are struck] with glowing iron spikes the color of fire, with molten copper and other metals,
with tin, lead, brass, bronze, and so forth, as well as with caustic lye and lac.
In the hells, the ears are gradually filled with well-heated sharp oil and adamantine paste, as well as other torments.
O Lord, those who have gone to the abode of the gods and arrived there for the sake of service undergo these torments by wandering through them all in succession.
Or else, elsewhere, those who are overcome by intoxication and delusion,
being greedy, go to the wives of others with longing eyes.
Those cruel-eyed men who knit their brows at the guru have their eyes pierced by needles glowing with the color of fire.
And by means of all [substances] such as caustic alkali in succession, all the tortures are experienced in the body by those fools who,
out of lust for touch, have sexual contact with the wives of others.
Their hands are pierced with needles glowing with the color of heated fire;
thereafter, their entire bodies are smeared with caustic substances and the like.
And they undergo agonies of great suffering in all the hells;
moreover, they violently cast others onto the blazing iron śālmali tree.
Furthermore, on their backs they are struck by fearsome and mighty beings with a powerful,
jagged, and extremely sharp saw.
Beginning with Śīla and others, those who commit adultery are slain by their own offspring through terrible deeds, each in the very form [of the offender].
A woman embraces tightly a blazing man made of iron;
she embraces that blazing man made of iron from a previous time.
Women of evil conduct embrace him tightly and say:
"Why do you run away so swiftly? Now you have no delusion left."
"Since you have transgressed against your husband, now experience that evil;
you shall be cast slowly, one by one, into a copper cauldron with its lid closed. (BhS 36.89)
They are cooked by a mild fire, like men by their own sins;
they are pounded with mortars and the like, and crushed upon slabs of stone.
They are cast into blind wells and bitten violently by bees;
their entire bodies are pierced by worms and shattered in hundreds of ways.
Immediately thereafter, those evildoers are cast into wells of extremely sharp razors,
and they are cooked on all sides in the hell of great flames.
Burning with its flames, they run hither and thither;
having been brought along on his back, his two shanks are placed together, joined and bound.
Having pulled them by the middle, he bound them all very firmly together with the ropes of sin, fastening them tightly against each other across the backs of their arms.
Fierce bees made of sharp iron bite this person who has formed a mass [of sin]:
those terrible ones that belong to the arrogant, the wrathful, and the thieves.
In the Mahājvāla hell of Yama,
the torments are said to consist of being bound into balls and having one's limbs encircled by straight cords and smeared with mud.
They are cooked like dried cow dung and die by that means,
as well as on stone slabs heated by the fire of their karma with extremely sharp alkaline water.
Due to the destruction of their non-virtue, the sinful are rubbed away like sandalwood;
for men are constantly [consumed] by worms within their bodies.
They are devoured intensely by creatures with fierce mouths until their bodies are utterly destroyed,
having been cast into heaps of putrid flesh amidst swarms of worms.
They remain with agitated hearts, tormented within the mountains;
their bodies are smeared with a highly heated adamantine paste.
With their faces turned downward and their feet upward, they are surrounded and tormented by fire,
as a well-heated iron ball is thrust deep into their mouths.
Those who, out of greed, plucked the flowers of a divine grove with their own hands, eat while dependent on others and are beaten with mallets.
Those of deluded minds smell [the foul odor] and even carry it upon their heads;
their heads are then pierced with fiercely heated iron spikes.
Then, by means of blazing alkaline substances, oil, copper, and so forth, in succession,
there are various most terrible torments of hell within the body.
The tongues of those who speak pleasant words that are untrue are torn out in many ways with a well-heated pair of tongs, while they are tormented from the feet up to the chest.
And the tongue of this speaker of false scriptures protrudes forth;
it is split apart by sharp plows as wide as half a *krośa*.
Those cruel ones who revile their mother, father, or teacher—
because of that, their mouths are torn open by diamond-venomous leeches.
Then it is again sprinkled with caustic alkali, copper, and tin;
its opening is excessively filled with molten and heated metals.
Those who revile the Great-Souled One, the Teacher and instructor of the Dharma, are bound by the servants of Yama as they run hither and thither once again.
And for those deluded ones who are devotees of Viṣṇu, as well as their eternal dharma here,
[it appears] upon their chest, throat, tongue, and the joints of their teeth.
Upon the palate, the lips, the nose, the head, and all the joints of the limbs,
there are iron spikes, glowing like fire, intensely heated, and three-pointed.
They are repeatedly placed upon these spots with hammers;
thereafter, they are [further] treated with heated caustic, copper, and tin.
They are filled on all sides with everything such as molten iron and the like,
and they undergo various and manifold tortures throughout their entire bodies.
Thus they wander again in succession through all the hells without exception—
those who seize the property of others and those who touch a Brahmin with their feet.
In some places, the limbs of divine implements and knowledge are depicted;
they are filled on all sides by the blows of hands and feet.
Furthermore, they are burned in succession by blazing substances such as alkaline liquids and copper;
moreover, in all the hells, there are various tortures of the body.
Many painful afflictions arising from the hands and feet occur for the worshiper who has offered [something] to the God of Gods or in His name. (BhS 36.117)
Furthermore, those who forcibly seize the livelihood of others who receive only half a foot-measure of grain are indeed cooked in the pits of hell by their own actions.
Those who frequent the courtyards of temples, groves, ponds, wells, and monasteries undergo further torments; they do not pass beyond the courtyard of Yama. (BhS 36.119)
The most wicked kings harass them and dwell there;
[they provide] exercise, rubbing with fragrant powders, oil massages, bathing, and the drinking and eating of food.
They engage in play, sexual intercourse, gambling, and impurities;
and they are tormented by various terrible machines, such as the sugarcane press and others.
They are cooked in the fires of hell as long as the moon and stars exist,
[or] somewhere within the precincts of a temple or a divine grove.
Those fools who discharge feces or even urine [inappropriately],
their penis along with the testicles is struck by iron hammers.
With needles that are as red-hot as fire and possessed of thorns,
they are impaled through the anus until the needles emerge from the crown of their heads.
Then, the anus and the penis of embodied beings are intensely filled with molten copper and tin of great corrosiveness.
Since it has been stated that the mind and all the sense-faculties are set in motion [by it],
therefore, through the suffering of the sense-faculties, that [mind] becomes intensely afflicted.
Those fools who neither give nor even approve of food and drink when it is not being given, and who, despite possessing wealth, do not bestow gifts due to craving; (BhS 36.127)
Those who, while in the householder stage of life, disregard a guest who has arrived at the proper time,
become deprived of splendor and are bound with their hands and feet unrestrained in battle.
With their limbs stretched out, men remain for a hundred years withering away,
pinned to their hands, feet, and foreheads by iron spikes.
It is eternally deformed and crooked, pierced by two stakes,
and infested with worms, fierce creatures, and iron-beaked crows.
The mouth is tormented within by various kinds of afflictions;
then the tongue is further pierced deeply with a heavy chain.
And they stand suspended, perfectly round like iron hammers;
then, having torn out their own flesh in pieces the size of sesame seeds, [they eat it].
Blood is given to them to drink with the point of a needle,
until they have repeatedly become fleshless over time in many ways.
Then that body is smeared with blazing caustic;
it is split apart by showers of rain and dried up again by the wind.
Furthermore, they are drenched on all sides with well-heated oil;
thus they are tormented by various kinds of horrific sufferings born of their own karma.
The most wicked do not die at all until their evil is exhausted;
therefore, one should not commit sin while life remains so fickle.
Thus, defiled and distinguished by their remaining karma,
embodied beings are born again upon reaching the earth.
Various stationary beings, cruel and distinguished as grasses, shrubs, and so forth,
having experienced sufferings there, are born among the wombs of insects.
Having emerged from insect births, they are born as birds in due course;
afflicted by their state as birds, they come to exist among the species of wild animals.
Having traversed the difficult path, they are born among the animal species;
gradually reaching the womb of a cow, they are then born again as humans.
Even by skipping through the stages, human birth is attained through the weight of merit;
then, having attained that state of humanity, one experiences various [consequences] according to their respective sins.
Consequently, living beings exist joined with the marks of evil;
therefore, having bathed, wearing the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, being self-restrained and tranquil in mind, one should approach the deity.
Undistracted by other tasks, he himself should personally take fruits and other offerings, as well as perfumes and flowers, according to his ability.
He by whom all these [offerings] were made, dedicating gold to Hari— let him properly propitiate the Teacher of the World with offerings and the like.
He is satisfied by leaves, flowers, or fruits offered according to one's ability,
and even by water that is easily obtained without effort.
One should go to the temple on foot alone, free from sloth;
whether one is incapable or capable, wealthy or poor.
He is considered equally authorized over the sovereignty of the Creator of the World;
for the moon does not withhold its moonlight even from the house of a caṇḍāla.
Nor do streams of plaster rain down upon the palaces of emperors;
their abode of enjoyment is but a single form, this wretched body.
The donor bestows grace upon him; for this, there is no rule regarding high or low status, as Viṣṇu is the supreme goal.
Here in this world, the deity is the one supreme light, the one Supreme Person alone.
That very same one is divided manifold in the world through his own illusory power;
he himself, known as Viṣṇu, having manifested his own illusory nature (māyā) as primordial matter (prakṛti), becomes twofold.
And abiding in three ways according to the distinction of the qualities such as sattva,
he is known by the names Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, and is traditionally held to be the performer of maintenance, creation, and dissolution.
His forms, beginning with Viṣṇu, should be understood as fourfold, distinguished by dharma, jñāna, and so forth; they are based upon the Vedas, the castes, and the ages.
Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha—
through the fivefold divisions of the Upaniṣads, he has attained the state of the great elements.
Through the six limbs consisting of the mind, the ears, and so forth, as well as the heart and other organs, this [Self],
which is eternally composed of six syllables, is differentiated by the sages.
This [Self], being divided sevenfold by means of the seven vyāhṛtis, the worlds, the meters, and likewise the sacrifices, is to be understood by the wise.
Through the eight primary natures and likewise through the eight forms,
he is eternally composed of the eight syllables and is divided eightfold.
Nārāyaṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha, and Vāmana, as well as Rāma, Brahmā, Indra, Sūrya, and Candra— by them no destruction of the established order occurs.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta— these are the ten.
Distinguished by the eleven sense organs, as well as by the twelve means of measurement,
he likewise exists in thirteen ways through the Viśvedevas and the others.
That Lord should be known as divided fourteenfold by the Manus beginning with Cākṣuṣa, and likewise divided fifteenfold by the lunar days (tithis). BhS_36.160.
Its expansion is to be understood as manifold: divided sixteenfold by the vowels, likewise by the directions, intermediate points, and corners, and by other forms.
One, two, three, four, five, six, and so forth— these varieties of faces are declared to belong to that Viśvātman, Hari, who faces in every direction.
Two and more arms are recorded as the various types of arms of Viśvataḥpāṇi;
they are long, adorned with various ornaments, and bear various weapons.
And his heads were described as having shimmering crowns and earrings;
their curly locks of hair, arising from the beauty of golden upper tufts, were beautifully curled.
With lips reddened by smiles, gentle, and showering the nectar of grace,
there are a thousand feet and countless eyes in the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
Hiraṇyagarbha is manifold in nature; he is proclaimed to be stainless, dark-blue, blue, yellow, red, and indeed of various colors.
The moon and sun are said to be his left and right eyes;
they call Brahmā his head, and the trees his hair.
His mouth consists of the infinite Vedas, and his water is indeed blood;
furthermore, it is said that his uvula is the hundredfold Upaśruti.
Likewise, one should know Rudra situated between the eyebrows and Bhṛgu residing in the mind;
the eleven Rudras are known to have taken refuge in his throat.
The constellations, planets, and stars are his teeth, and the Maruts are likewise;
furthermore, righteousness and unrighteousness are proclaimed to be his upper and lower lips.
Indra and Agni are his two palates, and Sarasvatī is his tongue;
the cardinal and intermediate directions are recorded as being his two ears.

Vāyu is to be known as residing in the vital breaths (prāṇas); the Sādhyas are remembered as being in the fingers; the sages (ṛṣis) are in the pores of the skin; and the oceans are in the region of the bladder.
The rivers, the earth, and the nāgas are situated in his shanks;
the two divine Aśvins are situated in his knees, and the mountains are situated in his thighs.
The Guhyakas are to be known as his secret [treasures], the Vasus reside in his chest,
and likewise the divine medicinal herbs are to be recognized in the tips of his nails.
The two nostrils should be known as the southern and northern solstices;
the seasons are at the bases of the arms, and the months are upon the palms of the hands.
Likewise, the Siddhas are at the tip of the forehead; the clouds with lightning are between the eyebrows;
and the Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Daityas, and Dānavas are likewise [located there].
Rākṣasas and Cāraṇas have taken refuge within his belly,
as well as the Pitṛs, Pretas, Kūśmāṇḍas, Vetālas, and Pramathas.
Those whose domain is the netherworld (pātāla) should be known as resting upon his pair of feet;
on his two sides are the ritual actions praised by the Vedas.
The rites such as the Agnihotra, those beneficial to the castes and stages of life,
and all the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ— these all reside within his heart.
They recite a hundred, a thousand, or even an infinite number of names,
which correspond appropriately to his infinite and manifold forms.
All his forms are proclaimed to be beyond numbering;
the forms of all beings, beginning with the gods, are contained therein.
Therefore, he is proclaimed as infinite; this is declared in the Puruṣasūkta:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. (BhS 36.182)
From whose mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born, from whose arms the Kṣatriyas, and from whose thighs the Vaiśyas—these, O men, are the castes on earth. (BhS 36.183)
The moon was born from the mind, and likewise the sun from the eyes;
Indra and Agni were born from the mouth, and Vāyu arose from the breath.
From the navel of that God the intermediate space was born, and from his head the sky;
from his feet the earth arose, and from his ears the directions were manifested.
Such is Mahāviṣṇu—immeasurable and free from affliction;
without his grace, it is impossible to know him or to speak of him.
Viṣṇu consists of all the gods, and all the gods have him as their essence;
so too does this entire realm of speech, the world with its light and darkness, and all that is moving and unmoving.
The entire space between the directions is pervaded by the power of Viṣṇu, just as the atmosphere is filled by the wind;
