indeed, all the gods are proclaimed in all the scriptures to be composed of Viṣṇu.
Pervading in two ways by way of the relationship between the container and the contained,
He remains both partless and possessed of parts for the sole benefit of all beings.
Thus, the eternal Viṣṇu is to be known as both partless and possessed of parts;
his hands and feet are everywhere, and his eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all;
it appears as the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all the senses.
Unattached yet supporting all, devoid of qualities yet the experiencer of qualities;
undivided among beings, yet appearing as if divided.
That should be known as the sustainer of beings, as both the devourer and the progenitor;
it is said to be the light of even lights, beyond darkness.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge abide in the hearts of all;
and He is the primordial Lord of the worlds, the Supreme Lord, the Highest God.
Viṣṇu resides in the heart of all in the form of the higher and the lower;
the Blessed One likewise exists in a threefold manner as the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
He is remembered as the powerful one, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu;
for he is indeed known as the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
The Vairāja and the Laiṅgika [forms] exist both externally and internally in every respect;
they are composed of consciousness, consisting of sound and the other sense objects, and pervading the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The wise person should seek these three—inhalation, resonance, and sound—within the Veda, in the teaching of the Blessed One, and likewise in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (BhS 36.198)
In the Dharmaśāstras and the Purāṇas, it is constantly recited by all sages, gods, and humans: "The entire universe is pervaded by Viṣṇu."
Whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever is present—
namely, the sense faculties, the objects of the senses, the elements, and the internal organs.
The unmanifest, the three qualities, Māyā, Vidyā, as well as Dharma and the others, Niyati, Kalā, Kāla, and everything else is composed of that.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme deity, abiding within all beings; and all beings indeed abide in him. There is nothing here that is not he.
Gods, asuras, and others; mortals and beasts; reptiles; trees, creepers, grasses, and medicinal herbs; great clouds, thunderbolts, and lightning.
Mountains, oceans, rivers, gardens, cities, and lakes;
the worlds, infinite time, fire, the abode of pretas, and the dwellings of serpents.
The seven worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ and known as Brāhma, Śaiva, and Vaiṣṇava,
are all pervaded by Viṣṇu alone, who is the Self of all selves.
Varāha, Bhārgava, Siṃha, Rāma, Śrīdhara, Vāmana, Aśva, and Kṛṣṇa— by these [incarnations] in the various directions, the entire cosmic egg along with its worlds [is sustained].
And whatever has not been stated in its entirety, these are the manifestations of Viṣṇu;
it is because of his pervasion of the universe that he is proclaimed as "Viṣṇu" by the elders.
He is known as Puruṣa because he lies within this body which is designated as "puruṣa";
he is proclaimed as Satya because his object is uncontradicted, and as Nitya because of his eternity.
He is called Acyuta because he is indeed unshakable;
that Hari is likewise proclaimed as Aniruddha because of his non-obstruction by anything whatsoever.
Having attained the state of Vāsudeva while dwelling within all beings,
the Lord who is drawn forth from the Primordial Form is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Pradyumna is so called because his back is radiant; he is Tridhāman because of his three abodes;
and he is called Vaikuṇṭha because of his stainless color, which is the state of Vaikuṇṭha.

Because Keśa and Ava dissolve within him at the time of dissolution, he is Keśava; and because he is the creator of man (nara) and woman (nārī), and because he is the refuge (ayana) of men, he is Nārāyaṇa.
He is Nārāyaṇa because he is the refuge (ayana) for men (nara) and because he is beyond the waters (apa);
he is remembered as Mādhava because he was born among the Madhus, or because he protects (dhavati) Śrī.
He is called Govinda because he finds the cows, or likewise because they find him;
he is Madhusūdana because he slays the Asura named Madhu.
This Trivikrama pervaded the universe with his three strides;
he is Vāmana due to his connection with dwarfishness, and Śrīdhara because he carries the goddess Śrī.
He is called Hṛṣīkeśa because he is the lord (īśa) of the senses (hṛṣīka);
and since a lotus (padma) arose from his navel, he is therefore known as Padmanābha.
Because he has a rope (dāman) around his belly (udara), Hari is called Dāmodara;
because he is the Supreme Person (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ), he is called Puruṣottama.
Because he is perceivable by the senses in a reverse manner, he is called Adhokṣaja;
half-lion, half-man, he is declared to be Narasiṃha.
Because he torments wicked people, he is Janārdana;
because he became the younger brother of Indra, Hari is called Upendra.
Because he removes all sins, Hari is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
because he draws away the heaps of evil, the all-pervading Hari is Kṛṣṇa.
He is called Rudra because he causes weeping; Brahmā, because of his act of expansion (bṛṃhaṇa);
and Indra, because of his supreme sovereignty; while Vahni is so called because of his carrying (vahana).
He is Yama because he restrains men; likewise, he is Varuṇa because he encompasses them;
he is Vāyu because he moves; and he is Soma because he gladdens. He is Īśa, for he exercises lordship over all people.
"Āditya is so called because he is the son of Aditi, and Candra because he gives delight"—
thus, by means of words functioning through qualities, even a single entity is designated in many ways.
Brahman, known by the name Viṣṇu, is proclaimed by the Vedas and never anything else;
and through the sovereignty of that Lord, all this proceeds.
For the entire world must have a Lord; it can never be without a Lord.
Therefore, men should cast the burden of all things upon Govinda by becoming absorbed in Him.
Those fortunate ones who perform that sacrifice cross the ocean of existence;
therefore, men should make an effort with their whole being to accomplish it.
Everyone should always go to the Lord of the World with devotion bowed;
for that which is pleasing to that God is indeed the honoring of Him. (BhS 36.227)
The god is ever-present with him in whose heart Janārdana dwells;
Hari is pleased with him through generosity and austerity, and not by any other means.
Whether it be a man, a woman, a child, an elder, or even one who is afflicted by illness, whoever shall ascend a cart and go to the temple of Viṣṇu, [attains great merit].
Those mortals, whether men or other living beings, who drive those [animals], have no merit to be gained after death; instead, they are born as draft animals themselves.
They shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu because they move at his feet;
yet those fools who drive living beings [as beasts of burden] surely fall as well.
The fool who torments those very beings while on his way there,
having reached the tortures of Yama, is tormented by the servants of Yama.
Furthermore, having fallen into the state of an animal, that man is driven by other animals or men,
or else he is used as a beast of burden through being hired out for wages.
Whether he causes [others] to carry it or carries it himself, he too will go to a miserable state,
especially in the shoreless and difficult saṃsāra that is bound by karma.
Having utterly abandoned their own duty, they fall into an impure hell;
thereafter, having attained the state of animals, they remain upon the earth for a long time.
Even one who enters a temple while wearing sandals is reborn as an animal after death and is born here as a sick person.
If one of deluded intellect should offer salutation to Hari while standing upon his sandals or his vehicle, Hari remains very far away from him.
With the intention of praising the gods, one should not approach in this manner;
even if one arrives without effort, one should descend from one's vehicle.
Having set aside his sandals and other such items, and having sipped water for purification,
he should enter the first enclosure wall again, becoming fully composed.
One should not enter the abode of the god with vehicles and such;
seeing such a person, one should instruct him according to one's ability.

This would indeed be the first transgression; thereafter, it becomes something that must be remedied with effort, as when one who has gone into the midst of a cremation ground should then proceed to the temple of a deity.
A person is liberated from the merit accumulated over seven lifetimes at that very moment;
thereafter, having entered the womb of a jackal, he shall pass through three births.
Those who, having gone outside to another temple, return home after bathing there, shall become poor and foolish for three lifetimes. (BhS 36.243)
Due to delusion regarding the God of gods, his sin would become very great;
thus, he himself, hungry, went from house to house seeking alms.
A man who fails to obtain alms anywhere is born poor;
and for four births, until the end, he remains so—except for the wise one.
One enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla for fifteen births;
regarding this, Kāśyapa and others cite the following distinction:
Viṣṇu consists of all the gods; Hari consists of all the Vedas.
There is nothing whatsoever beyond him; the distinction therein shall now be explained.
All beings in the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are situated within the universe according to their respective karmas.
From that alone the entire world is produced at the time of creation;
and into that very same [source] it is completely dissolved again at the time of dissolution.
He who is declared to be the primordial, ancient, and imperishable Puruṣa, the supreme state beyond Prakṛti— he alone, as the self of all beings, is designated as Nara.
The principles born from Nara are called "Nārāṇi";
he for whom these alone are the "ayana" (path or abode) is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the highest reality.
Likewise, some [call him] Viṣṇu and so forth, while others call him Vāsudeva and so forth.
By means of various designations, the great-souled ones always worship Him,
who is everywhere complete in all ways and in all things.
Nothing whatsoever is ever found that is not pervaded by him;
therefore, having placed everything within that Lord of the lords of gods, [one should remain in equanimity].
Whatever worship there may be, that should be considered appropriate by the wise; for if worship were to take place after having superimposed [the object] elsewhere, it would not be so.
That worship would indeed be something else; therefore, its fruit is limited.
Even those who are devotees of other deities and sacrifice, endowed with faith—
They too worship that very Lord of Gods, though not according to the prescribed rites;
those others—Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the rest—are remembered as deities.
Those Vaiṣṇava incarnations which were proclaimed in the scriptures of old do not differ in the ultimate sense; there is no mutual distinctness among them.
Furthermore, from one abode of Viṣṇu to another abode of Viṣṇu,
or from those places to their respective deities, there can never be any difference.
Now, where the scriptural injunction is different and is not even found there,
one should recognize that as something else, provided one does not desire a confusion of scriptures.
Having served the god Hari while seated upon his vehicle, that best of brahmins then beheld another person on the street,
likewise seated upon a vehicle at that same time.
Even he who incurs sin becomes purified by meditating on Viṣṇu;
wherever there is a festival of the Lord of Gods, whether in a village or even in a city.
On a mountain peak, on the bank of a great river, or in difficult forests,
a person should go there with devotion and respectfully attend the festival.
Accompanied by his sons, ministers, and surrounded by all his attendants,
that man should go to the sacrificial ground of Viṣṇu and perform service there.
Having heard the commencement of a festival for the deity, that man who, out of a sense of helplessness, fails to employ his own power in those rites as is appropriate; BhS 36.265.
He shall remain lame for a thousand lifetimes;
that birth will be fruitless, and his life will be merely a burden to the earth.
When the festival of the Lord of Gods, which yields great fruit, is properly underway,
that man who is occupied elsewhere and does not go there becomes dejected.
No atonement has been prescribed for him; that sinner shall go to hell.
He who goes to a sacrifice uninvited, or likewise goes to the teacher’s household [uninvited], [is such a one].
Whoever, desiring to go to a sacrifice here, waits for a moment or the like,
his previously acquired merit perishes at that very instant.
That evil-minded mortal who, for any reason whatsoever, seeks to prevent another from attending a festival of the gods while they are making an effort to do so, [commits a grave offense].
Whether it be fruitless or even fruitful, it surely falls without a doubt,
on the five days of Viṣṇu or on other auspicious days as well.
But for one who, having fasted and heard of the festival of the Lord of Gods,
does not go there out of sheer force of will at that very moment, great sin shall accrue to him.
He who lies upon a bed while that festival is taking place,
remaining seated or lying down there, shall undergo the torments of Yama.
He who goes before the Lord of Gods and does not perform a salutation is the most sinful person in the world; for him, no atonement exists.
When the time for the departure of the vital breaths has arrived,
one should restore them by means of rising to meet [the teacher] and saluting him.
The immutable Lord Hari is the vital breath of all;
all living beings possess consciousness, yet he alone is the one who bestows life upon them.
Otherwise, there is great fault and human beings are destroyed;
the sin incurred by a single prostration with one hand cannot be matched by any other means.
Two hands were fashioned by the Creator; what good deed could be accomplished with them?
One should instead join the two hands in reverence and supplicate Madhusūdana.
If a person of dull intellect should bow to Hari with only one hand,
that hand of his shall remain solitary even for hundreds of future births.
In this very world, one is indeed born lame or diseased; of this there is no doubt.
Why this construction of a body with such numerous and diverse instruments?
If not even a single one of these is suitable for his service,
why serve an action that is under one's own control with a hand that is already under one's own control?
Being unable [to perform full prostrations], deprived of their independence, and struck down by sin, they are ruined; however, a salutation with one hand must especially be avoided.
He who returns the greeting to one who has saluted him with only one hand—
both of them go to hell, because their meeting was equal [in fault].
The deities, becoming apprehensive, curse such a fool who performs his own circumambulation before the deity. (BhS 36.284)
That wise person would be like one who betrays himself by acting against his own self;
for previously, [he failed to do so] before the image of the god and the auspicious form of the goddess. (BhS 36.285)
But when [the Buddha] is present, one should not disregard him; for there is no circumambulation of another.
Where there is mental worship, that should be considered mental.
That very Hari who exists within the heart as the partless Inner Controller (antaryāmī),
having become manifest with parts, is he who has been established in the image.
Therefore, one should never commit a transgression in any complete act of worship;
a wise person should never become impure while engaged in his own ritual duties.
If one voids excrement or urine on the road and does not perform purification immediately,
one remains impure from that point until then, being unfit for all ritual actions.
Furthermore, that man who casts nails, body hair, head hair,
or bones into a temple of the deities would be a slayer of a Brahmin.
Depending upon the womb of a honeybee, one is born and dies again;
for seven births one goes to that very place, and thereafter to hell.
He who throws chewed betel leaf into the presence of a deity goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Released from that [state], the great sinner Śunaka remains for three more births; of this there is no doubt.
That sinful man who spits in the temple of the Enemy of Madhu shall fall into the terrible hell named Kṛmibhakṣya.
He who, being of deluded intellect, voids urine in the temple of Keśava, is born as a śleṣmātaka tree for five lifetimes.
He indeed falls headlong into the Mūtragarta hell;
once released from there, he takes refuge in a nimba tree that is red with blood and other fluids.
There is no doubt that he who voids excrement here in the house of the Blessed One will be born as a sow for seven lifetimes. (BhS 36.297)
He goes to twenty-one terrible hells in succession;
then, once released from those, that evil-souled one is born as a worm in excrement.
He who even once voids urine near a temple shall remain in the terrible Raurava hell for ten million years.
Even after being released from that, the person attains the state of a village pig;
having undergone a hundred births in a village, he likewise becomes a pig dwelling in excrement.
But he who, having discharged semen either intentionally or unintentionally,
should go to a temple of the gods without having bathed, perishes immediately.
Whoever cleanses his teeth or scrapes his tongue in a temple dedicated to a deity—that sinner will certainly perish. (BhS 36.302)
That man whose entire body has been anointed with oil and likewise rubbed with fragrant unguents who enters the temple of the Supreme Lord, the God— [is purified].
He becomes a house lizard for fourteen births;
however, he who follows a deceased person goes to the abode of the gods.
If one then goes to dwell in order to propitiate [the deity], one shall go for ten thousand years to the womb of a crow-eater (a vulture),
indeed for very many births.
Having performed the funeral rites for the deceased in this manner, one must especially not enter the house; for if one enters, one perishes.
Having taken recourse to the womb of a Caṇḍālī, he will undergo nine and five births;
likewise, he will again become separately cruel and harsh.
He who, having eaten at a non-śrāddha meal in another's house, goes to the temple of Viṣṇu or worships there especially, becomes a wicked sparrow.
Having undergone a hundred births there, he then enters the body of a lizard;
yet, by approaching the shadow [of the deity] out of delusion, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Or if one should intentionally stand while circumambulating [the Buddha], that fool would become impure; this indeed is the fruit of his sin.
He might dwell in a desolate forest, surrounded by many thorns and devoid of fruits, flowers, and the like, or he might attain the state of a hollow tree in a cemetery.
Having placed the sacrificial thread below, and especially having placed it upon the ear, and having indeed worn it over the right shoulder (apasavya), and having worn it like the nivīta; BhS 36.312.
A man should not go to a temple with his hair unbound, nor without wearing a loincloth; he should not go naked, nor with his loincloth trailing behind, nor wearing only a single strip of cloth.
With empty hands and an empty bowl, and even with his upper garment cast aside;
even while chewing betel or eating offerings and the like.
He should never enter a temple; his sin would be great.
For a man of wicked conduct does not attain a long life in this world. (BhS 36.315)
Living beings tremble before him and likewise revile him;
therefore, one who possesses proper conduct alone should perform the Vedic rites.
Even for one of evil body, right conduct destroys inauspicious marks;
dharma is characterized by conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by their character.
And this characteristic of conduct, as it truly occurs among the virtuous,
makes a person who practices dharma recognizable by mere report, even if they have not been seen.
People do what is pleasing to him as he performs his own duties—
even those who are atheists, inactive, and transgressors of their teachers and scriptures.
Ignorant of the Dharma and of evil conduct, they become short-lived;
lacking moral discipline and the boundaries of righteousness, they are constantly engaged in promiscuous sexual intercourse.
Those men who crush clods of earth, cut grass, or bite their nails become short-lived and go to hell in this world. (BhS 36.321)
The ever-impure Saṃkusuka never finds favor anywhere with those who dwell near the abode of Viṣṇu and have come there for the sake of serving Viṣṇu.
One should not perform a ritual bath after touching even outcastes (śvapacas) or those who have fallen from their caste;
for he who bathes during the festival of Vāsudeva out of fear of such contact [commits a fault].
The ancestors dwelling in heaven fall into the impure hell for him;
one should drink the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, or especially that of one's gurus.
In that regard, O best of the twice-born, one should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) there, just as in the case of the Soma sacrifice;
likewise, those who worship Hari with offerings intended for other deities [should not do so].
For seven births, even those five [qualities] become deluded;
for two births, however, those deluded men indeed attain the state of Śūdras.
The man who, having offered flowers, smells their fragrance will certainly become afflicted with a foul odor and will surely become a leper.
At the end of that, three births of a similar nature occur;
for one who has either a birth or a death, impurity is prescribed.
One who is unworthy for all ritual acts should not be led to the temple of the deity;
however, according to the ancients, sapinda-relationship extending through seven generations is prescribed for the birth of a male child.
Likewise, in the case of the birth of a daughter, the sapinda relationship extends to three generations;
the same applies to those under a vow, those performing a sacrificial session, ascetics, and celibate students.
The wise do not declare that he is impure, just as Śātātapa has said:
"By the mere resolution for a vow, one becomes a performer of the vow. (BhS 36.331)
One who has merely put on the [sacrificial] garment is likewise proclaimed a *satrin* in a *sattra*, and by the mere wearing of the saffron robe and staff, one is considered a *yati*. (BhS 36.332)
Whether he dwells in the teacher’s family after being initiated or not, in due order,
the young celibate student either studies the Veda or does not study it.
Likewise, for those who carry out the king’s commands, for kings, and for a *snātaka*,
as well as for others of this kind, an internal state (*antarbhāva*) has been declared here.
One should not perform prostrations, nor should one offer a formal greeting;
one should not present offerings, nor should one frequent sacred fords and the like.
If a Brahmin who is in a state of ritual impurity should worship the God out of delusion,
he shall incur extreme poverty for seven births.
Having undergone a hundred births as a dog, he shall thereafter become a caṇḍāla, he who,
having eaten in a temple, leaves his leavings there.
He might go elsewhere or cast it away; even he, being deluded, comes to ruin.
But as for one who, having stretched out his feet somewhere at the door of a temple—
He sleeps and slumbers due to delusion, and he goes to ten thousand hells;
furthermore, having attained birth again, he does so many times in low-born wombs.
Having experienced torments as if they were real, that fool who, deluded by intoxication, lies down in a temple of the gods, shall fall into the state of a degraded Brāhmaṇa.
There, by depositing leftovers and by the winds of intense exhalations, a foul odor arises; such a mortal undergoes five births.
Then, having attained the state of a pig for fourteen births,
he suffers through many hardships and shall not lie in the abode of Hari.
The fool-minded person who occupies a bed provided with pillows and the like, especially in a temple or even within a rampart, [incurs demerit]. (BhS 36.343)
He shall indeed become unfortunate and is born among the wombs of serpents for twelve births;
thereafter, he may attain the state of a human being.
That evil-minded person who, being afflicted by disease, sleeps in a temple of the gods,
shall become dejected and miserable both in this life and in the life hereafter.
That fool who sleeps with a woman in the temple of the Blessed One shall become a eunuch for twelve births.
Yogis practice these postures especially for the sake of attaining yoga; they are indeed innumerable, yet one should not perform them in a temple.
Just as those devoted to mantra-yoga do so, likewise these are performed by those dedicated to laya-yoga,
by haṭha-yogins, and by rāja-yogins.
The Svastika, the Sarvatobhadra, the Siddha, and likewise the Siṃhāsana;
the Savya, the Khūla, the Sukha, as well as the Gomukha and the Garuḍa.
The peacock, the fish, the lord of fishes, the frog, the mallet,
the deer, the elephant, the cock, the serpent, the wood, the krauñca bird, and the tortoise.
The sword, the burner of desire, the tiger-skin seat, the bamboo seat,
the womb-seat, the dwelling, the steadfast one, and likewise the lotus-seat.
The Vārāha, the Paryaṅka, and the Patagāsana;
the Tripada, the Hastikarṇa, and likewise the Hemamardhāsana.
These and others are the eighty-four postures;
furthermore, there are other specific ones established in the scriptures.
But the wise man, having ascended those [steps], should stand before the foremost of the gods;
he who eats in the temple of a deity is sinful and dejected in mind.
Having been afflicted by diseases of the womb for fifteen lifetimes,
he will thereafter attain the state of a jackal and surely fall into an impure hell.
Or whoever, being of dull intellect, might out of delusion cause a meal for Brahmins to be prepared—
especially in a temple— he shall become a person censured by the world.
One should especially not eat food in the inner sanctum, in the intermediate space, likewise in the half-pavilion, or in the middle of the great pavilion.
Having placed food into a vessel made of leaves or similar materials,
one should eat that meal only after having performed the *āpośana* rite.
One should not perform the *āpośana* rite over water held in the hollowed palms after having received the favor of a deity; if one were to do so, that would be considered improper.
But he who leaves behind drinking vessels that have been used for water shall go to cruel hells for as many eons as there were drops of water.
They remain in the vessel for as many autumns as there are [offerings], of this there is no doubt;
especially so when it has been offered before the God of gods.
One should indeed bestow [the offerings] in due order, according to the regulations for the castes and stages of life;
all the devotees, moreover, should eat while holding [the food] in their cupped hands.
Having directed [this] toward the God who is the friend of Brahman, the Person dear to the Brahmins,
Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, and the Lord of all lords.
One should feed Brahmins for the sake of achieving perfection in the ritual action,
as well as for the accomplishment of expiation, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
One should never cause the feeding of twice-born men in places other than those specified;
however, that brahmin who, filled with devotion, causes food to be given to the twice-born, [attains merit].
What has been offered for the satisfaction of the Lord and of oneself—
by that the Lord of Gods is pleased, but the taker perishes.
The receiver shall incur all the manifold evil previously accumulated by the giver through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
For even the favor of Your Majesty never purifies a man who delights in the maturation of others;
it would not purify him at all, nor indeed would it ever purify him.
Just as one who is content with whatever is obtained by chance is like one who has received the best of alms,
so too is the fool-minded person who disregards the majesty of divine grace.
By that [act], sin would be incurred by the giver alone; of this there is no doubt.
[This is] the fruit obtained from satisfying ten thousand Brahmins.
The fruit of that [merit] is quickly destroyed by even a single grain of food from one who is impure;
now, the fault regarding the sale of food is described by those most learned in the rules.
Sinful sellers of food go to the torments of Yama;
after death, they become jackals for fourteen births.
But he who sells food in the house of the Blessed One, especially so,
is born as a caṇḍāla after death and shall wander about perpetually hungry.
But those Brahmins who sell [their knowledge], having set their eyes upon trade, as well as those who offer food, oblations, and other things in a temple of the gods; BhS_36.374.
They too go to a most terrible and exceedingly dreadful hell,
where not even a single drop of water from the palm of a hand will ever exist.
There may not even be a grain of food;
yet those people suffer there who, being hungry, take that food and eat it.
Or those who provide assistance to them are called "eaters of forbidden food.
Food is the life-force of human beings; everything is established upon food.
One should know that food has Brahman as its essence; one should know it to be the body composed of food. But those who sell food are considered sellers of their own life-force.
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon its purchase and sale;
one should not perform the worship of deities in the house, nor the rites for prosperity or the feeding of guests at a śrāddha ceremony.
One should not eat even after leaving aside rites such as the *śrāddha*, nor should one eat in the temple of Hari; therefore, with every effort, one must not eat there. (BhS 36.380)
He who, having entered the temple of Hari, engages in idle conversation,
is like one who abandons a treasure already perfected before him to beg for a mere cowrie shell.
But that wicked person who, having entered a temple, engages in idle conversation,
abandons prepared food and wanders about for alms.
Whether for a moment or even for an instant, if the Supreme Self is not contemplated— that is my loss, that is my great flaw, that is my delusion, and that is my perturbation.
Like one robbed by bandits, like one scorched by a forest fire,
like one afflicted by diseases, or like one dragged away by death.
Like a creditor threatened by fear, like one oppressed by kings,
like one sinking in the great ocean, or like one struck down by a whirlwind.
He who is released from it cries out as if crushed by stones;
there are many locations and, in particular, various rules.
For the sake of accomplishing the journey through this world, and for the maintenance of the body,
a person should go to the temple and not be intent on anything else.
"Whatever is spoken in connection with the name of Hari, yet in which neither He nor His greatness is attained—all that is said to be in vain; some even declare it to be false. (BhS 36.388)
For one should never speak an untruth in the presence of the Lord;
since the Blessed One is the very embodiment of truth, he would not conceal the truth from him.
Truth alone is the supreme Brahman; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme sacred learning.
Truth awakens among the gods; truth is the fruit of the tree of Dharma;
and austerity, sacrifice, merit, and the worship of the gods, sages, and ancestors [all depend upon it].
The primary ritual and knowledge—all is established in truth;
truth is the sacrifice, likewise the Vedas, and the goddess Sarasvatī is truth.
Likewise, the practice of vows, truth, the syllable Oṃ, and truth itself:
by truth the wind blows, and by truth the sun shines. (BhS 36.393)
Fire burns by means of truth; one goes to a good rebirth by means of truth;
Parjanya pours down water upon the earth by means of truth.
The study of all the Vedas and bathing in all the sacred fords, when weighed against speaking the truth in this world, would not equal it; of this there is no doubt.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
the weight of truth surpassed that of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
By truth the gods are pleased, as are the ancestors and the brahmins;
they say truth is the supreme dharma, they say truth is the supreme state.
They say that truth is the supreme Brahman; therefore, one should not violate the truth.
Those who are devoted to truth, whose oaths are truth, and whose prowess is truth—[they attain the highest state].
Those great-souled ones, the best of sages, attained supreme perfection;
devoted to truth, they rejoice in heaven together with the gods.
They travel about in celestial palaces crowded with hosts of Apsarases;
one must always speak the truth, for there is nothing superior to the truth.
In the stainless, pure, and true ford, the lake of purity, those endowed with mental discipline should bathe; that bathing is remembered as the supreme.
Those men who do not speak falsehood for the sake of the gods, for the sake of others, for the sake of their sons, or likewise for their own sake, go to heaven.
The man who speaks the truth and does not utter falsehood,
having reached the stainless worlds and dwelt there for eternal years, [attains the highest state].
For those liberated through devotion to the Blessed One, who are born into illustrious families, all these deities beginning with the Sun serve as witnesses. (BhS 36.404)
They always examine a person in all circumstances;
therefore, one must not speak an untruth, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Those fools who speak falsehoods and take oaths,
especially in a temple of the gods, perish along with their entire lineage.
Those who [indulge in] singing, instrumental music, dancing, and the like, as well as meritorious narratives and stories, go for a hundred births many times into the wombs of insects.
Furthermore, those wicked ones who revile the Enemy of Madhu with harsh words within his temple go to hell and are born into low wombs.
In that way, those evil-minded ones shall also attain the womb of a female donkey;
likewise, at the end, the cruel ones [shall pass through] nine and five births.
Those who engage in incoherent chatter within a temple of the gods are born as partridges for five lifetimes.
That man who, abandoning the divine language, praises [the deity] in regional dialects within a temple, especially in the presence of the God; BhS_36.411 //
For him, there will quickly be great fault, and there will be no fruit from worship;
moreover, there are many worthless treatises upon the surface of the earth.
In those scriptures where the greatness of the Lord is not elaborated upon,
whatever scriptural meanings have arisen therein are particularly [limited].
For all arguments and counter-arguments are indeed nothing but conditioned formations (saṃskāra), like various artistic crafts; there is no doubt about this, and therefore a person is not liberated.
That alone is true knowledge which praises Hari; that alone is true action which is His worship;
whatever else is merely a livelihood that results in evil consequences.
For if a man, having gone to a temple, should spend even a moment of time with unpalatable meanings of the scriptures, that is an insult to the deity.
Having created the entire vast expanse of speech, the Lord Hari, the Creator,
enters into its very core through the distinction between the signified and the signifier.

Because he always benefits all those who are devoted to him, this embodiment of the mass of consciousness exists for the sake of the discernment of human beings; therefore, all the best of devotees are ever [devoted].
Having set aside all other words and thoughts with respect,
one should likewise avoid recitation that is impoverished by even the scent of talk concerning his greatness.
One should never perform the teaching or the writing and so forth of Hari’s [scriptures] within the house;
he who commits such a transgression becomes a defiler of letters.
He would even betray those who consist of speech; therefore, one should be more disciplined than he who, having gone to a temple, weeps out of affection.
If one who is suffering praises the deity, that would be a mental impurity;
for he who, with a dejected mind, [praises] the state supreme in Nirvana, [is likewise stained].
Whether it be a woman or even a man, whoever goes to a temple anywhere and serves [there], yet does not know that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, [attains no fruit]. (BhS 36.423)
One should not weep, nor shed tears, nor even cause another to weep;
for as many tears as fall from those who weep in the temple of the gods, [so many births shall they endure].
For as many thousands of years as that, they dwell in the abode of Yama,
having experienced there the torments of intense retribution.
Having attained the state of a *tittiri* bird, they shall dwell on earth for a long time;
therefore, one should never commit violence against living beings that causes them suffering.
Non-violence, Vedic ritual action, meditation, restraint of the senses, austerity, and service to the teacher— these are declared to be the six gateways to dharma.
A self-controlled and wise person, having laid down the triple staff toward all beings, should practice the Dharma based on non-violence, being pure.
Having restrained both desire and anger, they then attain perfection;
yet those who strike harmless beings with punishment do not.
One who seeks his own happiness alone will not find happiness after death;
but that man who treats all beings as he treats himself shall indeed find happiness.
Having renounced violence and conquered anger, he prospers in happiness after death—
he who has become the self of all beings and beholds all beings as himself.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path as they seek the footprints of the trackless one;
therefore, one should not do to another that which is disagreeable to oneself.
This is the Dharma that gathers [disciples], which proceeds differently from [mere] desire;
it operates in both proclaiming [the teaching] and in giving, as well as in [dealing with] pleasure and pain, the agreeable and the disagreeable.
By means of self-comparison, a person attains the standard of measure;
the seers, the brahmins, and the gods especially praise this.
A wise man, by describing the authority of the Vedas, [establishes] the Dharma characterized by non-violence; for he never commits an act of violence through his actions.
By means of both speech and mind, one is then liberated from suffering;
for this non-violence has been taught by the teachers of Brahman as being fourfold.
If one fails in even a single one of these, there will be no success; of this there is no doubt. Just as a four-legged animal cannot stand upon only three legs.
In the same way, this [teaching] is specifically proclaimed by means of three causes,
just as all other footprints of those who walk are contained within the footprint of an elephant.
Just as all footprints are encompassed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too has non-violence been declared in the worlds as the ancient dharma.
For there is nothing in this world or in the next equal to that which consists of compassion and non-violence toward all beings here.
No fear ever exists here for a compassionate man;
through compassion, these worlds belong to ascetics even in the next life.
"He who, devoted to compassion, grants fearlessness to all beings—
to him all beings grant fearlessness," so the Śruti has proclaimed.
Whether wounded or fallen, whether stumbling, drenched, or struck down,
all beings protect one another on both even and uneven ground.
Wild beasts do not kill him, nor do piśācas or rākṣasas;
he is liberated in times of fear—he who delivers others from danger.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of life;
for it is certain that in this world, nothing is as dear to oneself as one's own self.
Death is said to be the most undesirable thing for all living beings;
indeed, at the time of death, trembling arises immediately within them.
In the ocean of saṃsāra, sentient beings constantly revolve amidst the sufferings of disease, birth, and old age,
and they tremble with fear at death.
In the dwellings of the womb, they are cooked by alkaline, sour, and pungent fluids, and by the harsh,
extremely cruel substances of urine, sweat, and excrement.
And those born there, being powerless, are seen being cut again and again, and being slaughtered while helpless by men who seek to kill them. (BhS 36.449)
Having entered various wombs, they are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell;
being attacked and slaughtered, they terrify one another again and again.
Indeed, throughout the entire earth, there is nothing dearer than oneself;
therefore, among all things that provide protection, one who possesses self-mastery should be compassionate.
With whichever body a person performs whatever action,
with that very same body they experience the corresponding fruit.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; likewise, non-violence is the supreme self-control.
Non-violence is the supreme gift; non-violence is the supreme austerity.
Non-violence is the supreme sacrifice, and non-violence is the supreme fruit;
non-violence is the supreme friend, and non-violence is the supreme happiness.
Neither the gift given at all sacrifices, nor bathing at all sacred fords,
nor even the fruit of all possible gifts is equal to non-violence.
The austerity of one who practices non-violence is inexhaustible; the non-violent person always triumphs.
One who is non-violent toward all beings is like a mother and like a father.
Therefore, one who is non-violent should constantly observe the vow of fasting;
the fruit of fasting has been proclaimed at length by Aṅgiras.
For three nights, five nights, or even seven nights, one who is non-violent should not even harm grains; for him there shall be non-injury.
As long as one does not eat, for that long one is deprived of merit;
through the lack of food, the body suffers.
While his body is undergoing ascetic heat, the sense organs remain under his own control, like servants under the command of kings.
He who restrains the very senses is happy and wise;
through the restraint of the senses, as well as through generosity and self-control.
A person obtains everything that he desires with his mind;
thus is the fast of non-violence, the root of all, proclaimed.
Whatever desires a person mentally longs for with devotion from Mādhava,
Hari, being pleased by his vows and fasts, bestows them upon him.
In this manner, one should practice this with certainty month after month.
This vow of fasting shall yield infinite fruit for him who,
on the eleventh day, remains without food and worships the imperishable Hari.
Having drunk that water from his feet and likewise having eaten the *tulasī* offered to him, one should observe the vow of fasting.
But that deluded soul who does not consume [the water] from a sacred ford accompanied by the auspicious *tulasī* on the day of fasting shall go to the Raurava hell. (BhS 36.467)
For a man should never engage in dispute after having entered a temple;
that place is not for dispute, therefore one should avoid it from afar.
He whose mind is unstable is not fit to worship Hari;
only he whose mind is stainless is worthy for all ritual acts.
A heart free from passion and the like, speech free from faults such as falsehood,
and a body free from violence and the like— this triad [is required] for the worship of Keśava.
Hari does not make his abode in a mind defiled by passion and other such afflictions;
a swan never sets foot in muddy water.
A person corrupted by speech through falsehood and the like is not fit to praise Mādhava,
just as the moon obscured by clouds is unable to destroy the darkness.
A body defiled by violence and other such acts is not fit for the worship of Hari, just as a reed shrouded in darkness cannot serve to clarify the minds of people.
For those who are free from mental defects, how could there not be no fault?
Otherwise, a beloved wife is embraced with one kind of affection, while a daughter is embraced with another.
The minds of ascetics and of lustful men alike are otherwise inclined toward the form of a woman;
thus, generally, the world is deceived by the untrained mind.
The world recoils at the sight of a red lotus, yet craves the wine from the mouth;
therefore, a man should go to the temple with pure senses.
Since dispute is born of anger, one should therefore avoid it;
for who, when angry, would not commit evil, or who, when enraged, would not even slay their own teachers?
An angry man may revile the virtuous with harsh speech;
this causes distress to the good and holy ones and is an insult to the virtuous.
He burns his family down to the seventh generation; there is no doubt about this.
When enraged, he never distinguishes between what should and should not be said.
For you who are angry, there is no deed that should not be done, nor is there anything that should not be spoken at any time—
yet he who casts away the arisen anger through patience is truly great.
Just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin, so indeed is that person called; those best of men who, through patience, cast off arisen anger are worthy of honor.
Those who constantly extinguish the blazing fire with water, who do not speak slander of others, and never speak what is unpleasant; BhS_36.482 //
No resentment whatsoever should be harbored by great beings in the presence of the gods;
rather, they should especially apply their own attention to the work of the gods.
One should consider oneself as nothing at all within the creation of the Blessed One;
he alone is the divine Lord, omniscient and endowed with all powers.
He is the Lord of all, the knower of all, and intent upon both restraint and grace;
therefore, no one else ever possesses the power for either wrath or favor.
Having reflected thus once more upon all living beings,
one should practice compassion while remaining in the presence of the Blessed One.
Whatever is destined to be—whether yet to come, present, or past—that is its own activity;
for if one relies on egoism, one is deluded by the intoxication of independence and pride.
Whether in punishing or in favoring, he who makes known his own power goes to a terrible hell; fate does not tolerate him.
Likewise, excessive intimacy with women should be avoided,
whether one has reached a temple of the deities at the prescribed times or at other times.
For men who are excessively attached to women, there is a loss of life, fame, and austerity;
for women who are excessively attached to men, that same loss is equal.
Noble, beautiful, and well-protected women remain within the bounds of propriety; yet that very fault is censured in women.
Indeed, there is nothing else more evil than women;
for women are the root of all defects—of this there is no doubt.
Having encountered men who are renowned, possessed of supernatural powers, handsome, and established in their respective stations,
women are incapable of discerning them as they truly are.
Indeed, this is generally an unrighteous state among women on earth,
in that they associate with men who are more sinful than themselves, having abandoned all sense of shame.
For women desire only that man who seeks them, approaches them closely, and performs service for them with eagerness.
Because men do not desire them and out of fear of their attendants,
women— who are themselves beyond restraint— remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands.
There is no one who is inaccessible to them, nor do they abide by any fixed age; whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Neither out of fear, nor out of compassion, nor for the sake of wealth in any way,
nor due to ties with their family or kin, do women remain faithful to their husbands.
Women of noble family long for those women who, being in the prime of youth, adorned with polished ornaments and fine garments, live according to their own will.
Even those beloved women who are constantly cherished and protected may become attached to hunchbacks, the blind, the lame, and the deformed.
Among those who are lame, afflicted by leprosy, or other men who are despised,
there is no one here in this world who is declared to be off-limits to women.
If the destiny of men cannot be established there in any way,
then they would even act toward one another, for they do not remain faithful to their husbands.
"Those of wicked conduct, devoted to evil, untruthful, and shrouded in deceit, are for the most part possessed of little insight"—this is what is determined. (BhS 36.503)
Indeed, due to the lack of men, out of fear of their attendants,
and also out of fear of execution or imprisonment, they protect themselves.
Fickle by nature, difficult to serve, and likewise difficult to grasp in their true intent;
as are the dispositions of a wise man, so too are women.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women ever satiated with men.
This and another secret concerning all women should be understood:
upon merely seeing another man, the womb of a woman becomes moistened.
Wicked women cannot endure their own husbands, even though those husbands are givers of sensual pleasures, providers of mental comfort and consolation, and protectors.
They do not value extensive enjoyments of sensual pleasures, nor the accumulation of ornaments for their sake,
as much as they value the favor shown in [the attainment of] delight.
The Ender, the Subduer, Death; the underworld, the submarine fire;
the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire—these are on one side, and women are on the other.
For these [senses] deceive men here in this world with their own illusions;
and no man who has once fallen into their hands is ever released.
Like cows seeking fresh grass, these [women] seize whatever is new and new;
such is the illusion of Śambara, and such is the illusion of Namuci as well.
All those women are known to belong to Bali and Kumbhīnasa;
they laugh when he laughs, and they weep when he weeps.
If one accepts what is unpleasant through pleasant words at the appropriate time,
even if that person is deceitful, they may live for a thousand autumns.
Devoted to no other task, one should meet death without speaking of the faults of women;
for Uśanas knows that scripture which Bṛhaspati also knows.
They cannot be distinguished by the intellect of women, nor are they easily guarded;
they call what is false "true," and likewise what is true "false."
Thus, how can those women—who are difficult for men to sustain—be guarded? Even when honored by men, they turn their minds against them.
Furthermore, women immediately transform the mind even when rejected;
it is an established principle of dharma that there are no [forbidden] actions whatsoever for women.
For women are without sense-faculties and lack sacred instruction; such is the Vedic revelation.
They [desire] beds, seats, ornaments, food, drink, and ignoble conduct. (BhS 36.519)
The Lord of Creatures gave Durvāgarbha and Rati to women;
it is not possible for men to guard them in any way whatsoever.
How much less, then, could it be done here by ordinary men—
whether by speech, or by execution and imprisonment, or likewise by various kinds of afflictions?
Women cannot be guarded, for they are eternally unrestrained;
they lead astray both the ignorant man in this world and even the wise man.
For there is nothing whatsoever that women can do to lead one who follows the sway of desire and anger onto a wrong path, beyond this [seduction by a woman]. (BhS 36.523)
Just as they know that association with men is the supreme fruit of this,
women, impelled by passion, act according to their own will.
And they are not burned as they go, even by the intensely heated sands;
nor are there wind, fire, Varuṇa, or any other gods [to obstruct them].
Women are indeed fond of pleasure and devoted to sexual enjoyment;
among thousands of women, it is said that perhaps only one might ever be obtained as a beloved.
Likewise, even among hundreds of thousands, if there should be some woman devoted to her husband,
these [beings] do not know her father, nor her family, nor her mother.
Playing wantonly, they destroy their family— neither brothers, nor husbands, nor sons, nor brothers-in-law— just as the great rivers destroy their banks.
Those drops of semen that fall from a man who exerts himself with women should not be considered sources of happiness, for they are like drops born of perspiration.

Those who know the truth understand that the pleasure women derive from scratching or applying heat from fire is like the pleasure of a leper or one afflicted with scabies when being tormented by worms.
Whatever pleasure is found when an itch and its pus are removed, such should be understood as the pleasure found with women; nothing more exists in them.
Just as the sensation of a knot is felt when a wound has burst open, so too should it be understood regarding women: there is no happiness in the ultimate sense.
The pleasure that arises from the discharge of feces and urine is exactly the same as that which is found with women; nothing greater than that exists in them.
Upon investigation, not even a particle of happiness exists;
thus, the pursuit of festivals for the gods and the like is forbidden.
For a woman can never go to another place by her own volition;
nor do the elderly build temples for the gods as a mere pastime.
Therefore, for the sake of the amorous play of those who desire pleasure,
it would be more appropriate if the father, brother, husband, or son were to follow her.
Then she may go to the temple, but never otherwise, O passionate woman;
for in a man who dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born;
from anger comes delusion; and from delusion comes the confusion of memory.
From the loss of mindfulness comes the destruction of the intellect; from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
The powerful host of the senses drags away even the wise man.
Therefore, a wise man should never be excessively attached to women;
for that reason, one should not indulge in attachment toward women even in the house of a deity.
In the same way, one should not direct the mind toward the wives of others;
men who desire prosperity must not go to the wives of others.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world.
There is nothing here in this world so detrimental to the lifespan of men as the number of pores created upon the bodies of women.
For that many thousands of years they dwell in hell;
therefore, one should abandon excessive attachment to women in the temple of the gods.
One should avoid such vulgar speech by which a meaning is conveyed through several indecent words or even through a single word. BhS 36.545.
Furthermore, from indecent speech, there arises agitation among men;
and in the abode of the Blessed One, the minds of the devotees would become turbid. (BhS 36.546)
The mind should be withdrawn from that [world] and fixed upon the Supreme Self;
therefore, a person who utters vulgar speech becomes intent on sin.
Having attained the state of a caṇḍāla, he is born so for a hundred lifetimes; due to his suffering, he shall not enter the temple of the Lord, the Supreme Self.
When this body has become like the wind, in the activity of the movement of the vital airs,
there is the discharge of waste and air, especially in a temple.
One might cause even a man who has reached the further shore of the Vedānta to fall;
therefore, one should never discharge the odor of excrement.
Alternatively, if there is suppression of the wind, an aggravation of disease will occur;
therefore, one should indeed release the wind without hesitation.
Thus, one who is afflicted by disease does not at all deserve to go to a temple;
this is especially true for one with leprosy, as well as those tormented by other sinful diseases.
And [he went] to gaze upon the Lord of Gods, Madhusūdana, in his temple,
to worship him, to serve him, and likewise to offer a multitude of riches.
For it is not possible that the evil attached to that [object] could be transmitted;
otherwise, one would immediately become a sinner. (BhS 36.554)
For nine or even five births, one is born as a worm feeding on filth;
however, when one enters the temple of Viṣṇu for the sake of serving the Enemy of Madhu, [this fate is avoided].
Having properly arranged the beautiful upper garment like a sacred thread (upavīta),
one who is always pure and wears the sacred thread should serve the Lord of Gods.
One whose body is covered by a bodice (kañcuka) should not go to the temple of Hari;
nor should he perform a salutation, for such a person is said to be unworthy of being saluted.
One who wears a turban should not serve, nor one who holds a weapon in his hand;
having covered the body with a cloth, whether a woolen blanket or another kind.
The fool who cuts the bonds of yoga, or even he who bows down to Hari, the abode of Viṣṇu, is born as one afflicted with leprosy for nine and five births.
Or that man who, clothed in linen garments and the like, bows down to Hari,
enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla for fourteen births.
Even when faced with a superior, one should never address them as "thou";
whether it be the use of the word "thou" or actual killing, such conduct is not permitted among the wise.
Censuring others will result in the censure of another person;
and the censuring of a teacher is the censuring of another. (BhS 36.562)
Censuring others arises from anger; through anger, one is immediately destroyed.
Indeed, by censuring others, those who were censured are remembered [in turn] by them.
Therefore, a person should first avoid finding fault with others,
and likewise, one should properly renounce the praising of others.
A person should not offer praise, nor cause another to be praised, before that Supreme Self, the Ancient Puruṣa, who is proclaimed as the Highest. BhS 36.565.
But if one should worship another who is superior to the Lord of All, or if one should consider such a person worthy of worship in His presence, one's residence [in heaven] perishes.
The entire world is indeed the very nature of that Supreme Self;
nevertheless, it appears again in various forms characterized by degrees of gradation.
The Blessed One is worshipped by his devotees there; this is the path declared in the scriptures.
Therefore, whatever else exists—whether moving or unmoving—other than that Lord of Gods, [is subordinate].
In that abode, there exists an object especially worthy of worship;
therefore, one should undoubtedly offer worship, praise, and other honors to others as well.
That man who, while being capable— especially out of greed or other such motives— would abandon [the temple] and consider his life to be lived happily within a temple, should be cast out.
He who worships Viṣṇu with the secondary services as they have been described does not possess merit; he merely practices a false scripture.
To whatever extent the fruit for the wealthy and the poor is proclaimed in the scriptures,
that is [attained] only through the offering of one's own power, and by means of wealth and so forth, according to what is appropriate.
Just as the Lord of the Gods is pleased by pearl necklaces from kings,
he is pleased in exactly the same way by a garland of *tulasī* even from a poor man.
Therefore, one should exert effort; never at all should one harbor greed for power.
For if one acts otherwise, one will not attain the fruit at all.
Having died, that deluded man who cooks poison for himself is born five times as a cat. BhS 36.575.
Whoever should eat even a single grain of food that has not been offered to Viṣṇu, he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin; he eats only pus and blood.
Whatever one should drink, whatever one should eat, whatever one should smell,
wear, or anoint— one should offer all that first to the Enemy of Madhu.
One should eat or utilize only what remains after it has been offered to Him;
that lowest of men who does not eat what has been offered to Viṣṇu [is a sinner].
Even in a hundred million eons, no atonement for this is found;
yet, by giving to those devotees of Viṣṇu what has been offered to him, [atonement is achieved].
May the Blessed Lord be pleased; let the person be devoted to Him alone.
If one of dull intellect should say that what has been offered is "leftover," [he is lost]. (BhS 36.580)
But he, having fallen into an evil state, undergoes the torments of Yama,
despite having relied upon the eternal and infinite prosperity of that [Lord].
This earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, is truly prosperous,
for it constantly produces many things in this world.
In the same way, a man should offer all medicinal herbs, as well as flowers and fruits,
according to the prescribed rite, for the sake of discharging his debt to them.
But he who does not offer to Viṣṇu the various crops, medicinal herbs, fruits, and flowers that arise in their respective seasons— ||| BhS_36.584 |||
A man who has accumulated, according to his ability, new grains and other crops that have grown in their proper season, may become a partaker of Brahman.
They meditate upon the Lord of the gods and strive to approach him;
for those fools who treat him with contempt, this [meditation] is their supreme petition.
Those who remain indifferent or consume [the offerings] themselves—
those ungrateful ones go to many terrible hells.
All medicinal herbs curse [one who consumes them improperly]; therefore, one should especially offer with devotion fresh grain, fruit, flowers, curd, milk, ghee, and honey.
Whatever is fit for offering, one should present it all before Him;
whatever has been offered as leftovers out of greed, delusion, or ignorance, one should likewise offer.
That man would be especially sinful who offers to the Lord of Gods what has been left over by another deity.
Even he, having attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, will surely perish; of this there is no doubt—this applies to whoever offers [an oblation] to the deity with what has been left over from a meal.
Whether among these gods or even among humans,
that evil person is born for a thousand lifetimes in the wombs of dogs.
For having gone to the temple of a deity, one should not sit with one's back turned;
a devoted person should face the deity with their whole being.
One who intends for the welfare [of others] should never show their back before the gods;
rather, while moving along the side, they should return toward the monastery.
Having entered the temple of Hari, one should never bow down to anyone else;
for he who dwells there, the Lord of Ramā, is the Sovereign of All and the Supreme Support.
He alone is worthy of worship and worthy of salutation, and no one else therein;
the fool who pays obeisance otherwise goes to ten thousand hells. (BhS 36.596)
Having entered the womb of a Caṇḍāla, he repeatedly undergoes torment—
he who [neglects] the Vaiṣṇavas, the beloved of the Lord, when they have arrived at a temple of the gods.
Furthermore, he who does not honor the teacher, the officiating priests, the worshippers, and the attendants by observing silence perishes along with his lineage.
Whatever may be desired by the officiating priests, for the sake of fulfilling that very wish,
the devotees— and especially those residing in the village— should attend upon them.
Otherwise, the fault of pride would ripen for everyone;
for he who excessively praises himself is possessed by the conceit of egoism.
Disregarding his teachers and destiny,
and acting without restraint, the arrogant man does not recognize the fault inherent within himself.
A man who is arrogant on account of his noble lineage, learning, asceticism,
and accomplishments finds neither happiness nor good fortune, since he exalts himself.
Therefore, by performing self-praise, a person certainly falls;
thereafter, having undergone hundreds of births, he especially enters the womb of a deer.
He who, having gone to a temple of the gods, desires honor for himself, is born and dies repeatedly; his sin shall be great.
He undergoes thirteen births— nine and five—
in successive order through the castes for the sake of serving the Lord of Gods.
The qualification has been fully explained; one should not disregard its sequence.
Those who follow the Vaikhānasa-sūtras enter the womb as a house.
One who is not a Vaikhānasa must never enter the inner sanctum;
however, for those whose place is in the intermediate space, that shall now be explained.
Other twice-born ones also remain there according to the sequence of the stages of life;
those twice-born ones and their wives likewise enjoy themselves, gathered together there.
And those born of the kṣatriya caste, having taken their places in the half-pavilion,
as well as the women belonging to him, attend upon the Lord of Gods.
Those born of the Śūdra caste and those born of the inverse order (pratiloma) have gathered together;
having taken their place in the great pavilion, they serve Puruṣottama.
Those born of the *anuloma* castes and others who belong to the *mleccha* tribes,
standing outside the city gate, serve the temple of Hari.
Having understood this gradation, one should constantly serve Hari;
even that sinner who reviles the deities is liberated.
He who considers Puruṣottama to be equal to any other deity enters the womb of a Caṇḍāla for fourteen births.
If one should steal that property or other items after having first denied it to the gods,
he becomes a "slayer of the gods" (devahā) and truly is born in the wombs of dogs and other such creatures.
Likewise, one who disregards the gods as well as the scripture of the Blessed One and performs actions according to his own whims— that man also would be a slayer of the gods.
When the discourse of the Lord, the enemy of Madhu, is being told,
those men who depart without showing respect are evildoers.
In a forest devoid of water and exceedingly fierce, they are born as mere empty trees for seven lifetimes; thereafter, they fall into the state of being Caṇḍālas.
Indeed, one should not exercise authority over gods, cows, brahmins, or even temples, if by doing so one would fail to attain spiritual growth.
Furthermore, many faults are recorded by the wise in that sovereignty;
for everything he does, whether intentionally or unintentionally, [is subject to censure].
Therefore, it would lead only to evil; thus, one who desires prosperity should abandon that [practice].
If one were to take [such] a hand, he would fall instantly along with it;
however, that which is offered with devotion by devotees in the presence of the God is accepted.
Whether it be a leaf, fruit, root, gold, clothing, or anything else that is an inheritance, he who out of delusion denies it to the worshippers— (BhS 36.622).
Or if he should consume it himself, that sinner would go to hell;
whereas those devotees who, permeated by devotion, offer [it] to Hari.
By means of that name, worshippers alone are known as partakers of the fruit,
because through it the worship of both the stationary and the moving is accomplished.
Therefore, whatever is given in a temple to the deity in the name of the Blessed One— setting aside ornaments and the like, as well as garments and other personal belongings— [is what is intended].
Only the officiating priests shall take those items suitable for the adornment of the deity that are especially valuable; let no one else obstruct them.
But whoever, out of pride in his authority, enters a temple and desires to frequent it at an improper time, he too shall go to a miserable rebirth.
Alternatively, even if one should desire to serve for some reason whatsoever,
a wise person should serve only at the times already mentioned.
At the conclusion of the final worship, once the door is closed,
it shall remain so until it is opened again at dawn.
One should not worship Hari at all during that time, especially at an improper hour;
however, one may perform worship through mantra at the beginning or end of the night, or at any other time.
And even when the door was fastened at that particular time,
there was no such loss as there would have been had it remained unfastened without the mantra.
Furthermore, even at the time when worship is due,
many improper times for serving devotees have been declared, as well as those mentioned by Yavāsika.
Therefore, one should avoid untimely practice according to the rule,
especially for those whose minds are overcome by sense objects and who do not perform the worship of Viṣṇu.
In the land of karma, the birth of humans is certain, and their actions are likewise constant;
yet one who regards the human state toward the guru as a mere stone, and the divine state toward the deity [likewise], [is lost].
He comes to regard mantras as a means of livelihood, sacrifices as acts of violence,
and the act of worship by those who perform it as something devoid of flavor.

Indeed, his life is to be censured in every way, for it is fruitless. Now I shall explain the supreme procedure for the mantra of patience (kṣamā-mantra), which is distinguished by its excellence. (BhS 36.636)
By reciting this, a person is liberated from all transgressions;
even if an offense was committed knowingly and under one's own volition, one is freed from it.
One is not released even by the recitation of a thousand *kṣamā* mantras;
indeed, the *kṣamā* mantra is said to be capable of destroying all sins without exception.
“O Nārāyaṇa, homage be to you; homage to you, O one devoted to your devotees! Homage, homage, homage be to you; homage be to you, homage, homage! (BhS 36.639)
Whatever offense has been committed through ignorance, greed for wealth, passion, hatred, or negligence— forgive that, O Supreme Person.
Whatever offense has been committed during the two twilights, by day or by night, while awake, dreaming, or in deep sleep— forgive that, O Puruṣottama.
Whatever offense has been committed by body, mind, or speech, or even by all combined— forgive that, O Supreme Person.
Whether standing, walking, or lying upon a bed or seat,
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed.
Whether bathing, reciting prayers, performing sacrifices, or offering oblations,
whatever offense has been committed by me, forgive it, O Supreme Person.
O Supreme Person, please forgive those offenses committed by me while I was enjoying pleasures, dwelling in meditation, and indulging in the objects of the senses.
"O Supreme Person, whatever offense has been committed by me, or by my attendants, or even by my kinsmen, please forgive it."
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the king, or by his ministers, or even by the king’s servants.
O Puruṣottama, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the preceptor, the worshipper, the devotees, or the attendants. BhS 36.648.
O Puruṣottama, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the singers, the dancers, or the players of musical instruments.
O Puruṣottama, forgive the fault of performing the rites from the syllable *praṇava* to the final *visarga* according to the prescribed rules without the mantras during this worship.
O Supreme Person, forgive the fault committed through a lack of faith in various activities, from the drawing of water to the making of a bed.
Who is able to worship you, O God, who are without beginning or end and immutable?
Therefore, O Supreme Person, forgive my ignorant conduct.
I pray to you, the God of gods; be gracious toward me, O Blessed One.
May she who dwells upon the expanse of your chest be gracious to me.
The Goddess Īśānā is the sovereign of the world, the mother who is eternal and never-failing;
may all the gods be gracious toward me through the grace of you two.
May there be well-being for us through the compassion of you two, who are so well-pleased,
by means of the services I have performed daily under the pretext of ritual offerings.
"O Supreme Person, forgive all these transgressions," thus one should petition him again, permeated by devotion and awe. (BhS 36.656)
Being supremely pleased by that request, the one whose banner is a bird becomes gracious;
he should bestow this mantra of forgiveness, but never upon one who is unwilling to listen.

"This is the most secret of secrets, to be guarded at all times by the preceptors. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, concerning miscellaneous matters, in the *Siddhānta* proclaimed by Bhṛgu within the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Bhagavat Śāstra*.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter: The Exposition of the Dharma of the Three Ages (*Tiyugadharma*).
Now, I shall describe the dharmas of the ages (yugas) according to a concise account; thereafter follows the fourfold age-cycle consisting of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
Whatever was desired should indeed be done at that time;
there, the dharmas do not perish, nor do the subjects truly decline.
Therefore, that age is called the Kṛta Yuga according to its true quality;
in that conjunction of ages, there was neither sexual intercourse nor the decay of the senses.
There was no quarreling, nor weeping; no arrogance and no backbiting;
no conflict, no hatred, no falsehood, and no deception.
Then there is neither fear nor distress, neither greed nor pride;
that is the supreme light, the Brahman, the stainless state of the forest-dweller.
That single goal of the yogins who desire no rebirth is known as the white Nārāyaṇa, the god Viṣṇu, the soul of all.
But when that Hari, the inner controller who consists of all the worlds,
himself attains whiteness, everything will become transparent.
In the Kṛta age, all human beings— Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— become devoted to the Blessed One and intent upon their own respective duties.
The entire world continuously becomes endowed with true asceticism, right conduct, truthfulness, devotion to austerity, and filled with higher knowledge.
United by a single Veda and performing the rites according to a single dharma,
they followed one dharma while remaining devoted to the single Veda.
By that action performed in accordance with time, those living in the four stages of life attain the supreme goal through the union of desirelessness and effortlessness.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the fourfold system of the four castes is eternal and possesses all four quarters;
this is called the Kṛta Yuga, which is devoid of the qualities of the three guṇas.
Then comes the age named Tretāyuga, wherein Dharma loses one foot;
the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, moreover, assumes a reddish hue.
And men who act according to truth, devoted to the duty of giving,
worship the faultless Nārāyaṇa with various sacrifices.
Since the elders have become established in the station of dharma, the Brahmins and others engage continuously in their own respective duties; thus they have attained the Dvāpara age.
Because its dharma is decaying, they call this age Dvāpara;
Viṣṇu attains a yellow hue, and even the Veda is divided.
When the Dvāpara age has arrived, unrighteousness arises from two parts;
likewise, some possess two Vedas, some one Veda, and others are without a Veda.
Devoted to various scriptures, people engage in diverse activities;
becoming intent on giving, they constantly praise the act of charity.
By resorting to a rajasic state of being, the progeny become rajasic;
for those falling away from sattva, diseases become exceedingly terrible.
There will also be other calamities, with things turned upside down;
due to the shortening of time, the fourth age shall be the Kali Yuga.
Since the God who assumes a perceptible form is not seen in the Kali age as He was in the Kṛta and other ages, that very age is called "the three-yuged" (triyuga) Kali.
In the Kali age, indeed, Dharma shall proceed by means of a single quarter;
but when that [Kali] has fully arrived, Dharma does not proceed at all.
Having reached the Tāmasa Yuga, Hari attains a dark form;
yet whoever here may be righteous in soul and devoted to ritual action and yoga, [he shall attain liberation].
Seeing a man devoted to righteousness, everyone becomes envious;
those whose conduct is based on the duties of their caste and stage of life will undoubtedly perish.
Vows, observances, meditations, sacrifices, and so forth will perish;
indeed, calamities will arise from the prevalence of unrighteousness.
In the Kali age, all people will be devoted to envy, intent on hypocritical conduct, and all living beings will have short lifespans.
All dharmas perish when Kṛṣṇa has attained the state of Kṛṣṇa (the dark age),
because Kali is most terrible and the accomplisher of all evil.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras will turn their backs on dharma; the twice-born will turn their backs on the Vedas.
All are devoted to deceptive dharma, corrupted by the arrogance of the elderly;
everything is constantly cast aside by men who fancy themselves wise.
"Every person contends, 'I alone am superior';
likewise, all the twice-born are greedy for unrighteousness."
Therefore, in the Kali age, all will be short-lived;
because of the short lifespan of human beings, there will be no acquisition of knowledge.
Due to the lack of engagement in the acquisition of knowledge, unrighteousness prevails;
all subjects, intent on fulfilling their sinful desires, die out of order.
Likewise, the castes beginning with the Brahmins become intermingled with one another;
they are deluded, devoted to desire and anger, and filled with the vain conceit of "I."
All people will harbor enmity, desiring to kill one another; they will be devoid of compassion and utterly lacking in courtesy.
Devoid of austerity and truth, they will become equal to Śūdras;
the high-born will fall to a low state, and likewise, the low-born will attain a high state.
Kings are devoted to material wealth and are intent upon greed and delusion;
though clothed in the cloak of dharma, they are destroyers of dharma.
Whosoever is rich in horses, chariots, and elephants, he shall become the king;
and the twice-born shall become servants to the Śūdras.
The Mlecchas and the Yavanas protect the earth,
for the most part keeping their eyes fixed upon the sky out of fear of drought.
In the Kali age, all men will always be distressed by the fear of hunger;
men will have little fortune but many offspring.
Disregarding their husbands' words and always intent on the houses of others,
women of immoral character will desire those of wicked conduct.
When the Kali age has arrived, women will always be speakers of harsh and untruthful words, devoid of bodily refinement, and excessively talkative.
In cities and villages, people, terrified by the fear of thieves and other dangers, construct wooden mechanical devices upon their walls and watchtowers.
People, being excessively afflicted by famine and the oppression of taxes,
