will reach regions rich in wheat and barley food, even though they themselves are suffering.
Other human beings feel affection for others only until their own purpose is accomplished;
even monks are constrained by bonds of affection toward friends and the like.
They accept disciples from all sides on account of the pretext of food;
likewise, women scratch their heads with both hands.
Disregarding them, they will disobey the commands of their principal lords;
they will be devoted to conversing with heretics and will associate with people of heretical sects.
When the Brahmins become such, then the Kali age shall reach its full growth;
the clouds will yield little water, and the earth will produce meager crops.
Likewise, cows will yield little milk, and from that milk no clarified butter (ghee) will be produced;
furthermore, even the four castes will become of a single color.
There is no distinction of caste there;
men will go to their dissolution, both the virtuous who languish and the wicked who sport, all around.
May there be love for strangers and enmity for one's own kin;
sons die even while their fathers are still alive, right before their eyes.
In the Kali age, even for the sake of a mere cowrie shell, people will abandon their friendships after falling into conflict;
they will give up their dear lives and even slay their own kinsmen.
When the Dharma was overrun by heretics, when kings were mostly like bandits, and when men subsisted on various livelihoods such as theft, falsehood, greed, and violence; BhS_37.52 //
When the castes consist mostly of Śūdras and the cattle consist mostly of goats,
the base Śūdras will likewise assume the outward marks of those who have gone forth into the religious life.
Clad in saffron robes, with matted hair and smeared with ashes,
they follow impure practices and subsist on food cooked by others.
Sinful people will desire worship in the dwellings of gods and the twice-born; likewise, evil-minded Śūdras will become renunciants.
There, those who live by bribery and are devoted to great sins will arise; likewise, there will be heretics, skull-bearers, and wicked mendicants.
The lowliest Śūdras, who are favorites of the king and possess the outward marks of renunciation, will proclaim the doctrines to the twice-born who are habituated to destroying the Dharma.
When the Kali age has arrived, Brahmins will be devoted to singing and instrumental music, turning their backs on the discourse of the Vedas, and will follow the path of the Śūdras.
In the Kali age, people will be takers and not givers;
they will be devoid of faith and treacherous toward the Vedas, the gods, and the twice-born.
Those who speak of the unconditioned and are free from passion and hatred will then have a maximum lifespan of sixteen years.
In the fifth or even the sixth year, a girl gives birth;
likewise, men give birth at eight years and nine years of age.
In the Kali age, all will abandon their own duties; they will be ungrateful, of broken conduct, beggars, and indeed slanderers.
Men are always intent on insulting others, devoted to praising themselves,
and constantly devising means to seize the property of others.
They constantly revile their paternal and maternal families;
though they speak words of dharma, their minds are greedy for evil.
The lowest of men strive to conceal their own faults born of evil deeds,
yet they openly display their misdeeds upon the innocent.
In the Kali age, sinful kings of barbarian origin will arise and will revile the one who proclaims the path of Dharma.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other castes— all of them, being excessively lustful, will intermingle with one another.
There will be no disciple and no teacher, no son and likewise no father;
there will be no wife and no husband, for everything will be thrown into total confusion.
And in the Kali age, even those who are wealthy will become beggars;
and in the Kali age, they will also become sellers of liquids.
Husbands bestow the marks of a paramour upon their lawful wives;
sons hate their father, and disciples hate their teacher.
In the Kali age that has arrived, there is no doubt that a woman hates her husband;
with minds overcome by greed, all people are characterized by evil deeds.
The twice-born will be constantly greedy for the food of others;
they will all be devoted to the wives of others and intent upon the wealth of others.
They will live by means of the flesh of mortals, milking goats and sheep,
and they will cultivate medicinal herbs on the banks of rivers with spades.
In the Kali age, the fruits of these [virtues] will become exceedingly small;
women will instead direct their longing toward the beauty and character of courtesans.
There will be obstacles to the Dharma for both women and men;
no one will ask for a daughter in marriage, nor will there be any man who gives away a daughter.
O twice-born ones, girls and suitors will generally choose one another by their own free will, even in the presence of wretched relatives.
They will plunder the wealth of various virtuous people;
indeed, people will no longer perform sacrifices, offer oblations, or practice austerities.
They will not give gifts and the like, nor will they worship Hari;
relying on the discourse of causal reasoning, they will not be established in the Dharma.
In that way, men perform acts of giving only to unworthy recipients,
and they cultivate affection for cows merely for the sake of the pretext of milk.
The Brahmins do not perform such rites as bathing and purification;
they are intent on actions at improper times and are experts in fraudulent reasoning.
Devoted to reviling the gods and likewise devoted to reviling the brahmins,
the twice-born will wander about having abandoned the sectarian mark, the topknot, and the sacred thread.
The mind of no one at any time would ever be intent on devotion to Viṣṇu;
rather, seeing someone devoted to the worship of the gods, everyone would mock him. (BhS 37.82)
And those deities who are proclaimed in the scriptures as the retinue of the Enemy of Madhu—
men, driven by the power of Time, abandon them out of delusion.
At that time, they will make other gods dependent on the doctrine of causality;
the king’s servants will even bind the twice-born themselves for the sake of taxes.
In the Kali age, which is filled with sin, others do not respect the twice-born;
indeed, some twice-born sell the fruits of their gifts, sacrifices, and recitations.
These twice-born ones accept gifts even from outcasts and the like;
they are devoted to the company of Śūdra women and are greedy for sexual union with widows.
In the Kali age, there will be those who marry women in their menses;
they will be devoted to the food and drink of Śūdras and become almost indistinguishable from Śūdras.
In the Kali age, the countryside will have its pillars of justice as its main concern, crossroads will have their pillars of auspiciousness, and women will have their pillars of hair.
And there will be deceitful people there, experts in sophistry,
heretics who remain revilers of the stages of life (āśramas).
Nor did he practice service to the twice-born— which turns one away from all dharmas—
among his kinsmen who were mostly householders yet resembled ascetics.
Then, day by day, righteousness, truth, purity, compassion, and forbearance— all these,
as well as lifespan, strength, and memory— perish through powerful Time.
In the Kali age, for men, wealth alone gives rise to birth, conduct, and virtues;
mutual affection is the cause of marital union, while mere illusion prevails in worldly dealings.
Indeed, strength alone is the cause for the establishment of dharma and justice;
womanhood alone is sweet in enjoyment, while the sacred thread alone is [the mark] of Brahminhood.
The external mark alone is the cause for the designation of a stage of life; it is improper [to rely on it] as the cause of one's livelihood.
Furthermore, in the absence of a livelihood there is weakness, and even in scholarship, one's words are fruitless.

In marriage, the very act of acceptance is considered a ritual bath; in the pursuit of one's own ends, the mere filling of one's belly is regarded as truthfulness; and in fact, audacity alone is what constitutes it.
In skillfulness, in supporting the family, and for the sake of fame, there is the practice of dharma;
thus, when the Kali age has arrived, all dharma decays.
When there is illusion, falsehood, sloth, sleep, violence, addiction to poison,
grief, delusion, fear, and dejection— that is known as the Kali age, characterized by tamas.
Whenever there is a decline of virtuous, Vedic, twice-born men,
then and there the wise man should recognize that the Kali age has arrived.
Alas, what suffering! Alas, what great suffering! Alas, what great suffering! Alas, how immense is the inherent nature of this most terrifying cycle of existence, so difficult to bear!
In the womb-dwelling, filled with feces, urine, and pus,
due to the pressure within that impure and most loathsome place, there is suffering that is utterly unbearable.
And there is suffering for those being born, consisting of the pain of the breaking of limbs and so forth;
for those being impelled by the wind, it brings about fainting and extreme terror.
In childhood, for those lacking discernment, there arises [delusion] regarding the elements, the deities, and the self;
and likewise in youth, in old age, and in death, which is exceedingly terrible.
One hundred and one deaths are to be known as established within the body;
among them, one is designated as "Time" (kāla), while the remaining are recorded as adventitious.
Those [afflictions] mentioned here as adventitious are pacified by medicines, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, and gifts; however, death at its appointed time is not pacified.
Various diseases, weapons, living beings such as serpents and the like, poisons,
and malevolent spells are the doors of death for embodied beings.
Neither medicine, nor austerity, nor charity, nor sacred mantras, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person afflicted by the death that is time.
Even death at the appointed time can be overcome by great-souled men who are diligent and have attained perfection through elixirs, austerities, recitation, and yoga.
There is no suffering equal to death; there is no fear equal to death.
[It takes away] one's virtuous wife, sons, friends, and the pleasures of sovereignty and royal power.
And when enmities have been bound, death destroys everything;
there is no suffering anywhere in this world equal to that which a living being experiences at the time of death.
Like a frog swallowed by a serpent, the world is devoured by death,
even while embraced by kinsmen and surrounded by loved ones.
Sighing long and hot breaths with a parched mouth,
he turned repeatedly over the four sides of his bed.
Deluded, he flails his hands and feet excessively here and there;
he desires the floor from the bed, and from the floor, he seeks the bed, and then the floor again.
Naked and devoid of shame, drenched in urine and excrement, he begs for water with his throat, mouth, and palate parched. (BhS 37.113)
Thinking, "To whom do these riches belong when I am dead?",
he scratched the ground with his fingernails, dragged by the noose of Time.
While others are looking on, it dies and makes a "khura-khura" sound in its throat;
like a leech, this living being enters from one body into another.
Having attained a body in a superior lineage, he casts off his former one;
that which is the separation of men through the dissolution of the body occurs due to the exhaustion of karma.
Death is designated as such, yet in the ultimate sense there is no destruction;
thus one is born and dies by means of the actions one has personally accumulated.
Surrounded by cold, heat, thirst, hunger, fierce fevers, and other such afflictions,
a person remains in this state at all times until the end of his life.
For that which constitutes the ultimate limit of suffering for humans at the end is indeed not happiness;
it has no comparison whatsoever and is inferred only through its effect.
When I recall that most unbearable suffering of being dragged by the men of Yama, it causes my body to tremble.
And furthermore, there is that which occurs during his transition into the womb,
as well as the suffering of one dwelling within the womb, which is exceedingly difficult to endure and intense.
Furthermore, for one who is being born again, there are these endless sufferings arising from childhood and youth experienced by those dwelling within the cycle of existence.
Deluded by the illusion of happiness, people experience [these things] as pleasure;
yet there is not even a fraction of true happiness here, for this state brings only extreme suffering.
In the perils of saṃsāra, there are always base people whose minds are attached to sense objects, even when they have encountered a favorable opportunity.
They do not fix their minds upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of all worlds;
nevertheless, the Vaiṣṇavas, who are dear to the Blessed One, do not fear this.
Those who are devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu and intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu should be known as equal to Viṣṇu himself; indeed, the Kali age does not afflict them.
This illusion of Viṣṇu may indeed cause living beings to fall again;
yet it becomes surmountable and attainable by those who have fixed their minds upon Mādhava.
Without abandoning the householder's life and likewise without performing ascetic penance,
one who is devoted to the worship of Keśava indeed cuts through the māyā of Viṣṇu.
Even while enjoying sense objects without opposition, those who worship Mādhava cross over this insurmountable illusion of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā).
Since this is so, having obtained this bodiless instrument for action, men should perform only auspicious deeds for its purification. // BhS_37.130 //

When this [system] is propitiated, all desires are placed in the hands of everyone through their respective duties according to caste and stage of life; and in the end, liberation stands within reach.
His forms, which bring about the welfare of the world, exist for the sake of his purpose;
therefore, by perceiving him as possessing form and through devotion, one shall attain perfection.
And relying upon this scripture, one should worship the imperishable Viṣṇu;
for that meditation which is taught in the scripture as being absolute is sometimes described as having no external support.
In that case, there is no qualification for one established in action due to the weakness of the faculties,
just as [there is none] for one who desires the fruit of a tree standing on a mountain precipice.
One should apply oneself tirelessly to the means; likewise, one should exert effort in such a way that effort is applied progressively in all matters, and not by mere desire alone.
Through the application of body, speech, and mind, one should desire the supreme goal in due order;
however, in the formless [state], worship or meditation performed with devotion is what is desired.
That which appears delightful is actually the cause of misfortune;
for his senses, through birth, lead toward the manifestation of gross existence.
They do not perceive what is subtle and clear, either after a long time, let alone immediately;
moreover, it is impossible for anyone to meditate upon a fault without [first perceiving] its form.
For when the intellect has ceased from all forms, where does it abide?
When the intellect has ceased, it becomes languid and is overcome by sleep.
Therefore, the wise person should worship Him with the intellect at all times;
one should recollect that His existence is something beyond direct perception.
A wise person, having been instructed in every aspect, should not abandon the Supreme Deity, whether for the sake of liberation or for the sake of some other fruit.
Pleased by the worship performed with devotion,
the Lord first manifested in his four-armed form to bestow grace through that worship and other favors upon Prajāpati.
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa, endowed with that very form of modesty and splendor, should always be meditated upon, served, and worshipped by the wise.
Whatever worship, praise, or even meditation is performed toward this [deity] with form,
according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, it becomes as if performed toward that [very deity] itself.
In the Kali age, a certain highly intelligent person will come into being who, for the sake of public proclamation, will especially treat that very worship of Viṣṇu with contempt.
As long as there shall be the decline of Dharma and the increase of Adharma,
for that long the Lord Mahāviṣṇu creates himself by means of himself.
In Śrīnivāsa-janāvāna, Hari himself, Śrīnivāsa, will descend upon the earth; he is proclaimed as Śrīnivāsa.
Even as he is about to be born, shining with his own splendor,
he shall destroy the cruel mass of darkness that obscures the world.
Then, at only five years of age, he had mastered the entire multitude of arts;
refined by all purificatory rites, he was endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge.
The god who is the Lord of all worlds, Śrīnivāsa, the husband of Śrī,
four-armed, with noble limbs, adorned with divine ornaments.
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark, possesses mighty arms, and holds the conch, discus, and mace;
he is adorned with a crown and diadem, and is marked by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
His lotus-face shines with the beauty of golden vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
and he is constantly worshipped by the highly fortunate forest-dwellers (vaikhānasa).
In the Kali age, his family deity has taken up residence there, being praised by Vedic verses beginning with "O one-eyed Arayi. (BhS 37.153)
"He is especially worshipped by the Vaikhanasas with the supreme mantras beginning with 'rayiḥ kakudmān' and various other mantras pertaining to the Supreme Self. (BhS 37.154)
Complete with auspicious qualities, possessing a divine and auspicious form,
self-manifested, the supreme light, the highest Brahman, beyond the transcendent.
He will worship the God according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures;
the God, with a face gracious through favor, will himself [act] toward his own self-born child.
And bowing his head, he will take upon his neck a garland woven with divine, radiant flowers and tulasī leaves.
The Prince himself, together with the Kumāra, will consume the sacrificial offerings;
thus was the Treasure of Compassion entreated by the satisfied Kumāra.
In the temple, together with the highly fortunate Vaikhānasa ascetics,
he will supervise the sacrificial offerings and comfort the prince.
He will proclaim the greatness of the incarnation in worship to the worlds;
devoted to his worshippers, the God will do everything for them.
Thus honored with affection and respect by Śrīnivāsa,
he shall perform various other sacrifices for the Lord of Sacrifice.
Upon the vast surface of the earth, crowded with many refinements,
he will establish images of Viṣṇu in every village and in every house.
There were ancient cities inhabited by people, as well as the houses of householders,
alongside the beautiful temples of the Lord of Lakṣmī that were bowed with prostrations.
They will be adorned; they will devote themselves to the true nature of the world.
From here is the instruction of the teacher; from here is the approach of the disciple.
Right here is the frequent socializing of householders; right here is their consultation;
right here is the selection of a teacher; and right here is the seeking out of artisans.
Here is the gathering of the sacrificial grass, here the grasping of the wood;
here is the performance of the initiatory rite, and here the examination of the ground.
From here comes the proclamation of auspiciousness, from here the recitation for a day of merit;
from here the laying of the first brick, and from here the rite for the topmost brick.
From this side there is the seizing of a spear; from that side, the binding with the rope of enmity;
from this side the refinement of clay; from that side the scratching of colors.
From here is the preparation of beeswax; from here the fashioning of ornaments;
from here the construction of the banner; from here the gathering of the devotees.
From here [proceeds] the ritual resolve for installation, from here the opening of the eyes;
from here the consecration, and from here the offering of abundant oblations.
From this [world], there is the churning of fire; here, the oblation increases bliss. Here is song, here is dance, and here is instrumental music that delights the ear.
Here is the consecration of the deity, and here is the feeding of the twice-born;
here is the seasonal festival, and here, during the month of Dhanus, is the morning festival.
The offering of mung-bean rice, jaggery-rice, and clarified butter—
does Vaikuṇṭha, who was reclining upon the Ocean of Milk, arise today?
Today is the completion of the vow undertaken by Hari with firm resolve;
today, at the conclusion of her own vow, the Goddess shall perform the marriage ceremony, an auspicious event for the world.
Today is the full moon day of Pauṣa, and today is also the auspicious Ekādaśī;
today they shall perform the ceremonial bathing of the God with hundreds of water-pots.
Today the son of Daśaratha was born on the twelfth lunar day of the month of Māgha;
today the Mother of the World was born on the Revatī constellation during the month of Phālguna.
Today the lords perform the Damanaka festival for the God;
indeed, the month of Caitra is said to be most pleasing to the God.
O lord of men, people celebrate a divine festival in the spring;
for today there is the water-sport festival, and in some places the Caitra procession of Hari.
"A festival of ketaki, mālatī, jātī, mallikā, and dolikā flowers is being held today; it is a festival of fragrance. When will the day of the full moon arrive? (BhS 37.179)
When was the meritorious Ekādaśī, or when was the twelfth day?
When was Nṛsiṃha born? It is remembered that today is the thirteenth day.
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the annual festival is celebrated;
when does the full moon occur that the Candrikā festival is performed?
When will the festival of Jyeṣṭha take place? When will the auspicious full moon occur? When will the festival of the water-stations be held? And when will the month of Āṣāḍha arrive?
And when will the asterism Śravaṇa occur, under which the high-minded son of the Wind-god was born, having taken up the burden of service to Rāma?
And when will the month of Śrāvaṇa come, in which Nārāyaṇa Hari brought himself forth for the sake of the welfare of the world?
When will the month of Bhādrapada arrive, and on which day therein will the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) fall—for that [day] they know as Vaikhānasa, Vikhanasa, and Viriñca? BhS 37.185.
When will the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) come, which destroys all sins,
wherein they shall offer a sesame-cow (tiladhenu) in the presence of the Lord?
When shall the month of Āśvina arrive, and within it the auspicious tenth day,
so that the festival of Hari’s horse-ride may take place and we may follow after Hari?
"When will the new moon day occur on which he was slain in hell?
Or when will the month of Kārttika, so dear to Hari, arrive?"
When should the offering of lamps take place there? When is the auspicious Kārttikī full moon? And when are the Yugādis and other such special times of merit?
When will the chariot procession of the high-souled Hari take place?
When will the elephant procession occur, or when the mounting of the palanquin?
When will the beautiful Lord of Gods wander through the village streets?
When shall I obtain the most purifying sacred ford of Hari?
When will she obtain the favor of the god Kaṇa?
When will she be adorned with divine marks such as the conch and the discus?
The sandals of the God of gods will sanctify my head;
or when shall I offer the meritorious tulasī at his feet?
I shall eat [only what is offered], and I will indeed wear upon my head the Vaiṣṇavī [garland]—
when, indeed, shall I receive even a single holy flower offered to the God?
I shall bear him upon my head and smell his many fragrances;
when shall I behold the God of Gods, beautiful in every limb?
"From the feet up to the crown of the head, his body is sweet with loveliness"—
such stories as these will circulate among the people there.
All will be devoted to the Dharma, all will have Nārāyaṇa as their ultimate refuge,
and men will take delight in the worship of Vāsudeva.
Thus, in due time, the Guru will restore Kāleya to life;
he shall long worship Śrīnivāsa, the abode of Śrī, upon this earth.
He will indeed restore the Vaiṣṇava dharma, which has been overwhelmed by heretics,
and he will ensure that this scripture of the Blessed One endures for a long time.
Independent in all treatises, he will compose many works and will teach that essential meaning to countless disciples.
Having thus established the order of the Dharma in this most terrifying age of Kali,
he shall go to the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
And at the end of the age, Hari alone will take up the name;
then the great hero Hari will become known by the name Kalki.
Having brought about the destruction of unrighteousness, he will establish righteousness;
[this is] this narrative of the descent of the divine incarnations of Hari.
Whoever should read or even hear this shall also go to a happy destination;
blessed are those best of men in the ocean of existence that is difficult to cross.
Those of undecaying soul who, even in the Kali age, shall remember the name of Viṣṇu,
will obtain the same merit as one who meditates on Viṣṇu in the Kṛta age or performs sacrifices in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
Whatever fruit one obtains in the Kali age merely by remembering Hari, that same fruit is attained when His name is chanted even once; it removes all sins.
In a world abounding in heretics and extremely terrifying due to the Kali age,
he who recites that name should be known as the best among the virtuous.
Therefore, with every effort and endowed with supreme devotion, one should perform the worship of the embodied [deity]; otherwise, one shall not attain liberation.
The Lord is praised in succession by the first nine chapters:
the rites beginning with the examination of the ground, and the construction of celestial palaces (vimānas).
The detailed procedure for the construction of various images is taught;
then, in the tenth [chapter], the planting of the seed-syllable (aṅkura) is proclaimed by two [verses].
The ritual for the consecration of the Lord of the World yields ultimate fruit;
thereafter, the ritual for the ten incarnations is proclaimed by means of four [sections].
Likewise, in the seventeenth [chapter], the ritual for the primordial form was taught;
thereafter, in the eighteenth, the worship of Madhuvighātin along with its ancillaries was described.
Then, by means of two [verses], the sequence for gathering the materials for worship was stated;
in the twenty-first [chapter], the procedure for special worship was correctly proclaimed.
The bathing ceremony is taught in the twenty-second [chapter], and specifically in the twenty-third;
the ritual for the festival wheel is proclaimed in two [chapters], and then the festival itself.
Then, the detailed exposition of expiation (prāyaścitta) was declared in six chapters;
thereafter, in the thirty-second [chapter], the mixed castes (saṃkīrṇa-varṇas) were described.
The greatness of the incarnations in the form of images is proclaimed in the thirty-third [chapter],
and the distinctions such as the self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and others are illuminated in the thirty-fourth.
In the thirty-fifth [chapter], however, the fruit based on kriyā-yoga is fully proclaimed;
in the thirty-sixth, the transgressions that provoke the gods' anger are described.
And the dharmas of the Kali age have been specifically proclaimed in thirty-seven chapters;
thus, by the power of the Guru’s grace, [they are contained] in exactly thirty-seven chapters.
The constituent of ritual action has been described in six thousand verses.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the section on miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇādhikāra*) within the *Sāhitā* of twenty-four thousand verses, as proclaimed by Bhṛgu, in the venerable *Vaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
This concludes the *Kriyāpāda* (Section on Ritual Action) in the illustrious *Prakīrṇādhikāra*.

Salutations to the great preceptor Vikhanas, the illustrious one! Salutations to Vikhanas, the knower of the meaning of all the Vedas, by whom every ritual action—whether based on the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, or otherwise—was systematically codified.
Victorious is the Lord of the Self, the beloved guest of the palace of profound meditation, the glorious resident of Pampāpurī, Śrī Rāma, whose wife is Sītā.
Homage to Śrī Rāmacandra!
